# Research — The Ninth Line

## Contents
1. Decree 770: The Law and Its Enforcement Machinery
2. Going to the Hospital: The Danger and the Calculus
3. The Someș Valley: Geography and the Town of Dej
4. Daily Life in 1984: Scarcity, Rationing, and the Texture of November
5. The Miliția: Structure, Procedure, and the Criminal File
6. The Securitate Informer Network at Neighborhood and Workplace Level
7. The Factory Bookkeeper: Communist Accounting and the Ledger
8. Names, Address Forms, and Period Vocabulary

---

## 1. Decree 770: The Law and Its Enforcement Machinery

### The decree and its core prohibition

Decree 770 was signed personally by Nicolae Ceaușescu in October 1966. It prohibited abortion
in almost all circumstances (exceptions: women over 40 or 45 depending on the period; women who
had already raised four or more children; cases of rape, incest, or fetal deformity; and a narrow
category of life-threatening conditions). [cite:01] Contraceptives were simultaneously removed from
sale. [cite:01]

### Monthly gynecological examinations

**All women of childbearing age (generally defined as 15–45) were required to undergo mandatory
monthly gynecological examinations.** [cite:01] Where those examinations were conducted varied, but
the workplace was the primary site in industrial settings.

One documented literary account, Adrian Sângeorzan's "The Bicycle Factory" (published in English
translation in Words Without Borders, 2012), describes the procedure from the examining physician's
perspective: the factory physician was assigned to perform gynecological check-ups on forty to sixty
female workers each week in less than two hours; foremen lined women up and brought them to be
checked; the factory floor examination was the enforcement mechanism in industrial settings. [cite:20]
One worker's sardonic response — that the doctor "searches us for eggs, like hens" — was remembered
by the narrating physician as capturing the daily register of the examinations. [cite:20]

From 1984, the requirement at state institutions was formalized further: women working for or
attending any state institution were required to undergo at least annual gynecological examinations
at their place of employment, with investigations into all miscarriages. [cite:03] The monthly
requirement remained the practice at most factories regardless. [cite:02]

All detected pregnancies were followed until birth; a woman found to be pregnant was effectively
tracked by the state from detection through delivery. [cite:01]

### Physician obligations and penalties

Doctors were legally required to notify prosecutors of any abortion intervention, either beforehand
or within twenty-four hours. [cite:04] Doctors who performed abortion for health reasons and failed
to report to higher authorities faced one to three months imprisonment. [cite:05] Between 1967 and
1973 alone, 83 doctors were indicted alongside 187 health workers. [cite:04] Each administrative
region had a Disciplinary Board for Health Personnel that conducted investigations and occasional
show trials. [cite:03] Medical practitioners were held partly responsible for the national birthrate.
[cite:03]

Despite these pressures, many doctors helped women by falsely diagnosing qualifying conditions
(diabetes, hepatitis) or prescribing drugs known to cause miscarriage. [cite:03] The enforcement
system therefore coexisted with widespread evasion by sympathetic physicians — which is part of what
made the Securitate's hospital surveillance so intensive.

### The 1984 secret action plan

A third secret action plan, approved by Internal Affairs Minister George Homoștean in the spring of
1984, mandated surveillance of "all medical units, including those without obstetrics and
gynaecology, as well as units where most of the staff is female." [cite:04] The plan placed
informants throughout healthcare facilities. In Cluj County alone, 54 doctors were recruited as
Securitate informants under this plan. [cite:04]

Securitate agents were stationed in or near operating theatres. If doctors performed a dilation and
curettage, agents would assess whether the uterus showed signs of infection — if it did, they
concluded the woman had had a failed illegal abortion. [cite:04]

### Maternal mortality statistics

This is the most precisely documented element of the decree's consequences. The figures are:

- **1980**: 132.1 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births [cite:02]
- **1985**: 137.4 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births [cite:02]
- **1989**: 169.4 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births (the highest ever recorded in Europe) [cite:02]

By the late 1980s, Romanian women were dying at rates more than ten times higher than those in
Western Europe, despite Western European rates declining during the same period. [cite:03] Over 9,000
women died between 1965 and 1989 from complications of illegal procedures. [cite:03] Unsafe abortion
deaths accounted for more than 80% — one source states 87% — of all maternal deaths by the late
1980s. [cite:02]

**The November 1984 setting of the book falls between the 1980 and 1985 data points.** The actual
rate in November 1984 is not in the sources; a value near the 1985 figure of 137.4 is the closest
anchored estimate.

**Source disagreement:** One source (Wikipedia, Decree 770) does not provide year-by-year figures
and refers only to the rate becoming "the highest in Europe." Another (Decree Chronicles, "Guardians
of the Decree") provides the specific year-by-year figures. The Decree Chronicles figures are the
most specific and are used above. A third source ([cite:06], the 1984 CSMonitor article) does not
address maternal mortality directly but confirms the general political and enforcement climate in
the period.

---

## 2. Going to the Hospital: The Danger and the Calculus

### Why hospital was dangerous

This section is directly load-bearing for the book's premise and must be handled precisely.
**The research scope explicitly excludes the medical content of the circulated document.**
What follows describes only the hospital environment and the enforcement regime.

Women who arrived at a hospital with complications from an illegal procedure were not simply
treated. The documented practice was: **Securitate agents or prosecutors would arrive at the
bedside and require the woman to name who had performed the procedure before treatment was
authorized.** [cite:04] One documented case describes a woman with severe hemorrhage being withheld
treatment for five days while being threatened; she died. [cite:04] Another formulation: "state
security operatives would hover at hospitals, forcing women to give up the names of underground
clinics even as they bled to death." [cite:02]

This enforcement created a lethal calculus: going to the hospital meant interrogation and the
near-certainty of naming someone; not going meant managing the complication at home. The timing
of the decision — how long to wait before the risk of staying home exceeded the risk of going —
is precisely the subject of the circulated document.

### What the hospital would know

Hospitals were required to report all cases to the Miliția and to prosecutors. **Every doctor who
treated a woman for complications of an illegal procedure was in theory liable.** [cite:05] The
enforcement agents were looking not just at the woman's condition but at whether the attending
physician had been complicit. [cite:04] This created a situation where even sympathetic doctors
were constrained by the presence of agents.

**Inference (not in sources):** A woman arriving at the district hospital in Dej in November 1984
who was already gravely ill would have been assessed first by the duty physician, who would have
been required to classify the case and notify the relevant authorities (prosecutor and, for a death
or near-death, Miliția). The specific notification form or chain is not documented in the sources
consulted, but the obligation to report is consistent across all sources.

### The "say she began bleeding on her own" instruction

The canonical document in the brief (N1) includes the line: *Say she began bleeding on her own
and you do not know why.* This specific framing maps directly onto the documented hospital
enforcement regime. If a woman could plausibly present as a spontaneous miscarriage, the 
attending physician had cover to treat without triggering a prosecution investigation. The
instruction is accurate to the actual enforcement environment. [cite:03], [cite:04]

---

## 3. The Someș Valley: Geography and the Town of Dej

### Location and rivers

Dej is a municipality in Cluj County, Transylvania, 60 kilometres north of Cluj-Napoca. [cite:11]
The town sits at the confluence of two rivers: **the Someșul Mic (Little Someș) and the Someșul
Mare (Large Someș) join approximately 4 km upstream of Dej at a village called Mica, and the
combined Someș then flows through and past the town.** [cite:12] The town itself lies at the left
bank of the river at an elevation of approximately 285 meters above sea level, within the valley
corridor. [cite:11]

The Someș is 415 km long. It flows west and northwest from Dej toward Satu Mare and eventually
into the Tisza in Hungary. The valley at Dej is a wide alluvial basin where the Transylvanian
Plateau slopes down to the river. [cite:12]

### Population

Census data: 32,345 residents in 1977; 41,216 in 1992. [cite:11] **Inference: The 1984 population
was likely in the range of 35,000–38,000.** The 1977–1992 growth reflects heavy communist-era
industrialization and rural-to-urban migration characteristic of all Romanian towns with significant
industrial enterprises. No census figure for the 1980s was found in sources consulted.

### Industry during communism: the fiber enterprise

The research confirmed one major industrial facility in Dej during the communist period:
**the Artificial Fiber Enterprise (Intreprinderea de Fibre Artificiale, or AFE)**, which produced
celofiber (cellulose-based synthetic fiber) and employed approximately 1,500 workers. [cite:13]
This facility was located approximately 2 km from the Someș river bed. [cite:13]

Celofiber is a regenerated cellulose fiber (similar to rayon) used in textile manufacturing.
**Inference:** A mill town with a fiber enterprise would have downstream textile production —
weaving and finishing facilities that used the fiber — as well as the AFE itself. The brief's
"textile mill" (fabrica de textile) is consistent with the known industrial profile of Dej. The
exact name and ownership structure of the textile operation (as distinct from the AFE itself) is
not confirmed by sources consulted; the AFE is the documented industrial anchor.

Historical salt mining also operated at Ocna Dej (Ocna Dejului), one of the villages administered
by Dej. [cite:11] The salt works predate communism but continued through the period.

### November in the Someș valley

**Average temperatures in November, Transylvania:** daytime maximum 8–11°C; nighttime minimum
approaching or below 0°C. [cite:21] Precipitation averages 40–58mm for the month — moderate rain
with occasional early frost and, by late November, the possibility of snow. [cite:21]

River valleys in Transylvania are characteristically foggy in autumn and early winter. The Someș
valley between Dej and the confluence point would collect ground fog on still mornings. **Inference:**
The industrial fiber enterprise, which involves hot-wet processes and produces effluent into the
river, would add steam and chemical haze to the natural valley fog in cold weather. No source
confirmed this specific industrial detail for the AFE at Dej; it is an inference from general
knowledge of rayon/celofiber production.

### The district hospital at Dej

**Inference (not in sources):** A town of 35,000–38,000 with an established industrial base would
have had a district/municipal hospital (Spitalul Orășenesc Dej or similar designation) as part of
the communist-era healthcare infrastructure. The brief specifies that Ana dies at the "district
hospital in Dej." No primary source describing the specific hospital's layout, staffing, or
conditions was found. Given the documented power-cut conditions across Romanian hospitals in
1983–84 [cite:07] — including the death of dozens of neonatal patients from power cuts to
incubators in winter 1983 — the brief's implication that the hospital was understaffed and under
power constraints is historically grounded.

---

## 4. Daily Life in 1984: Scarcity, Rationing, and the Texture of November

### The rationing system (cartelă)

Romania introduced formal food rationing by county decree in December 1980, intensifying through
1981–1989. [cite:09] In December 1983, a new dietary program for 1984 established even lower
allowances. [cite:07]

**The documented monthly/daily rations for 1984:**

| Item | Allowance |
|------|-----------|
| Bread | 300 g per day (approximately half a loaf) [cite:10] |
| Meat (pork or beef) | 500 g per month [cite:08] |
| Chicken | 1 kg per month [cite:08] |
| Eggs | 8–12 per month [cite:08], [cite:09] |
| Butter | 100 g per month [cite:08] |
| Oil | 750 ml – 1 liter per month [cite:09] |
| Sugar | 1 kg per month [cite:08] |
| Cheese | 500 g per month [cite:08] |

The government framed these quantities as a "Rational Nutrition Programme," claiming Romanians
required only 2,700–2,800 calories daily. [cite:09] Official rations were theoretical minimums;
actual availability was frequently lower. One account: "If you were able to get 500g of meat during
whole month then it was huge success." [cite:09]

### Food substitutes and queue culture

Coffee had entirely disappeared; the substitute was **nechezol**, a horse-feed-based mixture of
chicory, chickpeas, and barley. [cite:08] Meat was often replaced by **soy salami** (salam de soia)
and smoked pig feet colloquially called **adidași** (a joke: they had "stripes" like Adidas
shoes). [cite:08] Vietnamese shrimp chips (imported under a trade arrangement) appeared on shelves
when nothing else did. [cite:08]

Food queues were a daily institution. Citizens stood for hours — sometimes overnight — only to be
turned away when supplies ran out. [cite:08] Bread walks (buying bread from the assigned state
store) were organized by family, with different members taking different days. [cite:10] One
contemporary journalist (CSMonitor, January 1984) witnessed "people lined up to buy broken eggs
being handed out in paper cups" and "two lines of people spread from the back of a van selling
freezer-burned chickens." Food prices had increased 35% in a single year. [cite:06]

Hoarding food beyond the ration was criminalized starting in 1981. [cite:08] Rural people with
private plots had an advantage; urban industrial workers had almost none. [cite:08]

### Electricity and heating

**One 40-watt bulb per household** was the effective norm in 1984; this was not a legal limit but
the result of a government-mandated 50% energy consumption reduction combined with ongoing
shortages. [cite:06] Indoor electric heaters were banned; if one person in a building used one and
was caught, power was cut to the entire building. [cite:07]

District heating (centralized hot water through apartment-block systems) was cut frequently and
without notice to save energy. Hot water availability was limited to approximately one day per week
in most apartments. [cite:07] The government's own 1984 target was 50% reduction in all energy
consumption. [cite:06]

The consequences for hospitals were documented: in the winter of 1983 (one year before the book's
setting), dozens of babies in neonatal intensive care units died from power cuts to incubators.
[cite:07]

### The texture of a November workday

**From the 1984 CSMonitor article, directly observed:** Police and armed soldiers on street corners.
No visible protest. Even hotel rooms stripped of extra light bulbs. People waiting at vans for
meat, at state stores for eggs, starting at dawn. [cite:06]

**Inference:** November in an industrial town like Dej in 1984 would mean: darkness at 4:30 pm;
unheated hallways in apartment blocks; the night shift arriving at the factory while it was still
dark and leaving after dark again; block committees responsible for turning off stairwell lights
after a set hour; coal furnaces in older buildings for those who could get coal; heavy coats worn
indoors in offices where the district heating had not come on.

---

## 5. The Miliția: Structure, Procedure, and the Criminal File

### Organization

The Miliția was the civilian police force of the Socialist Republic of Romania, established by
decree in January 1949, under the Interior Ministry and directly controlled by the Romanian
Workers' Party (later Romanian Communist Party). [cite:14] It was modeled on the Soviet Militsiya
with Soviet advisors providing ideological guidance. [cite:14]

Three branches: Territorial Militia, Railroad Militia, Prison Militia. Each territorial district
had a militia with a Population Section, Investigations Section, and Information Office. [cite:14]

### Rank structure

Personnel held military ranks. The documented officer ranks include (ascending): Sub-Locotenent,
**Locotenent**, Locotenent Major, Căpitan, Major, Locotenent-Colonel, Colonel, then general
officer grades (General Major, General Locotenent, General Colonel). [cite:14]

The book's character Vasile Munteanu is a lieutenant (Locotenent), which is a mid-level officer
rank — plausibly the rank of someone handling a county criminal investigation in a district town,
reporting to a superior (căpitan or higher) at the county inspectorate level.

### Relationship with the Securitate

The Miliția handled visible public order and ordinary criminal matters. The Securitate (Departamentul
Securității Statului, DSS) handled political intelligence and repression. The two operated in
parallel, both reporting through the Interior Ministry. [cite:14] In practice, the Securitate
frequently co-opted Miliția manpower for arrests and surveillance. [cite:14]

A suspicious-death investigation touching on Decree 770 (which was enforced partly by the
Securitate) would almost certainly draw Securitate attention, but the initial file (dosar penal)
would be opened by the Miliția's Investigations Section and referred to the procuror (prosecutor)
for classification. **Inference:** Whether a specific death was handled as a criminal matter by
Miliția alone or was escalated to Securitate involvement would depend on whether it had political
implications. In the book's setup, it begins as a Miliția investigation that has not yet attracted
Securitate attention because it has been classified as an administrative matter — which is
consistent with Munteanu's handling of it.

### Criminal procedure and the dosar penal

Romania's Penal Code was reformed in 1969 under Ceaușescu. The basic unit of criminal
investigation was the **dosar penal** (criminal file). [cite:17] Under Romanian criminal procedure,
the procuror (prosecutor) was involved from the outset in classifying deaths — natural, suspicious,
or criminal — and the Miliția's Investigations Section conducted the physical evidence gathering
under prosecutorial supervision. [cite:17]

**Inference (not confirmed in sources for this specific period):** A suspicious death at a district
hospital — a young woman who arrived mortally ill and died within hours — would generate a hospital
report, a death certificate, and a notification to the local procuror and Miliția. The attending
physician was required to report. The Miliția's Investigations Section would be assigned to
determine whether a crime had occurred (i.e., whether the death resulted from an illegal procedure).
The file would move from the district office to the county inspectorate (Inspectoratul Județean de
Miliție, Cluj County) if it could not be resolved locally or if escalation was required.

**The book's fixed deadline** — after which the file moves from a lieutenant who wants the truth
to an office that wants a name — reflects the real administrative pressure in this system, though
no specific statutory deadline was found in sources consulted. **Inference:** In the communist
administrative culture, a case that remained unresolved beyond a set period (likely 30 days for
an initial investigation) would generate pressure from above to produce a result, and county-level
or central offices would demand a "name on the file."

### Investigative methods available to Munteanu

What a Miliția lieutenant could actually do in November 1984, based on documented organizational
capacity [cite:14]:
- Knock on doors (explicitly: the Miliția's Population Section maintained population registers)
- Demand identity documents (buletin de identitate, see §8)
- Summon individuals to the county Miliția building for questioning
- Collect and compare physical objects (the paper copies in the book)
- Contact the hospital for the patient's admission record and any statement given before death

What a Miliția lieutenant could **not** easily do without Securitate involvement:
- Tap telephones (required Securitate authorization and equipment)
- Run surveillance across multiple neighborhoods simultaneously
- Access Securitate files on individuals without a formal request

---

## 6. The Securitate Informer Network at Neighborhood and Workplace Level

### Scale

By the mid-1980s: **approximately 11,000–13,000 full Securitate agents and approximately 450,000
informants** across a population of 22 million. [cite:15], [cite:16] One summary formulation: one
person in every thirty Romanians had been recruited as an informant by the 1980s. [cite:16]

The network grew significantly over time: approximately 12,000–13,000 informants in 1958; 30,000 by
1960; 80,000 by 1963; 110,000 by 1967. By the 1980s, the figure had reached several hundred
thousand. [cite:15]

### The shift from repression to social control

In the 1970s and 1980s, the Securitate **shifted from open violent repression to pervasive
monitoring.** [cite:16] Its primary function in the 1980s was to track and report to party
leadership on "economic, social, ethnic, and political grievances" — the state of mind of the
population. [cite:15] The fear this created was pervasive but not usually spectacular. As one
source puts it: the defining atmosphere was "fear rather than terror." [cite:16]

### Recruitment and coercion

Informers came from all social categories: neighbors, coworkers, students, family members. [cite:16]
Blackmail was the primary recruitment tool — discovering a vulnerability (an illegal act, a foreign
contact, a moral "irregularity") and threatening disclosure. [cite:16] The Securitate also used
appeals to civic duty, framing informing as voluntary participation in the protection of the state.
[cite:15]

Close friends were among the most productive informers; many Romanians discovered from their
post-1989 files that intimate friends had been reporting on them for years. [cite:16]

### What informers reported

Informers were required to produce written reports covering: who a target met with, what places
they visited, what was said about the regime, the country's economy, and its leadership. [cite:16]
In the 1980s context, the Securitate was particularly interested in: signs of collective organizing,
contact with foreigners, illegal economic activity (black market, hoarding), and — for the
Decree 770 enforcement — reproductive violations.

### How ordinary people managed surveillance risk

**No primary-source account of specific individual risk-management strategies was found** in the
sources consulted. What the sources confirm:

- People refrained from criticizing Ceaușescu in public, aware that anyone could be an informer.
  [cite:16]
- "Private space in apartment buildings could easily turn into public space," meaning neighbors
  could report on what happened inside flats. [cite:15]
- The telephone was a risk. Phones were tapped; the Securitate intercepted mail; typewriters were
  registered. [cite:16]
- The assumption that any neighbor might be reporting was sufficiently pervasive that it structured
  ordinary social behavior. [cite:16]

**Inference:** In the context of the book — women sharing information about aftercare — the most
rational behavior would be: no telephone, no written list, face-to-face only, strictly limited
disclosure (only people already known and trusted), and the assumption that any transaction that
became visible to a neighbor or building superintendent (locatar de bloc) was potentially reported.
Doina's silence about the woman on the bus — refusing to name her — is precisely the behavior
the surveillance system trained ordinary Romanians to adopt as rational self-protection.

---

## 7. The Factory Bookkeeper: Communist Accounting and the Ledger

### The accounting system under communism

In Romania's centrally planned economy, enterprise accounting served the state, not the enterprise.
[cite:17] As documented in academic analyses of Romanian communist-era accounting: "Accounting
information was exclusively prepared for the state, and public disclosure was non-existent." [cite:17]
The enterprise's accounts were submitted to the Ministry of Finance and the State Planning Committee;
they were instruments of plan verification, not business management.

The principle that governed the work: **"Accountants cannot journalize anything in accounting unless
they have a primary document."** [cite:17] This emphasis on documentary evidence was fundamental to
the communist system and persisted into the post-communist period as an institutional legacy. The
significance for the book: every transaction required a supporting document; a bookkeeper who kept
clean records was legally protected; a bookkeeper whose records had gaps was exposed.

### Role of the enterprise bookkeeper (contabil)

Under communism, accounting at Romanian state enterprises was "largely a matter of clerical
bookkeeping." [cite:17] The chief accountant (contabil-șef) was responsible for the accuracy of
the enterprise's books and for producing records on demand for state auditors and inspectors.
[cite:17] The enterprise had no ability to withhold records from the state; the books were, in
principle, government property.

**What an enterprise bookkeeper was legally required to produce on demand:**

- Production plan fulfillment records
- Payroll registers (stat de plată)
- Material consumption records
- Inventory registers
- Cost-per-unit calculations

**Inference:** The specific forms and ledger names in use at a Romanian textile enterprise in 1984
are not documented in the English-language sources consulted. Romanian communist accounting used
standardized forms issued by the Ministry of Finance, updated periodically through the Five-Year
Plans. A bookkeeper like Ilinca, responsible for the accounts of a textile mill (fabrica de
textile/industrie textilă) in Dej, would have maintained the following categories: production
records, wage/salary registers, material input/output, and annual balance submitted to the county
financial office. A state audit could arrive without notice and demand any record going back up to
five years. The ledger Ilinca uses to hide the master document is a ledger she is "legally required
to produce on demand" — this is accurate to the actual exposure: the ledger is not a private object.

### The bookkeeper's physical workspace

**Inference:** A mill bookkeeper in 1984 would have worked at a desk in the enterprise's
administrative building (separate from the production floor), with access to a telephone (a risk),
a typewriter (registered with the Securitate by serial number), and the physical ledgers and forms.
Calculations were done by hand or, in larger enterprises, on a mechanical adding machine. The
accountant's office smelled of paper, carbon copy paper, and the mill production (synthetic fiber
mills produce a distinctive chemical smell). No source confirmed the specific physical layout or
equipment of the AFE or its associated textile facilities.

## 8. Names, Address Forms, and Period Vocabulary

### Surname structure

Romanian surnames standardized in the nineteenth century from patronymic forms. Common suffixes:
**-escu** ("child of," as in Petrescu = "child of Petru"); **-eanu/-anu** (place-based, as in
Munteanu = "man from the mountains/munte"); **-aru/-ată** (occupational); **-oiu** (Slavic
influence). [cite:18], [cite:19]

Male and female versions of the same surname are often identical in modern usage, though some
surnames have gender-inflected forms. [cite:18]

**Validation of the book's surnames:**
- **Roșca**: Romanian adjective *roș* (red); common Romanian surname. [cite:18]
- **Petrescu**: -escu suffix from Petru; one of the most common Romanian surnames. [cite:19]
- **Munteanu**: from *munte* (mountain); very common throughout Romania, especially in Transylvania. [cite:18]
- **Marcu**: Romanian form of Marcus/Mark; used as both given name and, occasionally, surname. [cite:18]

### Given names

**Female given names** almost always end in -a. [cite:18] Traditional names come from the Orthodox
saint calendar. [cite:18]

**Validation of the book's given names:**
- **Ilinca**: Romanian diminutive of Elena/Ileana; documented in use. [cite:23]
- **Doina**: Romanian given name meaning "folk song" (a distinctively Romanian lyric form); used as
  a given name, especially in Transylvania. [cite:23]
- **Ana**: directly from the Orthodox calendar (Saint Anne); extremely common in Romania. [cite:18]

**Male given names** end in a consonant. [cite:18]

**Validation:**
- **Vasile**: Romanian form of Basil (Vasiliu in some older forms); major Orthodox saint's name;
  very common in Romania. [cite:18]

### Forms of address

Standard formal address: **Domn/Domnul** (Mr.) + surname for a man; **Doamnă** (Mrs./Madam) +
surname for a woman. [cite:22] These forms were retained through communism for civilian interactions.

**Inference:** In the communist context, the forms "tovarăș" (comrade, m.) and "tovarășă" (comrade,
f.) were also in official use, especially in party/workplace settings. A Miliția officer might
address a woman he was questioning as "Tovarășă [Surname]" in a formal setting, or "Doamnă
[Surname]" in a more civil interaction. No source confirmed the specific preference between these
forms for a 1984 Miliția interrogation setting; the distinction is an inference.

### Other period vocabulary

**Buletin**: the identity card (buletin de identitate), issued by the Miliția, 8-page booklet format
in the communist era, containing photograph, occupation, and registration stamps. Required to be
carried at all times. [cite:22]

**Bloc**: the standard communist-era apartment block; residents were organized in bloc committees,
with a building superintendent (administrator de bloc). The bloc as social unit was also a
surveillance unit. [cite:15]

**Cartelă**: the ration card. Issued by county, valid for one month or three months depending on
region. Non-transferable; losing it meant forfeiting the ration. [cite:09]

**Contabil-șef**: chief accountant at a state enterprise, the senior bookkeeper responsible for
all records. [cite:17]

**Dosar**: file. **Dosar penal**: criminal file, the unit of a Miliția investigation. [cite:17]

**Procuror**: state prosecutor, involved from the outset of any criminal matter in classifying
the nature of the death or incident. [cite:17]

**Inspectoratul Județean de Miliție**: the county-level Miliția office, to which district cases
were escalated. [cite:14]

**Locotenent**: lieutenant; the rank of the book's investigator Munteanu, in the lower-middle of
the officer hierarchy. [cite:14]

**Tovarăș/tovarășă**: comrade; the official form of address in institutional and party contexts.
**Inference**: not from a specific source but consistent with documented communist-era Romanian usage.

# Pitch — The Ninth Line

Romania, November 1984. Eighteen years into Ceaușescu's Decree 770, which banned abortion and contraception and made pregnancy a matter of state accounting, women in the mill town of Dej pass a piece of paper hand to hand. Not instructions for ending a pregnancy — what to do afterwards. How to keep a woman warm, what to count, when the number is too many, and the one thing the paper exists to say: when to stop managing it at home and take her to the hospital, and what to say when you get there.

On the fourth of November a nineteen-year-old named Ana Petrescu arrives at the district hospital in Dej. She dies four hours later, nine hours after she should have come. The copy of the paper her sister-in-law followed said to take her in *in the morning*. The original, written by forty-one-year-old mill bookkeeper **Ilinca Roșca** and folded into the spine of a ledger she is legally required to produce on demand, says no such thing.

What sits between the original and the dead girl is a chain of twenty-two handwritten copies, five generations deep, each a physical object distinguishable by paper stock, handwriting, and the small errors of transmission. Two people are collating that chain from opposite ends: Ilinca, quietly, because a woman she knows may die next; and **Lieutenant Vasile Munteanu**, thirty-four, county militia, who has worked out that the copies are not identical, that the differences are inherited, and that a family of documents can be climbed to its source. He is right. He is also faster, because he can knock on doors.

**Nineteen-year-old Doina Marcu**, night-shift mill worker, has a copy folded in her geography book. It came from a woman on the bus whose name she doesn't know. Her copy is clean — still has the bracket that matters. Munteanu reaches Doina before she can prove that. The book ends in the only place it can: Ilinca handing Munteanu the original and the cellar copy she made herself, the one where the bracket became a numbered line. Ilinca is taken. Doina is released. The paper is gone. The ninth line — the bracket included — is memorised.

# World — The Ninth Line

## Period and location

November 1984. Dej, Cluj County, Transylvania, Romania. A municipal town of approximately 36,000 people, 60 kilometres north of Cluj-Napoca, at the confluence of the Someșul Mic and Someșul Mare rivers. The two Someșuri join four kilometres upstream at the village of Mica and arrive at Dej as one river, wide and flat, carrying the cold of the Transylvanian plateau downhill toward Satu Mare.

## The town

Dej is a mill town in the late stages of communist industrialisation. The dominant employer is the Artificial Fiber Enterprise (Intreprinderea de Fibre Artificiale — AFE), which employs roughly 1,500 workers producing celofiber, a cellulose-based synthetic fiber used in downstream textile manufacturing. The mill keeps two shifts. The administrative building sits apart from the production floor; the factory physician's office is two doors down from the personnel office, and both shifts of female workers above fifteen are examined monthly.

The town is served by a district hospital (Spitalul Orășenesc Dej), a county Miliția station, a procuror's office in the same building, and the usual apparatus of bloc-committee surveillance: building superintendents (administrator de bloc) who know whose light is on at 2 a.m. and who came home at what hour.

## Physical texture — November 1984

**Light and heat.** District heating comes on when it comes on. On the nights it does not, the unheated stairwells of apartment blocks are colder than the street. One 40-watt bulb per household is the effective norm — not a legal limit, the result of a 50% energy-consumption reduction decree and chronic shortage. Indoor electric heaters are banned; a neighbour who reports one to the bloc committee can cut power to the whole building. Darkness falls by 4:30 p.m. Night-shift workers walk to the factory in the dark and walk home in the dark.

**Food.** The ration card (cartelă) is issued monthly. Documented 1984 allowances: 300 g bread per day; 500 g pork or beef per month; one kilogram chicken per month; eight to twelve eggs; 100 g butter; one litre oil; one kilogram sugar; 500 g cheese. Actual availability is frequently lower. Coffee has been replaced with nechezol — chicory, chickpeas, and barley — and nobody pretends to like it. Queues form before dawn for bread, for eggs, for the occasional van selling freezer-burned chickens. Hoarding beyond the ration has been a criminal offence since 1981.

**Weather.** Daytime high in early November: 8–11°C. Nights approaching or below zero. The Someș valley collects fog on still mornings. The AFE's wet-heat production processes add steam and chemical haze where the valley fog has already settled. By late November, frost and the possibility of early snow. Rain is frequent, 40–58 mm for the month. The outdoor cold is a constant background condition: the kind of cold that makes unheated rooms feel like the outside continued indoors.

**Paper and hands.** Carbon paper, mechanical adding machines, ledgers in standardized Ministry of Finance format. Typewriters are registered with the Securitate by serial number. A telephone is a risk. Writing a list is a risk. The act of not writing things down is its own kind of record-keeping.

## Enforcement atmosphere

Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion and contraception; Decree 770 and its successor instruments are enforced by a layered apparatus. All women of childbearing age (15–45) are subject to mandatory monthly gynecological examinations at their place of employment. Detected pregnancies are tracked from detection through delivery. Every physician is legally required to notify the procuror of any abortion-related intervention within 24 hours; physicians who fail face imprisonment. Securitate informants are stationed in or near hospital operating theatres. In Cluj County alone, 54 doctors have been recruited as informants.

The result: a woman who arrives at the district hospital with complications from an illegal procedure faces bedside interrogation before treatment is authorized. The documented practice includes withholding treatment until the woman names who helped her. The timing of the decision to go to the hospital — how long to wait at home before the risk of staying exceeded the risk of going — is the decision that kills women. That is what the paper is for.

At the neighbourhood level: approximately one in thirty Romanians has been recruited as an informant by the 1980s. The defining atmosphere is fear rather than terror — pervasive, structural, not usually spectacular. Private space in apartment blocks is effectively public. Close friends have been reporting on friends for years. Nobody mentions Ceaușescu critically in a space where a neighbour can hear.

## The Miliția

Civilian police force under the Interior Ministry, modelled on the Soviet Militsiya. Three branches: Territorial, Railroad, Prison. Each district office has a Population Section (population registers, identity documents), an Investigations Section (criminal files, dosar penal), and an Information Office. The Securitate operates in parallel; a Miliția case that acquires political dimensions can be co-opted. Lieutenant-rank officers handle district-level criminal investigations, reporting to a captain or higher at the Inspectoratul Județean de Miliție (county Miliția inspectorate) in Cluj-Napoca. Identity documents: the buletin de identitate, an 8-page booklet issued and stamped by the Miliția, required to be carried at all times.

## Period vocabulary in use

- **Cartelă** — ration card
- **Buletin** — identity booklet
- **Dosar (penal)** — (criminal) file
- **Procuror** — state prosecutor
- **Contabil-șef** — chief accountant at a state enterprise
- **Bloc** — apartment block, also a surveillance unit
- **Tovarăș/Tovarășă** — Comrade (m./f.); official address in institutional contexts
- **Nechezol** — the coffee substitute
- **Locotenent** — Lieutenant (Miliția rank)

# Characters — The Ninth Line

## POV characters

### Ilinca Roșca — POV 1, third person present
**Age:** 41  
**Role:** Chief bookkeeper (contabil-șef) at the textile mill in Dej  
**Background:** Born 1943; grew up in the Someș valley. Has worked the mill's accounts for fifteen years. Unmarried, lives alone in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a bloc a fifteen-minute walk from the factory. She has never been caught doing anything.

**Inner drives:** Ilinca's mind runs in columns: incoming, outgoing, balance. She organises information the way she organises ledger entries — every item has a place, a provenance, a corresponding document. This is not coldness; it is how she manages terror. The paper exists because she could not stop thinking, after a woman she knew did not go to the hospital in time, about the decision and whether it could be made better. She made it better. She made it worse. She does not know yet.

What she wants is to undo one night in a coal cellar without undoing everything that followed from it. She will discover, chapter by chapter, that the two things cannot be separated. The climax is her choosing not to separate them — handing Munteanu both documents, the master and the cellar copy, which exonerates Doina and ends Ilinca.

**Voice:** Close third person, present tense. Spare declaratives. Her interiority runs in procedures and tallies — "line nine is not" is a thought and a fact simultaneously. She notices things in the order she notices them, which is the order she can act on them. She does not name her fear; she catalogues its symptoms.

**Relationships:**  
- The women she has handed copies to, personally, over two years — each known by name, each a counted entry in a private ledger she has never written down  
- The woman in the coal cellar (November 3, 1983): unnamed, unnamed deliberately; Ilinca knew her, made the copy fast, did not check it after  
- Munteanu: does not know him until Act III, when he comes to the mill

### Doina Marcu — POV 2, first person past
**Age:** 19  
**Role:** Night-shift worker at the textile mill  
**Background:** Born 1965; from a village outside Dej, moved to town two years ago when the factory offered her a place in a workers' hostel. She is intelligent and bored, which is a dangerous combination under the circumstances. She has never been in any trouble that mattered. She has a copy of the paper she has never used, folded inside a geography book, because the woman on the bus gave it to her before she could think of a reason to say no.

**Inner drives:** Doina wants to survive and she wants to be the kind of person who deserved to. She is funny — not funny the way characters in this library have been, which is wry-and-restrained, but genuinely funny, capable of a digression that is also the truth. Her first-person past tense is the voice of someone who survived and is recounting it straight, without the benefit of having been smart at the time. Her silence about the woman on the bus is not heroic self-sacrifice; it is the thing the world she lives in trained her to do, and she is not fully sure why she is doing it even as she does it.

**Voice:** First person past. Longer sentences than Ilinca; room to digress; wry observation that lands sideways on the terror. She can say things that would read as dark comedy if the reader did not already know about Ana. She is never arch; she is nineteen and honest.

**Relationships:**  
- The woman on the bus: never named, never found, never appears; Doina's silence about her is the source of Doina's danger and the book's sharpest irony

### Lieutenant Vasile Munteanu — POV 3, third person past
**Age:** 34  
**Role:** Miliția lieutenant, Investigations Section, Dej district  
**Background:** Born 1950. Career Miliția officer; joined at 22. Married, two children; lives in a Miliția-assigned apartment. He is not a party enthusiast. He is a man who is good at his job and has organised his life around the fact of being good at his job, and who has not looked too carefully at what his job serves.

**Inner drives:** Munteanu is a puzzle-solver, and the copies are the most interesting puzzle he has been given. He has worked out that differences between copies are inherited, not random — that a family of documents can be collated, like a genealogy. He is right. He is pursuing the truth, in good faith, which is the thing that makes him dangerous rather than merely menacing. He understands, with the flatness the brief names, that his arithmetic will lead him somewhere his captain will not like, and he is going to follow it anyway.

What he cannot see — what the reader sees and he does not — is the difference between solving the tree and deciding what the tree means. He never holds the proposition `ninth-line-is-a-warning-not-a-step`. He solves for origin, not for culpability in the way the book means culpability. He is wrong about what to do with Doina not because his arithmetic is wrong but because his arithmetic is the wrong arithmetic.

**Voice:** Third person past. Deliberate; the pipeline's own default register. Restrained and literary. He thinks in cases, precedents, what will and will not survive being described to his captain. His interiority is orderly and procedural in a different way than Ilinca's — hers is a private discipline she chose; his is an institutional one he has inhabited for twelve years.

**Relationships:**  
- His captain at the Inspectoratul Județean in Cluj-Napoca: the deadline is the captain's deadline, not Munteanu's; the captain wants a name on the file  
- Doina: the arrest, around chapter 19, is the most power he has over anyone in this book and the moment his arithmetic most visibly fails  
- Ilinca: he does not know she exists until chapter 22 or later; when she comes to him, it recontextualises everything

# Style — The Ninth Line

## POV and tense

Three POVs, each with its own grammatical contract:

- **Ilinca — third person close, present tense.** Her interiority moves in columns and tallies. The present tense is there because she does not know how her collation ends. Sentences are short and declarative under pressure; longer only where the counting takes time.
- **Doina — first person, past tense.** She survived to tell it; the reader should feel that as ground before it is confirmed. Longer sentences; room for digression; wry, honest, nineteen.
- **Munteanu — third person close, past tense.** Deliberately the pipeline's own default literary register — restrained, procedural, careful. The irony is never explained: the state's investigator speaks in the voice the model reaches for by default.

These three voices must remain genuinely distinct throughout. A chapter header is a date only; the voice must be legible before the end of the first sentence.

## Register

Cold, exact, and physical. Weather. Paper. Hands. The smell of a synthetic-fiber mill in November — hot-wet chemistry and the cold coming in through every door. Short declaratives under pressure; longer sentences only in Doina's voice, where being nineteen allows digression.

Fear is rendered as procedure: what characters do with their hands, which door they use, what they do not write down, what they say is the influenza. Fear is almost never named. The reader assembles the political situation from its effects — the reporting requirement, the monthly examination, the queue, the fact that a telephone is a risk — not from any character's explanation of it. **Nobody explains the regime to anyone else, because everyone already lives there.**

## Narrative distance

Close third for Ilinca and Munteanu. First person for Doina. In all three cases: the narrative distance lives *inside* the character's professional or personal idiom. Ilinca's interiority runs in accounting categories. Munteanu's in case procedure and what will and will not survive being described to his captain. Doina's in the voice of someone recounting something they are still figuring out.

## Dialogue

Dialogue is sparse but load-bearing. Characters in this book do not talk to manage their feelings; they talk to transact information or, more often, to withhold it. Dialogue tags are minimal — said, asked, no more. No dialogue is followed by a paragraph interpreting it.

## Chapter structure

No prologue. No epigraph. No framing device. A date is the only chapter header. Chapters are not self-contained episodes; they are stations in two simultaneous collations. Chapters in Ilinca's and Munteanu's voices are procedural; Doina's chapters are the only ones with room for reflection.

Endings: mixed by design. Quiet endings where the chapter wants them; hard cuts where it does not. Do not settle into a uniform closing mode.

## Quotation from the documents

**The full text of any node is printed at most four times across the entire book**: the master (N1) early, Ana's copy (N17) beside it at the reveal-to-reader, Doina's clean copy (N14) once, and the master and cellar copy (N4) together at the climax. Everywhere else: fragments only, attributed to the specific node the scene's character holds. A fragment quoted must be the fragment as *that character's copy* renders it — which may differ by exactly one word or formatting choice from every other node. This is the book's central discipline.

Before re-quoting any node in a chapter, `read_record` it and reproduce it exactly. **The 22 nodes differ from each other by design; no editor or repair pass may reconcile, harmonise, or "correct" any variant toward any other.** The line `9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.` in `copy-n11` and `copy-n17` is correct as written. It is the murder weapon.

## Failure modes

The AI-author patterns most tempting in this story's register. The drafter should actively avoid these; the compression pass should cut them.

- **Sentence-after-the-sentence** — an image lands in a declarative; the next sentence glosses what it means. This register wants the image to sit without explanation. The glossing sentence is almost always the one to delete.
- **Meta-commentary on cognition** — "She registered." "He noticed." "She felt the familiar weight of." The prose already shows what the character is doing; labelling the cognitive act softens the cold-procedure register this book depends on.
- **Post-scene subtext naming** — a paragraph after a scene that names what the scene was *really* about. This book's argument is carried entirely by the document tree, never by a character — or narrator — articulating it. Any sentence that begins to say what the mutations mean is an instance of this failure.
- **Thesis restatement** — an abstract sentence re-stating the book's argument about state culpability, conditions, or what the paper means. The brief is explicit: "that is the argument of the book, and it must be carried entirely by the tree of copies — never stated by a character." The narrator obeys the same rule.
- **Redundant transition / re-summary** — a paragraph at the opening or close of a chapter that recaps what the reader already knows about where the collation stands. The two ladders (nodes held, days elapsed) are the clock; the reader tracks them. Restating them in prose is padding.

## Lean-into patterns

Patterns the drafter and editors should NOT treat as failures, because this register depends on them.

- **Variants that differ from each other by a single word or a formatting mark** — the 22 document nodes intentionally diverge. Across-chapter differences in how a line appears are not continuity errors; they are the book's mechanism. Never smooth them.
- **`copy-n11` and `copy-n17` saying "in the morning"** — this is correct. It is the fatal mutation. Any pass that edits this line toward the master is destroying the book's subject.
- **Doina's longer, wry, digressive sentences** — her register is not the book's default. A compression pass should not shorten Doina's chapters toward Ilinca's cadence. The length is the nineteen.
- **Procedural repetition in Ilinca's voice** — she counts the same kinds of things more than once. Counting is her idiom; it is not redundancy when it is in character.

# Continuity — The Ninth Line

Hard facts that must not break in later drafting. Every numbered item is binding. **No editor, repair, or compression pass may contradict any item in this list.**

---

## The document — N1, the master

1. **N1 (the master)** was written by Ilinca Roșca in October 1983. It has exactly eight numbered lines plus a ninth line written across the bottom margin inside a hand-drawn bracket. The bracket line is NOT a numbered item. RecordId: `master-n1`.

2. **The text of N1 is canonical and fixed.** It is reproduced verbatim under `master-n1`. It must be reproduced exactly, including bracket and indentation, wherever quoted in full. The full text is printed at most four times in the book.

3. **N1's ninth element reads:** `[ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning. ]` — it is a bracketed marginal override, not a sequential step.

---

## The poisoned branch

4. **N4 (Ilinca's cellar copy)** was made by Ilinca herself on 3 November 1983 in a coal cellar, by the light of the door, in a hurry. Lines 1–8 are identical to N1. The ONLY difference: the bracketed ninth element has been transcribed as a numbered line 9. Every word is correct; the formatting is different. RecordId: `copy-n4`. This is a second-generation copy (G2).

5. **N11 (the regularised copy)** is two generations from N4 (G4). Lines 1–8 are identical to N1. Line 9 reads: `9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.` — **this is correct as written and must not be changed by any pass.** RecordId: `copy-n11`. The phrase *in the morning* is the fatal mutation; it is a loss of urgency, not a wrong quantity.

6. **N17 (Ana's copy)** is a fifth-generation copy (G5), descended from N11. It is identical to N11 in every line. RecordId: `copy-n17`. It is a separate physical object with separate provenance. The full text of N17 is printed once in the book, beside N1, at the Act I close that establishes the dramatic irony.

7. **The fatal mutation is a loss of urgency.** The warning "Do not wait for the morning" became a step "take her in in the morning" through a chain of two formatting transcriptions made in good faith. No one in the chain was careless. No quantity, substance, dose, or procedure was ever wrong.

---

## The clean branch

8. **N14 (Doina's copy)** is a fourth-generation copy (G4), descended from N3 (a G2 branch that is NOT the poisoned N4 branch). N14 still has the bracket. It is clean. Doina did not use it. Doina received it from a woman on the bus whose name she does not know. RecordId: `copy-n14`.

9. **Doina's copy is clean; Munteanu does not know this.** Munteanu's collation reaches Doina and is arithmetically correct — her copy points upward in the tree. He arrests her because he can reach her, not because his arithmetic is wrong. His wrong belief (`doina-copy-is-clean` = false in his stance) is the book's second dramatic irony.

---

## The tree structure

10. **Twenty-two nodes, five generations.** G1: N1. G2: N2, N3, N4 (N4 is the poisoned ancestor). G3: six copies. G4: seven copies including N11 (from N4) and N14 (from N3). G5: five copies including N17 (from N11). Every node is a distinct `record` with its own recordId; no two nodes share a recordId. **Intentional cross-node differences are not continuity errors.**

11. **All 22 nodes differ from each other by design.** Differences between nodes are inherited through the copy chain. No editor, repair pass, or continuity agent may reconcile, harmonise, or "correct" any node toward any other. Nodes off the poisoned branch may differ from N1 only in incidental ways (spelling, dropped comma, line-break, numbering style) that never touch lines 7, 8, or 9.

12. **Only the poisoned branch (N4 → N11 → N17 lineage) touches line 9**, and only in the two ways described in items 4–6 above. Every other node carries line 9 as the bracketed marginal element.

---

## The compounding mechanism

13. **Two monotonic ladders, moving in opposite directions, under every chapter:**
    - *Nodes held*: Ilinca's collation count and Munteanu's collation count each increase. Neither ever loses a node. The reader tracks both.
    - *Days since Ana died*: against the fixed 31-day administrative deadline. When the deadline passes, the file escalates from Munteanu to the county inspectorate — from a lieutenant who wants the truth to an office that wants a name.

14. **Each chapter advances exactly one of these ladders by one rung, and names a specific foreclosure** — a woman is now known, a branch is now closed, a name is now on a list. No chapter re-measures a count already taken or re-walks a copy the reader already holds. This is monotonic: the situation only gets worse.

---

## The ending

15. **The ending is fixed and must be delivered in full, on the page:**
    - Ilinca produces the master (N1) and the cellar copy (N4) to Munteanu. This is the climax and it happens in scene.
    - Munteanu's collation is completed by this handover — he now has the top of the tree.
    - Doina is released.
    - Ilinca is taken.
    - The last chapter is Doina, carrying nothing, having memorised the ninth line — the bracket included.

16. **Do not soften this ending into hope, and do not withhold it.** The paper is what killed Ana; the memorised line is what survives. The ending is not ambiguous.

---

## Safety constraints (absolute — override all other direction)

17. **The circulated document is aftercare and when-to-seek-help ONLY.** It contains no method, no substance, no dose, no procedure, no route of administration, at any node, in any chapter, in any variant. Ana's pregnancy and its ending are never described. These constraints hold at every generation of the copy chain, in every node registered as a record, in every in-prose fragment, in every variant.

18. **The fatal mutation is a loss of urgency** — a warning that stops reading as a warning — not a wrong quantity of anything. If any phase finds itself specifying medical technique, it has misread this brief.

---

## Characters and events

19. **Ana Petrescu** dies on 4 November 1984 at the district hospital in Dej (Spitalul Orășenesc Dej). She is 19. She is never a POV character and never appears in a flashback scene.

20. **Ilinca Roșca** is 41. She is the mill's chief bookkeeper (contabil-șef). She wrote N1 in October 1983.

21. **Doina Marcu** is 19. She works the night shift at the mill. Her copy (N14) came from a woman on the bus. She is innocent and cannot prove it because she cannot name the woman on the bus without identifying her.

22. **Lieutenant Vasile Munteanu** is 34. Miliția lieutenant, Investigations Section, Dej district. He never holds the proposition `ninth-line-is-a-warning-not-a-step` at any point in the book. His collation is arithmetically correct and morally beside the point.

23. **The woman on the bus is never identified, never found, and never appears.** Doina's silence about her holds.

---

## What no character ever does

24. No character draws the document tree, explains the tree, diagrams it, or uses the word "tree." The collation happens in kitchens, on a bus, in a mill office, in a militia room with copies laid on a desk — in objects and hands, never on a whiteboard.

25. No character delivers a speech about the regime or the decree. Nobody explains the political situation to anyone else, because everyone already lives there.

26. No torture, no interrogation set-piece, no Securitate melodrama. Munteanu's power is paperwork and knocking on a door in the afternoon.

**Securitate (DSS — Departamentul Securității Statului)** — the state security apparatus. Distinct from the Miliția; handles political intelligence. ~11,000–13,000 full agents; ~450,000 informants nationwide by the mid-1980s. In Cluj County: 54 doctors recruited as informants. Agents stationed in hospitals. Co-opts Miliția investigations when they acquire political significance.

**Someș** — the river at Dej; the Someșul Mic and Someșul Mare join 4 km upstream at the village of Mica. The combined river runs through the town at 285 m elevation. Fog collects in the valley in November.

**Spitalul Orășenesc Dej** — the district hospital at Dej. Where Ana Petrescu dies on 4 November 1984.

**Tovarăș / Tovarășă** — Comrade (m./f.); official form of address in institutional and party contexts.

**Vasile Munteanu** — 34, Miliția lieutenant, Investigations Section, Dej district. POV character, third person past. Assigned Ana's death as an administrative matter; turns it into a real investigation. His collation is arithmetically correct. He never understands what the ninth line means.

# Themes — The Ninth Line

## The conditions of transmission

The paper is not wrong. The chain of women who passed it were not careless. The mutation that killed Ana Petrescu entered the chain in a coal cellar on a November night when the conditions for safe copying — light, time, a second reading — were the conditions the state had made unavailable. The book's argument is that the state's culpability lives in the conditions, not in the content: speed, darkness, no second chances. It made those the conditions of the work, and then the work failed the way work fails under those conditions. This argument is never stated. It is carried entirely by the tree of copies and the circumstances of each transcription. The reader assembles it; no character names it.

## The arithmetic of innocence

Everyone in this chain acted correctly, given what they knew and what they had. Ilinca copied fast to avoid being late. The intermediate copyists were tidy; they made a numbered list out of what they received, which was a numbered list. Ana's sister-in-law followed what the paper said. Munteanu's collation is arithmetically correct; he is not wrong about the tree. And yet a girl is dead, and Ilinca will be taken, and the machine that produced these outcomes is not in this book's courtroom. There is no villain. There is no exoneration. There is only the record: who held which copy, and when, and what it said.

## What silence does

Doina's silence about the woman on the bus is the silence the surveillance state trained every ordinary Romanian to maintain. It is not heroism; it is the rational behaviour of someone who has learned that naming a person gives them to a system that will use the name in ways you cannot control. Her silence is also the thing that keeps her in the cell: Munteanu cannot close the chain above her because she will not give him the next link. The book does not resolve this into a lesson. The silence is both protective and damaging and it remains both. The woman on the bus is safe because Doina did not name her. Doina is in a cell because she did not name her.

## Survival and what it costs

The last chapter is Doina, memorising the ninth line — bracket included. The paper is gone. Ilinca is gone. What survives is the knowledge: not written, not copied, not transmittable by the method that killed Ana, but held in a person. This is not offered as hope. The memorised line is what the network had to become to continue existing, and it has become it at the cost of the woman who built the network. The book does not tell the reader how to feel about this. It gives them the fact of it.
