# 10 November 1984

The November payroll forms are in the wooden tray beside the secretary's elbow, folded in half the way they come from the print room. She takes them without sitting down.

Pântelimon says: there has been some unpleasantness with the Petrescu matter. A Miliția officer has been speaking with people.

He says it as a statement in an open room. The outer door of the office is propped; two women from the personnel section are at their desks with their coats still on. He is watching Ilinca's hands.

She folds the forms once more and tucks them under her arm. A tragic business, she says. She is glad the family has someone looking into it.

She goes back to her office.

---

She closes the door and puts the payroll forms on the left side of the desk, beside the October figures. She does not open them yet.

An officer has been speaking with people. The secretary told her this in the tone of a man who has information and would like to exchange it. She gave him nothing except the obvious, which is the kind of exchange that costs her nothing and may give him something to think about later, if he is the type who thinks about things later. She does not know what type he is.

She thinks: he has not come to the administrative building. If she were a name in the file, someone would have been at her door by now. The administrative building is not a production section and it is not a residential bloc. It sits on the other side of the main gate, which is a distance that means something, practically speaking, about whose names come first.

A man working outward from Ana Petrescu's house works from the sister-in-law, then from whoever the sister-in-law named, then outward from there. That is how it goes. There is a sequence to these things and she is not at the front of the sequence. She knows this because nobody has knocked on her door.

She opens the middle drawer and takes out the October summary sheet and places it to the right of the payroll forms. She does not look at either of them.

She has time. Not an abundance of it. Enough to do the next thing.

---

At nine she takes the materials-usage report from the filing cabinet behind the door. The October comparison columns for Hall B show a discrepancy on the last week of the month: the production log records sixty-eight kilograms of raw fiber allocation, but the stores ledger shows seventy-two kilograms issued over the same period. Four kilograms. Small enough to be a transcription error; large enough that it cannot stay in the month-end summary without an explanation and a countersignature.

She needs Georgeta for this.

This is the difficulty and also the solution to the difficulty, and she takes a moment to look at it as both. It is the second time in a week she will have occasion to speak with Georgeta. Once in a week is reasonable. Twice is one more than she prefers, for a woman who has always been careful about how often she appears in the same place as the same person. But the discrepancy is real. The stores ledger is here in her hand. She needs a production supervisor's countersignature before the month-end summary can go to the director's office, and Georgeta is the supervisor for Hall B. The legitimacy of the reason is sufficient. She has used worse reasons than this.

She writes the discrepancy figures on a separate sheet: *issued, 72 kg; production log, 68 kg; variance, 4 kg.* She clips the sheet to the October comparison figures and puts both in her document folder.

She waits until ten. She does not look at the clock between nine and ten.

---

At ten she goes to the supplies corridor.

Georgeta is already there. She is doing the quarterly inventory, which she does on the tenth of every month — Ilinca has countersigned the inventory sheets since 1978 and knows the schedule. Georgeta's clipboard is in her right hand; she is making ticks with a pencil, working along the shelves from the door end.

Ilinca sets her folder on the table near the window end and opens it to the October comparison sheet.

A materials discrepancy, she says. Hall B, last week of October. Seventy-two kilograms issued against sixty-eight in the production log. I need to know before the month-end summary which figure is correct, or whether there is a stores entry that explains the difference.

Georgeta does not stop her ticks. She finishes the shelf she is on. She sets the clipboard against the wall and comes to the table.

She looks at the comparison sheet. The last week of October, she says. We had two days of reduced intake on the spooling machines in the second bay. Some of the raw fiber arrived late. I logged it in the first week of November to keep the production records clean. If stores logged it in October because the delivery arrived in October, that is where your four kilograms are.

Ilinca writes this down. She says: I will need the delivery receipt to confirm the date. Can you get me the November intake log for the first four days?

By afternoon, Georgeta says. The materials office will have the receipt; I will send someone.

Ilinca closes the folder and clips the note inside it. She says: that should close it for the month-end summary. Then, without a pause that could be read as a pause: and how is Livia keeping?

Georgeta's pencil is in her hand. She does not tap it against anything.

Her daughter stopped by on Tuesday, she says. She says Livia is fine. Quiet. She's been at home, not seeing people.

Ilinca says: hasn't given anything to anyone?

Georgeta shakes her head, once, as if she is agreeing that the delivery receipt will settle the discrepancy.

No, she says. She kept it to herself.

Good. Ilinca picks up her folder. I'll have the countersignature form ready when the intake log comes. If you send it by two, we can close this before Friday.

She goes back to her office.

---

She closes the door. She sits in the chair.

N2 branch: Georgeta. From Georgeta to Livia — Georgeta's neighbor on her street. Livia gave the copy to nobody. She has been at home, not seeing people. No Miliția contact; Georgeta's daughter went by on Tuesday and she was fine. The branch runs from the master, then to Georgeta, then to Livia, and there it stops. A dead end is what the branch was designed to be; not every copy was meant to go further. Livia had kept it to herself for more than a year and had not used it and had not passed it and was now sitting quietly in her apartment while a man with a notepad asked questions on streets that were not her street. The branch contains no one who is in a file.

*No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.*

She has followed this herself. The cousin, the borrowed pot, the materials discrepancy. She has not made a telephone call she did not need. She has not opened her door to anyone who was not expected. What she has done in the past week to close her accounting of the branches — the routes she took, the words she used, the questions she turned sideways — are all consistent with the instruction on line five. She knows line five the way she knows all of them. She wrote it, which is a different kind of knowing than reading it, because writing a thing is choosing every word separately, and she chose those words and has not needed to reconsider them.

The N3 branch is confirmed through Elena Florescu. The N2 branch closes now, with Livia. What remains is the cellar copy — the third copy she made from the master, on November third of last year, in the coal cellar behind Strada Dorobanților, by the light of the door, in ten minutes, for a woman who could not wait for a better time. She has gone over it. She knows what she wrote. She drew the bracket — two strokes and a corner — and she wrote the words inside it, and the words were the words from the master. She is certain of this the way she is certain of her own handwriting.

She counts: four nodes in her private account. The master. The N2 branch, now closed and clean. The N3 branch, closed and clean. The cellar copy, which she holds as correct. Four entries. She cannot write any of this anywhere. She cannot write the count or the confirmation or the four-kilogram discrepancy in the same column. The private account has no ledger. It exists in the hour between nine and ten when she does not look at the clock.

The man asking questions in the production sections will work outward from what he has and will eventually reach what exists to be reached. What exists to be reached, on the N2 branch, is Livia, who is fine and has kept herself quiet and has given nothing to anyone. That branch is closed. If he reaches it, it dead-ends. It has no information that points back to her.

She opens the payroll forms.

---

The November columns are blank. She fills them from the October summary, adjusted for the two new employees in Hall C and the reduced hours from the repair week. She uncaps her pen and writes the first entry at the top of the column. She checks the form header. Alphabetical, surname-first, which has been the format since October per the new directive from the financial office. She has been using this format since October. The entry is in the right place.

The numbers go in one column at a time. Gross hours, deductions, net. She runs the figures by hand first, then checks the tape. The tape agrees with her column for the first twelve entries and disagrees by three lei on the thirteenth. She finds the error: a transposition in the gross hours, twenty-two where the source sheet says twenty-two point five. She corrects it with a single line through the wrong figure and the right figure beside it.

She fills the column to the end of the first page. She turns to the second.

The fog from the river burned off before ten. The sun comes in through the window now at an angle that crosses the desk; she moves the October comparison sheet out of the light and continues. By eleven the second column is complete. Twenty-seven entries on the first page, three on the reverse. The countersignature line for the materials discrepancy will go at the bottom when Georgeta's intake log arrives. That should be before two.

She sets the pen down and looks at what she has done. The column is correct. The figures are in the right order. When the delivery receipt confirms the dates, the four-kilogram discrepancy will have an explanation and the explanation will go into the correct column and the month-end summary will go to the director's office by Friday and the October accounts will be closed.

She clips the payroll forms together — original, personnel copy, summary page — and puts the set in the out tray.

She leans back in the chair. The chair has a creak at the back joint that she has meant to report to the maintenance office since spring. She has not reported it. A creak is not a problem; it is the kind of sound that stops being heard after the first week, the kind that only a person paying close attention to her office and her habits would notice in the middle of a morning. She has not reported it.

She sits forward and puts both hands flat on the desk.

N2 branch closed. Four nodes confirmed. The officer who has been asking questions has not come to the administrative building. She has time still — not much, but enough to do the next thing, and the thing after that.

The delivery receipt will arrive by two.

She uncaps the pen and pulls the October comparison sheet back into the light and reads the figures again from the beginning. This is what she does after a column is finished: she reads it again. The thing you miss is always in the line you read first, when your eye has not yet learned what it is looking for. She has learned this about herself over fifteen years and she does not argue with it.

The lamp is off. She has not needed it since the fog cleared.

# 11 November 1984

He had left the two copies on his desk the previous evening, spread flat and held at their corners by the evidence folder, and when he came in Monday morning they were as he had left them.

He took off his coat and hung it on the back of the door. Sandu's desk at the far end of the investigations room was empty; Sandu was in the field on the Cuzdrioara registration matter and would not be in until afternoon. The coal stove in the corner had been lit by whoever was on overnight duty and was burning with the damp smell of lignite that never quite cleared in November, which meant it had been going long enough to take the edge off the cold without quite producing warmth. He moved the folder to the left side of the desk and sat down.

He had read both copies on Thursday — the day he had collected them — and again on Friday before the weekend. He knew what they said. What he was doing now was not reading for content. He was reading the way he had learned, over twelve years, to read a statement taken from two different people about the same event: not for what the words said but for where the words diverged, and whether the divergence was something that would have happened accidentally or only by design.

He was not a graphologist. He was a man who had spent twelve years reading statements.

Line one of the first copy: *Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.* Small careful hand. The o in 'lying' and the o in 'whole' pressed closed by a pen held at a narrow angle.

Line one of the second copy: the same line, the same words. Different hand. Larger letters, a slight rightward lean, the downstrokes of the l and the t in 'lying' longer than was strictly necessary, as though the writer had thought they were about to run out of room and then discovered they had more than enough.

He went line by line.

Lines one through eight: close to identical. He noted where they were not. Line three on the first copy: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.* Line three on the second copy: the same sentence, until the last four words — *on the paper beside the bed.* He looked at the two phrases. The instruction was the same. The prepositions were not. Someone had written *beside* where the other document, or its source, said *by.* That was either a copying error — the copyist's own preposition substituting itself for the original's — or it was a variation already present in whatever the second copy had been made from.

He had no way to know yet which of these was true.

He turned to the back page of his cardboard folder, which served as his case notes, and wrote below Saturday's entry: *L3 variant: 'by the bed' / 'beside the bed'. Two hands, two sheets, different paper stocks. L9: identical — see below.*

Line nine was the same on both copies. He read it on the first document — *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning* — and then on the second, the words arriving in the same order, set down in a different hand on different paper, but unchanged: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* He held the two sheets up briefly, each in one hand, and read the ninth line again on each. 

Nine words. Twice. In two separate acts of writing by two people who had not been in the same room.

A woman who had stayed until morning had been following a document that told her to wait for morning. He had understood this from the first reading, on Thursday. What he was looking at now was something additional: the instruction had not entered the chain at the point where the first copy had passed to the Petrescu household. It was present in the neighbor's copy as well, which was a separate document obtained separately from a separate address. If the instruction was already in both copies, and both copies had been made by different people from whatever they had each received, then the instruction had been present in what they had each received. The instruction was earlier.

He closed the folder.

---

The address he needed was a three-story bloc on Alecsandri street, east of the mill workers' market. Three hundred metres. He walked.

November had gone cold and wet in the last week, the kind of damp that came off the Someș in the morning and did not lift before noon. The market was open but thin — mid-month, the queues had already moved through whatever there was to move through. A woman at the corner stand near the market entrance had something under an oil cloth. She watched him come up the street and watched him go past without moving. He did not stop. He counted the doorways until he had the right building.

Interior stair. The third floor smelled of cabbage soup and wet wool. He knocked at the indicated door.

The woman who answered had the expression of someone who had been expecting a particular knock for some number of days and had made a decision about how she would receive it. She was in her late forties, heavy-shouldered, her hair pinned close to her head, wearing a house coat. She was holding a dish cloth. When she looked at him she folded the cloth in half, and then in half again, until she had a square she had nowhere particular to put.

He introduced himself. He said he was investigating the death of Ana Petrescu and that he had questions about a document she might be able to help with.

She said: come in.

The flat was a kitchen and one other room. The kitchen had a table in the centre and two cups on it, which she moved to the counter without comment. She put the folded dish cloth on the counter beside them and sat down across from him at the table.

Her name was Lucia Gal. She worked the day shift in the second weaving hall at the AFE mill. She had worked there since 1972. She said this directly and without elaboration, with the particular quality of someone who has decided that the correct response to official interest is to offer official information precisely and let nothing else slip through in the offering.

He told her: he was aware that a document of a certain kind had been circulating in the area. That he was trying to understand how it had moved. That if she had such a document and was willing to give it to him now, that cooperation would be noted in the file. Voluntary surrender was better than the alternative. He said this simply, without emphasis on the word 'alternative,' because emphasis was the thing that made people stop cooperating. He had learned this.

She got up and went to the counter. Second drawer from the left. She took out a folded sheet, carried it to the table, and set it in front of him.

He put on his gloves before he picked it up.

The paper was different from the other two copies. It was lighter, greyer, the stock of a mill production form — the front side carried official printing, department designation and output-tracking columns and a foreman's signature box, in the regulation black ink. On the reverse: the document, written in blue pencil. He had not seen blue pencil before on any version of this document. The handwriting was careful — more careful than either of the copies he had collected on Thursday, the numerals at the start of each line formed with a deliberateness that was close to elegance, the lines spaced evenly from top to bottom of the sheet.

He put it in an evidence envelope and wrote her name and address on the flap.

He asked: had she given a copy of this document to anyone else?

She said: no. She held his eyes when she said it. He wrote *denies further transmission* in his case notes.

He asked: where had she received this document?

She said: from a woman she worked with, on the production floor, in the second hall. She gave him the name without prompting. He wrote it. He wrote the hall number and the shift.

He asked: and did the woman she named live in this building, or elsewhere?

She gave him the address. He wrote it.

He thanked her. She held the door.

---

He had three copies.

He laid them side by side on his desk and weighted the corners with whatever was nearest, which turned out to be a stapler and three unopened tins of shoe polish. He read each copy through separately first, going from line one to line nine. Read separately, they said nearly the same thing. He read them again together, line by line across all three sheets.

He put the grey mill-form paper on the left, the two Thursday copies on the right, and went from the top.

Lines one through eight: close to identical across all three. He moved slowly, each line in sequence across all three sheets before going to the next. Line one was the same. Line two was the same. Line three: the grey-paper copy said *by the bed*. The first of the Thursday copies said *by the bed*. The second of the Thursday copies said *beside the bed.*

He stopped.

Two of his three copies agreed in line three. The third differed from both of them by one word. He marked the positions in his notes. It was a small difference — a preposition, nothing more, the instruction unchanged — but it told him something about the arrangement. Two copies that agreed with each other in a particular line were either copied from each other or copied from the same source. A third copy that differed from both of them had either introduced the variation itself or had inherited it from a different source. He was looking at two copies that agreed, and one that did not. The two that agreed were probably closer to each other in the chain.

That was not a complicated observation. It was arithmetic.

He continued down the page.

Lines four, five, six, seven, eight: no differences of consequence. Minor variations in spacing, in the exact formation of particular letters — the d in 'down' on one copy made with a loop, on another without it. The kind of variation that appeared whenever a person was copying something by hand and was not aware that the variation was there. He noted these without significance.

Line nine he read last, going left to right across all three sheets.

The grey-paper copy, in blue pencil: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

The first Thursday copy, the small careful hand: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

The second Thursday copy, the slightly larger hand with the opened o's: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He sat back and looked at the three line nines.

The same instruction, three times. Three different hands, three different sheets, three different acts of writing. The same nine words. He had taken his pen up when he started reading line nine across the three copies and he set it back down without writing anything.

The instruction had been present in the grey-paper copy, which was a step earlier in the chain than the two Thursday copies. The grey-paper copy was the one the woman in the flat on Alecsandri street had given him — the woman who had named a woman on the production floor as the person she had got it from. If the instruction was already present in the grey-paper copy, it had not been introduced by Lucia Gal. It had been there when she received it. It had been present before the grey-paper copy was made.

He looked at the three sheets again. The grey-paper copy and the first Thursday copy agreed in line three — *by the bed*. The second Thursday copy said *beside the bed.* That meant the second Thursday copy had probably been copied from the grey-paper copy or from something that had already introduced *beside* — but either way, the grey-paper copy was probably the oldest document in front of him, or closest to the oldest. And the oldest document in front of him already had the morning instruction in line nine.

He turned to the fresh page at the back of the cardboard folder and wrote: *Three copies in evidence. L3 variant: 'by the bed' (x2) / 'beside the bed' (x1). L9 consistent across all three: 'take her in in the morning.' Instruction not introduced at points of collection. Present at minimum in copy acquired today (earlier in chain). Source is upstream. Next: [the name from the Gal interview].*

It was the kind of finding that would not survive being described to his captain in its present form. Captain Niculescu had looked at the file on Wednesday and asked when Munteanu expected to have something writable. He had said: by the end of the week. That had been a realistic estimate at the time. He had thought, on Wednesday, that the chain would be short — three, maybe four people, the kind of small informal thing that didn't go far and died at the edges for want of someone to carry it. He thought less of this now. The instruction in line nine had been present before the three copies he held. Before the woman on Alecsandri street, before the woman on Strada Gării, before the Petrescu household. The chain behind it was longer than three people.

He was going to have more names in this file before he was done.

He stood and took his coat from the back of the door.

The name from the Gal interview was the production-floor woman who had given Lucia Gal her copy. One step further back. One step closer to wherever the instruction had entered. She worked the same hall, the day shift. She had not been expecting him this morning, because he had not known her name this morning. Now he did.

He put on his coat and picked up his case notes.

# 12 November 1984

She is on the last two lines of the October column when the knock comes.

Stela Ionescu, from the personnel section: a maintenance request across the desk, the boiler-room work order for the second heating pipe joint, which has been leaking since October and bleeds heat from the second-floor corridor before it reaches the administrative wing. The description of the repair is specific — sealing the joint with a wool-and-resin compound, three hours of work after the Sunday shift. The date is correct. The series number matches the maintenance register. Ilinca picks up her pen.

She has known Stela by the corridor and the elevator and the bathroom sink at the end of the hall: eleven years of proximity without occasion for more. Stela has a quiet manner and flat shoes and keeps her coat buttoned in the building until the heating comes on, which in November means until six, which in the administrative wing means until somewhat after that.

While Ilinca signs, Stela says — as a separate sentence, as something entering the air from the side — that her friend from the bloc committee was called in this morning. About the Petrescu matter. Someone had been asking about a piece of paper that was going around the district. Something about what to do when a person was ill.

Ilinca hands the form back.

Stela says: the person asking had a copy with him, and he had read the ninth line aloud from it. The exact wording, as her friend had told her: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

She adds that she thought Ilinca would want to know, given that everyone in the building is talking about it.

Ilinca says thank you. Stela goes, pulling the door not quite shut behind her. A two-centimeter gap of corridor light. Ilinca watches it for a moment. Then she gets up and closes the door properly.

She goes back to her desk. She sets her pen on the blotter. She does not pick it up.

---

The 1983 ledger is on the second shelf between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission. The brown tape at the top of the spine has held since February. It is a Ministry of Finance form-book, four hundred pages, a state document she is required to produce on demand.

She takes it down from the shelf and carries it to her desk. She sets it flat with the spine uppermost and holds it by the boards, opening the spine at the top, fitting two fingers along the gap between the pages and the board where the paper sits. The paper is folded twice in one direction and once across, a small square. She takes it out by the corner.

She opens it flat on the desk between the ledger and the lamp. She does not touch it again.

The paper has been folded and refolded many times in the fourteen months since she wrote it in October of last year. The creases have gone slightly furry — the fiber pressing up at each fold line into a faint nap — and the outer edge has taken on a soft, handled quality. The ink is still sharp. She used the blue-black she keeps for fair copies. The page shows everything she has asked of it.

She reads from the beginning.

---

1. Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.
2. Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.
3. Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.
4. If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.
5. No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.
6. Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
   [ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why.
     Do not wait for the morning. ]

---

She reads the bracket three times.

She drew it in October of last year because she understood, before she finished writing, that the ninth instruction was not the same kind of thing as the other eight. A numbered list is a sequence. Lines one through eight are a sequence: what to do first, what comes next, what follows. The bracket is not a step in a sequence. It is a different order of information entirely — not what comes after eight, but what overrides everything above it when the conditions are met. She drew the two strokes and the corner precisely because she needed the shape on the page to carry that difference. In fourteen years of bookkeeping she has used brackets for the same reason every time: to mark what operates on the column, not what continues it. An item inside a bracket is not the next entry. It is the instruction that changes what the other entries mean.

*Do not wait for the morning.*

She reads the phrase once more. Then she looks away from the document without looking at anything in the room.

She has been given the exact wording of the ninth line as it exists in another copy. *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* She holds the two texts beside each other and reads the difference.

The bracket: *take her in. Do not wait for the morning.*

The numbered line: *take her in in the morning.*

Both contain the word *morning*. In the bracket, *morning* is the limit — the threshold you do not wait for. In the numbered line, *morning* is the time — it is when you go. The bracket says: the sequence has ended; when condition 7 or 8 is true, go now. The numbered line says: when condition 7 or 8 is true, go in the morning.

A bracket given a number has become a step in a list. The word *now* — which is what *do not wait for the morning* means — is gone from it. What is left is a sequential instruction with a time attached: *morning.* The woman who made that copy was being tidy. She saw nine pieces of information and she numbered them one through nine, because that is what a careful copyist does with nine pieces of information and a numbered list on the page in front of her. The hand that has just written *8.* has the *9.* ready.

Ilinca counts down the page. Eight numbered lines. Then the bracket.

She counts again. Eight. Then the bracket.

---

She puts the two accounts together and runs the entry that reconciles them.

The master is here, in front of her — eight numbered lines and a bracket, exactly as she wrote it. The three copies she made from the master in the thirteen months since October 1983 are the second generation. She has traced two of those three branches.

The N2 branch goes from Georgeta to Livia: dead end, closed, no Miliția contact, no further transmission. Clean.

The N3 branch goes through her cousin to Elena Florescu: confirmed clean on Day 5, no outside approach, no contact.

The N4 branch — the cellar copy, Strada Crișan, the third of November of last year, twenty minutes, by the light of the door gap — she has not confirmed directly, because confirming it directly means identifying herself in the chain. She has no route to N4 that does not require a name.

But she made N4. She holds the memory of making it the same way she holds a column: in order, line by line. The cellar: the smell of coal dust, the cold at the door, the paper on her knee. The pencil moving down the page. Eight numbered lines, written in sequence — one through eight, each checked as she went. And then the bracket: two strokes and a corner, the corner at the bottom of the last stroke. The text inside the bracket, written inside it, not below it, inside. She checked the copy once after finishing. She is almost certain the bracket was there when she handed it over.

If the N2 branch is clean and the N3 branch is clean, and if N4 is clean — and she is almost certain — then the mutation entered in a generation after her second generation. Someone downstream received a copy with a bracket at the bottom and copied it as a numbered step, because that is what the hand does when it has been moving down a numbered list and arrives at the bottom of the page with the number nine ready. The mutation entered there. Not in anything she made.

This is the direction the entries point.

She knows the wording of the mutation now exactly. She has added one node to her accounting: the fact of the mutant line, confirmed, the exact words of it, the distance between those words and the words in front of her on the desk. Her count is five.

---

She refolds N1 along the furry creases. Once in one direction, once across. The paper makes a soft sound that is the sound of paper that has made this fold many times before. She tucks it into the ledger spine, fitting it along the gap between the pages and the board until it seats at the outer edge. She carries the ledger to the second shelf and sets it between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission, spine flush with the edge of the shelf.

She goes back to her desk. She picks up the pen.

But before she takes the October column from where she left it, she does what she always does when two accounts that cannot both be correct must be held together: she sets them in the same column and reads what is there.

She knows lines one through eight. She wrote them. She holds each of them complete and exact.

She has been given line nine verbatim — read aloud by a man she has never met, repeated by a woman she has known for eleven years by proximity, delivered to her desk at a quarter past four in the afternoon. She sets both texts in the same column and she reads:

---

1. Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.
2. Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.
3. Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.
4. If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.
5. No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.
6. Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.

---

Lines one through eight: hers. Correct.

Line nine: not hers. Someone who received a copy with nine pieces of information numbered them one through nine, because that is what nine pieces of information look like when they are arranged in a column on a page. The person was being careful. The error is in the being careful.

She puts her pen to the October column and begins.

The heat comes on at twelve minutes past six: the knock of the joint at the baseboard corner, and then the dull expansion of the pipe along the wall. She does not look up. The figures run to the end of the page. She checks the column twice. Both times it totals correctly.

She caps her pen and sets it in the groove at the right side of the desk. She takes her coat from the hook behind the door and turns off the lamp. The office goes dark except for the yellow line of corridor light under the door. She steps through, closes the door, tries the handle once.

N1 is in the ledger spine. The ledger is on the second shelf. The mutation entered somewhere downstream — in a copy she did not make, in a hand she cannot name, in a generation she has not yet reached.

She walks.

input.content:
# 13 November 1984

The bridge over the Someș was always the worst part, and I say that as someone who spent two years crossing it in the dark at four-thirty in the morning, which gives me more authority on the subject than I would have liked.

It was the fog. Not the cold — I was used to the cold by then, or I had at least stopped expecting anything better from November in the Someș valley, which is not the same thing — but the fog came off the river in autumn and settled on the bridge deck in a way that had nothing to do with temperature and everything to do with the specific disposition of this particular valley toward the people who lived in it. You walked into it and it erased the railings and the far bank and the road beyond, and for thirty or forty seconds you were just a person in white nothing, which at four-thirty in the morning, when you were already thinking about things you should not be thinking about, was not an experience I found helpful.

On the street before the bridge: one lamp still burning in a third-floor window of the first bloc, a woman in a dark coat going the opposite direction who did not look up. I did not look up either. This is the social compact of the four-thirty shift change, and I had always appreciated it in the abstract, but I appreciated it more that November than I ever had before.

The mill smell reached you from two hundred meters out. Hot and wet and chemical — the celofiber production hall, the fiber drying unit, the pressing-and-sizing vats all combining into something that had no single good description and that I had long since stopped smelling as a smell. Two years on the night shift. Somewhere over seven hundred crossings of that bridge. I had done the arithmetic once and been depressed by it and had not done it again. The smell was the smell of being here, which was where I was, and had been for two years, and which was not looking like it was going to stop being the case any time soon.

I went along the road below the water treatment plant, past the parking area with the three bicycles that had been chained to the fence since before I arrived — the chain on the middle one had been rusting for longer than I knew — and around to the production entrance in the side of the weaving hall. The door was propped open during shift change. The guard in the hut was drinking from a metal cup. I showed my shift pass. He did not look at my face.

Inside: the locker bay, then the production corridor. I hung my coat and put my bag under the bench and closed the locker. The geography book was on the shelf above the coat hooks, between the corner of the locker and the wall seam — the shelf is too short for anything except exactly that. I did not look at it directly, because I had found in the last ten days that not looking at the geography book directly was a habit I was developing, like the habit of checking the lock twice, like the habit of taking the river path home instead of the main road. I checked the lock a second time and went to the floor.

---

The production floor in the morning was the loom noise. I don't know how to convey the loom noise, which is why I keep stating it as a fact and moving on.

The looms were Hungarian-made, retooled for celofiber yarn some years before I arrived. When all forty-eight were running, which they were when I came onto the floor at five past five, conversation was not possible in any practical sense — not because of any rule, but because anything produced at mouth level was absorbed immediately into the ambient volume, and the person next to you had no particular reason to suspect you had spoken. I had worked in this for two years, and in the last ten days I had come to regard it as one of the more comfortable environments available to me in the district of Dej in November of 1984. I want to be precise about this: I was genuinely grateful for the loom noise in a way I had not anticipated when I signed my contract.

I threaded the machine. Two minutes later my hands knew what they were doing and I had the rest of myself free for other purposes.

What I did with it: watched the women near me without appearing to watch them. Row across from mine: Anca, who has the kind of face that conveys nothing and who I had once seen win an argument in the break room without appearing to have an argument; past her, a woman I had worked beside for six months without ever learning her name, who today had her hair loose on both sides instead of pinned on the left; at the end of the row, a third woman attending her machine with the focused precision of someone who has decided that the machine is the only object in the room.

I recognised that last one as a decision. I had been making a version of it myself.

Three women who looked like they had not slept. I can't tell you now what it looked like exactly. I'm telling you what it looked like and I'm telling you I was getting better at seeing it. Something around the eyes. A quality of attention that was paying attention to something else entirely.

---

The break room was off the production corridor, across from the bathroom. Two long tables, eight chairs each. At the back there was a hot-water urn that had probably been there since the founding of the republic and that produced something technically classifiable as tea if you held your cup under it long enough and did not ask anything more specific from the transaction. I got my cup and sat at the far end of the first table.

Marta — she worked the adjacent loom on my section, she lived on the fourth floor of my bloc, she had a son in the fourth form and a husband who drove for the transport depot — sat down across from me but toward the middle of the table, not beside me, which I noted as a kind of tact. She looked at her cup. She said, without looking at me: they took Floarea and Geta in on Monday.

Both of them from the finishing section. Both from the other end of the hall.

I said: what did they ask them?

She said: what do you think they asked them.

She picked up her tea and moved to the far end of the table, where some other women were already involved in something about the bread queue on Victoriei, and within two minutes she was involved in it too.

I sat with my cup.

---

I knew Floarea the way you know someone from six months of sitting behind them on the morning bus — the back of her head, her posture, a blue coat she wore on cold days. Her name I had heard once in the break room. That was the full extent of my knowledge of Floarea.

I did not know whether she had a copy of any paper. I did not know whether she knew anyone who did. I did not know whether, in the specific context that now had a context, she knew that Doina Marcu from the night shift existed in any relevant sense.

Here is what I had been trying to think clearly about for ten days, and what kept refusing to go clear: this was not built like something that has a diagram. It was not a thing where you could stand at any point and draw lines outward and eventually reach all the other points. It was: one person knowing one person, the paper traveling between those two, neither of them necessarily knowing anyone else in the exchange. The woman on the bus had not asked my name. She had put the paper in my hand before I had finished deciding whether I was accepting it, and by the time I thought to say something she was looking out the window at the November fields outside Bonțida, and the moment had passed.

So what I knew about Floarea's connection to any of this was: nothing certain. There might be six steps between her line and mine. There might be none in common. They might share a branch with me that went all the way back to the same source, or they might be on a branch I had never had any connection to at all, in which case the fact that they were now in the file had nothing to do with my locker and I was fine.

I thought: it's probably fine.

Then I sat with the specific texture of "probably fine" for a moment.

Then I went back to the floor.

---

The second half of the shift, I worked. I want to be accurate about this because I remember being faintly surprised by it at the time: I worked. My hands moved. The loom ran. At some point the light coming through the clerestory windows above the machines changed from the flat dark of five o'clock to the particular grey of November morning — grey through a layer of hall condensation, but light — and this helped, in the way that light always helps even when you can't account for why it should.

The thing you can say about a loom is that it requires you to be there — not your feelings, but your hands, which is what I had to offer, and which held.

The woman at the end of the row kept her eyes on her machine. Anca did too. Near the end of the shift Anca looked up and caught my eye for a second. We both looked back.

---

After the shift most people went left from the production entrance, toward the main road and the bus stop and the bread shop on Victoriei that was already open by seven. I went right, along the wall of the fiber drying unit — forty meters where the heat coming off the ductwork almost reached the backs of your hands — and then around and down toward the river path.

The fog was still on the Someș at half past seven. Light was coming up behind the eastern ridge in the flat grey-gold way it comes in the valley in November: the sun above the ridge line, spreading flat along the bottom of the cloud layer without appearing in any particular place, so that everything was lit from nowhere and nothing had a shadow. The fog sat on the water in long horizontal shapes that moved with the current but went nowhere. The clay path alongside the river was wet and soft. My boots had not been fully waterproof since September, which I had known about and continued not to address, the same way you continue not to address things that are below the current top of your list.

*Keep her warm, and lying down.* Line one. It came to me the way things lodged in that particular slot come up — not because I had thought of it but because I had been not-thinking of it long enough and hard enough that it surfaced on its own. I knew line one the way I knew my hostel room number: by repetition, without intending to. I knew line three. I knew line seven. I knew the bracket at the bottom, the whole bracket. I could have recited it in order if there had been anyone to recite it to, which there wasn't and wasn't going to be, because the whole point was that you recited it to nobody. *Someone stays with her the whole night.*

The geography book was in my locker. My locker was locked. I had the key on my ring with the hostel key and my aunt's spare — the small brass key she had pressed into my hand when I moved to the hostel in 1982, which I had carried for three years and had never once needed to use. The man in the good coat had been asking questions at the mill and in the blocs for two weeks. He had taken Floarea and Geta in on Monday, both from the finishing section on the other side of the hall. He had not come to the locker bay.

The river path turned at the end onto the hostel road. I walked past the bench where people sat in summer. The kiosk on the corner was shut. The corner lamp was still on from the night.

I did not know if not yet was the same as not going to.

The fog moved on the Someș behind me. My feet were cold. I walked.

# 14 November 1984

She does the variance three times. The third time it comes back twelve lei.

The October third-shift payroll: seventeen line discrepancies, all resolved since Tuesday, and one aggregate variance of twelve lei that has had no explanation since she found it. She has been doing the rest of the column around it, leaving the line empty, returning after other work to see if the answer has appeared. It has not appeared each time she has returned. She marks the line with a pencil stroke and turns the page.

She will find it. It is twelve lei and it has been here since Tuesday and it will be there when she finds it.

What she is thinking about this morning is the N4 branch.

She made the copy on the third of November of the year before, in the coal cellar of a building she had been brought to by someone she trusted — a connection specific to that night, not a connection before and not a connection after. The woman from that night was waiting in the coal smell with her pencil ready. The light came in through the door from the courtyard; not enough light but enough to write by if you were fast. Ilinca had recited the lines while the woman wrote. She had watched the pencil to see if it was keeping up.

She can account for eight lines from that recitation.

*Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.* Line six. She had said it clearly. The woman had written it without stopping. Line six is the one that appears to go against the line before it and does not; she had been deliberate with it in the dark because of this. She can account for line six the way she can account for each of the eight: said it, watched the pencil move, line complete.

What she cannot account for is the bracket. The ninth element. She had said it. She is almost certain the pencil was still moving when she said it. She cannot say with certainty that the bracket was in the right position on the page, or in any position at all, because it is a margin note and not a numbered line and the difference between those two things in the dark, with a pencil moving fast, is a difference she could not audit in real time.

She has been proceeding on the assumption that it was correct. She has treated the cellar copy as: one transaction, her end closed. Made the copy, gave it over, left. What came after was the woman from that night's management, not a column Ilinca had any reading of.

This morning she does not believe the column ends there.

The woman from that night is not a full stop. She received the paper. People who receive this paper, and who know people who might need it, do with it what it is for: they pass it on, when the time comes, to someone they know. Ilinca has been counting on this. It is how the paper gets where it needs to go. It is also how a branch extends past a single transaction, and she has been treating the cellar branch as one transaction and nothing after, and she does not now believe that is accurate.

What she does not know: whether the woman from that night gave a copy to anyone, and if so to whom. She cannot ask directly. The cellar woman is not part of her usual network; a visit to that part of the city would be its own kind of visibility, the kind she cannot afford. She needs a route.

---

She has one.

The pharmacy is on Eminescu, near the second bloc, fifteen minutes from the mill gate. The woman at the counter knows her from the market queue and the monthly aspirin requisition and the bus stop on Thursdays. They have spoken about the bread allocation. They have spoken about the flour, about the new forms, about the bus that does not run on Saturdays when it should. They have not spoken about anything that matters.

She has needed aspirin since Monday. This is the first mid-morning she has had free.

She tells Lenuta from accounts she will be back before eleven and goes out through the rear exit, past the clinic door, which is still locked at this hour.

---

The cold on the street outside is particular to this valley in November: not at the floor yet, but past the point where the body argues about it. The boulevard trees have been finished with their leaves for several days. The pavement is wet with something that happened earlier without reaching the level of rain. She keeps her pace at the pace of a woman going somewhere she goes regularly, which she is. The market stand at the corner is closed until Thursday; she passes it.

Dorobanților runs behind Eminescu and connects to it at the north end. She does not go down Dorobanților. She goes straight to Eminescu and turns toward the pharmacy.

The pharmacy occupies a narrow single-story building between the corner post office and a shoe repair. Inside: the counter, the shelves with the permitted stock behind it, a warmth that is not present on the street. The woman at the counter has glasses repaired with thread at the right hinge and a way of standing that suggests she has been standing in the same position for a long time and has found it sufficient.

She copied Ilinca's buletin number into the register while the identity document lay open between them. She produced the aspirin. Ilinca pressed the requisition form flat with one finger and signed it.

She said, while tucking the identity document away: there is a woman I've been meaning to find. She gave a description — roughly her own age, a round face, a dark coat with a grey collar, the kind you see everywhere; added: her husband worked at the chemical plant on the south road. I thought she lived somewhere near here, on Eminescu or behind it. Do you know the family?

The woman at the counter restocked a shelf while she thought.

She said: there is a woman on Dorobanților — just behind the second bloc on Eminescu — who recently moved her sister in from the village. The sister works at the communal laundry on Strada Mihai. That's the closest I know to what you're describing.

Ilinca considered. She said: the husband at the chemical plant, that was the main thing I remembered about them.

The pharmacy woman said: I don't know about a husband. That family, that's all I know of them.

Ilinca thanked her. She said: perhaps it's not the right person. Don't trouble yourself.

She went out.

Three items to carry: *sister, laundry, Strada Mihai.*

She took the longer route back to the mill — eight minutes more, away from the bloc side of town — and arrived at her desk at twelve minutes past eleven.

---

She opened the November preliminary and started the December headers. At six minutes past noon she found the twelve lei: a digit misread in the October second-week line transfer, a three entered as an eight in the fourth column, a small error dated to the twenty-second. She corrected the entry and ruled the line. The column closed.

Then she worked. The afternoon documents came through: two sets of revised production tallies from the third shift, a ministry form that required countersignature, an internal memo about the December heating schedule for the administrative building that required no action but had to be filed. She processed them.

At half past two, through her window, she saw the delivery boy from the pharmacy cross the forecourt below with a cardboard box held level. He went past the personnel door, past the door she was sitting behind, and turned toward the clinic two doors down.

He did not come to her. She had not expected him to.

At twenty minutes to three, Lenuta knocked and opened the door: the clinic nurse had stepped out to the toilet, could Ilinca sign for the pharmacy delivery.

Ilinca went into the corridor.

The box sat on the shelf by the clinic door with the delivery notice folded flat on top. She lifted the notice and read it and signed the incoming column in the delivery ledger; while she was doing this she took from beneath the notice a slip of paper that she folded once and put into the pocket of her coat; she carried the box the three steps to the clinic ledge and set it inside and came back and returned the delivery ledger to its hook.

Lenuta was already back at accounts. The door between the two rooms was closed.

Ilinca sat at her desk. She took the slip from her coat pocket.

The pharmacy woman's handwriting: small, regular, not hurried. Three sentences about the December aspirin allocation and the new Ministry dispensing form taking effect in January, which all mill clinics would receive notice of separately. Below that, set a little apart, one sentence that was not the same kind of sentence as the others: *Regarding the family you were asking after — the sister is at the communal laundry on Strada Mihai, I am told, Tuesdays through Saturdays.*

She read the last sentence three times.

Then she folded the slip and placed it in the ledger between the October summary and the first November sheet, where it was a piece of paper among other pieces of paper, and she sat.

---

The cellar woman had a sister. The sister was in Dej. She worked the laundry on Strada Mihai, Tuesdays through Saturdays.

This was not the same as knowing there was a copy at the laundry. A sister recently arrived from the village is not automatically a woman who has received a copy of a specific document from a specific source. But: the cellar woman had received a paper she would not have requested for herself, because the emergency had been resolved by the time Ilinca brought the copy to her that night — resolved or past. She had taken the paper anyway. People take the paper for the reason people take anything useful that they cannot buy and cannot request through official channels: because someone they know may need it and they may need to give it.

The logic did not stop applying because the woman was the woman from the cellar.

She added the new entry. Five, and now this: six.

The problem was the laundry. She had no route to Strada Mihai. The laundry was not on her circuit; she had no contact there; a visit without a reason was the same problem as Eminescu. She needed a second route, the way she had needed the pharmacy for the first. She did not have one yet. This was a problem with a solution she had not found.

She reopened the December forecast and began the first column.

---

The shift bell rang at half past three. The building cleared in its usual sequence. Accounts first: she heard Lenuta and the two junior staff go down the corridor, the familiar pattern of their conversation about the Victoriei bread shop, which was closed on Tuesdays apparently. Then the personnel office, two women who had worked there since before Ilinca arrived and who left without speaking to anyone on the way out, which was their habit and not unfriendliness. Then, at a quarter to four, the two senior clerks at the far end of the corridor, whose footsteps she had learned to distinguish without intending to: the one with the uneven heel first, then the other.

She stayed at her desk.

Her office lamp was the only one burning in this part of the building. The lamp at the end of the corridor had gone off when Lenuta left. The clinic door lamp had been off since three. Through the window: the forecourt was dark except for the gate lamp, and beyond it the street, and beyond that the production building with its row of small high windows lit orange from inside. From three buildings over she could hear the frequency of the night shift at full run — not individual machines but the aggregate of them, the forty-eight looms at their register.

She still needed the route to Strada Mihai. She had six nodes and a gap she could not close from her desk.

The December first column was not going to finish itself.

She bent over the ledger and kept working.

# 15 November 1984

The two copies occupied the right side of his desk. He had placed them there at ten past seven, when he arrived, in the order he was building them: Lucia Gal's copy from the eleventh on the near right, behind it and slightly above the copy he had collected from Ana Petrescu's sister-in-law on the sixth, which had spent time rolled inside something and dried with a crease in its upper quarter. To the left of Lucia Gal's copy: a gap of clean desk. The heating in the investigations room had come on overnight but was not yet warm; the radiator behind his chair made a low sound and produced the smell of hot metal without producing much else. He was the only person in the room.

He had the referral from Lucia Gal in his working notebook, on the page that began with the date of the Gal interview: the eleventh, a Sunday, the house on the far side of the rail crossing. She had given him a first name — Viorica — and a location: the laundry, she had said, and he understood her to mean the enterprise laundry facility on Strada Mihai, which handled finished goods before dispatch and was listed in the enterprise directory as a subordinate operational unit. She had not known a surname. She had been clear about this, in the way he had begun to recognize as a consistent feature of each of the four interviews he had conducted since the sixth: an avoidance of last names, a precision about first names and approximate locations, the address described rather than given. He no longer noted this as a limit of individual memory. It was a characteristic of the network. The document moved through it without a list, by design, and the design had consequences for him that were neither surprising nor convenient.

He signed out a personnel access form at the front desk and put on his coat and went out.

---

The enterprise administrative building was a ten-minute walk from the station, down the main road past the market. He had made this walk three times since the sixth, for different sections each time. The woman at the front desk acknowledged him with a nod and did not speak.

The personnel section occupied the second floor, three rooms behind frosted glass. He knocked and a clerk admitted him — not the woman he had seen on the fourth or the eighth, but one he had not met before. He showed his identification and stated his requirement: a worker in the enterprise laundry facility, first name Viorica, surname not known. The clerk went to the file drawers. She did not ask why.

She returned with a single card and laid it on the counter without comment. He read it in full before writing anything down. Damian, Viorica. Born 1949, Turda district. Transferred from internal production services to the enterprise laundry facility in February 1982. Registered address: Strada Mihai 14, bloc B, apartment 8.

He wrote the address in his working notebook. He thanked her and went downstairs.

---

Strada Mihai was two blocks east of the main road, past the old market building and a shuttered bakery whose sign was still up. The street ended at a courtyard shared between three residential blocs. The enterprise laundry occupied the ground floor of the first, its designation stenciled on the door: SERVICIU SPĂLĂTORIE. The smell reached him before he reached the door — heated water, lye soap, and below those, the warm chemical undersmell of processed fiber. He did not go to the laundry door. He went to the residential entrance at the far end of the same bloc and pressed the bell for apartment eight.

He waited. He pressed it again.

The outer door opened from the inside after a longer interval. The woman who appeared in the frame had dressed in the approximate direction of readiness: a grey wool robe, belted at the waist, her hair compressed flat on one side from sleep. She was between thirty-five and forty, broad through the shoulders. She took in his coat and his identification card in the same brief glance.

He told her his name and rank. He said he was sorry to disturb her at this hour. He was conducting an investigation in connection with the Petrescu matter, which had been in the district paper on the ninth. He asked whether he might come in.

She had already moved back from the door.

---

The apartment had the cold of a bloc that ran on central heating and had not received it since sometime before six. The kitchen was standard: a two-ring electric burner, a pot of water beginning to heat on the nearer ring, a row of tins on the shelf above the stove. The window had begun to fog at the lower corners. She sat across from him at the table and folded her hands and waited.

He said he was looking into the distribution of a particular document in connection with the Petrescu matter, and that he had received information suggesting she might have had access to such a document. He asked whether she had received one, and whether she still had it.

He did not describe the document.

She stood and took a tin from the shelf — the second one from the left, with a printed floral pattern, the kind that had once held tea. She set it on the table in front of him and sat back down.

He opened the tin. Inside: a sheet of paper, folded twice into quarters, the fold lines worn smooth from some months in the tin. He unfolded it and spread it flat on the table.

The paper was a factory form, written on the back. The front side showed through: column headings and the word PRODUCȚIE reversed, a date he could read only partially. On the writing side: pencil, small and regular, the letters shaped by someone who had written carefully. Nine numbered lines.

He read from the top.

---

Lines one through five he had seen before, in proportions that varied by a word here, a punctuation mark there. He did not slow down for them; he was accumulating pattern, not text.

Line six was different.

His copy — Lucia Gal's, which he had brought folded in his inside pocket — read: *Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.*

This copy read: *Burn nothing at all until she is well. Wash and keep.*

Two additional words. He wrote both versions in his notebook, side by side, and did not yet mark the relationship between them.

Lines seven and eight were as expected.

Then line nine: *7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

He set the factory-form sheet to the left and found the corresponding line on Lucia Gal's copy: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He looked at both for a moment.

The line on the left was longer — thirty-five words, roughly. It contained a sentence at the end about not waiting. The line on the right was twelve words, and it ended with the phrase *in the morning* in a position he would not have predicted from reading the line on the left. One of these versions had preceded the other, or both had descended from a third version he had not yet seen. He could determine from the texts alone neither which had come first nor what the difference meant. He could determine only that the two versions diverged, and that the divergence had entered the chain at some point between these two copies, or in a copy between them that he had not collected.

He noted both versions in his notebook, verbatim, with a line between them.

The woman across the table had not moved. She was watching him the way people watched him when they had decided the outcome of the interview was fixed — not fixed in their favor, but fixed.

---

He asked where she had gotten the document.

Her sister, she said. Her sister had given it to her.

He asked when.

She considered. Late autumn of last year, she said. November. She thought November.

He asked whether her sister was in Dej.

She said yes.

He asked for an address.

There was a pause — not a long one, but deliberate. Then she said: Dorobanților. Behind the second bloc on Eminescu.

He asked for a name and a building number. She gave them: Moga, Rodica, bloc three on the right, apartment fourteen. He wrote them in his notebook.

He asked whether her sister still lived there, as far as she knew.

As far as she knew.

He thanked her. He folded the factory-form sheet into his inner pocket with Lucia Gal's copy and stood. She stood with him. He let himself out of the kitchen and down the hallway and through the outer door without her accompanying him.

---

The cold on Strada Mihai was the same cold as when he had arrived. He walked back to the station.

---

At his desk, he laid the three copies out in order from left to right. The factory-form sheet from Viorica Damian on the far left, its printed columns showing through from the reverse, the pencil text dark against it. Lucia Gal's copy in the center — ordinary paper, black ink, a handwriting that had taken its time. The Petrescu sister-in-law's copy at the far right, with its crease at the upper quarter and its right edge curling where the paper had been wet.

He had been building this row for twelve days. On the sixth it was one copy. On the eleventh it was two. Now it was three, and there was a name written in his notebook that corresponded to the address from which the left-most copy had come.

He opened his working notebook.

First observation: *Line nine of the Damian copy reads, verbatim: "7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning." Line nine of the Gal copy reads, verbatim: "If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning." The Damian copy contains substantially more text in line nine. The change in wording between these two copies represents the earliest point in the current sequence at which this change can be placed.*

Second observation: *Line six of the Damian copy reads "Burn nothing at all until she is well." Line six of the Gal copy reads "Burn nothing until she is well." Difference: the addition of "at all." Both versions are consistent with independent hand-copying from separate physical sources, not with copying from the same original.*

Third observation: *The Damian copy is written on the back of an enterprise production form. The header on the printed side reads PRODUCȚIE; the date is not fully legible. The copy is consistent with having been made in a context where blank paper was not available.*

He read these observations over. He found them accurate and sufficient for the working notebook. He was more careful about the dosar penal, which his captain at the inspectorate would eventually review and which had to contain only what he could demonstrate.

He opened the dosar penal to the evidence section and wrote: *Physical document collected from V.O. Damian, Strada Mihai 14/B/8, Dej, 15 November 1984. Document intact. Content consistent with document family under examination. Witness cooperative. See working notebook, 15 November, for textual observations.*

He closed the dosar.

He sat for a moment with the three copies in front of him.

He had started at the last copy in the chain — the one that had been in the house when Ana Petrescu died — and he had been working backward, one name at a time, one copy at a time. Three copies now. He had not yet established how many copies there were in total, which meant he did not know how far he was from the beginning. He had a sense of scale. A document that moved through a network of this kind, through named individuals in specific relationships, without a list anywhere — a document like this did not travel through twenty hands; it was too narrow, too particular, too bound to specific contexts of trust. He had been in every house he had visited in twelve days, and none of them had felt like the house of a woman who had received this paper from a stranger. He was reading a chain of close contacts. The chain was not long.

He had the address on Dorobanților.

One copy before the Damian copy was where the chain had come from. He did not know, yet, if that was the beginning of the chain or one step into a longer sequence. He suspected — without evidence, without anything he would write in the notebook — that it was close to the beginning.

He closed the working notebook and stood and put on his coat and went downstairs.

The afternoon was grey and still, the cold sitting in the valley without moving. He turned toward the main road and walked.
