input.content:
# The Deadline

5 December 1984

He had been inside the building since six. The overnight duty officer had given him a nod from behind the entry logbook and returned to his numbers. The corridor lights were at half-strength, which they were until eight, when the day shift arrived and someone switched the panel over. In the duty-room kitchen: the powder tin on the upper shelf, water from the tap that ran brown for a moment before clearing. He carried the nechezol back to his desk in the tin cup — the one with the handle that held. The ceramic mugs had handles that separated from the body without warning; he had learned this in his first month at the Dej station, twelve years ago, and had not touched the ceramic mugs since.

The investigations room was empty. His desk held, left to right: his working notebook open to 4 December, the Petrescu dosar open to the blank determination form, and the two documents face-up in the center — he had left them there when he went home the previous evening, which he did not usually do with evidence — and the eleven evidence envelopes stacked on the left edge of the desk, labeled but not yet sealed. He had the labels written from yesterday afternoon. He had wanted to see everything one more time in the morning light before closing it.

He had come in two hours before the office filled because a determination written in an empty room was complete when he signed it, and a determination written while people moved past the desk sometimes needed to be written again. He had written two over twelve years that needed to be written again. He preferred to write things once.

He wrote the section headings in the left margin, uncapped his pen, and began.

---

*Nature of the death.* Petrescu, Ana, born 1965, age nineteen. Admitted to the Dej district hospital at 14:33 on 4 November 1984, died at 18:47 the same date. Cause of death certified by the duty physician: hemorrhagic shock following complications of an illegal procedure. Initial notification to the Procuratură received 5 November 1984. No additional certification required; case opened on that date under the relevant articles.

*The document.* A handwritten document circulating without authorisation among workers and residents of the Dej municipal area. The document contains aftercare instructions pertaining to the management of complications of illegal procedures; it does not describe or specify any procedure. Through examination of twenty-two physical copies and through the voluntary testimony of its originator, it has been established that the document exists in multiple handwritten variant versions, all derived from a single source copy designated Exhibit A. The variants differ from the source by minor transcription incidentals: punctuation, line-break, numbering style. In one branch of transmission, a formatting difference in the source's ninth element propagated a material change in the rendered instruction, resulting in the version present in the Petrescu household. That branch is the subject of this determination.

*Origin.* The source copy — Exhibit A, the master — was produced by Roșca, Ilinca, born 1943, contabil-șef at the Artificial Fiber Enterprise, Dej. Authorship was attested to in a voluntary interview of 4 December 1984. The document was written in October 1983. From the master, the originator produced three copies between October and November 1983: two distributed through named individuals on separate branches of transmission, and one — Exhibit B — made on 3 November 1983.

The originator confirmed that the ninth element of the master was set down in bracket format: a marginal notation attached to the eighth line, not a numbered list item. In Exhibit B, the copy made on 3 November 1983, the same element appears as a numbered line, item 9 of nine. The originator described the conditions of that copying as insufficient light and available time. She stated that she does not know why the transcription took the form it did. She acknowledges that it did, and that Exhibit B was the product of her hand.

*Chain of transmission.* He wrote the names in order from the second generation forward, working from the notebook. He had twelve names: eight women who had spoken to him, plus the responsible party, plus the two household members at the chain's end. Against those twelve he had two entries where a holder had declined to provide a name — recorded as *Name not provided to the investigating officer.* One entry near the bottom read: *Unidentified female, bus route 4, Dej, approximately spring 1984. Contact not established.* He underlined it and moved to the next line.

The chain as established ran eleven confirmed nodes from the master to the copy in the Petrescu household. Branches not connected to the fatal variant had been traced and confirmed as dead ends; they were summarised in an appendix. The central chain — from the master through Exhibit B, through two further transmissions, through the regularised copy, and through three further transmissions to the Petrescu household — had been documented through physical copy collection, voluntary interview, and the documentary evidence produced by the responsible party on 4 December 1984.

He reached the mutation section. He looked at the two documents in the center of his desk. He had read them both a dozen times since yesterday afternoon. He wrote.

*Formatting difference and its propagation.* The ninth element of Exhibit A (the master) reads, in relevant part:

[ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning. ]

The same element in Exhibit B (the copy made 3 November 1983) reads:

9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.

The wording was identical in both versions. The formatting differed: a marginal bracket notation in the master became a numbered list item in the copy. Two further transmissions downstream from Exhibit B, a copyist reading nine numbered lines regularised the ninth into sequence with the eighth, producing the following:

9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.

This wording was preserved through three further transmissions and was present in Exhibit C (node seventeen), the copy in Ana Petrescu's household at the time of the events of 4 November 1984. The introduction of the phrase *in the morning* and the omission of the phrase *Do not wait for the morning* both occurred in the course of regularisation from the numbered format of Exhibit B.

He drew a check in the margin and moved to the last heading.

*Responsible party.* Roșca, Ilinca, born 1943, contabil-șef, AFE Dej. Employment address. The relevant articles, which he had from memory. The voluntary interview; the documents produced by the responsible party in person on 4 December 1984. A note that the responsible party had appeared at the station before the end-of-day threshold at which formal preliminary charge would have been placed against the secondary holder. The secondary holder of a document on a clean branch of transmission — Marcu, Doina, born 1965 — had been released from preliminary detention on 4 December 1984, per order of the investigating officer. He wrote that sentence twice, because the first time the handwriting was not clear.

---

The determination was six pages. He read it from the heading. The facts were in the right order. The chain was documented. The mutation was described in the language he had chosen, which said what it said and nothing else. The responsible party was named and the secondary holder was cleared.

He capped the pen.

He picked up the two documents from the center of the desk. He read each one's ninth element once more before the envelopes.

The bracket, in the master: *[ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning. ]*

The numbered line, in the cellar copy: *9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

Every word the same. He slid Exhibit A into the first envelope and Exhibit B into the second. The labels were already written. He sealed both and set them with the other nine.

Eleven envelopes in a row on the left edge of the desk. He straightened them until the edges aligned and wrote the case number across the strip of paper along the top of the row. He wrote *Petrescu, A., 4.XI.1984 — evidence* and set the completed dosar on top, closed.

---

He thought about what the file contained.

It was complete. The origin, the chain, the mutation in exact language, the responsible party named, the secondary holder cleared in the final paragraph. Everything required by procedure was in it. He checked this the way he checked anything: by asking what was missing, and finding nothing.

Then he thought about what the file did not contain.

The file did not contain the reason the document had existed. It described the document, its origin, its chain of transmission, and the consequences of one variant of it. It did not contain the prior question: why a woman in this town had written eight instructions and a bracketed ninth, what the bracket was there to prevent, what kind of decision it was designed to help someone make. These were not in the file because the file was not that kind of file. No file he had written in twelve years was that kind.

The file did not contain the reason the cellar had been dark and the time had been insufficient. It contained "insufficient light and time pressure" as the originator's own description of the conditions in which Exhibit B was made. That phrase described a condition. It did not describe the condition that produced the condition. He had followed the chain from the death back to the source and had reached the source and had written the source's name in the determination. He had not followed it further than that. The file did not go further than that. He understood all of this correctly.

He had spent thirty-one days on the Petrescu matter. He had not sent up an innocent name. He had sent the correct name, through the correct procedure, on the deadline day. He was not comfortable with the things the file did not contain, and he understood that this was not a circumstance that was going to change by his sitting with it at his desk in the morning.

He closed it there.

---

He telephoned his captain at half past nine. Two rings before the answer.

He said: the determination in the Petrescu matter is on its way to you by messenger.

His captain said: good.

He said: the evidence can be transferred today or tomorrow, whichever is preferred.

His captain said: today. Then: was it as complicated as it seemed?

Munteanu said: it was exactly as complicated as it seemed.

A pause. His captain said: good. Understood. And the call ended.

He set the phone down. Whether "exactly as complicated as it seemed" had given his captain what he wanted or not was not something he could determine from this end of the line. He had answered what he was asked.

---

The dosar went with the courier at noon. At half past four he carried the evidence envelopes downstairs himself. The evidence room officer — a younger man, two or three years in the post — asked for the case name. Munteanu told him. The officer wrote it in the register. Munteanu watched the entry being written and did not speak again after that.

He went back upstairs and sat at the cleared desk for a few minutes. The notebook was in the inside pocket of his coat. The pen was in the drawer. The tin cup was on the corner, where it had been since six-fifteen that morning.

At six he put on the coat. He picked up the tin cup and drank what was left of the nechezol, which had been cold for several hours. Nobody liked the nechezol warm. Cold was not an additional problem so much as the same problem continued at a lower temperature. He set the cup on the desk and went out.

On Strada 22 Decembrie the air was several degrees below zero and the valley fog had settled back in, low along the Someș — the kind that sat from early evening until late morning, opaque at road level, thickening where the ground fell toward the water. He could make out the shape of the far hillside through the haze. He could not see the river. He turned his collar up.

The case was closed. December fifth, the day it was required to close, and it was closed on that day. Doina Marcu had been released the afternoon before. Ilinca Roșca was in the second-floor holding section, which he had not gone past when he came by it this afternoon.

He walked. His hands were in his coat pockets. The determination was in a folder on its way to Cluj-Napoca. The evidence was in a room in the basement, correctly labeled, signed for, sealed. The fog absorbed the sound of the road and the sound of the Someș below the embankment and the sound of his own boots, so that by the time he reached the corner where the road dropped toward the bridge the only thing he could hear clearly was the one thing he could not see.

He went home.

Chapter 29 — "The Deadline" — is complete.

## What the chapter does

**POV:** Vasile Munteanu, third-person past, in his deliberate house-voice register.

**Shape:** The formal determination of the Petrescu case, written on the deadline day. Five report sections, three quotation sites (N1 line 9 / N4 line 9 / N11 line 9 — all verbatim, all appearing through the prose of the determination rather than as set-off documents), followed by the sealing of eleven evidence envelopes, a brief interiority on what the file contains and does not contain, the captain call, and a coda walk home through valley fog.

**The book's final irony, maintained:** Munteanu writes "a marginal bracket notation in the master became a numbered list item in the copy. Two further transmissions downstream, a copyist regularised the ninth into sequence with the eighth" — genealogically exact, semantically blind. He never holds `ninth-line-is-a-warning-not-a-step`. # 5 December 1984

The officer who gave me back my coat was not one I'd seen in twelve days of faces, which was the first good thing about the morning. He set the items on the counter in a row: the coat, my buletin, and the bread roll that had been in my coat pocket when they brought me in, which was hard now and slightly flattened from eleven days in an evidence drawer. He put it on the counter with the same procedural neutrality as the buletin and pushed a form across for me to sign. I signed it. It said I was released following the determination of the case, which I knew was what the form would say because it was the only thing that would produce a morning where an officer I didn't know returned my coat instead of an officer I did know collecting me for a fourth session in the second-floor room.

A bread roll in an evidence drawer. I have thought about this since and I cannot improve on it as a description of the situation.

I asked once where my geography book was. Not hopefully — I had worked out, on approximately the fourth day, that the geography book was not coming back, and I had made a kind of peace with that, or at least the functional version of peace that you make with a thing you cannot change while you still have other things to think about. The officer checked a printed list. He said it was retained in evidence. I nodded and picked up the coat.

I put the buletin in my coat pocket and the bread in the other and I walked out through the public entrance. The duty officer at the front desk did not look up. The door was heavier than I remembered, or possibly I was lighter; twelve days of holding-section food takes something from you that you notice most when you have to push a door.

Outside it was cold and barely light. Dej at six in the morning in early December is the idea of a town rather than the actual one — the shapes of blocs in the gray, the outlines of streets, everything the same color as the sky with only texture to tell them apart. I stood on the step and worked out what day it was. I had gone in on a Thursday — I knew it was a Thursday because it was a shift day and I was supposed to be at the mill at six in the evening, and Munteanu had knocked on my hostel door at half past four in the afternoon, which had given me an hour and a half to not go anywhere. Twelve nights from Thursday was Tuesday. I was willing to accept some uncertainty in that count, because some of the nights in the holding section had been long enough to have contained two separate nights inside them — not literally, but in the way that a night without sleep and with nothing to do but recite something to yourself in the dark stretches until it does not resemble a single unit of time anymore.

Tuesday, I decided. Approximately.

I ate the bread standing on the step. It was better than nothing — that is the most accurate thing I can say about the bread, and I have spent some time since trying to arrive at a more nuanced assessment and I cannot manage one. It was cold and hard and stale in a way that suggested it had never been particularly warm, and it was breakfast. When it was finished I was still on the step because I had not decided where to go.

The Someș was two streets over. I could hear the particular quality of quiet that a wide river makes when there is December fog sitting on it — flatter than ordinary quiet, slightly muffled, as if the river has drawn something heavy across itself and is no longer available. I had been inside for twelve days. The fog in the Someș valley had been happening for twelve days without my participation and it had managed fine.

The geography book was in an evidence room somewhere in the building behind me, entered in a register, sealed in an envelope, labelled. The piece of paper that had been inside it for eleven months was in the same room, in a different envelope or possibly the same one — I did not know the procedure for that level of specificity. Either way, both of them were now state property, which meant they were in a place where they would be kept safe and used for nothing. I thought about the state holding that piece of paper and I thought: good luck. You have it. You will file it. You will never know what it is.

Something had determined the case. The form told me that much. I had a theory about what that something was — who it had been, what they had done, what it had cost them — and the theory was detailed enough by the end of twelve days in the second-floor holding section that I am going to leave it here as a theory. Some things I was still not writing down and this was one of them. What I knew was that I was out, and that someone had made that possible, and that I would know more eventually or I would not.

I tested myself.

Line one. I said it quietly, to the empty street in front of me, to the fog that was beginning to move in from the direction of the river.

*Keep her warm, and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.*

Line two.

*Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.*

Line three.

*Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.*

Line four. I started to say *every*. This had been the fault in my memorization from the first time I had tried to recall it — a groove cut into the wrong word, a word-shaped rut that my memory ran into before my attention could prevent it. I had corrected it every time I had gone through the document in the hostel room in November, and on the hostel bathroom floor with the test copy burning in the sink, and on the nights in the holding section when there was nothing else to do with the dark. I corrected it now.

*If she sleeps, wake her each hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.*

Line five.

*No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.*

Line six.

*Burn nothing until she is well. Keep and wash.*

Line seven.

*Two cloths in one hour is too many.*

Line eight.

*A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.*

I stopped there. A pigeon on the cornice of the building across the street watched me with the comprehensive indifference of pigeons. I stopped not because I had forgotten what came next but because what came next was a different kind of thing from the eight elements before it, and I had always given it a moment. There is no way to draw a bracket in memory. What you have instead is the space where the bracket was: the pause before the thing that overrides the sequence, the one that says the eight steps end here and here is what supersedes them. I had read it right. I had said it right in the hostel room in November when I had first gone through the whole document without the paper, and on the bathroom floor when I burned the test copy and checked it against the original and found the bracket still there, and on the nights in the second-floor room when the document was the thing I held against the dark and the dark didn't win.

I said it quietly, on the step, to the street.

*Seven or eight — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

The pigeon left. I went down the steps.

---

The fog was on the Someș when I got to the bank — white and thick, sitting on the surface of the brown water so that the river looked like it went on in both directions indefinitely without going anywhere. The water was running fast from the autumn rains and I could hear it more clearly than I could see it. There was no proper path along the bank, just ground that had been walked flat over enough years to stay flat. I walked along it with my hands in my coat pockets and the fog around me on every side.

I was not going to try to find the woman on the bus.

I want to be clear about this because it has come up since, in various forms, from various people who have heard different versions of the story. I did not know her name. I did not know her stop or where she was going or what she normally did on the number four bus in the morning direction. She had put the paper in my hand the way you pass someone the salt — before I could think of a reason to say no, which I suspect was not accidental, which I suspect was the technique of someone who had done this kind of transaction before and knew that the window for consent is narrower than the window for refusal. I had not said her name in eleven months of having the paper. I had not said it in twelve days of Munteanu asking me questions across the table in the second-floor room, in three sessions across three weeks, the third of which lasted long enough that I lost track of whether it was still the same day. I was not going to say it now, on the Someș bank in the fog, because I was cold and out and the bread was finished and the geography book was in an evidence room. The not-knowing was the correct version of not-knowing. She was safe or she wasn't, and I would go on not-knowing, and that was not going to change because the case was determined and I was standing on the flat ground by the river.

I thought about Ana Petrescu. Not for very long. I find I can hold that thought for a certain stretch before it tips into something I can't do anything useful with, and I try to keep it to the useful part. I didn't know her when she was alive. What I knew about her was what I'd known since November — her name, her house on Strada Someșului, her sister-in-law's account, the time she arrived at the district hospital, the time she did not come out. She was nineteen years old. I kept coming back to that, the way you come back to a number that doesn't add up — nineteen, the same as me, which is not a meaningful coincidence and I know that, it is just the number I could not set aside. She was nineteen and the paper said *in the morning* and she died in the morning, and the paper said *in the morning* because somewhere along the chain of hands through which it had traveled, someone had read a bracket as a ninth step in the sequence and written it down that way. Nobody in that chain had been careless. The conditions had been the conditions. A girl had died who should not have.

The fog was around me and the water was somewhere to my right, present as sound and smell rather than sight — the brown-water smell of the Someș in December, the cold that comes off a river moving fast in early winter. The far bank was somewhere I had to take on faith. The bloc-tops behind me on my side of the river went in and out of the white as I walked.

I turned around when the concrete apron ended and the bank became proper mud. I walked back the way I had come, into the fog from the other direction.

Eventually I would go back to the hostel. Eventually the hostel would let me in and I would sleep, and then there would be next things, because there are always next things at nineteen — the next shift to figure out, the next month, whatever the determination of the case meant for the rest of it, which I did not know yet and was not going to know on an approximately Tuesday morning on the Someș bank before the town had fully opened for the day. I had my coat. I had my buletin. I had the nine elements in my head, all nine, in order, the bracket included.

The fog did not come up. I got cold first.

# 6 November 1984

She pulls the November stat de plată from the in-tray and sets it flat on the desk to the left of the adding machine. Forty-seven lines. There are forty-seven workers on the administrative and technical rolls, each of them a column: name, labour category, days worked, deductions, net. She starts at line one.

The adding machine is a Felix 5010, original equipment from 1972, which she has run every working day for twelve years. It adds and subtracts; it keeps a running total on a paper strip and rings a note — more of a click than a ring, though she calls it a ring — when a column clears. She runs column one. It is clean. She tears the strip at the perforation, clips it to the form, and moves to column two.

The window behind her left shoulder gives onto the administrative courtyard. The heat pipe will not come on until after six in the evening, which is the November arrangement on the shared pipe, and the office in the morning is the temperature of the stairwell, which is approximately the temperature of outside. She has dressed for this since October: wool underneath, the heavy coat she keeps on until ten. She runs column three.

The stat de plată has the same forty-seven lines it had last month and the month before. What changes is the days-worked column, and occasionally the deductions when there is a medical absence on a note from the factory physician. In November there is one: the maintenance supervisor on the second floor, who had a respiratory illness last week. She enters the adjustment in his deductions column and continues.

She turns to look at the courtyard window twice in the hour: once when a truck from the transportation depot drives in, and once when it drives out. Both times there is nothing that needs seeing. The sky over the courtyard is the grey that will hold all day.

By nine she has worked through line twenty-eight. The materials consumption report for October is in the out-tray, waiting for the floor section chief's signature before she can send it to the district financial office. She does this every first week of the month; having a reason to be on the production corridor is something she is in the habit of accounting for. She finishes through line thirty-one, takes the materials form from the out-tray, and puts her coat on.

---

The passage between the administrative building and the production hall is covered but open at the base, and in November the cold collects along the corridor floor. She reported the gap at the bottom of the connecting door to maintenance in October 1979 and nothing was done. She walks through it and into the production corridor.

The loom floor is to her left, behind the baffle wall. The sound it makes is not quite a sound — it is a vibration below the range of what she identifies as noise, which she stopped distinguishing from silence after the first year. The smell is the synthetic-fiber smell: wet chemistry and steam heat, the exhaust of the wet-spinning process mixed with cold air through every unsealed gap. It has been in the walls of this corridor since 1974 and she stopped registering it years ago. What she registers now is the cold through the soles of her shoes.

The floor section chief's office is the third door on the right. She knocks once and goes in. He is on the telephone — receiver in one hand, a pen in the other, his eyes on the wall. She puts the materials form on the desk in front of him. He signs it without looking at it; she has had it typed cleanly. He does not stop talking. She goes back into the corridor.

Three women from the day shift are near the locker-bay door at the far end. She knows two of them by their coats. She does not turn toward them.

Georgeta Marin, the production supervisor for Hall B, is moving toward the women's bathroom at the far end of the corridor. She walks at the particular pace she uses when she has somewhere to be before the shift bell — not hurried, not slow. She has a ring of keys on a lanyard around her left wrist, tucked into her palm so they do not sound against each other. Three minutes to the shift change, perhaps less.

Ilinca walks to the bathroom.

---

One working bulb in the overhead fixture. Four sinks along the left wall; four stalls, two with latches — one of which has been difficult to close since August. The window above the sinks is painted shut, looking onto the outer wall of the fiber drying unit close enough to touch. The drain smell is more present in November.

Georgeta is at the far sink. Ilinca takes the one next to her and turns the tap.

"I've been thinking about the influenza," Ilinca says. "Whether it's going around. One of the women on the floor was ill last week."

Georgeta does not look up. Her hands are under the tap; she is washing them left over right, carefully.

"I had mine last year," she says. "I gave it to my neighbor on the street. Livia. No one else."

Ilinca runs cold water over her left wrist, then her right.

"And Livia?" she says.

"She's kept it to herself. She's a private woman — she doesn't pass things on. That's just her character."

The water is cold. Ilinca turns the tap off. In the mirror: the painted-shut window behind them, the single bulb above, Georgeta's keys in her palm.

"The influenza passes," Ilinca says.

"It does," Georgeta says, and goes.

---

Ilinca dries her hands and goes back up the corridor, through the connecting door, to her office. She hangs her coat. She sits.

Two pieces of information. She runs them in the order she can act on.

The first: Georgeta holds what Ilinca gave her, and it has not moved. The bathroom conversation said so, in the language that conversation is always conducted in, and Georgeta does not use that language carelessly. Ilinca has known Georgeta Marin for eleven years — from before the supervisor promotion, from a period when the section rosters put them in proximity and she learned what Georgeta's silences mean and what her assurances mean. What she heard in the bathroom was real.

The second: Georgeta gave one copy to her neighbor Livia, on her street, who has not passed it further. Livia is a private woman. Ilinca has seen her perhaps three times in eleven years — grey coming into her hair before it should, a manner of walking with her chin slightly forward. Livia's family name Ilinca does not know by heart. She could find it in the bloc registry at the street committee. She will not need to. She will not look.

Two nodes on this branch: Georgeta, Livia. She runs every name she can place in the Petrescu household, and every name she can place on Georgeta's street, and the two sets do not intersect. The branch does not reach Ana Petrescu. It is two copies deep and neither copy is the one she is looking for.

She thinks of the fourth line, the way she wrote it for Georgeta: *If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.* The copy she made for Georgeta — the third week of November last year, at this desk, by this lamp, in the blue-black ink she uses for fair copies — she can see the page as clearly as if it were in front of her. Line four. Numbered. In its place. The upstroke of the y in *properly*, where the nib caught slightly at the end of the word.

The branch is clean.

She enters both nodes into the account she carries in her head, which has no ledger and no supporting document and which she has maintained for thirteen months by discipline alone. The count is two.

She returns to line thirty-two.

---

Elena Florescu holds the other copy. Third shift now; when Ilinca first knew her they were both on the morning schedule, eleven years ago, when the roster rotation put them in the same section for two seasons. Since 1979 their paths cross in two ways: at the bakery on Strada Lungă, which Elena passes on her way to the morning handover and which Ilinca passes on her way home on certain days; and twice a year at the bloc committee office when the identity documents come up for renewal. Ilinca has counted fourteen exchanges at the bakery in three years. This is not friendship; it is adjacency, which is a more reliable thing.

Elena Florescu is not someone Ilinca knows well in the way of knowing — what she knows of her is procedural: the schedule she keeps, the coat she wears in November, the way she holds her bag on the same shoulder always. In this work, procedural knowledge is reliable in the way that other kinds of knowledge are not.

She cannot go to Elena today. Elena is on the floor, on the machine, and a visit from the contabil-șef without an administrative basis is a visit that anyone nearby can note. The bakery is the correct approach. Elena passes it on Friday mornings at half past five on her way to the handover. Ilinca passes it at that hour only when she has reason to, which she now has. She will be there on Friday.

She does not write any of this down.

---

The stat de plată is finished at quarter past three. She tears the final strip, clips it to the summary line, puts the folder in the out-tray with a rubber band. The next item in the in-tray is a letter from the district financial office about the Q4 consumption norms. She reads it, makes a note in the margin, and puts it in the pending tray.

At four-fifteen the door opens.

A boy she does not know — not older than twenty; she has not seen him in the building before, which means he started recently. He is carrying a folder from the cadres office: she reads the stamp before he speaks. He sets a form on the edge of her desk.

"From the cadres office," he says. "Supplementary materials-usage calculation, Q3. Needs to be back by the fifteenth."

She takes it. "Sign the receipt book."

He finds it in his folder. She signs the line. He closes the folder and goes. She listens: footsteps in the corridor, the connecting door, then nothing.

She holds the form.

It is a Ministry of Finance series form. Q3 is July through September, which closed in October. She submitted the standard materials-usage calculation on the twenty-second of October; the district financial office stamped it received on the twenty-fifth. She ran the numbers four times before submitting because the supplementary ministerial instruction from August had adjusted the Q3 norms mid-quarter, and she wanted the adjustment applied consistently through every line item. It was. If there is a discrepancy in the Q3 accounts, it is not here.

She turns the form over. The back is blank. The watermark is in the lower left corner, the serial number in the upper right, where it belongs. She received a supplementary form for a closed quarter once before, in 1981, during the audit year — but that year all enterprises in the district received supplementary requests for everything, and those circumstances were general and known. This is not that.

She is holding the form and she has not decided what to do with it yet.

In fifteen years she has learned that most things which appear to be something are nothing. She has also learned that a thing which is something looks, from the outside, exactly like the things which are nothing. A form that arrives because a number was transposed two months ago in the district office looks like a form that arrives because someone wants to observe what a person does when a form arrives. She knows what a test looks like. She has not been given one she could verify before, which means she has no way to compare now.

The shift bell sounds in the production hall — muffled through the baffle wall, but she knows the pitch of it, the duration; she has known it for fifteen years and this is it. Footsteps in the corridor. Voices, the brief noise of the shift change, and then the corridor going quiet again under the machines.

She has not moved. The form is in her hand.

# 12 November 1984

He had left the two copies on his desk the previous evening, spread flat and held at their corners by the evidence folder, and when he came in Monday morning they were as he had left them.

He took off his coat and hung it on the back of the door. Sandu's desk at the far end of the investigations room was empty; Sandu was in the field on the Cuzdrioara registration matter and would not be in until afternoon. The coal stove in the corner had been lit by whoever was on overnight duty and was burning with the damp smell of lignite that never quite cleared in November, which meant it had been going long enough to take the edge off the cold without quite producing warmth. He moved the folder to the left side of the desk and sat down.

He had read both copies on Thursday — the day he had collected them — and again on Friday before the weekend. He knew what they said. What he was doing now was not reading for content. He was reading the way he had learned, over twelve years, to read a statement taken from two different people about the same event: not for what the words said but for where the words diverged, and whether the divergence was something that would have happened accidentally or only by design.

He was not a graphologist. He was a man who had spent twelve years reading statements.

Line one of the first copy: *Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.* Small careful hand. The o in 'lying' and the o in 'whole' pressed closed by a pen held at a narrow angle.

Line one of the second copy: the same line, the same words. Different hand. Larger letters, a slight rightward lean, the downstrokes of the l and the t in 'lying' longer than was strictly necessary, as though the writer had thought they were about to run out of room and then discovered they had more than enough.

He went line by line.

Lines one through eight: close to identical. He noted where they were not. Line three on the first copy: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.* Line three on the second copy: the same sentence, until the last four words — *on the paper beside the bed.* He looked at the two phrases. The instruction was the same. The prepositions were not. Someone had written *beside* where the other document, or its source, said *by.* That was either a copying error — the copyist's own preposition substituting itself for the original's — or it was a variation already present in whatever the second copy had been made from.

He had no way to know yet which of these was true.

He turned to the back page of his cardboard folder, which served as his case notes, and wrote below Saturday's entry: *L3 variant: 'by the bed' / 'beside the bed'. Two hands, two sheets, different paper stocks. L9: identical — see below.*

Line nine was the same on both copies. He read it on the first document — *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning* — and then on the second, the words arriving in the same order, set down in a different hand on different paper, but unchanged: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* He held the two sheets up briefly, each in one hand, and read the ninth line again on each. 

Nine words. Twice. In two separate acts of writing by two people who had not been in the same room.

A woman who had stayed until morning had been following a document that told her to wait for morning. He had understood this from the first reading, on Thursday. What he was looking at now was something additional: the instruction had not entered the chain at the point where the first copy had passed to the Petrescu household. It was present in the neighbor's copy as well, which was a separate document obtained separately from a separate address. If the instruction was already in both copies, and both copies had been made by different people from whatever they had each received, then the instruction had been present in what they had each received. The instruction was earlier.

He closed the folder.

---

The address he needed was a three-story bloc on Alecsandri street, east of the mill workers' market. Three hundred metres. He walked.

November had gone cold and wet in the last week, the kind of damp that came off the Someș in the morning and did not lift before noon. The market was open but thin — mid-month, the queues had already moved through whatever there was to move through. A woman at the corner stand near the market entrance had something under an oil cloth. She watched him come up the street and watched him go past without moving. He did not stop. He counted the doorways until he had the right building.

Interior stair. The third floor smelled of cabbage soup and wet wool. He knocked at the indicated door.

The woman who answered had the expression of someone who had been expecting a particular knock for some number of days and had made a decision about how she would receive it. She was in her late forties, heavy-shouldered, her hair pinned close to her head, wearing a house coat. She was holding a dish cloth. When she looked at him she folded the cloth in half, and then in half again, until she had a square she had nowhere particular to put.

He introduced himself. He said he was investigating the death of Ana Petrescu and that he had questions about a document she might be able to help with.

She said: come in.

The flat was a kitchen and one other room. The kitchen had a table in the centre and two cups on it, which she moved to the counter without comment. She put the folded dish cloth on the counter beside them and sat down across from him at the table.

Her name was Lucia Gal. She worked the day shift in the second weaving hall at the AFE mill. She had worked there since 1972. She said this directly and without elaboration, with the particular quality of someone who has decided that the correct response to official interest is to offer official information precisely and let nothing else slip through in the offering.

He told her: he was aware that a document of a certain kind had been circulating in the area. That he was trying to understand how it had moved. That if she had such a document and was willing to give it to him now, that cooperation would be noted in the file. Voluntary surrender was better than the alternative. He said this simply, without emphasis on the word 'alternative,' because emphasis was the thing that made people stop cooperating. He had learned this.

She got up and went to the counter. Second drawer from the left. She took out a folded sheet, carried it to the table, and set it in front of him.

He put on his gloves before he picked it up.

The paper was different from the other two copies. It was lighter, greyer, the stock of a mill production form — the front side carried official printing, department designation and output-tracking columns and a foreman's signature box, in the regulation black ink. On the reverse: the document, written in blue pencil. He had not seen blue pencil before on any version of this document. The handwriting was careful — more careful than either of the copies he had collected on Thursday, the numerals at the start of each line formed with a deliberateness that was close to elegance, the lines spaced evenly from top to bottom of the sheet.

He put it in an evidence envelope and wrote her name and address on the flap.

He asked: had she given a copy of this document to anyone else?

She said: no. She held his eyes when she said it. He wrote *denies further transmission* in his case notes.

He asked: where had she received this document?

She said: from a woman she worked with, on the production floor, in the second hall. She gave him the name without prompting. He wrote it. He wrote the hall number and the shift.

He asked: and did the woman she named live in this building, or elsewhere?

She gave him the address. He wrote it.

He thanked her. She held the door.

---

He had three copies.

He laid them side by side on his desk and weighted the corners with whatever was nearest, which turned out to be a stapler and three unopened tins of shoe polish. He read each copy through separately first, going from line one to line nine. Read separately, they said nearly the same thing. He read them again together, line by line across all three sheets.

He put the grey mill-form paper on the left, the two Thursday copies on the right, and went from the top.

Lines one through eight: close to identical across all three. He moved slowly, each line in sequence across all three sheets before going to the next. Line one was the same. Line two was the same. Line three: the grey-paper copy said *by the bed*. The first of the Thursday copies said *by the bed*. The second of the Thursday copies said *beside the bed.*

He stopped.

Two of his three copies agreed in line three. The third differed from both of them by one word. He marked the positions in his notes. It was a small difference — a preposition, nothing more, the instruction unchanged — but it told him something about the arrangement. Two copies that agreed with each other in a particular line were either copied from each other or copied from the same source. A third copy that differed from both of them had either introduced the variation itself or had inherited it from a different source. He was looking at two copies that agreed, and one that did not. The two that agreed were probably closer to each other in the chain.

That was not a complicated observation. It was arithmetic.

He continued down the page.

Lines four, five, six, seven, eight: no differences of consequence. Minor variations in spacing, in the exact formation of particular letters — the d in 'down' on one copy made with a loop, on another without it. The kind of variation that appeared whenever a person was copying something by hand and was not aware that the variation was there. He noted these without significance.

Line nine he read last, going left to right across all three sheets.

The grey-paper copy, in blue pencil: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

The first Thursday copy, the small careful hand: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

The second Thursday copy, the slightly larger hand with the opened o's: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He sat back and looked at the three line nines.

The same instruction, three times. Three different hands, three different sheets, three different acts of writing. The same nine words. He had taken his pen up when he started reading line nine across the three copies and he set it back down without writing anything.

The instruction had been present in the grey-paper copy, which was a step earlier in the chain than the two Thursday copies. The grey-paper copy was the one the woman in the flat on Alecsandri street had given him — the woman who had named a woman on the production floor as the person she had got it from. If the instruction was already present in the grey-paper copy, it had not been introduced by Lucia Gal. It had been there when she received it. It had been present before the grey-paper copy was made.

He looked at the three sheets again. The grey-paper copy and the first Thursday copy agreed in line three — *by the bed*. The second Thursday copy said *beside the bed.* That meant the second Thursday copy had probably been copied from the grey-paper copy or from something that had already introduced *beside* — but either way, the grey-paper copy was probably the oldest document in front of him, or closest to the oldest. And the oldest document in front of him already had the morning instruction in line nine.

He turned to the fresh page at the back of the cardboard folder and wrote: *Three copies in evidence. L3 variant: 'by the bed' (x2) / 'beside the bed' (x1). L9 consistent across all three: 'take her in in the morning.' Instruction not introduced at points of collection. Present at minimum in copy acquired today (earlier in chain). Source is upstream. Next: [the name from the Gal interview].*

It was the kind of finding that would not survive being described to his captain in its present form. Captain Niculescu had looked at the file on Wednesday and asked when Munteanu expected to have something writable. He had said: by the end of the week. That had been a realistic estimate at the time. He had thought, on Wednesday, that the chain would be short — three, maybe four people, the kind of small informal thing that didn't go far and died at the edges for want of someone to carry it. He thought less of this now. The instruction in line nine had been present before the three copies he held. Before the woman on Alecsandri street, before the woman on Strada Gării, before the Petrescu household. The chain behind it was longer than three people.

He was going to have more names in this file before he was done.

He stood and took his coat from the back of the door.

The name from the Gal interview was the production-floor woman who had given Lucia Gal her copy. One step further back. One step closer to wherever the instruction had entered. She worked the same hall, the day shift. She had not been expecting him this morning, because he had not known her name this morning. Now he did.

He put on his coat and picked up his case notes.

# 13 November 1984

The bridge over the Someș was always the worst part, and I say that as someone who spent two years crossing it in the dark at four-thirty in the morning, which gives me more authority on the subject than I would have liked.

It was the fog. Not the cold — I was used to the cold by then, or I had at least stopped expecting anything better from November in the Someș valley, which is not the same thing — but the fog came off the river in autumn and settled on the bridge deck in a way that had nothing to do with temperature and everything to do with the specific disposition of this particular valley toward the people who lived in it. You walked into it and it erased the railings and the far bank and the road beyond, and for thirty or forty seconds you were just a person in white nothing, which at four-thirty in the morning, when you were already thinking about things you should not be thinking about, was not an experience I found helpful.

On the street before the bridge: one lamp still burning in a third-floor window of the first bloc, a woman in a dark coat going the opposite direction who did not look up. I did not look up either. This is the social compact of the four-thirty shift change, and I had always appreciated it in the abstract, but I appreciated it more that November than I ever had before.

The mill smell reached you from two hundred meters out. Hot and wet and chemical — the celofiber production hall, the fiber drying unit, the pressing-and-sizing vats all combining into something that had no single good description and that I had long since stopped smelling as a smell. Two years on the night shift. Somewhere over seven hundred crossings of that bridge. I had done the arithmetic once and been depressed by it and had not done it again. The smell was the smell of being here, which was where I was, and had been for two years, and which was not looking like it was going to stop being the case any time soon.

I went along the road below the water treatment plant, past the parking area with the three bicycles that had been chained to the fence since before I arrived — the chain on the middle one had been rusting for longer than I knew — and around to the production entrance in the side of the weaving hall. The door was propped open during shift change. The guard in the hut was drinking from a metal cup. I showed my shift pass. He did not look at my face.

Inside: the locker bay, then the production corridor. I hung my coat and put my bag under the bench and closed the locker. The geography book was inside, on the shelf above the coat hook — too narrow for anything except exactly that. I did not look at it directly, because I had found in the last ten days that not looking at the geography book directly was a habit I was developing, like the habit of checking the lock twice, like the habit of taking the river path home instead of the main road. I checked the lock a second time and went to the floor.

---

The production floor in the morning was the loom noise. I don't know how to convey the loom noise, which is why I keep stating it as a fact and moving on.

The looms were Hungarian-made, retooled for celofiber yarn some years before I arrived. When all forty-eight were running, which they were when I came onto the floor at five past five, conversation was not possible in any practical sense — not because of any rule, but because anything produced at mouth level was absorbed immediately into the ambient volume, and the person next to you had no particular reason to suspect you had spoken. I had worked in this for two years, and in the last ten days I had come to regard it as one of the more comfortable environments available to me in the district of Dej in November of 1984. I want to be precise about this: I was genuinely grateful for the loom noise in a way I had not anticipated when I signed my contract.

I threaded the machine. Two minutes later my hands knew what they were doing and I had the rest of myself free for other purposes.

What I did with it: watched the women near me without appearing to watch them. Row across from mine: Anca, who has the kind of face that conveys nothing and who I had once seen win an argument in the break room without appearing to have an argument; past her, a woman I had worked beside for six months without ever learning her name, who today had her hair loose on both sides instead of pinned on the left; at the end of the row, a third woman attending her machine with the focused precision of someone who has decided that the machine is the only object in the room.

I recognised that last one as a decision. I had been making a version of it myself.

Three women who looked like they had not slept. I can't tell you now what it looked like exactly. I'm telling you what it looked like and I'm telling you I was getting better at seeing it. Something around the eyes. A quality of attention that was paying attention to something else entirely.

---

The break room was off the production corridor, across from the bathroom. Two long tables, eight chairs each. At the back there was a hot-water urn that had probably been there since the founding of the republic and that produced something technically classifiable as tea if you held your cup under it long enough and did not ask anything more specific from the transaction. I got my cup and sat at the far end of the first table.

Marta — she worked the adjacent loom on my section, she lived on the fourth floor of my bloc, she had a son in the fourth form and a husband who drove for the transport depot — sat down across from me but toward the middle of the table, not beside me, which I noted as a kind of tact. She looked at her cup. She said, without looking at me: they took Floarea and Geta in on Monday.

Both of them from the finishing section. Both from the other end of the hall.

I said: what did they ask them?

She said: what do you think they asked them.

She picked up her tea and moved to the far end of the table, where some other women were already involved in something about the bread queue on Victoriei, and within two minutes she was involved in it too.

I sat with my cup.

---

I knew Floarea the way you know someone from six months of sitting behind them on the morning bus — the back of her head, her posture, a blue coat she wore on cold days. Her name I had heard once in the break room. That was the full extent of my knowledge of Floarea.

I did not know whether she had a copy of any paper. I did not know whether she knew anyone who did. I did not know whether, in the specific context that now had a context, she knew that Doina Marcu from the night shift existed in any relevant sense.

Here is what I had been trying to think clearly about for ten days, and what kept refusing to go clear: this was not built like something that has a diagram. It was not a thing where you could stand at any point and draw lines outward and eventually reach all the other points. It was: one person knowing one person, the paper traveling between those two, neither of them necessarily knowing anyone else in the exchange. The woman on the bus had not asked my name. She had put the paper in my hand before I had finished deciding whether I was accepting it, and by the time I thought to say something she was looking out the window at the November fields outside Bonțida, and the moment had passed.

So what I knew about Floarea's connection to any of this was: nothing certain. There might be six steps between her line and mine. There might be none in common. They might share a branch with me that went all the way back to the same source, or they might be on a branch I had never had any connection to at all, in which case the fact that they were now in the file had nothing to do with my locker and I was fine.

I thought: it's probably fine.

Then I sat with the specific texture of "probably fine" for a moment.

Then I went back to the floor.

---

The second half of the shift, I worked. I want to be accurate about this because I remember being faintly surprised by it at the time: I worked. My hands moved. The loom ran. At some point the light coming through the clerestory windows above the machines changed from the flat dark of five o'clock to the particular grey of November morning — grey through a layer of hall condensation, but light — and this helped, in the way that light always helps even when you can't account for why it should.

The thing you can say about a loom is that it requires you to be there — not your feelings, but your hands, which is what I had to offer, and which held.

The woman at the end of the row kept her eyes on her machine. Anca did too. Near the end of the shift Anca looked up and caught my eye for a second. We both looked back.

---

After the shift most people went left from the production entrance, toward the main road and the bus stop and the bread shop on Victoriei that was already open by seven. I went right, along the wall of the fiber drying unit — forty meters where the heat coming off the ductwork almost reached the backs of your hands — and then around and down toward the river path.

The fog was still on the Someș at half past seven. Light was coming up behind the eastern ridge in the flat grey-gold way it comes in the valley in November: the sun above the ridge line, spreading flat along the bottom of the cloud layer without appearing in any particular place, so that everything was lit from nowhere and nothing had a shadow. The fog sat on the water in long horizontal shapes that moved with the current but went nowhere. The clay path alongside the river was wet and soft. My boots had not been fully waterproof since September, which I had known about and continued not to address, the same way you continue not to address things that are below the current top of your list.

*Keep her warm, and lying down.* Line one. It came to me the way things lodged in that particular slot come up — not because I had thought of it but because I had been not-thinking of it long enough and hard enough that it surfaced on its own. I knew line one the way I knew my hostel room number: by repetition, without intending to. I knew line three. I knew line seven. I knew the bracket at the bottom, the whole bracket. I could have recited it in order if there had been anyone to recite it to, which there wasn't and wasn't going to be, because the whole point was that you recited it to nobody. *Someone stays with her the whole night.*

The geography book was in my locker. My locker was locked. I had the key on my ring with the hostel key and my aunt's spare — the small brass key she had pressed into my hand when I moved to the hostel in 1982, which I had carried for two years and had never once needed to use. The man in the good coat had been asking questions at the mill and in the blocs for a week. He had taken Floarea and Geta in on Monday, both from the finishing section on the other side of the hall. He had not come to the locker bay.

The river path turned at the end onto the hostel road. I walked past the bench where people sat in summer. The kiosk on the corner was shut. The corner lamp was still on from the night.

I did not know if not yet was the same as not going to.

The fog moved on the Someș behind me. My feet were cold. I walked.

# 14 November 1984

She does the variance three times. The third time it comes back twelve lei.

The October third-shift payroll: seventeen line discrepancies, all resolved since Tuesday, and one aggregate variance of twelve lei that has had no explanation since she found it. She has been doing the rest of the column around it, leaving the line empty, returning after other work to see if the answer has appeared. It has not appeared each time she has returned. She marks the line with a pencil stroke and turns the page.

She will find it. It is twelve lei and it has been here since Tuesday and it will be there when she finds it.

What she is thinking about this morning is the N4 branch.

She made the copy on the third of November of the year before, in the coal cellar of a building she had been brought to by someone she trusted — a connection specific to that night, not a connection before and not a connection after. The woman from that night was waiting in the coal smell. Ilinca had the pencil. The light came in through the door from the courtyard; not enough light but enough to write by if you were fast. She had written the lines while saying each one aloud, and had watched the pencil to see if it was keeping up.

She can account for eight lines from that recitation.

*Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.* Line six. She had said it clearly. The woman had written it without stopping. Line six is the one that appears to go against the line before it and does not; she had been deliberate with it in the dark because of this. She can account for line six the way she can account for each of the eight: said it, watched the pencil move, line complete.

What she cannot account for is the bracket. The ninth element. She had said it. She is almost certain the pencil was still moving when she said it. She cannot say with certainty that the bracket was in the right position on the page, or in any position at all, because it is a margin note and not a numbered line and the difference between those two things in the dark, with a pencil moving fast, is a difference she could not audit in real time.

She has been proceeding on the assumption that it was correct. She has treated the cellar copy as: one transaction, her end closed. Made the copy, gave it over, left. What came after was the woman from that night's management, not a column Ilinca had any reading of.

This morning she does not believe the column ends there.

The woman from that night is not a full stop. She received the paper. People who receive this paper, and who know people who might need it, do with it what it is for: they pass it on, when the time comes, to someone they know. Ilinca has been counting on this. It is how the paper gets where it needs to go. It is also how a branch extends past a single transaction, and she has been treating the cellar branch as one transaction and nothing after, and she does not now believe that is accurate.

What she does not know: whether the woman from that night gave a copy to anyone, and if so to whom. She cannot ask directly. The cellar woman is not part of her usual network; a visit to that part of the city would be its own kind of visibility, the kind she cannot afford. She needs a route.

---

She has one.

The pharmacy is on Eminescu, near the second bloc, fifteen minutes from the mill gate. The woman at the counter knows her from the market queue and the monthly aspirin requisition and the bus stop on Thursdays. They have spoken about the bread allocation. They have spoken about the flour, about the new forms, about the bus that does not run on Saturdays when it should. They have not spoken about anything that matters.

She has needed aspirin since Monday. This is the first mid-morning she has had free.

She tells Lenuta from accounts she will be back before eleven and goes out through the rear exit, past the clinic door, which is still locked at this hour.

---

The cold on the street outside is particular to this valley in November: not at the floor yet, but past the point where the body argues about it. The boulevard trees have been finished with their leaves for several days. The pavement is wet with something that happened earlier without reaching the level of rain. She keeps her pace at the pace of a woman going somewhere she goes regularly, which she is. The market stand at the corner is closed until Thursday; she passes it.

Dorobanților runs behind Eminescu and connects to it at the north end. She does not go down Dorobanților. She goes straight to Eminescu and turns toward the pharmacy.

The pharmacy occupies a narrow single-story building between the corner post office and a shoe repair. Inside: the counter, the shelves with the permitted stock behind it, a warmth that is not present on the street. The woman at the counter has glasses repaired with thread at the right hinge and a way of standing that suggests she has been standing in the same position for a long time and has found it sufficient.

She copied Ilinca's buletin number into the register while the identity document lay open between them. She produced the aspirin. Ilinca pressed the requisition form flat with one finger and signed it.

She said, while tucking the identity document away: there is a woman I've been meaning to find. She gave a description — roughly her own age, a round face, a dark coat with a grey collar, the kind you see everywhere; added: her husband worked at the chemical plant on the south road. I thought she lived somewhere near here, on Eminescu or behind it. Do you know the family?

The woman at the counter restocked a shelf while she thought.

She said: there is a woman on Dorobanților — just behind the second bloc on Eminescu — who recently moved her sister in from the village. The sister works at the communal laundry on Strada Mihai. That's the closest I know to what you're describing.

Ilinca considered. She said: the husband at the chemical plant, that was the main thing I remembered about them.

The pharmacy woman said: I don't know about a husband. That family, that's all I know of them.

Ilinca thanked her. She said: perhaps it's not the right person. Don't trouble yourself.

She went out.

Three items to carry: *sister, laundry, Strada Mihai.*

She took the longer route back to the mill — eight minutes more, away from the bloc side of town — and arrived at her desk at twelve minutes past eleven.

---

She opened the November preliminary and started the December headers. At six minutes past noon she found the twelve lei: a digit misread in the October second-week line transfer, a three entered as an eight in the fourth column, a small error dated to the twenty-second. She corrected the entry and ruled the line. The column closed.

Then she worked. The afternoon documents came through: two sets of revised production tallies from the third shift, a ministry form that required countersignature, an internal memo about the December heating schedule for the administrative building that required no action but had to be filed. She processed them.

At half past two, through her window, she saw the delivery boy from the pharmacy cross the forecourt below with a cardboard box held level. He went past the personnel door, past the door she was sitting behind, and turned toward the clinic two doors down.

He did not come to her. She had not expected him to.

At twenty minutes to three, Lenuta knocked and opened the door: the clinic nurse had stepped out to the toilet, could Ilinca sign for the pharmacy delivery.

Ilinca went into the corridor.

The box sat on the shelf by the clinic door with the delivery notice folded flat on top. She lifted the notice and read it and signed the incoming column in the delivery ledger; while she was doing this she took from beneath the notice a slip of paper that she folded once and put into the pocket of her coat; she carried the box the three steps to the clinic ledge and set it inside and came back and returned the delivery ledger to its hook.

Lenuta was already back at accounts. The door between the two rooms was closed.

Ilinca sat at her desk. She took the slip from her coat pocket.

The pharmacy woman's handwriting: small, regular, not hurried. Three sentences about the December aspirin allocation and the new Ministry dispensing form taking effect in January, which all mill clinics would receive notice of separately. Below that, set a little apart, one sentence that was not the same kind of sentence as the others: *Regarding the family you were asking after — the sister is at the communal laundry on Strada Mihai, I am told, Tuesdays through Saturdays.*

She read the last sentence three times.

Then she folded the slip and placed it in the ledger between the October summary and the first November sheet, where it was a piece of paper among other pieces of paper, and she sat.

---

The cellar woman had a sister. The sister was in Dej. She worked the laundry on Strada Mihai, Tuesdays through Saturdays.

This was not the same as knowing there was a copy at the laundry. A sister recently arrived from the village is not automatically a woman who has received a copy of a specific document from a specific source. But: the cellar woman had received a paper she would not have requested for herself, because the emergency had been resolved by the time Ilinca brought the copy to her that night — resolved or past. She had taken the paper anyway. People take the paper for the reason people take anything useful that they cannot buy and cannot request through official channels: because someone they know may need it and they may need to give it.

The logic did not stop applying because the woman was the woman from the cellar.

She added the new entry. Five, and now this: six.

The problem was the laundry. She had no route to Strada Mihai. The laundry was not on her circuit; she had no contact there; a visit without a reason was the same problem as Eminescu. She needed a second route, the way she had needed the pharmacy for the first. She did not have one yet. This was a problem with a solution she had not found.

She reopened the December forecast and began the first column.

---

The shift bell rang at half past three. The building cleared in its usual sequence. Accounts first: she heard Lenuta and the two junior staff go down the corridor, the familiar pattern of their conversation about the Victoriei bread shop, which was closed on Tuesdays apparently. Then the personnel office, two women who had worked there since before Ilinca arrived and who left without speaking to anyone on the way out, which was their habit and not unfriendliness. Then, at a quarter to four, the two senior clerks at the far end of the corridor, whose footsteps she had learned to distinguish without intending to: the one with the uneven heel first, then the other.

She stayed at her desk.

Her office lamp was the only one burning in this part of the building. The lamp at the end of the corridor had gone off when Lenuta left. The clinic door lamp had been off since three. Through the window: the forecourt was dark except for the gate lamp, and beyond it the street, and beyond that the production building with its row of small high windows lit orange from inside. From three buildings over she could hear the frequency of the night shift at full run — not individual machines but the aggregate of them, the forty-eight looms at their register.

She still needed the route to Strada Mihai. She had six nodes and a gap she could not close from her desk.

The December first column was not going to finish itself.

She bent over the ledger and kept working.
