# 5 November 1984

The woman from the third floor told us the way you tell a thing you don't want to be the one to tell. She was already in her coat. She said it toward the wall at the end of the hallway — *she died at the hospital in Dej, the younger Petrescu* — and then she went downstairs and left us standing there. Nobody moved first. We all stood in the hallway waiting for someone else to be the person who stopped standing there.

I didn't know Ana Petrescu. I knew the name the way you know names in a mill town — she worked the day shift, I worked nights, we had never been in the same building at the same time as far as I could reckon. What I knew about her was that she was nineteen, which is what I also am, and now she wasn't. The woman from the third floor was already gone. I went back to my room and got my jacket and my gloves and my bag. The shift started at six and if I didn't leave now the section head would have a reason to remember my face, and I didn't want that, and so I put my gloves on and went downstairs, and that was November fifth, 1984, which is where this begins.

---

It was dark at five-thirty. In November in the Someș valley darkness is not an event, it is the default condition that the daytime interrupts briefly and incompletely. The streetlamps along the road to the mill make yellow haloes in the fog rather than light on the pavement, and this is the light I have walked to work by for two years: more fog than lamp, more direction than illumination. I know the road by the soles of my shoes. I know the stretch where the cobbles are loose near the transformer station and the bend where the puddle collects against the cracked kerb and the place where the smell of the mill arrives before you can see the mill's lights — the hot-wet chemical sweetness of the fiber process mixed with the river cold, the smell that lives in my coat whether I notice it or not.

The women ahead of me I knew by their coats. Mariana's was the navy one with the collar lining coming loose on the left side — she had pinned it twice and the pin kept giving way. Costina's was the brown one with the wooden toggles, short on her because she is taller than it was made for. The two women from Shift B whose names I had not learned in fourteen months, for reasons that say something about me or about fourteen months and I am not sure which. I fell in behind their backs and followed them through the dark and the fog and the mill smell and didn't say anything, because it was five-thirty in the morning and the woman from the third floor had said what she said and I didn't have anything to add to it.

By the time the smell of the mill was strong I could see the lights over the production floor. They are always on. It is the most reliable thing about my life in Dej, and I am not going to pretend I don't find it comforting. I showed my cartelă at the gate. I went to put my things in the locker.

The geography book was on the shelf above the coat hooks, where I had put it on my first day two years ago and never moved it since. It was published in 1978, purchased for me by my mother when I was twelve, and neither of us has ever read it. I brought it to Dej because I thought I ought to look like a person who read things, and then when I got to the hostel and understood the situation I decided the factory locker was more private than the hostel room, and I left the book on the shelf and walked away from it. For eleven months it had been just a thing I owned, the way the coat is a thing I own. I did not look at it. I went to work.

---

On the production floor the looms are twelve metres high and if you want to say something to someone standing two metres away, you put your mouth near their ear and shout. If what you want to say is not the kind of thing you shout, you wait. Everyone waits. We have all been waiting for years at whatever volume is required by the job, and we are all very good at it.

What this meant on the morning of the fifth was that I had six hours in which nothing was required of me except to watch the thread and count the revolutions and do what I was there to do. The woman from the third floor had said what she said and Ana Petrescu was in the past tense and the name was in my head and I was on the production floor where the looms make other things impossible. I watched Costina's hands on her machine — she has been here eight years and knows things about it that the maintenance record doesn't, and I have learned more from watching her hands than from anything the section head has ever said directly to me — and I counted what I was supposed to count, and I was very grateful for the noise, which is not something I say lightly because the looms are genuinely very loud.

The loom on my left has been running a small vibration in the tensioning arm since September. The section head signed off that it was within tolerance. I don't know if this is true but I have decided to agree with him about it, because I am nineteen and this is my job and I need it. I note this because it is one of the things I was thinking about on the production floor on the morning of the fifth rather than thinking about what was in the geography book on the shelf in the locker. The vibration in the tensioning arm. Whether Costina's method of clearing a thread jam is actually faster than what I was taught, which I believe it is, though she has never shown me directly and I have only seen it from across the aisle.

Six hours. The break is twenty minutes. I had been not-thinking for six hours and I was very tired from it.

---

I went to my locker and took the geography book off the shelf.

Nobody has ever opened my geography book, including me. I want that on the record because of everything that came after: I received the paper that was inside it on the bus from Gherla, eleven months before the fifth of November. The woman who gave it to me had a face like a closed shop and she put it in my hand the way you pass someone the salt — without asking if they wanted salt, without looking at them while they took it. I had eleven minutes between the stop at Bonțida and the stop before Dej and I read what was on the paper in those eleven minutes and I understood that it was the kind of thing you kept somewhere safe and I needed to decide, in eleven minutes, where safe was.

The hostel was not safe. The hostel room has a door with a latch that can be lifted from the outside with a fingernail. I know this because the woman across the hall demonstrated it in the second week, not as a threat but as a fact worth knowing, and I have been grateful for it since. The factory locker locks. I am the only one with the key. I have not lost the key in two years and I do not intend to.

So I put the paper inside the geography book, between pages 34 and 35, which is a double-page diagram of the watershed drainage of the Northern Carpathians, illustrated in blue and grey. I put the geography book on the shelf in the locker. For eleven months it sat there. I want to be clear about this: I never used it. I never showed it to anyone. I could not have told you what was written on any line of it if you had held me upside down. It was just a thing I owned, the same category as the coat — the green wool one with the loose button on the left cuff that I keep meaning to resew.

I took the geography book to the bathroom. There are four stalls and two of them have latches that work. I took one of the ones with a latch.

---

I sat on the edge of the lid with the book on my knees and opened it to pages 34 and 35 and took out the paper. It was folded three times — twice across and once along — and the fold lines had softened over eleven months into the kind of creases that will hold their shape for years without being asked to.

I read it straight through.

Lines one through eight are instructions, numbered, imperative. I am not going to set all of them out here. What I want to say is that I read each one and it was legible and I continued to the next. At the bottom of the page, below the eighth numbered line, there is a bracket. It is drawn in pencil — a hand-drawn rectangle around the last part of the document, with lines that are mostly straight. Inside the bracket it says:

*7 or 8 — take her in.*

And more. The bracket holds more than that — it says what to say when you get there, and one other thing, one line that I didn't retain on the bus and didn't retain in the first week at the hostel and didn't retain now. What I retained, this time, was the bracket itself. The drawn line around it. It was not a ninth step in the same sequence. It was something else — a different kind of instruction, the kind you draw a box around to show it overrides the sequence rather than continuing it.

I had never been able to tell you what was inside that bracket before the fifth. Not if you had asked me on the fourth or the third or at any point in the previous eleven months. I read the paper three times in my life before the fifth of November and each time I read it the way you read something you have been handed and don't know what to do with yet — looking to find out what it is, not to understand it. I retained almost nothing, which I am telling you now because of what came after. I am not asking you to believe it changed anything. I am asking you to believe it is true.

On the fifth of November what I saw was the bracket. It was drawn there. I could see that the thing at the bottom was bracketed, which made it different from the lines above, and today that difference mattered in a way it hadn't mattered before. I didn't know why. I know why now.

---

I folded the paper back along the three creases and put it between pages 34 and 35. I closed the geography book.

The women's bathroom at the AFE production floor has a window above the sinks that is painted shut. In the fluorescent light the walls are a colour that started as pale yellow and has become something else over a number of years I will not guess at. I stood at the sink and ran cold water on my wrists, which does something to my heart rate that is worth doing in certain situations, and then I went back to the locker and put the geography book on the shelf above the coat hooks.

What I told myself: this is still a thing I own, like the coat. Not evidence of anything I did. I had received it on a bus, from a woman I had never seen before and have not seen since, and I had not used it and I had not shown it to anyone and I could not recite a single line of it from memory, including the line inside the bracket. Eleven months of owning it and I had done nothing with it except leave it on a shelf. Same as the coat. Same category entirely.

What I also told myself: the locker locks. The factory has a gate and a guard. I am a woman who tends the looms and has not been in any trouble that mattered, and there is no reason for anyone to open my locker, because there is no reason for anyone to look at me.

I went back to the production floor and worked until two.

---

After the shift I walked back through fog that had not lifted. In November in this valley it often does not. The hostel is ten minutes from the mill gate on a clear day and fifteen when you have to navigate by memory, and on the fifth it was closer to fifteen. I signed in at the desk and went upstairs to my room.

The ceiling of my room has a water stain in the upper left corner. It has been there since before I moved in and it has not grown in two years, which I find reassuring. It does not look like anything. Some water stains resolve into shapes — a face, an animal, a map of somewhere — but this one is just a stain. I find this restful.

I lay on the bed with my coat on.

The geography book was in the locker. The locker was in a building with a gate. I had not used the paper. I had not shown it to anyone. I had not recited it to anyone, could not recite it to anyone. What had gone wrong for Ana Petrescu had gone wrong before the fifth, before I read the bracket or the numbered lines above it, before I ran cold water on my wrists and put the book back on the shelf. I had not been any part of it. I was as innocent as I had been when I got on the bus from Gherla, and the geography book in the locker was the geography book in the locker, and that was the afternoon of the fifth.

Whether that was the right place for it, I did not know. I did not know what the right place was, or whether there was one, or whether the bracket being there rather than not being there made any difference to anything that had already happened or was going to happen next. I lay there with my coat on and I did not know any of it, and so I did nothing, which is itself a kind of decision, as I found out later.

The ceiling stain was in its corner. The light through the curtain was the grey of mid-afternoon fog. I stayed on the bed until it was dark enough that the grey went away.

# 6 November 1984

She pulls the November stat de plată from the in-tray and sets it flat on the desk to the left of the adding machine. Forty-seven lines. There are forty-seven workers on the administrative and technical rolls, each of them a column: name, labour category, days worked, deductions, net. She starts at line one.

The adding machine is a Felix 5010, original equipment from 1972, which she has run every working day for twelve years. It adds and subtracts; it keeps a running total on a paper strip and rings a note — more of a click than a ring, though she calls it a ring — when a column clears. She runs column one. It is clean. She tears the strip at the perforation, clips it to the form, and moves to column two.

The window behind her left shoulder gives onto the administrative courtyard. The heat pipe will not come on until after six in the evening, which is the November arrangement on the shared pipe, and the office in the morning is the temperature of the stairwell, which is approximately the temperature of outside. She has dressed for this since October: wool underneath, the heavy coat she keeps on until ten. She runs column three.

The stat de plată has the same forty-seven lines it had last month and the month before. What changes is the days-worked column, and occasionally the deductions when there is a medical absence on a note from the factory physician. In November there is one: the maintenance supervisor on the second floor, who had a respiratory illness last week. She enters the adjustment in his deductions column and continues.

She turns to look at the courtyard window twice in the hour: once when a truck from the transportation depot drives in, and once when it drives out. Both times there is nothing that needs seeing. The sky over the courtyard is the grey that will hold all day.

By nine she has worked through line twenty-eight. The materials consumption report for October is in the out-tray, waiting for the floor section chief's signature before she can send it to the district financial office. She does this every first week of the month; having a reason to be on the production corridor is something she is in the habit of accounting for. She finishes through line thirty-one, takes the materials form from the out-tray, and puts her coat on.

---

The passage between the administrative building and the production hall is covered but open at the base, and in November the cold collects along the corridor floor. She reported the gap at the bottom of the connecting door to maintenance in October 1979 and nothing was done. She walks through it and into the production corridor.

The loom floor is to her left, behind the baffle wall. The sound it makes is not quite a sound — it is a vibration below the range of what she identifies as noise, which she stopped distinguishing from silence after the first year. The smell is the synthetic-fiber smell: wet chemistry and steam heat, the exhaust of the wet-spinning process mixed with cold air through every unsealed gap. It has been in the walls of this corridor since 1974 and she stopped registering it years ago. What she registers now is the cold through the soles of her shoes.

The floor section chief's office is the third door on the right. She knocks once and goes in. He is on the telephone — receiver in one hand, a pen in the other, his eyes on the wall. She puts the materials form on the desk in front of him. He signs it without looking at it; she has had it typed cleanly. He does not stop talking. She goes back into the corridor.

Three women from the day shift are near the locker-bay door at the far end. She knows two of them by their coats. She does not turn toward them.

Georgeta Marin, the production supervisor for Hall B, is moving toward the women's bathroom at the far end of the corridor. She walks at the particular pace she uses when she has somewhere to be before the shift bell — not hurried, not slow. She has a ring of keys on a lanyard around her left wrist, tucked into her palm so they do not sound against each other. Three minutes to the shift change, perhaps less.

Ilinca walks to the bathroom.

---

One working bulb in the overhead fixture. Four sinks along the left wall; four stalls, two with latches — one of which has been difficult to close since August. The window above the sinks is painted shut, looking onto the outer wall of the fiber drying unit close enough to touch. The drain smell is more present in November.

Georgeta is at the far sink. Ilinca takes the one next to her and turns the tap.

"I've been thinking about the influenza," Ilinca says. "Whether it's going around. One of the women on the floor was ill last week."

Georgeta does not look up. Her hands are under the tap; she is washing them left over right, carefully.

"I had mine last year," she says. "I gave it to my neighbor on the street. Livia. No one else."

Ilinca runs cold water over her left wrist, then her right.

"And Livia?" she says.

"She's kept it to herself. She's a private woman — she doesn't pass things on. That's just her character."

The water is cold. Ilinca turns the tap off. In the mirror: the painted-shut window behind them, the single bulb above, Georgeta's keys in her palm.

"The influenza passes," Ilinca says.

"It does," Georgeta says, and goes.

---

Ilinca dries her hands and goes back up the corridor, through the connecting door, to her office. She hangs her coat. She sits.

Two pieces of information. She runs them in the order she can act on.

The first: Georgeta holds what Ilinca gave her, and it has not moved. Ilinca has known Georgeta Marin for eleven years — from before the supervisor promotion, from a period when the section rosters put them in proximity and she learned what Georgeta's silences mean and what her assurances mean.

The second: Georgeta gave one copy to her neighbor Livia, on her street, who has not passed it further. Ilinca has seen her perhaps three times in eleven years — grey coming into her hair before it should, a manner of walking with her chin slightly forward. Livia's family name Ilinca does not know by heart. She could find it in the bloc registry at the street committee. She will not need to. She will not look.

Two nodes on this branch: Georgeta, Livia. She runs every name she can place in the Petrescu household, and every name she can place on Georgeta's street, and the two sets do not intersect. The branch does not reach Ana Petrescu.

She thinks of the fourth line, the way she wrote it for Georgeta: *If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.* The copy she made for Georgeta — the third week of November last year, at this desk, by this lamp, in the blue-black ink she uses for fair copies — she can see the page as clearly as if it were in front of her. Line four. Numbered. In its place. The upstroke of the y in *properly*, where the nib caught slightly at the end of the word.

The branch is clean.

She enters both nodes into the account she carries in her head, which has no ledger and no supporting document and which she has maintained for thirteen months by discipline alone. The count is two.

She returns to line thirty-two.

---

Elena Florescu holds the other copy. Third shift now; when Ilinca first knew her they were both on the morning schedule, eleven years ago, when the roster rotation put them in the same section for two seasons. Since 1979 their paths cross in two ways: at the bakery on Strada Lungă, which Elena passes on her way to the morning handover and which Ilinca passes on her way home on certain days; and twice a year at the bloc committee office when the identity documents come up for renewal. Ilinca has counted fourteen exchanges at the bakery in three years. This is not friendship; it is adjacency, which is a more reliable thing.

Elena Florescu is not someone Ilinca knows well in the way of knowing — what she knows of her is procedural: the schedule she keeps, the coat she wears in November, the way she holds her bag on the same shoulder always.

She cannot go to Elena today. Elena is on the floor, on the machine, and a visit from the contabil-șef without an administrative basis is a visit that anyone nearby can note. The bakery is the correct approach. Elena passes it on Friday mornings at half past five on her way to the handover. Ilinca passes it at that hour only when she has reason to, which she now has. She will be there on Friday.

She does not write any of this down.

---

The stat de plată is finished at quarter past three. She tears the final strip, clips it to the summary line, puts the folder in the out-tray with a rubber band. The next item in the in-tray is a letter from the district financial office about the Q4 consumption norms. She reads it, makes a note in the margin, and puts it in the pending tray.

At four-fifteen the door opens.

A boy she does not know — not older than twenty; she has not seen him in the building before, which means he started recently. He is carrying a folder from the cadres office: she reads the stamp before he speaks. He sets a form on the edge of her desk.

"From the cadres office," he says. "Supplementary materials-usage calculation, Q3. Needs to be back by the fifteenth."

She takes it. "Sign the receipt book."

He finds it in his folder. She signs the line. He closes the folder and goes. She listens: footsteps in the corridor, the connecting door, then nothing.

She holds the form.

It is a Ministry of Finance series form. Q3 is July through September, which closed in October. She submitted the standard materials-usage calculation on the twenty-second of October; the district financial office stamped it received on the twenty-fifth. She ran the numbers four times before submitting because the supplementary ministerial instruction from August had adjusted the Q3 norms mid-quarter, and she wanted the adjustment applied consistently through every line item. It was. If there is a discrepancy in the Q3 accounts, it is not here.

She turns the form over. The back is blank. The watermark is in the lower left corner, the serial number in the upper right, where it belongs. She received a supplementary form for a closed quarter once before, in 1981, during the audit year — but that year all enterprises in the district received supplementary requests for everything, and those circumstances were general and known. This is not that.

She is holding the form and she has not decided what to do with it yet.

In fifteen years she has learned that most things which appear to be something are nothing. She has also learned that a thing which is something looks, from the outside, exactly like the things which are nothing. A form that arrives because a number was transposed two months ago in the district office looks like a form that arrives because someone wants to observe what a person does when a form arrives. She knows what a test looks like. She has not been given one she could verify before, which means she has no way to compare now.

The shift bell sounds in the production hall — muffled through the baffle wall, but she knows the pitch of it, the duration; she has known it for fifteen years and this is it. Footsteps in the corridor. Voices, the brief noise of the shift change, and then the corridor going quiet again under the machines.

She has not moved. The form is in her hand.

# 7 November 1984

He read the folder in his car with the engine off. The station was behind him; the Someș was somewhere ahead in the fog, down past the junction at Strada Gării, invisible from here. The folder held three items: the hospital's notification form, the death certificate stamped by the district procuror's office, and a handwritten sheet giving the name of the next of kin who had been notified. He read them in that order.

Ana Petrescu, nineteen years old. Admitted to the Spitalul Orășenesc at nineteen hundred hours on the fourth of November. Death recorded at twenty-three hundred and twelve on the same date. Cause of death: complications arising from hemorrhage. The hospital's notification form, submitted to the procuror's office on the morning of the fifth, classified the case as requiring investigation under the applicable decree. The hospital had done what it was required to do. His captain had made that clear, yesterday afternoon, when he had put the folder on Munteanu's desk and remained standing in the doorway: it was not the hospital under examination. What remained to establish was whether a criminal act had occurred, and on whose part.

The assignment had come to him on the afternoon of the sixth as an administrative case — the kind his captain classified as requiring a determination, not an investigation. Look at it, write down what happened, decide whether there is a basis for charges, close the file or pass it up. Munteanu had read the file the previous evening and concluded that these instructions would not cover what the file contained. He had not said this to his captain, because the determination had not been written yet and it was possible he was wrong.

He put the three sheets back into the folder in the order he had found them. He started the car and drove to Strada Gării.

---

The valley fog had not lifted by half past eight. It lay in the basin of the Someș below the road, dense in the low places, thinning only at the height of the bloc roofs. He drove with the window cracked. The market square was empty, the bread queue already dispersed — whatever had been available this morning had been available early. Past the square the road narrowed; the houses on Strada Gării ran close together, each with a small winter garden behind wire or concrete fencing: maize stalks cut low, a few cabbages still in the ground, a cold frame with nothing in it. Number forty-one had a metal gate that was not locked.

He parked and looked at the house for a moment before getting out. A single-storey building, extended at the back, with a kitchen light on behind a curtain not quite closed. He noted the gate, the cracked concrete of the garden path, the fact that the curtain had moved slightly while he was looking at it.

---

She came to the door before he had finished latching the gate. She had been watching from the kitchen window. A woman who knew the Miliția would eventually arrive, watching for when it arrived, was a woman who had been thinking about what to say. That was not deception. That was the preparation a person made when they understood that a conversation had consequences.

Her name was Rodica Petrescu. She was the wife of Ana's eldest brother and had been living in the house since the spring. She was not yet thirty and she had not slept.

He introduced himself: Locotenent Munteanu, Secția de Investigații. He said he was sorry for her loss. He was, in the way that he was always sorry at the beginning of this kind of interview.

She asked him in. The kitchen was small. A pot on the stove, the burner turned low, the smell of onions cooked an hour earlier and still in the air. She sat at the table with her hands in her lap; he sat across from her and took the notebook from the inside pocket of his coat.

He asked her to tell him what had happened from the evening of the third of November onward.

She had been telling it to herself for three days. He could hear it in the quality of the account — not rehearsed, exactly, but worn into a groove by repetition, the way a path is worn by the same feet going back and forth across it. Ana came home ill on the evening of the third; this was not the first time she had been unwell, so Rodica did not immediately understand what kind of ill this was. She stayed with her through the night. She counted the cloths, because the paper told her to, and she sat beside her and brought water in small amounts, because that was also on the paper. By noon on the fourth she understood that what she was counting had crossed a threshold. By the evening she understood that staying home was no longer the decision she was making.

She stopped speaking. He waited.

She said: she did not take her to the hospital until the evening of the fourth because going to the hospital was — she stopped again. She said, more quietly: because she did not know what to say when she arrived.

He wrote: *did not know what to say at the hospital.*

He asked: was there a piece of paper in the house.

She was very still. Then she said yes, and rose from the table and went into the next room. He waited. The pot hissed against the burner and went quiet. Outside, somewhere on the street, a cart moved across frozen gravel.

She came back with a folded piece of paper and put it on the table between them. It had been kept somewhere specific — she had returned without hesitation, without searching. The paper was folded twice, both folds going in the same direction. He could see handwriting through the sheet where the paper had gone thin at the creases.

He looked at it without touching it. Then he took an evidence envelope from his coat, held it open, and she put the paper into it. He sealed the envelope and held it in his lap.

He asked where the paper had come from.

From her neighbor, she said. A woman in the next bloc on the street. She gave the name. He wrote it.

He asked nothing else about the paper. He wrote the time in the margin of his notebook, wrote his station number on a card, and left the card on the table. She did not speak again. He put his coat on and went out the way he had come.

---

The neighbor's bloc was a hundred meters up the street. He walked slowly enough to look at the other houses: a light on behind frosted glass, a light on in an upstairs room, a dog behind a wire fence that watched him and did not bark. The fog was thinning; he could see to the end of the block now, the bare lindens black against the white-grey sky.

He found the address and rang the bell.

The woman who came to the door wore her kitchen apron and her coat at the same time. She read his identification card for a long moment — she read it properly, not just the top line of it — and stepped back.

The kitchen was slightly warmer than the previous one. A clothesline ran along the back wall with two towels folded over it. She stood near the stove with a dish towel in her hands, which were not still: she moved the towel from one hand to the other, set it on the counter, picked it up again.

He asked for her copy of the paper.

She said: what paper.

He said: the one you gave to Rodica Petrescu, on the street.

She was quiet. She looked at the dish towel and then at him. She put the dish towel on the counter and went to a drawer — second from the left, beneath the counter — and took out a folded piece of paper and brought it to him. Her hands were steady when she placed it in the second evidence envelope. It was the pause before the drawer that had not been steady.

He sealed the envelope. He asked her a few further questions: when she had last spoken with Rodica Petrescu, whether she had discussed Ana Petrescu's illness with anyone in the past three days, whether she had anyone else living in the household. She answered each question separately. He wrote the answers. He did not ask her who had given her the paper, and she did not say.

He thanked her. He left his card on the counter and went back out to the street.

---

He drove to the station and sat at his desk with both envelopes in front of him.

The investigations room held four other desks, only one of them occupied — Sandu, on the far side of the room, writing something in a ledger with his back to the window. The overhead fixture cast yellow light that reached only as far as the middle of the room. Munteanu turned on his lamp. He put his coat on the back of the chair. He set the two evidence envelopes side by side and looked at them for a moment.

He opened the first envelope and laid the paper flat on the right side of the desk. He opened the second envelope and laid the paper flat on the left. He moved the stapler to weight the right-hand sheet and a bottle of correction fluid to weight the left. Then he read them.

Line nine on both copies was the same. He read it on the right-hand sheet, then read it on the left: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He read from the top of each copy. Line one: the same on both. Line two: the same. Line three: he stopped.

On the right-hand sheet — the one Rodica Petrescu had given him, the one that had been in the house during the night of the third — line three read: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.*

On the left-hand sheet it read: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper beside the bed.*

He read both sentences again.

The handwriting was different. Not only different hands, but different enough in their letterforms that one person could not account for both. The right-hand script was small and even, the letters placed with some care; the left-hand script was slightly larger, the o's in *cloths* and in *hour* formed differently, opened where the right-hand script closed them. These had not been produced by the same person.

He read lines four through eight on both copies. In line six, the right-hand sheet had a full stop after *well* and the left-hand sheet had a comma — but the word was the same on both. Lines seven and eight were identical between the copies. Line nine was identical: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He held both sheets up toward the lamp. Not to see through them — the lamp was not strong enough for that — but to hold them in proximity, as two things that were related to each other. Then he set them back on the desk.

He had seen forged documents before. He had seen copied documents: a will transcribed in a different hand, a typed letter produced on two machines. In those cases, the second document had tried to be the same as the first, and what was interesting was where it had not succeeded. This was different. Both of these documents had tried to be the same as some third thing — something they had each been copied from — and both had succeeded, and each had arrived at something slightly different from the other. *By.* *Beside.* Neither of them wrong. Neither of them the other.

The variation between *by* and *beside* was what happened when a person read a word and wrote the word that was in their head, and the word in their head was slightly different from the word on the page. That was not an error of copying. That was copying. That was what copying produced, line by line and hand by hand, generation by generation. A word at a time.

And if both of these copies had drifted one step from the same source, then the source existed. And the source had come from somewhere.

He did not say any of this aloud. He did not write it down.

Line nine was the same on both copies: *take her in in the morning.* Nine numbered lines on both sheets, the ninth sitting square in the column with the rest.

He picked up his pen. He pulled the folder toward him and turned to a fresh page at the back, behind the death certificate and the notification form and his notes from the morning. He wrote the neighbor's name at the top of the page. He drew a line under it.

The neighbor was where the chain between his desk and the Petrescu household stopped, at the moment. Behind her name was whoever had given the paper to her. Behind that name was another, and behind that name another still. He did not know yet how many. He did not know yet where the nine-line version of this document had come from, or when, or in whose hand.

He wrote the date in the margin and began.

# 8 November 1984

She is at the window when the heating pipes knock. Seven o'clock. She has been up since half past five — there is no point lying still after five thirty in November, because the cold that comes through the bloc wall at that hour is not a cold she can sleep through, and the heating will not come on for another ninety minutes.

The nechezol is in her hand. She drinks it standing. The glass has condensation in the lower corners; there is a clear strip across the centre where she can see the street — two bare lindens, the pavement, and then nothing. The fog sits in the valley, pressed down against the cold, not moving. On still mornings it fills from the river to the rooftops and higher. The Someș is somewhere behind it, wide and flat, invisible.

She thinks: what she holds.

N2 branch: Georgeta, Livia. Both confirmed. Both clean.

N3: Elena Florescu, third shift, production floor. Not yet confirmed. Today.

The cellar copy. November third, last year. One entry. She lets it stand.

Three copies. One branch still open. She will reach Elena today, and then the count will be settled.

The pipes hiss and then go quiet. The heat is still in the radiator — she can feel it from where she stands, two metres away. By eight forty-five the radiator will be cold. She finishes the nechezol and rinses the cup. The adding machine is at the mill. Here there is only the pen and the pale-green notebook she keeps for grocery calculations, both of them on the corner of the kitchen table. She does not touch them. She puts her coat on and goes out.

---

The bread queue is on Strada Comercială. She is in it by seven twenty, and there are already eleven people ahead of her. The shutters of the alimentară are down and dark; there is no movement inside and no sign there will be, for another twenty minutes at least. The cold is dry, the kind that does not feel acute until you have been standing in it long enough. Her breath comes white. The breath of the woman ahead of her comes white. At the front of the queue a child shifts his weight from one foot to the other, his collar up, his hands in his pockets. Nobody looks at the child.

She knows three of the faces by sight: the woman from the second floor of her bloc, whose name she does not know but whose light was on at eleven the previous night; a man with a grey moustache who is in this queue every Thursday at this hour, regular as a ledger entry; a woman of sixty with a knitted hat she has worn every day since September, regardless of weather. Ilinca does not greet any of them. You stand in the queue. You do not calculate. You wait for the shutters to go up.

At five past eight the shutters go up. At twenty to nine she has her two loaves, wrapped in paper, and is walking back up Strada Comercială.

---

She leaves the bread on the kitchen table. She puts on her heavier coat and her boots, the ones with the rubber soles she bought at the universal shop in September, which have so far kept out most of the wet. She takes the pot from the corner of the kitchen where it has been standing since the first week of October: Marta's pot, cast iron, the large one she borrowed for the plum preserves. She has owed Marta the pot for six weeks.

Her cousin Marta lives on Bulevardul Victoriei in a second-floor flat. The walk is twelve minutes by the back streets and eleven by the main road. She takes the back streets. The pot is heavy; she carries it with both hands. The fog has not lifted yet from the street level and she walks through it, past the bicycle workshop that is never open in the mornings, past the bakery on Strada Lungă with its shutters still down, past a cluster of boys in school coats going the other way.

Marta opens the door before Ilinca has reached the top of the stairs. She is in her apron and indoor shoes, and she has flour on one hand, which means she has been at the kitchen table. She looks at the pot and says: you didn't need to make a special trip.

Ilinca says: I was passing.

She was not passing. Marta works the day shift in hall A, production floor, and returned from her shift two hours ago. She has known Ilinca since childhood and she knows when Ilinca is not passing. She looks at her with the particular expression of a woman who has decided not to ask.

The kitchen smells of dough and of something earlier in the day — onions, a broth that has cooked down. It is warmer than Ilinca's kitchen, larger, with a window over the courtyard and a rug that has always been there as long as Ilinca can remember. Marta sets the pot on the counter and pours a second nechezol without asking. They sit at the table. Marta talks: the new tram schedule, which is two months old now but which she has only recently begun to need; her youngest daughter's classroom, where a window has not closed properly since August and the teacher has taped cardboard over the gap, which helps with the draught but not the light. Ilinca listens. She notes the clock above the stove.

After nine minutes she says: I heard Elena Florescu has been unwell.

Marta says: has she.

Third shift, Ilinca says. Lives in your next bloc over. If you happen to see her — tell her I said to keep the influenza quiet. Not to come in until she's better. No reason to make it worse.

Marta looks at her cup and then at Ilinca and then back at her cup.

Ilinca says: it's nothing urgent. Only if it's convenient.

Marta says: I can go now. She'll be in at this hour.

She takes her apron off and hangs it on the back of the door. Her daughter, who is eleven, has been doing schoolwork at the table in the other room; Ilinca can hear the scratch of a pencil, steady, not hurried. Marta puts her coat on. She says: ten minutes.

Ilinca says she will wait in the stairwell.

She goes down and stands on the second-floor landing, below the working light bulb, and waits. The stairwell smells of cabbage and of the particular cold that accumulates in enclosed spaces that are not quite as cold as the outside. Somewhere above her a door opens and closes. On the street, the sound of a cart, and then nothing.

Seventeen minutes. Then the front door and Marta's youngest on the stairs, coat on, satchel on her back, going to the afternoon school shift. She stops when she sees Ilinca.

Marta's voice from above: tell her what Elena said.

The girl says: Elena says she's fine. She's been careful. She hasn't seen anyone she doesn't know.

She goes out the door. Ilinca stands for a moment on the landing.

---

She takes the long way home. It adds twelve minutes and goes along the embankment. The fog has lifted from street level; she can see to the end of the block, and beyond it the bare tops of the willows over the river. The Someș is brown and fast and cold-looking. Yellow leaves turn in the slow current near the bank. The sky is white-grey and not moving.

She walks, and she accounts.

N2 branch: confirmed. N3 branch: confirmed, this afternoon. Both clean, both quiet. No contact, no names said, no questions asked from any direction she has not herself sent. The count is three. All three branches she seeded herself. All three accounted for.

Which leaves one that she does not think of as a question.

November third, last year. The door to the street was open just enough for the light from the lamp outside to fall onto the paper — a rectangle of yellow, not steady, because the hinge moved slightly in the draft from the coal chute stairs. She had the master in her left hand and the pen in her right. Ten minutes. Less, possibly; she did not look at the time. The woman could not wait. The woman had come a long way and could not be late and could not be seen standing.

She counted the lines as she wrote them. One through eight, in order, each numbered in sequence, identical to the master. She can see the lines. She can see the numbers.

And then the bracket. In October she had drawn it herself: two strokes — one down, one across the bottom — and a corner, making the three sides of a rectangle around the words. An override, not a step. In the cellar she drew it again: two strokes and a corner. She remembers the pressure of the pen tip on the paper. She remembers drawing the corner last. And inside it she wrote: *7 or 8 — take her in.* And then: *Do not wait for the morning.*

Those words are in her handwriting, in the bracket, on that copy.

She has checked this before. She found it correct before.

She was in a hurry, and she was careful, and she has been both at the same time her entire working life. She counted the lines. She put the bracket.

A woman passes her on the embankment path with a bicycle. A door somewhere in the bloc row to her left opens and shuts. The willows at the edge of the path are bare and black, roots in the river mud, branches reaching across the path and not quite reaching the other side.

She is almost certain.

---

She is home by half past four. She hangs up her coat and her scarf on the door hook and stands for a moment in the kitchen. The heating will come on again at six, if it comes on.

She sits at the table. The pale-green notebook is where it always is. The pen is beside it. She thinks about the adding machine at the mill: the weight of the crank, the sound it makes, the column of figures it confirms without ambiguity. Here, only the pen. She picks it up and holds it. She puts it down.

She thinks about writing something.

She does not open the notebook.

Outside the window the grey is deepening into the grey before dark, and she watches it change without moving to turn on the second lamp. The forty-watt bulb on the table makes a circle and leaves the rest of the kitchen in shadow. This is enough light. She has worked in worse.

She gets up and goes into the bedroom and lies down on the bed with her shoes on and looks at the ceiling. The ceiling is white in the last light from the window and then less white as the light drops. On the street below: a cart, the sound of a metal door on a hinge, something with an engine that does not accelerate. Nothing she needs to account for.

N2. N3. The cellar copy.

Three. Confirmed, confirmed, and — she was careful, she counted, she drew the bracket.

The second lamp stays off. Outside, it is full dark now, and the block heating will come on at six or it will not come on. She does not get up. She is almost certain, and certainty of this kind is a column that balances; she has closed it before and found it correct.

She lies still.

# 9 November 1984

My old roommate Luiza, who transferred to the Cluj plant in September, used to say the bloc heating was like a sentence: it said something and then it stopped before you understood it. I don't know that she was wrong. The heating came on at seven and stopped at a quarter to eight. Forty minutes. Enough to warm your hands if you held them over the radiator and not enough to do much else, which was more or less Luiza's point.

The room had two cots, a shared wardrobe, and a window that looked onto the factory yard. From the window, at seven in the morning in November, you could see the loading dock lights and the upper edge of the mill roofline and approximately nothing else beyond that — the fog sat on the yard like something deliberately placed. Luiza had kept a photograph on her side of the wardrobe door: a man in a white shirt at some summer occasion, squinting into the sun. She took it with her to Cluj in September. Her side of the wardrobe door was bare now, which was the kind of thing you noticed even when you weren't looking.

I was in my coat. This is not a detail I mention for atmosphere. I mention it because being in my coat meant I didn't have to decide what to do with my coat, and that morning I had enough to decide about without adding coat.

The paper was not in the room. I want to be clear about this before anything else. The geography book was at the mill, in my locker — on the shelf above the coat hooks in the production floor locker bay, exactly where I had left it when the shift ended on Wednesday. The locker has a padlock. I lock it when I leave and unlock it when I arrive; I have done this every day since the week I understood what the geography book was carrying between pages thirty-four and thirty-five. When I left on Wednesday I had closed the padlock and heard it click and walked out of the locker bay and caught the tram home. I had no reason to doubt any of this. But the paper was not here in the room with me, which meant there was one kind of thinking available to me that morning and another kind that wasn't. I could think about the paper. I could not look at it.

So I thought about it.

Line one: *Keep her warm, and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.* I had that.

Line three: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.* I had that without trying. It was the kind of line you kept without deciding to, the way you keep a number that has stopped making sense by repeating it until it either makes sense or stops mattering.

Line seven: *Two cloths in one hour is too many.* That one I knew the way I knew the tram schedule — not by remembering it but by never having a reason to forget it.

The bracket at the end. *7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.* I had read it enough times that it was simply there: part of the furniture of the room, without me having unpacked it. The bracket was not a step. I understood it as a bracket. I had understood that from the first reading, in the eleven months since the woman on the bus gave it to me on the route from Gherla, between the stop at Bonțida and the stop before Dej, while I held it in my hand and she looked at the window.

I tested line four, because line four was the one I was least sure of. *If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.* I held that in my head for a moment, and then the doubt: every. Was it every? I went back through the text in my mind. No — the paper said *each hour*, not every. Each. I corrected it and sat with the correction. Every and each mean the same thing in ordinary speech, which is why the error was easy to make and not easy to catch. I had caught it. I didn't know what to do with that information except note it.

---

The question of burning it had come to me before. Several times, on several nights, with the seriousness you give to a question you're not going to answer but feel you should have considered properly at least once. I had considered it properly.

Burning it required fire. In the hostel room: no fire. The hostel room had a radiator that performed its duty for forty minutes a day and otherwise sat there cool and impersonal, taking up space under the window. No woodstove, no fireplace. The hallway had an ashtray on the communal table, which was for cigarettes — it was not, in practice, for papers. Burning a piece of paper in a hallway ashtray is the kind of event that gets a name: *remember the girl in room fourteen who burned something in the hallway* — and then a series of questions that don't get easier the more they're asked.

The factory yard in November was more watched than in summer, which sounds counterintuitive until you account for the fact that in summer there are more reasons to be standing outside at odd hours doing things with your hands. In November, the only people in the factory yard at the end of a shift were people with a specific destination in mind, and standing near a rubbish bin burning something was not a destination.

The hostel toilet was the final option, and I had looked at it long enough to conclude that it required the latch in stall two to hold for the duration of a burning paper, which was a duration I couldn't calculate precisely, and the latch in stall two had been holding for me roughly sixty percent of the time since August.

I didn't burn it. I kept it.

Keeping it was a decision I had made eleven months earlier without knowing I was making it. The geography book had been in the locker since my third week at the mill. Nobody had ever asked to borrow it, read it, or look at the spine. My last roommate Luiza had looked at it once, in the first week, the way you look at a book to see if it has anything on the cover that interests you, and then she had not looked at it again. I had never opened it past page thirty-three. Everything I knew about the Northern Carpathians watershed drainage system I knew from the edge of the diagram visible when I lifted the paper out: a watershed, hills, something running northward. That was sufficient.

The forty minutes of heat had warmed the room more than I expected. I went to the window and unlatched it and pushed it open a few centimetres. Outside: the factory yard, quiet in the mid-morning, with all the noise moved inside. Two women in production aprons went across the yard at a diagonal toward the canteen, not talking to each other. A cat crossed the loading dock. Someone had left a bicycle propped against the far wall below the sign that said bicycles were not to be left against the far wall. The sky above the mill roofline was white-grey and flat, the kind of sky that has finished deciding what to do and has decided to do nothing.

I had nowhere to be until the bread allocation. If I left it until tomorrow the loaf for the week would be smaller, which was a separate problem from the one I was sitting with but still a problem. The bread queue closed at four. I sat on the cot and looked at the water stain in the upper left corner of the ceiling, which had been there since I moved in and had no recognizable shape, which was something I had checked a number of times over two years, mostly in the middle of the night when I was awake and there was nothing else to look at.

It was ten to ten.

---

I went out in the early afternoon. The bread queue on my street was shorter than usual — nine people ahead of me when I got there, which was shorter than average for a Friday. Someone in line said the delivery had come late and the loaves were smaller than the allocation said they should be. The woman who said this was not saying it to me specifically; she was saying it to the air, in the way people have of putting a complaint where it can't be held against them. The cold was dry, the kind that doesn't feel acute until your nose stops working.

At the front of the queue: a child in a yellow coat, small, shifting weight from one foot to the other. His mother put her hand on his shoulder and he went still. The motorized cart somewhere around the corner made a sound and stopped making it. I was third from the front when I looked across the street.

Two women from the production floor. Second shift — I knew their faces from the locker bay and the break room, the way you know people you see at the same hour every day without ever having occasion to use their names. They should not have been on this street at this hour on a Friday morning. They were standing outside the locksmith's shop, close to the wall, in the attitude of people who have been placed somewhere rather than chosen to be there. A man was talking to them. He had a notepad open in his left hand, and while I watched he wrote something down.

Then I looked at the coat.

Factory coats are green-grey. They smell of fibre dust even when they're not in the factory; the smell gets into the weave after the first week and it doesn't come out after that. From across a street you know a factory coat by the colour and the cut and by the way the collar has gone lighter than the body from too many cold-water washes. The man's coat was not a factory coat. Bloc-committee coats are brownish, and the people who wear them have a way of carrying their shoulders that says the communal infrastructure is their professional responsibility, which they take seriously, which they would prefer you also took seriously — you can read it in the lapels from twenty metres. The man's coat was not a bloc-committee coat. It was darker and cut closer and longer, the coat of a job where you went to other people's places rather than to a fixed address. Where you arrived somewhere and wrote down what people told you.

The counter woman put my bread on the counter. I paid. I took my change and put it in my pocket without counting it.

I turned left instead of right. The long way back to the hostel was six minutes longer than the short way, along the block where the pharmacy had been closed since August. I took it. I walked at the speed of someone who had somewhere to be, which is faster than the speed of someone who is leaving a situation and slower than the speed of someone who is obviously leaving a situation. I did not look back. I did not cross the street to say hello to the two women from the production floor, who would have known my face from the locker bay, and who were standing outside a locksmith's shop talking to a man in a coat like that, and who were not where they should have been at this hour.

I went home.

---

In the hostel I went directly to my room. I shut the door. I sat down on the cot with the bread in my lap, and I did not take my coat off.

I thought about the locker.

The geography book was at the mill. Shelf above the coat hooks, production floor locker bay, second row from the left, the locker with the number plate where the seven looked like a one if you weren't paying attention. The padlock was on the locker when I left on Wednesday evening — I had locked it at the end of the shift, put the key on my ring, gone home. The key was on the ring with my hostel key and my aunt's spare key, which she gave me in 1982 when she thought she might need someone to look in on things and which she had never yet needed back. I found the ring in my coat pocket. I held it. Three keys.

The locker was locked.

The man with the notepad had been two hundred metres from the mill gate. The two women from the production floor had been talking to him on a Friday morning when they should have been in their section or at home. The coat said he had been somewhere before this street and would be somewhere after. The notepad said he was writing down what people told him, which was the kind of writing that, once written, moved somewhere you had no access to.

The paper was in the geography book, between pages thirty-four and thirty-five. The geography book was in the locker. The locker had a padlock, and I was holding the key.

I was fairly certain the locker was locked. I had locked it. I had the key in my hand.

I sat on the cot in my coat with the bread in my lap and the ring of keys in my other hand and thought about the word *fairly*, and how it was not the same word as *certainly*, and how it was the only word I had, and how it was something I had never needed to think about before this week.

# 10 November 1984

The November payroll forms are in the wooden tray beside the secretary's elbow, folded in half the way they come from the print room. She takes them without sitting down.

Pântelimon says: there has been some unpleasantness with the Petrescu matter. A Miliția officer has been speaking with people.

He says it as a statement in an open room. The outer door of the office is propped; two women from the personnel section are at their desks with their coats still on. He is watching Ilinca's hands.

She folds the forms once more and tucks them under her arm. A tragic business, she says. She is glad the family has someone looking into it.

She goes back to her office.

---

She closes the door and puts the payroll forms on the left side of the desk, beside the October figures. She does not open them yet.

An officer has been speaking with people. The secretary told her this in the tone of a man who has information and would like to exchange it. She gave him nothing except the obvious, which is the kind of exchange that costs her nothing and may give him something to think about later, if he is the type who thinks about things later. She does not know what type he is.

He has not come to the administrative building. If she were a name in the file, someone would have been at her door by now. The administrative building is not a production section and it is not a residential bloc. It sits on the other side of the main gate, which is a distance that means something, practically speaking, about whose names come first.

A man working outward from Ana Petrescu's house works from the sister-in-law, then from whoever the sister-in-law named, then outward from there. That is how it goes. There is a sequence to these things and she is not at the front of the sequence.

She opens the middle drawer and takes out the October summary sheet and places it to the right of the payroll forms. She does not look at either of them.

She has time. Not an abundance of it. Enough to do the next thing.

---

At nine she takes the materials-usage report from the filing cabinet behind the door. The October comparison columns for Hall B show a discrepancy on the last week of the month: the production log records sixty-eight kilograms of raw fiber allocation, but the stores ledger shows seventy-two kilograms issued over the same period. Four kilograms. Small enough to be a transcription error; large enough that it cannot stay in the month-end summary without an explanation and a countersignature.

She needs Georgeta for this.

This is the difficulty and also the solution to the difficulty. It is the second time in a week she will have occasion to speak with Georgeta. Once in a week is reasonable. Twice is one more than she prefers, for a woman who has always been careful about how often she appears in the same place as the same person. But the discrepancy is real. The stores ledger is here in her hand. She needs a production supervisor's countersignature before the month-end summary can go to the director's office, and Georgeta is the supervisor for Hall B. She has used worse reasons than this.

She writes the discrepancy figures on a separate sheet: *issued, 72 kg; production log, 68 kg; variance, 4 kg.* She clips the sheet to the October comparison figures and puts both in her document folder.

She waits until ten. She does not look at the clock between nine and ten.

---

At ten she goes to the supplies corridor.

Georgeta is already there. She is doing the quarterly inventory, which she does on the tenth of every month — Ilinca has countersigned the inventory sheets since 1978 and knows the schedule. Georgeta's clipboard is in her right hand; she is making ticks with a pencil, working along the shelves from the door end.

Ilinca sets her folder on the table near the window end and opens it to the October comparison sheet.

A materials discrepancy, she says. Hall B, last week of October. Seventy-two kilograms issued against sixty-eight in the production log. I need to know before the month-end summary which figure is correct, or whether there is a stores entry that explains the difference.

Georgeta does not stop her ticks. She finishes the shelf she is on. She sets the clipboard against the wall and comes to the table.

She looks at the comparison sheet. The last week of October, she says. We had two days of reduced intake on the spooling machines in the second bay. Some of the raw fiber arrived late. I logged it in the first week of November to keep the production records clean. If stores logged it in October because the delivery arrived in October, that is where your four kilograms are.

Ilinca writes this down. She says: I will need the delivery receipt to confirm the date. Can you get me the November intake log for the first four days?

By afternoon, Georgeta says. The materials office will have the receipt; I will send someone.

Ilinca closes the folder and clips the note inside it. She says: that should close it for the month-end summary. Then, without a pause that could be read as a pause: and how is Livia keeping?

Georgeta's pencil is in her hand. She does not tap it against anything.

Her daughter stopped by on Tuesday, she says. She says Livia is fine. Quiet. She's been at home, not seeing people.

Ilinca says: hasn't given anything to anyone?

Georgeta shakes her head, once, as if she is agreeing that the delivery receipt will settle the discrepancy.

No, she says. She kept it to herself.

Good. Ilinca picks up her folder. I'll have the countersignature form ready when the intake log comes. If you send it by two, we can close this before Friday.

She goes back to her office.

---

She closes the door. She sits in the chair.

N2 branch: Georgeta. From Georgeta to Livia — Georgeta's neighbor on her street. Livia gave the copy to nobody. She has been at home, not seeing people. No Miliția contact; Georgeta's daughter went by on Tuesday and she was fine. The branch runs from the master, then to Georgeta, then to Livia, and there it stops. A dead end is what the branch was designed to be; not every copy was meant to go further. Livia had kept it to herself for more than a year and had not used it and had not passed it and was now sitting quietly in her apartment while a man with a notepad asked questions on streets that were not her street. The branch contains no one who is in a file.

*No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.*

She has followed this herself. The cousin, the borrowed pot, the materials discrepancy. She has not made a telephone call she did not need. She has not opened her door to anyone who was not expected. What she has done in the past week to close her accounting of the branches — the routes she took, the words she used, the questions she turned sideways — are all consistent with the instruction on line five. She knows line five the way she knows all of them. She wrote it, which is a different kind of knowing than reading it, because writing a thing is choosing every word separately, and she chose those words and has not needed to reconsider them.

The N3 branch is confirmed through Elena Florescu. The N2 branch closes now, with Livia. What remains is the cellar copy — the third copy she made from the master, on November third of last year, in the coal cellar behind Strada Dorobanților, by the light of the door, in ten minutes, for a woman who could not wait for a better time. She has gone over it. She knows what she wrote. She drew the bracket — two strokes and a corner — and she wrote the words inside it, and the words were the words from the master. She is certain of this the way she is certain of her own handwriting.

Four nodes in her private account. The master. The N2 branch, now closed and clean. The N3 branch, closed and clean. The cellar copy, which she holds as correct. Four entries. She cannot write any of this anywhere. She cannot write the count or the confirmation or the four-kilogram discrepancy in the same column. The private account has no ledger. It exists in the hour between nine and ten when she does not look at the clock.

The man asking questions in the production sections will work outward from what he has and will eventually reach what exists to be reached. What exists to be reached, on the N2 branch, is Livia, who is fine and has kept herself quiet and has given nothing to anyone. That branch is closed. If he reaches it, it dead-ends.

She opens the payroll forms.

---

The November columns are blank. She fills them from the October summary, adjusted for the two new employees in Hall C and the reduced hours from the repair week. She uncaps her pen and writes the first entry at the top of the column. She checks the form header. Alphabetical, surname-first, which has been the format since October per the new directive from the financial office. The entry is in the right place.

The numbers go in one column at a time. Gross hours, deductions, net. She runs the figures by hand first, then checks the tape. The tape agrees with her column for the first twelve entries and disagrees by three lei on the thirteenth. She finds the error: a transposition in the gross hours, twenty-two where the source sheet says twenty-two point five. She corrects it with a single line through the wrong figure and the right figure beside it.

She fills the column to the end of the first page. She turns to the second.

The fog from the river burned off before ten. The sun comes in through the window now at an angle that crosses the desk; she moves the October comparison sheet out of the light and continues. By eleven the second column is complete. Twenty-seven entries on the first page, three on the reverse. The countersignature line for the materials discrepancy will go at the bottom when Georgeta's intake log arrives. That should be before two.

She sets the pen down and looks at what she has done. The column is correct. The figures are in the right order. When the delivery receipt confirms the dates, the four-kilogram discrepancy will have an explanation and the explanation will go into the correct column and the month-end summary will go to the director's office by Friday and the October accounts will be closed.

She clips the payroll forms together — original, personnel copy, summary page — and puts the set in the out tray.

She leans back in the chair. The chair has a creak at the back joint that she has meant to report to the maintenance office since spring. She has not reported it. A creak is not a problem; it is the kind of sound that stops being heard after the first week, the kind that only a person paying close attention to her office and her habits would notice in the middle of a morning.

She sits forward and puts both hands flat on the desk.

The delivery receipt will arrive by two.

She uncaps the pen and pulls the October comparison sheet back into the light and reads the figures again from the beginning. The thing you miss is always in the line you read first, when your eye has not yet learned what it is looking for. She has learned this about herself over fifteen years and she does not argue with it.

The lamp is off. She has not needed it since the fog cleared.

## 07-livia

### Meta-commentary on cognition

- **"She thinks:"** (before "he has not come to the administrative building") — cut the cognitive-act label; the free-indirect thought stands as a declarative in close-third present tense.

- **", and she takes a moment to look at it as both"** (end of "This is the difficulty and also the solution to the difficulty") — trailing clause names the act of contemplating a thing already stated. Cut; sentence ends at "difficulty."

- **"She counts:"** (before "Four nodes in her private account") — labels the counting about to happen. Cut; the accounting sequence is its own evidence.

- **"This is what she does after a column is finished: she reads it again."** — restates the action in the immediately preceding clause ("reads the figures again from the beginning") and labels it a habit. The explaining sentence that follows ("The thing you miss is always in the line you read first…") performs that characterization without the intermediate label. Cut entirely.

### Sentence-after-the-sentence

- **"She knows this because nobody has knocked on her door."** — glosses the inference the reader already drew from "If she were a name in the file, someone would have been at her door by now." The conditional set the logic; the concluding sentence merely announces it arrived. Cut.

- **"The legitimacy of the reason is sufficient."** — the previous three sentences have demonstrated the reason is real (real discrepancy, real procedural need, actual supervisor). The conclusion is already sitting there. Cut; "She has used worse reasons than this." retained as it adds distinct information (prior practice).

- **"It has no information that points back to her."** — "What exists to be reached, on the N2 branch, is Livia, who is fine and has kept herself quiet and has given nothing to anyone" already tells the reader everything. "Dead-ends" closes the image; this sentence explains the image. Cut.

- **"She has been using this format since October."** — "which has been the format since October per the new directive from the financial office" in the same sentence already says this. Exact repetition of the time-anchor. Cut.

- **Second "She has not reported it."** (closing the creak passage) — the first instance of the phrase earlier in the same paragraph is the image-close. The intervening sentence ("A creak is not a problem…") is the explanation; repeating the phrase after the explanation is a gloss on the gloss. Cut; the explanation sentence retained because it carries specific surveillance-calculation content not otherwise stated.

### Redundant transition / re-summary

- **"N2 branch closed. Four nodes confirmed. The officer who has been asking questions has not come to the administrative building. She has time still — not much, but enough to do the next thing, and the thing after that."** — closing paragraph before the delivery-receipt sentence. All four propositions were established earlier in the chapter: the branch-close was done in the private-account section; the four-node count was just made; the officer's absence from the administrative building was established in the opening section; the time formulation repeats "She has time. Not an abundance of it. Enough to do the next thing." verbatim. This is the failure mode the style guide names explicitly ("a paragraph at the opening or close of a chapter that recaps what the reader already knows about where the collation stands"). Cut entire paragraph.
