# 17 noiembrie

The district heating had come on for half an hour in the night and stopped before I was awake enough to notice. I know this because when I put my hand on the radiator at seven o'clock it was just barely warm — not warm enough to do anything useful, the residual warmth of a system that had fulfilled its obligation and moved on — and by eight it was the same temperature as the wall. By nine I had my coat on top of the blanket, which is a method that works until you have to move and only addresses one of the two problems in a cold hostel room in November.

I had the room to myself. Floarea has been on day shift since October, which means she is at the factory before six and back before four, and on my days off I have the room from seven in the morning until the afternoon, which is a quantity of solitude unusual enough that I still notice it and have been noticing it since October. My days off I normally spend sleeping until ten and then going to the market and then coming back and sleeping again, which is the correct use of a day off when you work nights. Today I had been awake since seven, lying on my back with my coat over the blanket and looking at the geography book on the table.

I had brought it home from the factory on Thursday. This is not something I do as a rule. The geography book lives in the locker in the women's changing room — second row from the left, the locker with the number plate where the seven looks like a one if you are not paying attention — in a space where nothing ever happens and no one has any reason to look. It has been there since I understood, in my third week at the mill, what it was carrying between pages thirty-four and thirty-five. Bringing it home means bringing the problem home, which is not the kind of problem that improves with proximity. But I had brought it home this time for a reason, which was that I needed the original in the room in order to find out whether I still needed the original in the room.

The test is simple in principle. You write the document out from memory, without looking at the original, and then you compare what you wrote against what is on the page. I have passed examinations this way; the method is not new. What was new was what I would have to do with the test paper afterward. But that was a manageable problem, and I had been managing it in my head since Thursday, so I got up.

---

The piece of paper was in the front pocket of my bag, where I had put it on Thursday for exactly this purpose. It was the back of a utility calculation form — the kind of form that is distributed constantly by the calculation office and turns up in pockets and bags and on windowsills without anyone being able to account for it. The front had numbers on it that had nothing to do with me. The back was blank.

I sat at the table with the geography book closed in front of me and the utility form turned over to the plain side and uncapped the pen.

*1.* I wrote, and then I waited for the line to come.

*Keep her warm, and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.*

The comma after *warm* I have been practicing. Without it the line runs *warm and lying down*, which is how I heard it in my head for the first several weeks — the comma does not arrive naturally, it has to be placed. I know why it is there: it makes two separate directives out of what otherwise sounds like one, and the document is precise about that kind of distinction in a way that I have come to understand as intentional. The comma is the document being careful. I placed the comma and moved on.

Lines two and three went down without trouble. Line four stopped me.

Line four is: *If she sleeps, wake her each hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.* The word that matters is *each*. I have been working on *each* since November began, since I first tried to recite line four from memory on the night shift and came out with *every* instead. Every and each mean the same thing in ordinary usage, which is exactly why *every* is what you write if you are not paying careful attention. I wrote the line and then read what I had written: *wake her every hour.* I put a line through *every* and wrote *each* above it. I continued to line five, finished the list through line eight, and went back to read from the beginning. At line four I had written *every* again. Not the crossed-out *every* — a fresh one, below the correction, as though I had decided the correction did not apply. I cannot account for this. I crossed out the second *every*, wrote the line over on the next available line of the form, said *each* aloud twice while I was writing it, and moved on.

Lines five and six. Six says *Keep and wash*, and I had the order right. Seven. Eight — *A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.* I paused at eight, the way I always pause at eight, for reasons I have been unable to isolate. Eight has the word *morning* in it. Since the beginning of November everything with *morning* in it has acquired a quality I do not have a name for.

I picked up the pen and wrote line nine.

Except there is no line nine. That is the thing. The ninth element is not a line nine in the sequence of the other lines; it is a bracket that sits below line eight and is surrounded by square brackets to signal that it is different from what is above it — a condition that overrides the sequence rather than extending it. I put the left bracket and wrote what was inside it: *7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.* New line, indented, the closing bracket.

I read it back. That was right. That was exactly what it said.

---

I tore the utility form into quarters. The hostel bathroom at the end of the corridor has a window above the middle sink that opens over the yard, and on the windowsill there is a tin ashtray with a bent rim, and there is always a box of matches beside it. I have known about the ashtray since my second week in the building. Three of the four women on this floor smoke, and the bathroom is where they do it in winter when the yard is too cold, and the ashtray is a fixture as permanent as the sink.

The bathroom was empty. On a Thursday morning at half past nine, with the day-shift women at the factory and Floarea in her section, there was no reason for anyone to be in the bathroom except me. I opened the window and the November air came in off the yard, carrying the specific smell of the yard in late autumn — concrete, a little mud, the bins.

I put the torn quarters of the utility form in the ashtray. I took the first match from the box and dropped it on the tile because my hands were colder than I had understood them to be. I took the second match. It caught.

The paper was dry and went fast. The writing I had done — all nine elements, the bracket, the two crossed-out *every*s and the correction — curled at the edges and went dark and then went to white, and the white crumbled when I touched it with the spent match. Thirty seconds, at most. A page and a half of my handwriting turned into a small pile of ash that occupied roughly the space of one cigarette-end, which is less than you would expect from a page and a half of handwriting.

I carried the ashtray to the toilet. The ash flushed without trouble.

I put the ashtray back on the windowsill. I closed the window. I went back to my room.

---

The geography book was on the table where I had left it.

I want to say something here about what the woman who gave it to me looked like, because I have been asked — later, in a different context, under circumstances I am coming to — and the honest answer is that I cannot give you a picture that would help you find her. She had a face like a closed shop. She sat two rows ahead of me on the bus from Gherla and she put the paper in my hand as we were coming into Bonțida, the way you return something to a person who has dropped it, quickly, and then she looked out the window at the fields going past and did not look back. I held the paper in my lap for the rest of the trip into Dej and when I got off the bus I put it in my coat pocket and when I got to the hostel I put it in the geography book because the geography book was the first thing I could think of that nobody would open. Including me. I did not know her name. I did not ask. She did not offer it and I did not ask, which in the moment was simply not asking, and which later I came to understand as the only answer to the question of how she had kept herself safe long enough to have a copy to give.

I sat down and unfolded the document and read it through.

1. Keep her warm, and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.
2. Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.
3. Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.
4. If she sleeps, wake her each hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.
5. No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.
6. Burn nothing until she is well. Keep and wash.
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
   [ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why.
     Do not wait for the morning. ]

The comma was there in line one. Line four said *each hour*, which was what I had eventually written on the utility form. Line six said *Keep and wash*, in that order, which was what I had written. The bracket was below line eight, with the text inside it and the closing bracket on its own indented line, and it said *Do not wait for the morning*.

Everything was where I had put it in my head.

I read the bracket a second time. Then I folded the document back the way it had arrived: twice along the horizontal, twice along the vertical, so that the writing was inside and the outside was the plain back of the paper, which is the colour of paper that has been folded and opened many times and handled by several sets of hands. I put it back between pages thirty-four and thirty-five. The water-bird diagram on page thirty-four — some kind of delta bird, a heron perhaps, the caption too small to read without glasses I don't have — looked the same as it always did. I closed the book and put it in my bag.

It would go back to the factory tomorrow. Back in the locker, on the shelf above the coat hooks, where it would stay.

---

I went back to the bathroom and took the ashtray off the windowsill and brought it to the room.

There was nothing in it. I had flushed the ash; I knew that; I had watched it flush. What was in the ashtray was the grey film that lives in an ashtray regardless of cleaning — the residue of cigarettes I had not smoked, a small mark where the tin had rusted at the base. The ash I had made was not in there.

I sat on the cot with the ashtray in my lap and looked at the grey film.

Here is what I had, at this point in the day: the document, between pages thirty-four and thirty-five. The document also in my head, comma and all, *each* not *every*, bracket and not a line nine, with the closing bracket on its own indented line. I had tested myself against the original and the two versions matched. What to do with having established it — what the relationship was between the paper and the fact that the paper was now also in my head, whether having both meant something different than having only one, what I would do when something changed — I had not thought through yet, and I did not think through it then. I was nineteen years old and I had the information and I had no instructions for the next step.

I cleaned out the ashtray with the inside of the sock I had been wearing, which was the only thing I had that would serve as a cloth. It took two passes to get the grey film out of the corners. I pulled the sock back on and took the ashtray back to the bathroom and put it on the windowsill where it lived.

In the room I got under the blanket and put my coat back on top of it and lay on my back and looked at the crack in the ceiling, which runs from the light fitting to the wall above Floarea's cot and has been there, as far as I can tell, since the hostel was built. It does not have a shape. I have checked.

The district heating came on again at four in the afternoon, briefly.

## 14-the-ash

**Operative kill list:** sentence-after-the-sentence, meta-commentary on cognition, post-scene subtext naming, thesis restatement, redundant transition / re-summary. (Doina's longer wry digressive sentences are lean-into — not touched.)

### Meta-commentary on cognition

**Cut:** `; I notice it and set it aside and continue`

From the line-8 paragraph: `…a quality I do not have a name for; I notice it and set it aside and continue.` → `…a quality I do not have a name for.`

The prose has already shown the pause at eight, the difficulty of naming the quality. "I notice it" labels the cognitive act the text is already performing. Cutting it leaves the named-namelessness to land without annotation, which is stronger.

### Sentence-after-the-sentence

**Cut:** `and which tells you something about what a page and a half of handwriting actually is when you take away the paper`

From the ash paragraph: `…which is less than you would expect from a page and a half of handwriting and which tells you something about what a page and a half of handwriting actually is when you take away the paper.` → `…which is less than you would expect from a page and a half of handwriting.`

The image (a page and a half of writing reduced to a cigarette-end of ash) already carries its meaning. The "tells you something about what handwriting actually is" clause glosses the image thematically — it points at the image and announces its significance. The image sits better without it.

### Redundant transition / re-summary (×2)

**Cut 1:** `That was what the morning had established, and that was all it had established.`

In the "Here is what I had" paragraph, the preceding sentence (`I had tested myself against the original and the two versions matched`) already states what was established. This sentence restates it without adding information. The following sentence (`What to do with having established it…`) picks up the referent naturally from the preceding sentence alone.

**Cut 2:** `, which was the condition I had been in since November began and which was not getting more comfortable with familiarity`

Closing the "Here is what I had" paragraph: `I was nineteen years old and I had the information and I had no instructions for the next step, which was the condition I had been in since November began and which was not getting more comfortable with familiarity.` → `I was nineteen years old and I had the information and I had no instructions for the next step.`

The relative clause performs two moves: (a) it re-summarises the situation (we know she has been in this condition since November — the whole chapter establishes it); (b) it labels the emotional state ("not getting more comfortable with familiarity"). Both are already carried by what came before. The bare landing — "no instructions for the next step" — is more in keeping with the procedural-cold register even inside Doina's voice, and preserves the "Leave One" rule: the interior beat is the paragraph, not its closing annotation.

### Flags

None. No continuity gaps opened.

# 18 noiembrie

The two women are at the table three seats down, and the one facing Ilinca is saying *Strada Mihai*.

Ilinca does not look up from the payroll summary. October, third section — fifty-two names in the roster column, four absences in the column to the left, dates in the correct format, certification status noted beside each. The pen moves to the next entry.

The woman facing her is from Hall B, the adjacent section. She has a green wool scarf she has worn every November Ilinca can remember; the scarf is knotted at the throat and slightly felted at the knot from repeated washing. The woman with her back to Ilinca has short grey hair, cut close, and she is not someone Ilinca knows by name. The canteen smells of boiled potato and beneath it the mill's own smell — hot-wet synthetic fiber, the close sour warmth that does not leave a building this size even in the hours when the machinery has stopped.

Someone from the investigations office came to the building last week. The neighbor on the friend's bloc, a woman with a young child, third floor — she was the one they asked for. She went in on Thursday. She came home and made supper and said nothing to anyone.

Viorica Damian's bloc is at the end of Strada Mihai. The neighbor on Viorica Damian's bloc, the woman with the child: she had confirmed this node through the bread relay on Day 13 — no name, just the existence of it, a woman who had asked for the copy and gotten it last spring. A G4 on the N4 branch. Munteanu has now gotten the name. Munteanu has been to the bloc neighbor and brought her in for questions.

He is in G4.

One step from Viorica Damian — the G3, the cellar woman's sister. Two steps from the cellar copy itself.

The grey-haired woman with her back to Ilinca asks something that the sound of trays on the serving ledge covers almost entirely. The green-scarf woman says: the neighbor came home pale. She made cabbage. She went to bed before eight.

Ilinca finishes the entry for absence four, draws the line beneath the third-section totals, collects the sheets, clips them with the correct clip, and sets them on the return tray. She carries the tray to the service window and slides it through the slot. The corridor back to the administrative wing is colder than the canteen; someone has left the door at the fire stair open. She can see the grey November courtyard through the gap. She closes the door as she passes.

The heating pipe is running today. She can hear it at the corner join — a low, intermittent sound, the heat finding its way through.

---

At her desk she opens the Q4 materials ledger to the page she was working before the canteen break, then does not continue it immediately.

She looks at the second shelf. The 1983 ledger sits between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission, where it has been since she placed it there fourteen months ago. She does not take it out.

N1: in the ledger spine. N2 and the Livia branch: closed, confirmed clean, two nodes, no further transmission. N3, Elena's copy: confirmed clean on Day 5, pending today's contact. N4, the cellar copy, made the night of 3 November 1983 in twenty minutes by the light of a gap in a coal-cellar door: correct, as she has always assessed it. N10, Viorica Damian, G3 on N4, the Strada Mihai laundry. N18, the bloc neighbor with the child, G4 on N4, name not held: now in Munteanu's dosar penal.

She is a contacted node — whatever she knows and whatever she said are now in a room Ilinca cannot enter, in a file she has no way to read.

Munteanu is in G4. He does not have the G3 — Viorica Damian has not been formally spoken to, not from what Ilinca can see. He does not have the cellar copy. He is two steps from N4.

She returns to the Q4 materials ledger and writes the next line.

---

Marta's youngest daughter is eleven years old. On Tuesdays and Thursdays she walks from the school building on Strada Crișan to the tram stop at Piața Bobâlna, leaving just before one o'clock. The route passes the far end of Strada Avântului. Ilinca has been tracking this since the last week of October — timed it on a Thursday afternoon from the entrance of her building, nothing in her hands and no reason anyone would note.

At five minutes to one she is at the building door. The November sky has held the same flat grey since morning: no wind, no break in the cloud, the daylight the colour of a corridor with one working bulb. The cold when the door opens is direct. At one minute to one the daughter comes around the corner from the school direction: coat buttoned, bag over one shoulder, the dark braid Marta has been putting her hair in since she was small. She does not break stride.

Ilinca says, in the register she would use for something she is not saying to the daughter at all: *Just checking that Elena is keeping the influenza quiet. Not coming in until she's well. Let us know if she needs anything.*

The daughter passes without turning. She goes around the corner toward the tram.

Ilinca goes back inside and upstairs to the administrative wing. She sits at her desk and opens the November payroll for the fourth section and writes the first name.

---

At eleven minutes past two the daughter comes back along the return route. She passes the building entrance at her usual pace and her voice carries close enough to reach through the open door:

*She says she's fine. She's been careful. And — there's a woman in the second stairwell, third floor, in her bloc. Has one. Not from Elena — from somewhere else. The woman has been asking around. About the questions.*

She is at the corner before the last word settles. Ilinca has the door handle in one hand and the cold of the stairwell at her back.

She goes upstairs. She sits at her desk. She looks at the fourth-section payroll for a moment, then folds it to the next page and continues from where she was.

---

A G4 on the N3 branch. A woman in Elena's bloc, second stairwell, third floor. She received her copy from an intermediate source — a G3 on the N3 branch that Ilinca has no name for, someone between Elena and this woman in the building Elena has lived in for six years. The N3 branch extends past Elena through a generation she cannot see, to a node in Elena's own building that Elena did not give to her.

The woman in the second stairwell has been asking around — which means she knows something has started, and she wants to understand how close it has come. Ilinca cannot reach her. She has a stairwell and a floor.

She counts: node eight.

Eight nodes held. Munteanu: three. The two counts have been moving in the same direction all month. She does not close the gap by adding a node; she only describes the shape of the thing that is larger than she thought.

She finishes the fourth-section payroll at a quarter past five, files it, collects her coat from the hook behind the door, and walks the fifteen minutes home through the November dark.

---

The lamp by the kitchen table is the forty-watt bulb on the extension cord. She has moved it so the light falls on the table rather than the counter, but at forty watts a cord's length makes a circle with edges and the edges are not far from the centre. Beyond the circle: the refrigerator, the window, the counter with the plate she rinsed when she came in and left to dry. The glass of water she filled at six she has not touched.

The pale-green grocery notebook is on the table near her right hand. She brought it out from the coat pocket and put it on the table. She has not opened it.

N2 is clean. She made N2 at her desk, in her office, in full light, with the blue-black ink she uses for fair copies. She can see that document clearly, even now: the upstroke of the y in *properly* at the end of line four, where the nib caught slightly on the paper grain; the bracket drawn below line eight in the same ink, two strokes and a right-angle corner — down, then across the bottom to form the angle, then down again — the bracket enclosing what the bracket was supposed to enclose. She was not in a hurry. She had the light she needed. She knows what she wrote in N2.

N3 she made in Elena's kitchen. Less light than her office, enough to work by. She checked it against N1 when she finished, line by line, and the bracket was there. She knows what she wrote in N3.

N4 she made in a coal cellar on Strada Crișan on the night of 3 November 1983. The cellar door was open the width of a hand — held with one foot and one elbow, because the woman who owned the cellar had not offered to hold it and there was no one else. Twenty minutes. Pencil — the one she had been carrying in the lining of the bag since October, short by November, still working. She copied eight lines. Then she copied the element below line eight.

She checked the copy once, forward, in sequence — presence, not category. Each element in the place where she had put it, in the order she had put it. She did not read it against N1. N1 was at the apartment. The cellar was not the apartment, and the woman at her shoulder could not wait any longer than she was already waiting.

She has been running the question away from this point for thirteen months.

The mutation is in the N4 branch. This she has understood since Day 9. The N2 branch is clean; the N3 branch is clean — Elena confirmed it again today through a child going to the tram. Whatever turned the bracketed ninth element into a numbered ninth line entered through the N4 branch. That is what the arithmetic shows. That is what the confirmed cleanliness of N2 and N3 requires.

The question she has not asked is: where in the N4 branch?

N1 has a bracket below line eight. She drew the bracket. Inside it she wrote — among the other words — *Do not wait for the morning.* She can hear herself writing those words in the cellar: the sound of a worn pencil on the back of a supply receipt, the cold coming through the door gap, the dark that was not complete but was nearly complete, the coal smell that has not left the inside of her nose in thirteen months. She wrote *Do not wait for the morning.* She is certain of the words.

The character that comes before the words is the one she cannot see.

A left bracket is two strokes. A nine is a circle closed at the left with a stem descending. She writes both in the course of her work — brackets in the margin columns, nines in the numerical sequences. She made the cellar copy without full light and without time to spare, and she checked it forward, in the order she had written it, and if a nine had stood where the bracket should have been, she would have read *nine* and understood it as correct. A person reading back a document they have just written in the dark reads intention, not error. The check confirmed that each element was present. The check did not confirm whether the bracket was still a bracket or had become something else in the twenty minutes and the near-dark.

She has not seen N4 since the night she handed it over. The cellar copy is on Strada Crișan, in a place Ilinca does not go, in the possession of the woman who waited at her shoulder. Thirteen months. She has been almost certain for all of them — almost certain of the bracket, of the two strokes and the right-angle corner, of the shape she knows how to make without thinking.

She picks up the grocery notebook and opens it to the first blank page. She looks at it for a moment. She closes it.

Outside the window the stairwell light on Strada Avântului is off. It went off at seventeen-thirty; it will come on again at eighteen-thirty. It is not yet eighteen-thirty. She is in the lamp's circle at the kitchen table, in the dark that the circle does not quite reach, and she cannot tell — in the account she keeps, in the column she has been maintaining for thirteen months without a single entry she could not defend — whether what she holds under N4 is a bracket or a nine.

# 20 noiembrie

The laundry on Strada Mihai occupied the ground floor of the first bloc at the end of the street, where the street bent south and the buildings ran close to the river. The original window frames had been removed when the laundry took over the space; in their place were long horizontal panes of industrial glass that condensed all day and ran gray water down the inside of the sill in thin, continuous channels. From outside, the glass was opaque with moisture. From inside, the light came through diffusely, without shadows, only a general brightness that made the steam visible as it moved between the wash lines.

Munteanu arrived at seven forty-five. The morning delivery rush began at eight. He knew this because he had confirmed it on Thursday, the week he first opened the Petrescu file, before he had any particular reason to come here.

He gave his name at the intake counter, which was a solid wooden shelf running along the right wall, covered in receipt books and a mechanical adding machine and two rubber stamps in their stamp pads. The woman behind the counter was not Damian, Viorica — she was younger, managing the intake receipts and the telephone and the door simultaneously, with the expression of someone accustomed to all three arriving at once. She called to a young woman in a rubber apron near the first wash line, who put down what she was carrying and went to look.

The laundry was a long room — thirty metres at least, possibly more. The ceiling was high enough to accommodate the lines strung from wall to wall in four rows, with institutional cottons and work shirts hanging in stages from dry to damp, so that the back of the room smelled different from the front: the front end smelled of wet and industrial soap and the mineral scale building up inside the caldrons; the back smelled of something on its way to being clean. Along the left wall three caldrons ran at temperature, releasing steam that collected at the ceiling and came back down as condensation. The condensation ran down every vertical surface. In November this meant the walls were wet to the touch. The floor near the caldrons was dark and slick.

Viorica Damian came from behind the fourth wash line.

She was in her mid-forties, broad-shouldered, with her hair pinned close under a cloth cap pushed slightly back at the forehead. She came down the length of the room at a steady pace — no hesitation, no change of speed when she saw him, nothing that would be visible from the intake counter. She looked at him the way she might look at a form that required filling: correctly, and without pleasure. Whatever he was, she had encountered the category before. She was wary in the particular way of people who had been through official questions before and had come out the other side without explanation. She was not frightened.

They sat at a folding metal table near the condensed window. The table had a ledger open on it; she closed it and moved it to one side before she sat, the gesture automatic, as if she cleared this table several times a day.

He told her he was there about a document. A handwritten document concerning health procedures that had been circulated in the community. He had reason to believe she was in possession of a copy.

She said: yes.

He said he would need it.

She said she would get it.

She went to the back of the room. She was gone perhaps two minutes. When she returned she was carrying a piece of paper folded twice into a compact square. She set it on the folding table. It was the back of a laundry work-order form — printed in pale green ink on institutional paper thin enough that the delivery columns on the other side showed through as faint ruled lines beneath the handwriting. The writing on the back was in pencil, careful and even, in a hand that was not hers. The paper had been handled enough that the fold lines had gone soft and the corners had rounded.

He put it in the evidence envelope without opening it.

He asked where she had gotten it.

From her sister, she said.

He took out his notebook and turned to the page he wanted. The name was already there, in his own handwriting, eight days old: *Moga, Rodica.* Below it the address: Dorobanților, the second bloc on the corner of Eminescu.

He turned the notebook toward her and asked if that was correct.

She looked at the page without touching it. She said: yes, that was correct.

He asked whether she had passed a copy to anyone else.

She said no.

He asked whether there was anything else she wanted to tell him.

She looked at the condensed window for a moment. She said she didn't think so.

He thanked her. He collected the evidence envelope and closed his notebook and stood. He went back down the length of the room — past the first wash line, past the second, past the caldrons and the rising steam that fogged his glasses at the temples — and let himself out through the entry door.

---

The street outside was cold after the heat of the laundry. He stood at the corner of the building and let his glasses clear. Three women were coming from the direction of the main road with laundry bundles, the beginning of the morning rush he had timed to miss. He walked in the other direction, toward the station, and the cold came through his coat collar and settled at the back of his neck.

There was fog off the river. It sat low along the street, below the level of the bloc windows, so that the buildings looked as if they were floating on it. He walked through it without looking at it particularly. The name already on the page, the address confirmed.

Moga, Rodica. G2. One step from the source.

He had not yet visited her. He had the name and address from eight days ago, from the interview with Lucia Gal, who had said she had gotten it from a woman she knew from before the mill — not from the mill itself, from before. He had written the name down and kept working in the other direction, outward and downward, because you built the tree — you mapped what you had — before you walked up it. By the time you reached the upper nodes you needed to know what you were looking for.

---

He was back at his desk by twenty past nine. He took off his coat and put it over the chair back without hanging it and sat down at once.

He opened the evidence envelope and placed the Damian copy on the desk beside the folder with the others.

Four copies. He laid them side by side and weighted the corners with what was at hand: a stapler at the left, a spare ink tin in the middle, an empty buletin folder at the right, and the flat spine of his working notebook pressed across the bottom edges to keep them from curling. The desk was not large enough for four full sheets without overlap; he arranged them in sequence, left to right, and accepted the slight overlap at the edges.

He read line nine on each in order.

The Gal copy first — he knew it, but he read it: *9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* Written in blue pencil on the grey AFE production form; the nine stood cleanly in the column, followed by the instruction.

The sister-in-law's copy, from the fourth of November: *9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* Smaller hand, black ink, ordinary household paper. The nine was the same.

The Damian copy — the one he had just collected, on the back of the green laundry form, pencil: *9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

He read this one twice. The instruction was longer than the other copies' line nine. The wording was different — not *in the morning* but *do not wait for the morning*, which was, strictly, the opposite direction. And yet the format was the same: a numbered nine, the instruction treated as a list item, sequenced after the eighth.

He wrote in his working notebook: *G3 (Damian/Str. Mihai). Line 9: numbered. Wording: "do not wait for the morning" — differs from G4 and G5. Numbered nine present at G3 level. Source of numbered nine: Moga, Rodica (address confirmed).*

He underlined the last sentence.

Then he picked up the fourth copy. He had collected it four days ago during the general canvassing — a woman who had produced it when he asked without needing to be asked twice, who had said she did not know exactly where she had gotten it: from someone she used to know, she thought, from before her current section. He had written that down and kept moving. The copy itself he had placed in the folder and had not examined closely since.

He laid it on the desk, at the far right, past the other three, and read the terminal section.

There was no line nine. There were eight numbered lines — the same format, the same block structure he had been reading for two weeks — and then below the eighth line there was a bracket. A hand-drawn bracket in ink darker than the surrounding text, as if the pen had been pressed down. Two vertical strokes and a horizontal bar connecting them at the top, enclosing two lines of text that ran slightly smaller than the list above:

*7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why.*
*Do not wait for the morning.*

He read it twice. Then he read the three numbered copies again. Then he read the bracketed copy again.

He laid all four side by side and looked at them.

Three copies had a line nine. One copy had a bracket below line eight. The content inside the bracket was close to what the Damian copy said in line nine — not identical, but in the same register, the same instruction. The difference was not in the instruction. The difference was in where on the page the instruction lived and what kind of thing it was treated as being.

A line in a list was a step. A bracket below a step was something else — an annotation, a condition, a note that interrupted the sequence to say something the sequence could not say. The three copies with a numbered nine had turned whatever the bracket was into a ninth step. The copy with the bracket had kept it as a bracket.

He wrote: *Two formats for the terminal instruction. Three copies: numbered line 9. One copy: bracket below line 8. The format is the variable. Which format is the source.*

He drew a line under the question. He did not answer it.

He thought about it for a moment — about which direction a change of this kind would run, from bracket to numbered step or from numbered step to bracket — and then he thought about the fact that he was still two nodes from the answer and the answer was sitting in an apartment on Dorobanților, eight days written in his notebook, unvisited.

He put the four copies back in the folder in order and closed the folder.

---

The call came through the front desk at seventeen minutes past four. He picked up on the second ring.

His captain said: good afternoon. The Petrescu matter — how was it proceeding.

Munteanu said it was progressing. He had traced the document chain through three generations on the principal branch and had today confirmed the G3 node. The chain now ran clearly from the G5 copy back to a G2 source — the next visit would be to that source, in the coming days.

His captain said he was glad to hear it. He paused briefly. He said: the fifth of December was the administrative deadline for filing a determination with the procuror's office. He assumed Munteanu was aware.

Munteanu said: yes.

His captain said: he was saying it because awareness and action were not always the same relation, in his experience.

Munteanu said he understood.

His captain said: good. He would speak to him Friday.

The receiver went down.

Munteanu looked at his desk. The folder was closed. The ink tin and the stapler and the buletin folder were where he had left them after he cleared the copies away. Outside the window the afternoon had gone dark without his noticing it; the courtyard light had come on at some point in the past hour, throwing a pale rectangle on the paving.

He opened his working notebook to the inside back cover, where he had been keeping his running figures.

He wrote: *20.XI — 5.XII.*

Below that, on its own line: *15.*

He looked at the number.

Fifteen days was not a short time. It was also not a long one — not for a chain this long, working from one end, with the other end still four addresses away. Fifteen days was the number he had. He was going to work with it.

He closed the notebook.

# 21 November 1984

She has not touched the November overtime summary. It sits on the right side of her desk, a pencil line at the third row where she stopped before eight. The adding machine has paper still rolled in it from yesterday's last column.

The administrative wing does not have heat until after six in the evening. She works in her coat. The sound from the weaving hall comes through the partition wall at a regular pitch — not a noise now, after fifteen years, just the condition of mornings.

She went to the bread queue at six-fifteen. She goes every Thursday unless the shift has changed and the queue has moved. Niculina Hora goes every Thursday too; Ilinca has known this for two years without making use of it until this morning.

Niculina Hora lives in the bloc on the corner of Avântului and Livezilor. Her husband was at the fiber plant before the accident. She has a knee that predicts weather and a daughter who lives near the Strada Mihai laundry. Ilinca has spoken to her for perhaps fifteen minutes in total over two years: mostly queue business, once the knee, once the heating fault in Ilinca's bloc and how long the building superintendent took to file the report.

She had said: there's a woman near the Strada Mihai laundry with a little boy, in the second or third bloc on the left side. Does she go to church?

Niculina had said: same church as my daughter. Why?

Ilinca had said: a friend is looking for a paper she lent out in the spring. A recipe, something small. She thinks it might have gone that direction.

Niculina had looked at her for two seconds. A measuring look, not a hostile one. Then she said: I can ask.

The overtime summary has not moved since. She has been at the desk since eight, with the ledger forms to her left and the adding machine paper curling out of the platen, and the pencil line at the third row of the overtime summary, and the column of figures she has not started. The weaving hall runs its regular pitch through the wall. She does the payroll forms for the second-shift bonus allocation instead. She does them correctly. She puts them in the outgoing tray.

---

At eleven minutes past one, Niculina appeared at the door of the administrative wing. She does not work at the mill. The lunch queue runs outside and people step in from the cold for reasons; nobody asked. She said: my daughter says yes. To a woman from their church — she comes from near the market, they don't know her well — she gave it. One thing. In October.

Ilinca said: thank you. That's exactly what I needed.

Niculina said: I hope your friend finds her paper.

She left. Ilinca ate lunch at her desk. The thermos of tea had gone cold at six-fifteen and she had not thought to reheat it.

---

She runs the count in the columns she keeps only in her head.

N2: two nodes. Georgeta and Livia on the Eminescu side. Both clean. Branch confirmed and closed.

N3: Elena on Crângului, and the fourth-generation woman in Elena's bloc she identified three days ago, and the G3 intermediate she has not traced directly but knows exists somewhere between them. Three nodes. All of it clean; the bracket where the bracket should be.

N4: the copy she made in the cellar. And below it, three she has traced working downward from the cellar woman: the sister at the Strada Mihai laundry. The bloc neighbor with the child. Now the church woman, near the market, no name.

Three nodes below the copy she has not looked at since the night she made it. None of them verified for the format of line nine.

There is also the arm she did not trace — the branch through Viorica Damian, which Munteanu reached before her. She knows from the mill what those copies say in line nine. Numbered ninth line. Morning. Both of them.

Every branch she has traced that is not N4 is clean. Every copy she has heard of with the mutant wording is on N4's branch.

She has now used every indirect route she has. She has worked outward through N2 and N3, downward through the branches she reached first. She has mapped nine nodes. She has not turned back toward Dorobanților.

She adds the church woman and makes the count nine. She opens the overtime summary and draws a line through the third row and starts the column again.

---

The stairwell in her bloc is dark when she gets home. The light goes off at five-thirty; it is quarter past six. She counts the stairs by memory: seventeen to the first landing, eleven to the second, thirteen to the third floor. Her right hand finds the banister before she reaches for it.

Inside, she lights the lamp. Forty watts. She hangs her coat and fills the kettle and sets it on the ring. She eats bread and the last of the dripping from the tin in the window alcove — she has been meaning to render more dripping for a week and has not done it — and she washes the plate and puts it away.

Then she takes the ledger down from the second shelf.

---

Four hundred pages. Ministry of Finance format. The spine retaped with brown tape in February of this year, after the binding cracked. Second shelf, between the quarterly labour-plan compliance records and the annual balance submission. She sets it on the table and does not open it; she puts her fingers inside the back cover and finds the paper in the spine by feel. Folded twice. The fold has gone furry at the crease — it has been wet once and dried badly, the paper giving at the corners. She unfolds it flat on the table under the lamp.

She reads from line seven.

```
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
   [ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why.
     Do not wait for the morning. ]
```

The bracket. Two short horizontal strokes and one vertical, drawn in ink at the left margin below line eight. She drew it in October 1983, at this table, by this lamp. Lines one through eight were a sequence: you did each one after the previous, for as long as you needed to. The ninth element was not a step in that sequence. It was a condition that answered a different question entirely: when to stop doing the previous eight and do something else. She drew a bracket because a bracket sits outside the list. It is not the next thing. It is the thing that says: if you are here, stop counting steps and do this instead.

The ink is slightly heavy at the base of the vertical stroke. She used the wide-nib metal pen she kept for ruling that month, not the narrow-nib; the narrow-nib was empty. The wide nib put down more ink at the base of each downstroke.

She holds the paper closer to the lamp and looks at the bracket.

Two strokes she can see clearly: the top horizontal and the vertical descending from it. The lower horizontal — the stroke that makes a bracket a bracket and not a descending line — at the base. In this light, in the circle of forty watts, all three strokes are distinct.

She tilts the paper away from the lamp until the lower horizontal goes into shadow.

She tries to bring up the cellar copy. She can see the workbench. She can see lines one and two in the strip of light from the door. She can see line eight and the way the light fell on the right side of the page, on the open field of the lines. She can see herself reaching the bottom of the numbered section.

She cannot see what she wrote below line eight. She cannot see whether the shape at the left margin, in that light, was a bracket or a nine.

---

Third of November 1983. She left the mill at half five and went directly to Dorobanților. She had not arranged it in advance; the woman came to her at the end of the shift with a particular brevity, and Ilinca had said: two hours. She went back for the master at six, when the administrative wing was empty, and carried it to Dorobanților inside her coat.

The cellar was on the ground floor off the interior courtyard. Coal and old timber; the smell was wet dust and something alkaline she had never identified. She pushed the door open two centimeters to check the courtyard — empty — then held it at six or seven centimeters to give herself a strip of light on the workbench. The workbench ran along the left wall. The light from the door fell across it from the right, across the open field of the page.

She placed the master flat and angled it clockwise until the numbers on the left margin came into the better part of the light. She wrote fast; she could hear the woman's shoes at the top of the cellar stairs, the weight-shifting of someone trying not to be impatient. Twenty minutes. She checked each line in turn when she finished: the words against what she had written. She was checking for presence. She was not asking herself whether the format had been preserved — a bracket or a numbered step, a margin notation or a sequence item. She read the words. The words were correct. She folded it and went up the stairs.

What was in the dimmer half of that strip of light: the left margin. The indented part. Where the bracket was.

She looks at the bracket now.

In that light, at that angle: the top horizontal stroke would catch the edge of the light coming through the door. The vertical would drop away from it into the darker part of the strip. The lower horizontal stroke, at the base — the third stroke, the one she cannot make out when she tilts the paper away from the lamp — would be in the worst of the light. The corner of the page that the door crack could not reach.

The top horizontal and the descending vertical, without the lower bar.

She has just shown herself what that looks like.

She made one check.

---

She folds the master along the furred crease. She puts it back in the ledger spine, back cover, where her fingers found it. She carries the ledger to the second shelf and sets it between the labour-plan records and the annual balance submission, where it has to be findable.

The lamp is on. She sits at the kitchen table.

She has spent seventeen days tracing N2 and N3 and the downward branches of N4, working outward and down from every node she could reach without going back to where she started. She has not been to Dorobanților since the night of the third of November 1983.

He has the address on Dorobanților in his notebook — she knows this from the bread queue, third-hand through people who know Rodica Moga's corridor neighbors, in the way that anything on Dorobanților eventually comes back around. He has not gone there yet. One node above the cellar copy. In the coming days. That was how it had stood for a week.

In the coming days.

The lamp is on. The heat is not. Outside the window, the fog from the river has moved onto the street; she can see it at the edge of the glass. The bracket on N1 is a bracket: she drew it in this light, at this table, in October 1983.

What she wrote in the cellar in twenty minutes by a strip of light from a cracked door: she does not know. She has shown herself this evening, with a forty-watt lamp and a tilted page, what the answer probably is.

She is not going to go to Dorobanților tonight. She is going to sit with what she probably knows for a little longer. She does not get up.

## 17-nine-or-bracket

# 22 November 1984

I was on the top bunk with my shoes on, reading, at half past two in the afternoon, when someone knocked on the hostel door.

Nobody knocks on hostel doors at half past two in the afternoon. Bloc committee women knock in the evenings, when the shift rotation accounts for people being home. Factory management knocks, but they send someone from personnel and they do it in the morning. The woman across the hall knocks when she wants to borrow salt, which she does regularly and which I find endearing rather than irritating, probably because she always returns it in exactly the same quantity — not the salt, a different salt, but the same amount. She was the only person I could think of who had reason to knock on my door at that hour.

I got off the bunk and stood in the middle of the room.

The geography book was not here. The geography book was at the factory, in my locker, between the thermos that didn't seal properly and the spare coat I kept because the November shift started in the dark and ended in the dark and some mornings there was frost in the seams of the window. The locker was metal, key lock, three-digit code I had changed in September to something I hadn't told anyone. The factory was a fifteen-minute walk from the hostel in either direction, and the afternoon shift didn't end for another two hours, and the combination was in my head, not on any piece of paper.

I want to put this on the record because people have asked me about it since: I did not think, in that moment, that the geography book was safe. I thought it was at the factory and I was at the hostel and those were two different places. That was all I had. I stood in the middle of the room and I held those two facts next to each other for the length of time it takes to get off a bunk and stand on the floor.

I did not look through the gap in the door. I opened it.

He was younger than I'd expected. I have been asked: how did you have an expectation, you'd never seen him. Which is true. But it is not how expectation works. The investigation had been going for nineteen days. In nineteen days of working the night shift and standing in the bread queue in the morning and eating in the canteen and saying nothing to anyone about the geography book, you develop a picture. Mine had been wrong about his age. The rest of it — the coat, the manner, the particular way of saying *Tovarășă Marcu* in a hallway — that came out about how I had pictured it.

He had a face that was not going to be remembered for anything in particular. Not unkind. Not especially notable. The face of a man who goes to other people's places and asks questions and writes the answers in a notebook. He wore a dark coat, close-cut, the kind that came from a different shop than factory coats or bloc-committee coats. He said his name and rank. He said he would like to speak with me about a matter.

He said it the way men in his position say it, which is in a way that means: you will come.

I said: I need to get my coat.

My coat was on the hook inside the door. I reached back and took it off the hook and put it on, in the room, facing him, without turning around to look at anything else in the room. I put on the coat and I went with him and the door closed behind me. I did not look back at the room and I did not look back at the stairwell and I did not think about going back to the factory and getting the geography book before we went wherever we were going. I put on my coat and I went.

I will remember that for a long time. Not as something I'm proud of and not as something I'm ashamed of. I went, and the geography book stayed in the locker.

---

Outside it was cold and the sky was already going from grey to the pale orange of streetlights coming on. He had a vehicle — a grey Dacia, parked at the kerb in front of the hostel gate with another man in the front seat who did not look at me. I got in the back. The drive to the station took six minutes on the route we took, which went up past the main square and past the department store with one window lit and one dark and the hardware shop closed early. The man in the front seat drove carefully, at the speed of someone who did not want to be noticed. I looked out the window. There was a queue outside the bread shop on the corner of the square — I recognised the angle of bodies, the way people lean slightly inward in a queue on a cold day, using each other as windbreak without making eye contact.

The station had a plain door on Strada Republicii. He showed me in, through a hallway that smelled like the inside of every official building in Dej — linoleum and a heating pipe doing its best — and into a room off the right side of the hallway. The room had a table and two chairs and a window with frosted glass. The frosted glass let in daylight but not anything you could see through. There was a lamp on the table, lit.

On the table, in addition to the lamp, there were four pieces of paper inside clear evidence envelopes. I could see from where I sat that they were paper documents, handwritten, roughly the size of what I had in the locker.

I did not try to read them from the far side of the table. I sat down and I looked at them without moving my head toward them and I put my hands in my lap.

He sat down across from me and set his notebook to the left of the envelopes and asked if I wanted tea. I said no. He said: we have reason to believe you may be in possession of a document that has been circulating in the factory district. He did not name the document. He did not describe it. He asked if I could tell him anything about it.

I said: I don't know what you mean.

He looked at me for a moment in the way of someone who has done this many times and understands that it takes a while for people to get to the place where they can speak to each other about what is actually being spoken about. He wrote something in his notebook. He said: Tovarășă Marcu, a piece of paper. Handwritten. Medical in nature.

I said: I found it.

I want to be clear about what happened in that sentence, because people have asked. I did not decide ahead of time to say those words. They arrived already decided, the way a thing arrives when you have spent nineteen days not letting yourself think about it.

He said: tell me more about that.

I said: I found it on the bus. Between the seats. I was sitting in the third row from the back and it was on the floor, between the seats, and I picked it up. He asked which route. I said the number 4, the morning direction. He asked when. I said last spring, I don't remember the exact month, sometime in April or May. He asked if I had been alone. I said: there were other people on the bus. He said: did anyone see you pick it up. I said: I don't think so. He wrote all of this down with his even handwriting.

He asked: and you kept it.

I said: I kept it because I didn't know what it was and I couldn't throw it away without knowing what it was. I had it in the geography book. I kept it in the geography book because the geography book is a thing I own but never open — it was there from when I was in school and I never gave it back — and I thought it was safer than keeping it in a pocket. That was all. I didn't think about it much after that.

He wrote. He was not rushing.

This is what I said and it was true. Every sentence of it was true, in the way that a set of true sentences can describe a true thing and leave the whole of the true thing sitting in the middle of them, in the space the sentences make around it, untouched. I found it on the bus, on the number 4, in the morning, in spring. I kept it in the geography book. Both of those things happened. The part I did not say — the only part, the single thing I did not say — was that when I picked it up from the seat, I picked it up because the woman sitting across from me, who had a face like a closed shop and had not spoken a word to me, had placed it there. Had put it in my hand first, actually, and I had looked at it for one second, and then she had looked out the window. She got off two stops later and did not look back and I have not seen her since.

That part I did not say. I will not say it.

He reached into the evidence envelopes and slid one toward me across the table, and through the plastic I could see the handwriting. Not just handwriting: my handwriting, the geography book cover, number 7 written in my hand on the front because I had numbered my school books and never bothered to change it. The locker had been opened. I had known the locker could be opened; this was a thing I had known, and had set next to the other thing I knew, and this was the result of that particular arithmetic.

He asked: can you identify this.

I said: yes. That's mine.

He asked how I meant that. I said: my copy. The one I found. He nodded. He picked up the envelope and read from it. He read:

*7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

He set it back down. He asked: is that how you read that section. The terminal section. Is that what it said.

I said: yes. That's what it says.

He looked at the other envelopes. He moved one a few centimetres toward me — not completely across the table, just enough that I could see the paper inside at an angle. He read from that one:

*If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He set it back. He looked at me. He said: you can see there's a difference.

I said: yes.

He said: you'd say your copy reads the first version, not the second.

I said: yes. That's what mine says.

I had memorized the whole document, every line of it, including the bracket, in the hostel bathroom five days ago. I knew what the difference was. I knew what it meant. I said yes, and I looked at him, and I did not say anything else about it, because I was nineteen years old in a room with a lamp and frosted glass and I had learned early that in rooms like this you answer what you're asked and you do not volunteer the rest.

He made a note. He said: you understand this document is evidence in a criminal investigation. I said: I understand. He said: we're going to hold you here for further questioning while we clarify a few things. I said: what things. He said: where you got the document.

I said: I told you where I found it.

He said: I know what you told me.

Not unkindly. Without any particular weight on it. He reached for his notebook, opened it to a new page, set his pen in the binding.

I sat back in the chair. The lamp put most of its light down on the evidence envelopes, and the rest of the room was November grey. Through the frosted glass, the street outside was dark now; the night shift had started without me. The geography book was in the locker at the factory, fifteen minutes from this chair, and it would stay there until someone with a key had a reason to go there and open it.

The man across the table from me reached for his pen.

## 18-the-hostel-door

Operative kill list (from `canon/style.md` `## Failure modes`): sentence-after-the-sentence, meta-commentary on cognition, post-scene subtext naming, thesis restatement, redundant transition / re-summary. **Cut B.** Removed the clause `and those two things follow from each other in ways I understood at the time and understand better now.` from the sentence ending paragraph 12. Sentence now ends: `I went, and the geography book stayed in the locker.`

# 23 November 1984

She is correcting the November payroll when Daniela Lungu opens the door without knocking.

Lungu is the factory committee secretary. She handles meeting minutes, internal correspondence, the directives that come down from the enterprise administration requiring annotations within fourteen days. She usually arrives with a form — the pale green of the personnel department or the off-white of the supply section — and she usually knocks. This morning she does neither. She stops one step inside the door and holds a personnel form against her forearm and looks at the desk without looking at Ilinca directly.

She says: Tovarășă Roșca. The October transport allocation correction. You'll need it for the quarterly submission.

Ilinca says: leave it on the corner.

Lungu sets it on the corner of the desk. She remains where she is. The radiator is off; it comes on at six in the evening, after the weaving hall has had the shared pipe first, and until then the administrative wing holds its cold completely. The chemicals from the fiber hall drift in through a gap somewhere above the window frame — a wet-acrid smell that Ilinca reported to the facilities division in January and again in March, both times receiving a form confirming that the matter had been registered. She has stopped reporting it.

Lungu says: I heard something this morning. Through Aurel in personnel.

Ilinca keeps her pencil on the paper. She says nothing.

Lungu says: one of the night-shift girls was taken in yesterday afternoon. She pauses. She says: Marcu. The one from the hostel on Strada Vasile. She had — a document, apparently.

Ilinca writes a number in the column. She looks at it and sees it is the number she meant to write. She says: I see.

Lungu goes. The door clicks shut.

---

Ilinca does not move for a moment. Through the south-facing window, the November morning is flat and pale, clouds that have come in low off the plateau and are not going anywhere. The looms are running in the hall beyond the administrative wing wall; she can feel the particular vibration of loom hall two, which has been running rough since mid-October, a tension problem that has been on the maintenance schedule since she reported it and has not been addressed. She has not reported it a second time.

She finishes the line she was on. She counts the remaining lines on the payroll sheet: three. She picks up her pencil and sets it down and picks it up again.

Doina Marcu. The name is in the payroll register the way every name is in the payroll register, in the column assigned to night-shift production workers, loom hall two. Started two years ago; came from a village outside town and was placed in the factory hostel. Monthly salary, corrected in June when the enterprise posted the wage schedule adjustment. Signed the mandatory health examination form in September — a handwriting that slants slightly to the right. Year of birth: 1965.

She has never spoken with her. She has never given her anything.

She knows Doina Marcu by the trace she left in forms that Ilinca is required to maintain and required to produce on demand. That is all.

The payroll sheet is waiting. Somewhere in loom hall two the rough vibration runs on. Outside, the clouds are sitting on the ridge above the river and the light is not going to improve before dark, which is four hours away.

---

If Munteanu went to Doina Marcu with her name already written in his notebook, he came to her through a branch. Not a canvass. Lungu said: *the one from the hostel on Strada Vasile*. An investigator running a general canvass of the mill's night shift would have spoken to many people; many people would have been mentioned. Lungu mentioned one, because there was one, because a single name had been given to Munteanu by someone below it on the same line.

A name before the visit.

Ilinca has the N2 branch: Georgeta, one neighbor in the next bloc, two nodes, both confirmed, end of transmission. Neither of them is a night-shift worker in loom hall two.

She has the N3 branch: Elena, two women Elena gave copies to, and the G4 node she traced — the woman in Elena's bloc whose daughter had asked. That G4 node is not a factory-floor worker. The N3 names she has collected in two months of careful relayed inquiry do not include a night-shift worker in loom hall two.

That leaves the N4 branch.

---

The N4 branch. She has mapped it at a distance, working through bread-queue acquaintances and delivery-relay contacts, counting nodes on a branch she has been unwilling to approach at the center. She has traced three G3 and G4 nodes below the cellar copy. The G5 node she added last week is the church woman near the market, whose name she does not know. Not one of those nodes is a night-shift worker in loom hall two.

Which means the branch is longer than she mapped. One of the G4 nodes she found — the bloc neighbor with the child, or the pharmacy acquaintance — gave a copy to someone Ilinca has not traced. And Doina Marcu is that untraced node. Or Doina is on the N3 branch, in the territory Ilinca has not fully walked, a G4 or G5 node below a G3 she never identified.

Either way: Munteanu, coming up from Doina, goes to whoever gave Doina her copy. Then to whoever gave that person theirs. One step at a time, backwards along a line. If the line is N4, it terminates at the cellar copy. And the person who made the cellar copy is Ilinca.

If the line is N3, it terminates at Elena's copy, then at N3, then at N1. And the person who made N1 is also Ilinca.

She has understood for two weeks, in an abstract way, that both branches terminate at her. What Lungu gave her this morning is the thing that was on the path before the terminus. A name from the payroll register. A year of birth. A hostel on Strada Vasile.

---

She does not know which branch Doina is on. She does not know whether Doina's copy carries the mutation. If Doina's copy is on the N3 branch, it has the bracket; it is clean; the mutation never passed through it. If it is on the N4 branch, it may or may not carry the mutation, depending on which generation it is and which path from the cellar copy it followed.

Munteanu has the copy — he would have it, that is the only reason a name would be in his notebook before the visit. He can see what it says. If the copy has the bracket, he can see she is on the clean branch. Whether that matters depends on whether he understands what the bracket means. Whether it matters further depends on whether understanding it is enough to release someone from custody.

Possession is enough for a charge. A clean copy is still a copy.

There is a nineteen-year-old girl who was not at work this morning, who is in a room somewhere on Strada Republicii, and who is there because she is a node in a network whose origin is the desk Ilinca is sitting at. Whether Doina's copy is clean or corrupted does not change that fact.

The nineteen-year-old does not know who made the first paper. She may not know how many generations she is from it. She is in the room because she has it, or had it, and because someone followed the line to her. If the line she is on is the N4 line, she is on the line that failed. If it is the N3 line, she is not.

Ilinca cannot determine which it is without asking, and asking is the one action she cannot take.

---

If she went to the woman on Dorobanților. If she asked to see the cellar copy. If the cellar copy showed what she has been afraid for two weeks it shows — the numbered ninth line where the bracket should be, written in a coal cellar by the strip of light from a door, by a hand that was working quickly because there was no time to work slowly. If all of that is true, then she could take two pieces of paper to the Miliție station on Strada Republicii. N1 and N4. The master and the copy. She could lay them side by side on a desk and say: here is what the ninth element is, and here is the copy where it stopped being that and became a line in a list. Here is the date I made it. November 1983. Here is the difference I did not see when I checked it once and folded it and gave it away. He would look at the bracket and then at the numbered line and he would understand the origin.

The girl from the hostel on Strada Vasile would go home.

Ilinca would not go home.

She knows this the way she knows the quarterly balance — not because she has worked through it step by step in this moment but because the arithmetic has been sitting in her since the fourth of November and she has checked it enough times that she does not need to check it again. The sum is the same every time. Two documents in front of Munteanu. One resolution. One accounting.

---

She gets up from the desk and takes the 1983 ledger from the second shelf. The standard Ministry of Finance form-book, four hundred pages, binding retaped in February with brown tape after the spine cracked during the winter. She sets it on the desk. She opens it to where she left off this morning. The spine lies flat. In the fold at the spine, N1 is there — she can see the pale edge of it, the paper that has been folded in a dim place for over a year and has gone slightly yellow at the crease. She does not need to take it out. She knows what it says. She wrote it in October 1983 at this desk, at this lamp, and she has read it perhaps forty times since then. She knows the bracket. She knows its three strokes — two horizontals and a vertical — and she knows the lines inside it and she knows the last line, which she added last because she was afraid of leaving it out, which she put in the bracket because it was not a step in the sequence of steps and she needed to make that visible. She can read it without unfolding the paper.

*Do not wait for the morning.*

She looks at the November payroll actuals. The column has three entries left to verify. She closes the ledger.

She sets it back on the second shelf in the correct position, spine forward, between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission. She sits down at her desk. The chair creaks at the back joint, as it has since spring. The payroll sheet is where she left it. The pencil is where she left it. Outside the south window the November light is the same as it was an hour ago.

Twenty days since the fourth of November. Thirteen days to the fifth of December.

The lamp is on. The ledger is on the shelf. The pencil is in her hand and she holds it without moving.
