# 24–25 November 1984

He came in before the duty officer brought her. The questioning room was on the north side of the building, facing the courtyard wall, and by eight in the morning it held only the remnant cold that the radiator had not yet addressed and a flat, grey light coming in through a window that hadn't been cleaned since spring. He set both envelopes on the table, took the contents out without removing the evidence log sheet from each, and laid them flat. He straightened both sheets so their left edges lined up and their top edges were even, and then he sat down and looked at them.

The first was Marcu's. He had spent two evenings with it already: returning to this room after the workday, switching the lamp on, sitting with both sheets in front of him and no notebook, not writing, just looking. The paper was school exercise paper — the red margin line running down the left side, seventy or eighty ruled lines per sheet, the kind sold in blocks of four at the school supply section of the Alimentara on Strada Republicii. Blue pen, medium nib, the letters slanting backward slightly, as if the writer had learned to write quickly and had slowed down for this and not entirely adjusted. Eight numbered lines, clean and evenly spaced, and then the ninth position: not a number. A hand-drawn bracket in the left margin, two horizontal strokes and one vertical, the text beside it running across two lines and ending below the lower margin of the numbered list.

*7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

The second envelope held a copy from the Petrescu chain. He had several; he had chosen this one because it was the clearest to read. Standard graph-rule notebook paper, the handwriting rounder and more even, the line spacing wider. He read the ninth line: *9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He had looked at these two ninth positions for two evenings and had not resolved what they meant for the case in any way he could write into the formal file. He had resolved what they meant for the document, which was a different thing.

The duty officer brought her in at eight forty-five.

She sat in the chair facing the lamp — the same chair she had used two days earlier, the same angle, her back to the courtyard window. She put her hands flat on the table and did not look at the two sheets.

He said: I want to show you these again.

She said: all right.

He indicated the first sheet — hers — and read the bracket text aloud. *Seven or eight — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.* He indicated the second and read the ninth line. *Nine — if seven or eight, take her in in the morning.*

He said: two different versions of the same instruction, in the same position in the same document. One says to take her in and not to wait. The other says to take her in in the morning. Your copy says the first version.

She looked at both sheets. She said: yes. That's what mine says.

He said: I need to know where you got the copy that says the first version. The difference between the two versions goes back to wherever your copy came from — every copy above yours will also say the first version. I'm going to follow that chain either way. I'd prefer to start from the right place.

She said: I found it on the bus. I told you that.

He asked: which bus.

She said: the number four. Morning direction. Last spring. She was the only one in that section of the seats.

He made a note in his working file: *Marcu, D., second questioning. "Found on bus." Consistent with prior statement. No additional information. Unable to verify or disprove.*

He waited ten minutes and asked again: had anyone mentioned this kind of document to her before she found it. She said no. He waited another ten minutes and asked whether she'd known, when she picked it up, what she was looking at. She said she'd read it and understood what it was for. He wrote: *Confirms she read it. Confirms she understood its function. Claims no prior contact with document or its contents. Claim is unverifiable from current evidence.*

He thanked her and had the duty officer take her back.

---

He sat for a while with the two sheets on the table. The radiator had made some progress; the room was no longer actively cold, only cool in the way that rooms are cool when they've been cold for a long time and the warmth hasn't yet moved through the furniture.

The bracket was older. If you read the Marcu copy and then the Petrescu-chain copy in the order they'd been made, the bracket came first: it occupied the margin, outside the numbered sequence, set apart from the eight numbered lines. Someone, at some point, had copied the bracket document and given the bracket a number — and from that copy forward, the ninth position was a numbered line. Every copy on the Petrescu chain had the number. The Marcu copy had the bracket. Which meant the Marcu copy had not been copied from the document where the number was assigned.

Her copy's ancestor had the bracket. Her ancestor's ancestor had the bracket, and so on, back to the point where the bracket branch and the numbered branch had come from the same place. That common point had the bracket.

He wrote in the formal file: *N14 (Marcu) — bracket format in ninth position. Divergence from numbered format in Petrescu chain pre-dates N14's entry into transmission. N14 probably descends from a different G2-level source than the numbered-format copies.*

What he did not write in the formal file was the rest of the reasoning. Because Marcu's copy was on the bracket branch, and because the mutation he was following — the numbered ninth line in its shortened form — had entered the numbered branch somewhere below its G2 source, her copy had not passed through the shortening point. She could still be a node in the transmission; her refusal to name her source was its own problem, unresolved. But the numbered branch and the bracket branch had different G2 ancestors. He needed the numbered branch's G2 ancestor, not the bracket branch's. And he had that address.

He slid both sheets back into their envelopes and put them in the drawer.

---

Mureșan knocked at half past three. He came in with an evidence envelope and set it on the desk. He said: a woman at eighteen, entry A, fourth floor, Strada Mihai. Same bloc as Damian. He'd been canvassing the building that morning as part of the production-floor sweep; she'd answered the door and handed over the document before he'd finished explaining why he was there. He'd taken a statement and sent her home.

Munteanu waited until Mureșan had closed the door. Then he put on his jacket against the cold from the courtyard window and opened the envelope.

The paper was mill stationery — AFE letterhead printed on the front, text written on the blank reverse. The paper had been folded lengthwise, once, and the crease was worn deep. The handwriting was precise, the letters slightly too large for the space, so the lines grew crowded near the right margin and the last word of each line was compressed. He read through the numbered lines.

Line six: *Burn nothing at all until she is well. Wash and keep.*

He had that phrasing from Damian's copy, and only from Damian's copy. No other document in his collection used it. He made a note in the margin of his working sheet: *"nothing at all" in line 6 — cf. Damian (N10). Probable descent from Damian or Damian's immediate source.*

He read to the end. The ninth line was a numbered line, the longer form — the same wording as the Damian copy's ninth position, different from the shortened form in the Petrescu copies.

He put the new copy in the third drawer. He wrote the count in his working sheet: six.

He checked the date on his desk calendar. November twenty-fourth. He wrote in the margin: *Damian bloc, 24 Nov. G4 on N4 branch (inferred from line 6 variant). Long form in line 9. Added to file.*

---

He stayed at his desk until past seven. When the room was dark enough that the desk lamp was the only light not coming from the street, he took all six envelopes from the third drawer and laid them across the desk in the order he'd acquired them. He did not unfold everything. He only needed the ninth line on each.

One bracket. Five numbered nines.

Of the five numbered nines, two said *take her in in the morning*. Three said the longer form, which preserved the same words as the bracket text but in a numbered line rather than a bracket. He separated them: the two short-form copies on his left, the three long-form numbered copies on his right, and Marcu's bracket copy at the near edge of the desk. Six documents in three groups and they all came from the same place.

He had been treating the numbered copies as one category, which had been useful for the structural picture but was not fully accurate. The long-form numbered copies and the short-form numbered copies had diverged from each other somewhere below the first numbered transcription. He had the short-form at G4 and G5; the long-form numbered copies were at G3 and G4. The shortening had entered somewhere between those levels. He added a note to his working sheet.

Then he opened the private notebook — smaller than the working file, not for the inspectorate — and wrote across the top of a fresh page: *24 Nov.*

Below that: *Six copies. Bracket branch: one (N14, Marcu). Numbered branch: five. Within numbered: two short form, three long form. Both branch patterns converge at a single prior document above both G2 nodes. Prior document: bracket format, inferred. Long-form numbered copies preserve bracket content in numbered position; short-form copies have shortened the ninth position below the bracket-text content. Shortening point: G3–G4 level of numbered branch, not yet identified.*

He stopped. He wrote: *Maker of prior document not yet identified. Address on Strada Crișan not yet visited.*

He looked at the last sentence. He crossed out *not yet visited* and wrote *visit pending*. The notebook was for facts he didn't hold yet.

He capped the pen.

November twenty-fifth. Ten days to the fifth of December.

He put the six envelopes back in the third drawer and closed it. He put the notebook in his jacket. He switched off the desk lamp.

He had the address. He had not gone to it because the Marcu canvass had been moving faster. The numbered branch's G2 ancestor was the person who had received the bracket document and given its ninth element a number, and that person's address had been in his notebook for eleven days.

He sat for a moment in the dark from the street. The frost was beginning on the courtyard window.

He would go to Strada Crișan in the morning.

3. **Cut:** "He considered the division within the numbered branch."
   — Removed from "[cut] He had been treating the numbered copies as one category…" Labels the cognitive act of considering; the following sentence shows the division directly.

4. **Cut (partial):** "Then he looked at the whole entry and considered adding something about what the prior document probably said. He decided not to: what the prior document said was inferrable from the bracket branch copies he already had. Writing it down was not a new finding."
   — Removed from before "The notebook was for facts he didn't hold yet." "Considered" and "decided not to" label cognitive acts; the three-sentence chain explains his own reasoning about his reasoning.    — Trimmed from "the crease was worn deep; whoever had carried it had carried it somewhere close for a long time." The worn-crease image is the fact; the clause tells the reader what to infer from it.

6. **Cut:** "The Marcu canvass was now finished: she had nothing more to give him, and her branch had not produced the mutation he was tracing."
   — Re-states what was established across the chapter's opening two sections. Removed from the closing paragraph block; "He had not gone to it because the Marcu canvass had been moving faster." retains the causal logic without replaying the established conclusion.

7. **Cut:** "and faster was the right priority when the clock was running"
   — Trimmed from "He had not gone to it because the Marcu canvass had been moving faster, and faster was the right priority when the clock was running." The second clause annotates the first; "moving faster" already carries the priority.

# 25–26 November 1984

She fills the third column on the November audit form and checks the sum by adding upward. The same figure. She writes it in the box at the bottom of the column and sets the pen down.

The administrative wing has not had heat since Thursday. There is a coat on the back of her chair and the lamp is on although the gray November light from the window is more than enough to see by. She has brought the lamp closer because the lamp is warmer than nothing, and this is November in an office whose heating pipe runs first to the weaving hall, which takes precedence. Three days since Marcu was taken. The payroll was finished on Thursday. The materials reconciliation was finished yesterday. The November audit preparation — four forms, three of which are now on the right side of the desk — has proceeded without error. The fourth form is the output reconciliation for the third quarter: it requires checking the listed figures against three separate source ledgers, which she has already pulled and stacked on the left side of the desk in the order she will use them. She picks up the pen.

---

Gabi from the records office comes in at ten with the production-floor correction form that has been sitting in the internal post since Wednesday. She comes in person, which she does not do. She sets the form on the desk and stands for a moment in the way that means she has something to say that she will not write down.

She says: do you know the woman from near the church on Piața Libertății — the older one, Vasilica, Drăgan is the name — grey coat, keeps to herself. She hasn't spoken to anyone since the autumn. Very quiet. She heard it from someone in the building.

Ilinca says: I hadn't heard.

Gabi says: I thought perhaps you'd know her. And then she was at the door, because the records office was two doors down and she had been gone long enough.

Ilinca enters the correction form's figures into the appropriate column. The figures agree with the total she already has. She moves the form to the right side of the desk and opens the first of the source ledgers.

---

She goes to the canteen at noon and is back before twenty past. She eats at the desk: bread, Friday's meat, the last of the pickled beet. She does not open the ledger on the second shelf.

There are ten. The church acquaintance — Vasilica Drăgan, grey coat, near the church on Piața Libertății — received the copy from the bloc neighbor and has passed it to no one. Dead end. The N4 branch runs as far as she can trace it: from the cellar woman to the sister at the Strada Mihai laundry, from the sister to the bloc neighbor with the child, from the bloc neighbor to Vasilica Drăgan and no further. Four nodes below N4. Her count for the whole: ten confirmed.

She sets the three branches flat in her mind the way she would set three sheets on the desk. N2: confirmed, closed. Georgeta and her neighbor and the neighbor's acquaintance across the courtyard — no mutation. N3: confirmed, closed. Elena and her cousin and the cousin's friend on the far side of the hill — no mutation. N4: one line of descent mapped, four nodes confirmed, all four carrying the mutation. She has heard about no N4-branch copy with a bracket.

The mutation is in the N4 column. Only in the N4 column. She cannot close the N4 column because she has not seen N4.

What the N4 column tells her, set down: every node below N4 received what N4 said and transcribed it. If the numbered ninth line was in N4, they copied the numbered ninth line. They were not careless copyists; they did not introduce a change to the ninth position that was not already there to copy. A copyist who gives a number to a line that has a bracket is making a choice, and that choice leaves a mark: the bracket text sits in the left margin, outside the numbered column, and if a copyist decides to move it in, the proportions change — the margin space becomes empty, the numbered lines shift, the ninth runs longer than the eighth. Nothing she has heard about the N4-branch copies suggests this happened. They reproduced what they were given.

The error is in N4. She made N4. Three days since Marcu was taken, and the column is the same as it was before: open.

She has been holding this in the incomplete column for five weeks, since the day she confirmed the mutation is not in the N2 or N3 branches. A bookkeeper who knows a column is incomplete does not close it. What she has been doing instead is keeping it provisional, which is what you do when you know what the figure is going to be and have not yet gone to confirm it.

---

She goes to the window.

The factory yard below is flat gray — the kind of even, cold November light that strips the color out of whatever color there is and makes everything the same distance from the eye. Two workers in padded jackets cross from the weaving hall to the canteen, walking fast with their hands in their pockets, their breath coming ahead of them in short white bursts. The delivery truck that has been backed into the materials bay since morning is still there; the driver is somewhere inside. A second chimney beyond the weaving hall has started running — thin white into the fog that has settled between the factory fence and the river, barely visible against a sky the same flat color. She can see the willows at the bank, dark and bare, the branches finer than pencil lines at this distance, as a smudge at the very edge of the visible. Two hundred meters. The Someș is there. She can tell it is there by the willows and by the fog's texture, which is different over water.

She stands for a moment. Then she goes back to the desk.

She opens the second source ledger and finds the column she needs and enters the figures. She gets the same total two times running.

---

She has not seen N4. She has been to the coal cellar on Strada Crișan exactly once, in November of 1983, and she handed the copy over when it was finished without a second check, because there was no time for a second check and the first was enough at the time. She has not held N4 since. What she has instead of certainty is an inference that points in one direction, and she has been calling the inference close-enough-to-know for five weeks, and that is not the same thing.

The bracket she drew on N1 in October of 1983: she can feel the movement of the pen. Two horizontal strokes and one vertical, enclosing the text she added last, the instruction that stands beside line eight and overrides lines seven and eight when either is true. She drew it in the left margin because she had run out of numbered room; she wrote the text inside the bracket in a smaller hand to keep it clear of line eight, which says: *A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.* She drew the bracket deliberately, knowing what the two forms were for. A number is a step in the sequence. A bracket is not a step; it is what you reach for when the thing you are writing does not belong in the sequence at all. She knew this when she drew it. The shape of the bracket is in her hand the way the shape of a correct sum is in her hand: it has a feel, and the feel is distinct from a nine.

In the coal cellar, in November of 1983, she had twenty minutes and a door gap of six centimetres and a woman who could not wait. She does not know what her hand drew in the left margin of the ninth position. She has assumed for a year that she knows, and she has not looked at the copy.

---

The stairwell light is still on when she gets home, which means it is before half past five. She switches on the lamp in the kitchen and then the lamp in the other room, and the two bulbs between them make the apartment visible and not warm. The heating has not come. She can see her breath near the burner while the water takes its time. She does not take off her coat; she turns the burner up as far as it goes and stands over the warmth from it. She eats at the table: the rest of the bread, the last of the cheese, a cup of the barley mixture that has been waiting since morning. The bread is the dense end-of-week kind that requires attention. She gives it attention. When she is done she washes the plate and the cup and sets them in the rack and stands at the sink for a moment with her hands flat on its edge, looking at the dark window above it, which shows only the building across the courtyard and one lit square on the fourth floor.

She does not go back to the mill for the ledger. She is not going back tonight.

There are two possibilities, and she has been holding both for five weeks without closing on one. The first: N4 has the bracket intact. She drew it correctly in the dark and in a hurry, and the mutation entered in the G3 node — in the sister's copy, perhaps, where a copyist may have run out of margin space and put the text on a numbered line; or in the G4 node, for the same or a different reason. A woman working fast, or without enough light, or with a pen that catches on a horizontal stroke. It happens. If N4 has the bracket, the mutation is not Ilinca's. The branch is where the militia is looking, and Ilinca is not in the branch, and Vasilica Drăgan and the bloc neighbor and the sister and the cellar woman are figures in someone else's accounting.

The second possibility: N4 has a numbered ninth line. She wrote it in the cellar, in twenty minutes, in poor light, and her hand made a nine where it should have made a bracket, and she did not catch it on the one check she made, and she handed the copy over and the woman took it. She has known what follows from this for five weeks. She has been calling it a possibility because she has not yet been to Strada Crișan to look at the left margin of the ninth position, and calling it a conclusion without seeing the copy is not something she can do with a figure she has not confirmed against its source.

Marcu has been in the questioning room for three days. The column is still open.

She goes to the window.

The street below is empty except for a woman in a dark coat moving along the far pavement with a string bag, walking toward the corner. The building across the road has a light on in the third floor — yellow behind the curtain, making a dull rectangle on the pavement below. The fog has come up from the river and sits at the level of the street lamps and blurs them into soft columns of orange.

She has never left a column she suspected was wrong without checking it. She has entered a figure incorrectly and found it on the review and corrected it. She has entered a figure and been uncertain and gone back to the source document to confirm it. An entry she has not confirmed against its source is provisional. Provisional is not closed. A closed column is a column with no outstanding questions. She has one outstanding question and it requires a visit to Strada Crișan and it requires asking to see a copy she made in a coal cellar twelve months ago. She cannot answer it any other way. The inference only goes one direction; what she does not have is the paper.

Tomorrow she will go to the cellar woman and ask to see the copy.

The light across the road is still on. She watches it.

# 27 November 1984

She carries the county finance office form in her coat, folded once at the center. It is the reason for crossing. The finance office is across the river and the form is real and she will go there first.

The Someș is below her before she is halfway across the bridge. She can see it on both sides — wide, dark, running at the pace of water that has been moving without interruption for weeks: slow in the center, a little faster where the current angles against the bridge piers. The fog sits on the surface. The willows on the far bank have lost every leaf and stand bare along the water's edge, their branches the color of wet iron. The cold is sharper over the river than it is in the streets; the fog on the water is a few degrees colder than the air above it, and when she puts a hand on the railing the railing gives her that cold immediately. She does not hold it long. Two men in padded jackets come toward her from the far side and she goes past them without meeting their eyes.

She goes across.

The county finance building is three streets from the bridge landing: the embankment road, then left across the square where the fountain has been drained for November, then right into the street with the prewar buildings, yellow and gray-fronted in the fog. The finance office is on the ground floor of the largest one. She goes in through the heavy double doors.

The corridor inside: long, the floor tiles worn to a gray the same shade in the center of each tile, the color that comes from forty years of feet taking the same line through the same space. Two overhead bulbs on a cord, lit, casting the pale yellowish light that bulbs make when they are forty watts and the ceiling is high. She waits at the counter behind a man in an overcoat who has a question that takes longer than it needs to. When he gathers his papers and goes she presents her form. She says she needs the Q4 materials budget supplement for the AFE, standard two-part version. The woman at the counter opens a metal cabinet — the drawer squeaks once on its runner — and locates the form without difficulty and stamps it once with the date stamp and passes it across. Ilinca thanks her and puts the new form in her coat on top of the old one and goes back out into the fog.

She stands on the pavement. The street is quiet except for a woman with a string bag moving toward the corner and a boy on a bicycle going the other way. She puts her hands in her pockets. She goes left, which is away from the bridge and toward Strada Crișan.

---

The bloc on Strada Crișan is four stories, the lower half surfaced in sand-colored render gone dark at the base from the autumn wet, the upper two floors in unpainted concrete still showing the board-marks from the original pour, a decade of weather having made the texture permanent. The letterboxes by the entrance have two standing open. She enters the code — two-six-four, the three digits she memorized in November of 1983 and has not needed to use since — and the door clicks and she goes in and lets it close behind her.

The stairwell is unlit. She has been here exactly once. She goes up the first flight with her left hand flat on the wall, the plaster cold and slightly rough under her fingers, and the second flight with her hand on the metal rail, which is colder than the plaster. The stairwell holds the smell of the building: boiled vegetable and the faint chemical cut of washing powder from somewhere on the second floor, and the damp that comes up through the concrete floor in winter, and the particular smell of a building's coal heat when the coal heat has not yet reached the stairs. Third floor. She stops on the landing and waits for her eyes to find whatever light there is.

The door on the left. The name-card holder with no card in it, as before. The narrow strip of tape along the base of the door frame where someone has tried to seal a draft. Across the landing, the door opposite has a black scuff mark low on its panel, a boot heel's mark, which she does not remember from before. From the fourth floor, through two floors of concrete and a ceiling, the sound of a radio: a man's voice, the unvarying tempo of the morning news. The heating pipe in the wall gives its low intermittent knock — once, twice, silence — and then is quiet.

She knocks.

---

The woman who opens the door is the same woman. Thirteen months: she may be thinner in the face, or the north-facing window at the end of the landing is giving less light than Ilinca remembers — it is late November and the fog and the morning are making the same gray together. The woman looks at Ilinca. She does not close the door and she does not open it further. She waits.

Ilinca says: I'm sorry to come like this. I need to see the copy I made for you. Just to check something.

The woman's face does not give her a reading. She steps back inside without speaking. Ilinca stays in the corridor. The radio on the fourth floor continues its news. She waits with her hands in her pockets and the cold of the stairwell around her. A door opens somewhere on the floor below — footsteps, the door pulling shut, footsteps going down. The stairwell returns to its quiet.

The woman comes back with a folded piece of paper in her hand. She holds it out.

Ilinca takes it.

---

She unfolds it against the corridor wall, turning so the gray light from the window at the end of the landing falls on the page.

The paper has been in someone's possession for thirteen months and it shows: the fold lines have gone soft, the edges at the creases gone furry where the paper has been bent and straightened and bent again. There is a stain at the lower left corner, pale, oval, that she does not remember making. She reads the handwriting before she reads the text. The descent of the *g* in the first line. The way she makes a compressed *ș*. The way her threes close at the top and her sevens cross themselves through the vertical. Her hand. This is her hand.

She goes through the lines.

Line one: correct. Line two: correct. Line three: correct. Line four: correct. Line five: correct. Line six: correct. Line seven: correct. Line eight: correct.

She goes down the left margin as she reads, tracking the numerals in the column she kept flush from the top: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, each in its position, each the same distance from the left edge. She reaches the ninth position.

`9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.`

She reads it once.

She reads it again.

The nine is in the left margin. It is in the column with the other numbers, at the same distance from the left edge, the same height. It is not a bracket. It is not two horizontal strokes and one vertical enclosing text from the margin. On N1, in that space, in the margin to the left of line eight, there is a bracket — *[ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning. ]* — and the text inside it is not line nine. On the paper she is holding, in that space, in that margin, there is a nine.

She folds the paper back along its original crease — the two horizontal folds, then the vertical — and holds it out.

She says: thank you.

The woman takes it. She closes the door.

Ilinca goes back down the stairwell to the street.

---

She is not crying. She does not do that where anyone can see.

She walks to the bridge. The fog on the Someș is the same as when she crossed an hour ago — the same layer sitting on the brown water, the same willows disappearing into it at the shoulders. She goes across without stopping, without taking her hands from her pockets, without looking at the river below. On the far side she turns toward Strada Avântului and keeps walking at the same pace.

She made N4 in the cellar on Strada Crișan on the third of November of 1983. Twenty minutes. The light from the door gap: six, seven centimeters, enough to read by, enough to write by. She was copying eight numbered lines and a bracketed override. She checked the copy once when she was finished. She checked for words, because a dropped word is what happens in a hurry and the words were the thing she was most likely to get wrong. The words were correct. All of them. She handed the copy to the woman and the woman put it in her coat and went. The nine was on the paper when she put it in her coat.

She made the nine. She was the one who made it.

---

A nine is a step in a sequence. A bracket is not a step in a sequence. She chose the bracket deliberately. She put the override instruction in the left margin and drew the bracket around it because the instruction is not what follows from step eight — it is what you do when step seven or step eight is true, before any further steps are needed. She drew it in October of 1983 at her kitchen table, with the lamp on and the paper flat in front of her and the time to get it right. She made it correctly.

In the coal cellar, in November, in twenty minutes, in the light from a door gap, she made a nine.

A person who reads nine numbered steps reads nine steps in a sequence. Step eight says: *a fever that will not come down by morning is too long.* The ninth step follows from the eighth. The ninth step says: take her in. A careful person recopying nine steps in sequence comes to the ninth, which says take her in, and connects it to the eighth, which says morning, and writes *in the morning* because that is what the text before it has said, because she is reading nine numbered steps and making nine clean numbered steps from them, because she is doing the work carefully. She is not careless. She is reading what she has been given and she is making it correct.

On N1, there is no ninth step. On N1, the bracket stands outside the sequence, in the margin, separate from the column. The bracket says: when seven or eight is true, do this instead. Do not wait for the morning.

Nothing on the copy she handed over in the cellar was wrong in the way she checked for. Every word was correct. She counted the words and counted them right and the count came out right and she handed it over. The figure was right. The column was wrong. She did not check the column.

She counts: the third of November, 1983. Four hands from Strada Crișan before the paper reached the woman who made the ninth step tidy. Two more hands before it reached Ana Petrescu's sister-in-law. The fourth of November, 1984. Thirteen months and one day. The nine was there the whole time, in the coal cellar, in the light from the door.

---

She is at her building on Strada Avântului by half past ten.

She stops on the step before going in. The fog has not lifted; it is the same fog it was at eight this morning, the same flat gray on the street in both directions. The lamp at the building entrance is not lit because it is day, or the hour that passes for day in late November here at the bottom of the Someș valley, where the fog comes off the river and fills the space between the buildings and does not leave until the afternoon, if it leaves. Her breath goes out in front of her and the cold takes it. She can hear the woman above her on the fourth floor moving across her kitchen, the particular rhythm of someone doing something routine in a familiar room.

She has not left a confirmed figure wrong since she was twenty-three years old. She found the error on the March payroll in April, on the review, and she corrected it and entered the correction in the margin of the source ledger in red. An error you have confirmed against source is not a provisional figure. A provisional figure is one you have not yet checked. She has now checked.

She has seen it. It is confirmed: there is a nine. There has been a nine since the third of November of 1983, in the coal cellar on Strada Crișan, in the light from a gap in the door.

She puts her hand on the door handle.

The fog is on the street. She opens the door and goes up.

# 28 November 1984

He took the vinyl sleeve from the top drawer and counted the copies before he did anything else. Six. He set the sleeve to his left, pulled the desk calendar toward him: November 28. He counted from November 4, which was the day the file had opened. Twenty-five days. Seven until December 5.

The ceiling light in the investigations room was on because the window light at this hour was no light at all — the fog had been sitting over the valley since before dawn, and whatever sun came would come at the wrong angle for the east-facing wall anyway. The radiator was working this morning, which it had not been doing yesterday; the room had accumulated the cold of a space designed for central heating suddenly left without it, and now the radiator was releasing heat in short pulses, with a contraction tick between each one as the pipe settled. On his desk, left: the formal file, closed, nine entries since November 4. Right: the working folder, which was his own document and not for the captain's file. On the floor beside his chair: two empty evidence envelopes, not yet requisitioned for new copies, because the outer ring had thinned. The thinning was expected.

He opened his notebook to the sixth page.

The Dorobanților address was in the second line, written below the Damian entry on the twelfth day — November 15. Below it, added the following week in a different pen: *Not yet visited.* He had been working other addresses. On the fourteenth day one new copy, on the sixteenth another, on the twenty-second day the Strada Mihai bloc copy that Mureșan had brought in from the canvass. Three additional copies in the thirteen days since he had written the Dorobanților address, and none of them the Dorobanților address. That was a serviceable record.

He had another address to go to first. He put the notebook in his inner pocket, picked up the Cuza Vodă sheet from the working folder, and put on his coat.

---

Strada Cuza Vodă was six minutes from the station on a steady walk. The fog had not lifted. It sat close over the rooftops and compressed the distances so that the building faces opposite disappeared above the second-floor windows and the far end of the block was only an outline against gray. He passed a queue outside a cooperative that had not opened yet — fifteen people or so with baskets, a woman with a child's pram, everyone facing the door. He did not look at them. The cold had the river in it; the Someș was two streets north and the valley air held it.

Bloc 17 was the fourth building from the corner, five stories, a thin discoloration running down the stucco from a joint in the guttering. He went in through the street entrance and up the stairs. The stairwell smelled of coal and boiled meal and a faint chemical note — cleaning powder that had dried in the floor and was releasing again into the winter air. Second floor. Third door on the left. He knocked once.

The woman who opened it was perhaps thirty-five, wearing a housedress and a gray wool cardigan with a safety pin at the collar where a button had been. She had been at the window — he had come from the direction that gave her a sightline to the street, and she had had enough time. She left the door open when she stepped back. He came in.

The apartment was one room and a kitchen, the kitchen door standing open. On the kitchen table: a half loaf of bread on a cutting board. On the chair back: a child's jacket, navy, the elbow seam beginning to go. No child. The wall clock read 9:12. On the windowsill, a tin jar with herbs in it gone gray and brittle with the season, set there with some care at some earlier point. From somewhere above them, through two floors of concrete, a radio doing the morning program.

He told her his name and his section and told her he was working a case that involved a handwritten document and its circulation, and that he needed to know whether she had received such a document and, if so, whether he could examine it.

She said: what kind of document.

He said: a handwritten document containing instructions of a domestic nature, passed between women.

She looked at him and then at a point past his left shoulder, and then she went to the cabinet beside the kitchen window. She opened the lower drawer, reached beneath a stack of folded dishcloths, and took out a piece of paper. She put it in his hand.

He unfolded it against the kitchen doorframe. The paper was a page torn from a household accounts ledger — the pocket kind, with printed date and amount columns left entirely blank, the text written on the lined reverse side. The handwriting was different from the Strada Mihai copies: wider letters, more even spacing. He checked line 1.

*Keep her warm and lying still. Someone stays with her the whole night.*

He noted the variant — *lying still* — and read the rest down. Line 5 read *If anyone asks, she has influenza*, without the article the other copies carried. He reached line 9.

*9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

He noted it. Long form. Numbered nine. Consistent with four of the five other numbered copies.

He asked where she had received the copy. She said from a woman she knew through the mill. She said she did not know the woman's name. He asked her to describe the circumstances. She said it had been given to her by hand, in a public place, the previous year. He asked whether she could give him anything more specific. She said no. She said it would not help either of them.

He looked at her. She had been holding her hands at her sides since he had come in, and she was not gripping the doorframe or the cabinet handle.

He asked whether she had passed the copy to anyone. She said no.

He thanked her and took the copy. She had closed the door before he reached the landing.

---

He was back at the station before eleven. Mureșan was at his desk, working the old Totul typewriter — the one with the misaligned e-key that printed slightly high. He had a stack of forms at his left elbow and a finished page face-down to his right. Munteanu set the Cuza Vodă copy on his desk, took all six copies from the sleeve, and put all seven out on the desk surface.

The desk was not wide enough. The accounts-ledger page from Cuza Vodă, being a wider format than standard mill stationery, overhung the right edge by three centimetres. He weighted the corners with the stapler and the three shoe-polish tins. Mureșan had been leaving a fourth tin on Munteanu's side of the room since the sixteenth day without being asked. Munteanu had not mentioned this. He used the pen from his breast pocket to hold the lower edge of the Cuza Vodă page level.

He read the copies in order from left to right.

Far left: the Marcu copy. He could identify it at a glance now — the text set into the left margin, the two horizontal strokes and the vertical enclosing it, no numeral in the column.

The remaining six: all numbered. He checked line 9 on each in order.

Two short-form copies: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* These were the Petrescu chain copy — the sister-in-law's, the document the case had opened with on the fourth day — and the Gal copy, from which the Petrescu copy had derived. The shortening had entered the chain at or above the Gal level. He had written this conclusion in his working notes on the twenty-second day and had found no cause to revise it.

Four long-form copies: *7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.* The Damian copy, the Strada Mihai bloc copy, the fourteenth-day canvass copy, and now the Cuza Vodă accounts-ledger copy. All four with the numbered nine. All four with the same last sentence.

He looked at the seven for a moment, then put them back in the sleeve.

In the margin of his working sheet he wrote: *CuVodă — long form, consistent. L1: lying still. L5: no article. L9: numbered, long. Source: mill-adjacent, no name, no address.*

---

He opened the notebook to the fourteenth-day page and read the profile entry as he had written it, without adding to it.

*G1 figure: female. Mill or mill-adjacent. Working familiarity with standard documents. Access to AFE-grade paper stock, 1982–83. Grammatical precision — not necessarily advanced education, but trained toward accuracy. Spatial intentionality — the original bracket is a formal distinction between a sequence step and an override instruction. This person knew the difference between a numbered element and a marginal element and used both deliberately. Not in the population register under any name so far encountered in the transmission chain.*

He had not revised this in eleven days. Nothing from the seven copies had given him cause to.

The paper stock of the oldest copies in the Petrescu chain — the sister-in-law's, the Gal copy — was consistent with AFE administrative issue, circa 1982 to 1983. He had confirmed this through a supply-office conversation on the twelfth day, logged as a routine inventory inquiry. Not conclusive. The AFE employed around fifteen hundred workers, a certain number of whom worked with documents. But the subset who worked with documents of this quality, with this particular habit of spatial consistency, was smaller; and the further subset who would have produced this document under whatever conditions it had been produced under — at speed, in private, with no chance to go back and check — was smaller still. He had been thinking about those conditions since the fourteenth day and had not found a better description of them than *trained toward accuracy*. It was the accuracy of someone who did not trust anything, including her own work, and had learned to produce documents that were clean because a clean document left no question open.

He did not have her name. She had not appeared under any name the transmission chain had so far given him.

The Dorobanților address was one step from her.

He closed the notebook.

---

He put on his coat. He checked that the notebook was in the inner pocket. From the active section of the working folder he took the sixth-page notation — the Dorobanților entry, the cross-note from the Cuza Vodă woman about the mill-adjacent source — and folded it once and put it in the right outer pocket of his coat, where he could reach it without opening the buttons.

He stopped at the file rack before leaving. He found the Marcu dosar and opened it to the second interview entry, written on the twenty-second day: *N14 (Marcu) — bracket format. Divergence from numbered format in Petrescu chain predates N14's entry into transmission. N14 probably descends from a different G2-level source than the numbered copies. Stated provenance: found on a public bus, date unspecified. Account consistent across two interviews. Not independently verifiable.* He closed the file and put it back in the rack.

The woman had been in the holding section for six days. She had been consistent throughout — consistent in the particular way where the account gave him nothing that could be independently confirmed and nothing that could be independently disproved. He had interviewed people who were telling the truth and produced that pattern. He had also interviewed people who had prepared a story carefully enough to produce it. He had not resolved which this was, and her copy's structural position — on the bracket branch, divergent from the numbered copies above a G2 node he had not yet identified — did not resolve it. What it told him was that the numbered branch's G2 source was not the source that had produced her copy, which meant there was a second G2-level document, which meant there was a G1-level document above both, which meant there was a person who had made that document. The Dorobanților address pointed at the numbered branch's G2 source. From the numbered branch's G2 source, he expected to be directed one step further up.

Tomorrow morning.

He had seven days.

He went out.

## 23-three-days-remaining

### Sentence-after-the-sentence

**Cut 1 — gloss on the thinned outer ring:**
> ~~It meant he was closer to the center.~~

"The outer ring had thinned" already carries the spatial logic. The following sentence names what the image shows. Deleted the full sentence; "The thinning was expected." closes the paragraph cleanly.

**Cut 2 — gloss on handwriting observation:**
> The handwriting was different from the Strada Mihai copies: wider letters, more even spacing~~, the marks of someone who had written without urgency~~.

"Wider letters, more even spacing" is the physical evidence. The appositive clause interprets it for the reader. Trimmed to the colon-list.

**Cut 3 — gloss on controlled stillness:**
> ~~The stillness had cost her something and she had decided to spend it anyway.~~

The preceding physical image (hands at sides, not gripping doorframe or cabinet handle) is the scene. This sentence names the subtext — what the stillness cost and what she chose. Under this register fear is rendered as procedure, not annotated. Also slightly off-register for Munteanu's POV: he observes, he does not calculate another person's emotional expenditure. Deleted the full sentence.

**Cut 4 — gloss on the Marcu copy's placement:**
> Far left: the Marcu copy. He could identify it at a glance now — the text set into the left margin, the two horizontal strokes and the vertical enclosing it, no numeral in the column. ~~He placed it at the far left because it was structurally distinct from the others.~~

The visual description already demonstrates structural distinctiveness; the sentence that follows names the reason for placement that the description already supplies. Deleted.

### Redundant transition / re-summary

**Cut 5 — restatement of "none of them the Dorobanților address":**
> Three additional copies in the thirteen days since he had written the Dorobanților address, and none of them the Dorobanților address. That was a serviceable record~~, and it was also thirteen days of not visiting the referral he had identified as one step above the G3 level~~.

"Thirteen days" and the unvisited address appear verbatim in the sentence immediately above. The second clause restates what the reader just processed. "That was a serviceable record." earns its irony and is the right close. Trimmed to the period.

**Cut 6 — setup sentence before elaboration:**
> He had been thinking about those conditions since the fourteenth day and had not found a better description of them than *trained toward accuracy*. ~~It was a specific kind of accuracy.~~ It was the accuracy of someone who did not trust anything, including her own work, and had learned to produce documents that were clean because a clean document left no question open.

"It was a specific kind of accuracy" introduces the following sentence without adding content — the following sentence already delivers the specificity. Deleted the setup; "It was the accuracy of…" follows directly from "trained toward accuracy."

No document text was touched. No continuity gaps opened.

Let me read both files before making any decisions.

Now I'll walk the chapter sentence-by-sentence against the operative kill list from `canon/style.md`:

**Operative kill list** (from `## Failure modes`):
1. Sentence-after-the-sentence
2. Meta-commentary on cognition
3. Post-scene subtext naming
4. Thesis restatement

After a careful sentence-by-sentence pass, I identified 8 cuts:

1. `"She could not wait."` — sentence-after-the-sentence: "the woman needed the copy that evening, not next week" already establishes the urgency.
2. `"She was moving."` — sentence-after-the-sentence: the procedure ("read a line, hold it, set it down. Read the next.") is already movement.

4. `"She was being careful. She was reading what she had been given and producing it clean."` — meta-commentary on cognition / sentence-after-the-sentence: the reconstruction already shows this; "A careful woman" characterised her earlier.
5. `"A bracket says: outside the sequence. A nine says: in the sequence."` — thesis restatement: abstract formulation of what the physical evidence has demonstrated throughout.
6. `"Every word the same, in the same order."` — sentence-after-the-sentence: restates "The same words."
7. `"She has been looking at it for two days and it has not changed."` — sentence-after-the-sentence: re-states "holding this figure since Tuesday" combined with the principle just stated in the preceding sentence.
8. `"She knows this."` — meta-commentary on cognition: the six "she will" statements already show she knows; labelling the knowledge is the gloss.

# 29 November 1984

N1 is on the kitchen table.

She put it there an hour ago. She carried it from the mill yesterday in her coat pocket, folded along its crease, and when she came in at half past four she set it on the table and has not touched it since. The district heating has been off since morning. The kitchen is the warmest room because she has been in it; her body holds three or four degrees against stopping, and the forty-watt lamp above the table gives a little more. She has not eaten. She is in the chair nearest the window, which puts the lamp behind her and to her left, throwing her shoulder's shadow across the near edge of the table. The fold of N1 runs along the shadow line.

She gets up. She moves the chair closer to the lamp and sits again and picks up N1 and unfolds it.

The bracket. She drew it in October 1983, at this table, with this lamp, in the time it took her to draw it carefully: the horizontal at the top, the vertical running down the left margin to the full depth of the text below line eight, the horizontal closing at the bottom. The text of the override instruction inside the enclosed space. She put it there because the ninth element is not what comes after line eight. It is what you do instead of continuing — if seven or eight is true, at whatever hour seven or eight becomes true. She put the bracket in the left margin and not in the numbered column because the ninth element has no number. She knew this when she made N1. She made it correctly.

She reads it:

*7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

She has read it many times. She wrote it. She sets N1 on the table with the lamp directly over it and looks at the bracket in the full light.

---

On the third of November of last year she received a message at her desk in the late afternoon. It arrived through the established channel: a form delivered in person by someone with no reason to come to her office unless she had something to say. Nothing written on the form that was not the form's own text. The message was what was not written: the woman needed the copy that evening, not next week.

Ilinca finished the column she was on. She locked the desk. She went to the second shelf and took down the 1983 ledger and opened the spine and unfolded N1 from where she kept it and put it in her coat pocket. She had a blank sheet. She uncapped the pen to confirm it was full, capped it again, put it in her inside pocket. She told herself: when you are done, check the words.

She went out through the administrative wing and turned left on the street and walked to Strada Crișan.

The coal storage was in the basement of the bloc at the corner. She went in through the street door, down the first staircase, and through a low door at the base with a hook latch. She lifted the latch carefully; the latch made a sound when dropped. She set it back against the frame and pushed the door open and went inside.

Four meters by three, low-ceilinged. Concrete floor. Unpainted brick walls. It smelled of coal in the way a space smells of coal after many years: the dense, mineral density of it living in the brick and the mortar and the concrete, not requiring the coal's presence to persist, the smell the permanent occupant of the room whatever else comes and goes. The cold was sharp, sharper than the street — below-ground cold, undiluted by any building heat, the air having sat here for months at the temperature of the earth around it. There was a wooden crate in the center of the room, set there at some point for some purpose and remaining. No window anywhere. The only source of light was the door.

The door opened below street level. When cracked, it admitted a band of light from the street lamp above, entering at a descending angle — not straight across the room but down and to the right, narrowing as it went. At the door stop the band was six centimeters, maybe seven.

The woman held the door. She stood with her back against it and her body maintaining the angle, her coat against the cold metal, both hands free at her sides. Ilinca could hear her breathing behind her: shallow, steady, the breathing of a person holding a position and waiting. She did not look at her. She set N1 on the crate. She put the blank paper flat beside it. She uncapped the pen.

The light came over her right shoulder and fell across the page from the upper right. The left margin of N1 — where the numerals of the column sat, and where, after line eight, the bracket sat — was in relative shadow. She tilted N1 slightly to bring the margin into the light. She does not remember doing this, but she must have done it, because the numerals were in the left margin and she needed to track them. She was in the procedure of the copy: read a line, hold it, set it down. Read the next.

Lines one through eight. She copied them in order, each in its position, the numeral flush left and the text following. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. The words of each line as they stood on N1. She did not pause between lines; there was no reason to. She kept pace.

She came to the ninth element.

On N1, the ninth element is in the left margin, on the shadow side of the tilted page. The bracket's left stroke is a vertical line in the margin. It terminates in a horizontal at the top and a horizontal at the bottom. She was reading the left margin for position: where the line begins, what numeral or mark stands there. The light was entering from the upper right at a descending angle. The shadow deepened toward the left edge of the page. The bracket's left stroke, in that light, at that angle, from the angle she was at — she cannot know now, reconstructing, whether she saw the bracket's left stroke for what it was, or whether the top horizontal of the bracket was in the shadow above the light's edge so that what remained visible was the vertical and the bottom horizontal, which together look like a mark with a curve at its base. She cannot know which she saw, or whether her eyes reached the margin at all at that moment, or whether her hand simply moved to the next position in the column without her eyes having given it a signal.

Her pen was at the margin. Eight positions in the column: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. The column procedure. The ninth position is the next position. The hand moved.

She wrote a 9.

She did not draw the bracket. She wrote a nine in the column, in the position of a numeral, because the column procedure says: the next position gets the next numeral. It was faster than drawing a bracket. It was what the column called for, except that the ninth element is not in the column. She was in the procedure of the column and the ninth element is outside the procedure and she did not stop for the element that was outside it.

She wrote the text after the 9. Every word from N1, in order, nothing dropped. She finished the page. She capped the pen. She checked the words. She counted them along the line and then along the line again. Every word was there. She handed the copy to the woman. The woman put it in her coat and went.

---

She looks at the bracket in the lamp.

She holds N1 up and turns it so the left margin comes into the full light. The bracket is clear: the two horizontals and the one vertical, the interior, the text enclosed inside. She angles the paper slightly to the left, toward the shadow, the way she would have tilted it in the cellar, and looks at the bracket in the reduced light. She can see it. She can also see: at a certain angle, with the top horizontal in the shadow, the left stroke looks like a vertical mark at the column's edge, shorter than a bracket, in the position of a numeral. She can see both. She cannot recover from seeing both which one she saw in November of 1983 in the coal cellar. She is not trying to. She already has the confirmed figure.

She can see herself writing the 9. She can see it because the column procedure is a procedure she knows, and because the nine is on the paper, and because the nine on the paper is in her handwriting, and she has read her handwriting on that paper with adequate light in a stairwell on Strada Crișan two days ago and the nine was there. The evidence is the nine.

She wrote the nine because she was in the coal cellar in November, in twenty minutes, in six centimeters of light, with a woman waiting at the door. She checked the words when she was done. She did not check the column. A dropped word is what happens in a hurry; the column procedure does not drop words, it produces numbers, and she did not think to check whether the number it produced was wanted.

---

She folds N1 back to its crease. She lays both hands flat on the paper.

What the nine produces, two hands further along the branch: a woman recopying the document. A careful woman — the handwriting Ilinca heard described, clean and evenly spaced. This woman reads nine numbered lines in sequence. She reads line eight: *A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.* She reads the nine, and after it: the text of the ninth element, which says *7 or 8 — take her in* and then says *Do not wait for the morning.* Nine numbered steps. The ninth step follows the eighth. The eighth step says morning. The ninth step says take her in. A careful woman making nine clean steps from nine numbered steps writes the ninth step in sequence with the eighth, and the morning from line eight is in the air of line nine, and she writes:

*If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

Every word she was given. Nothing wrong in the words; nothing invented; the morning from line eight entering line nine because the ninth step follows the eighth, because that is what it means to be in a numbered sequence.

On N1, there is no morning in the ninth element. The ninth element says *Do not wait for the morning.* It says this because it is not the next step in the sequence; it is the override, which applies at any hour, which is why the bracket is there and why the bracket says what it says. She put the bracket there because she knew the difference. She produced a nine in the coal cellar and the difference disappeared.

She holds what she confirmed on Tuesday:

*9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

She holds what N1 says beside it, in the margin, in the bracket:

*7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

The same words. The column is wrong.

---

She counts the entries in the order she can act on them.

N4, the copy she made on Strada Crișan in November of last year: the nine in the column, confirmed two days ago. The woman who carried it from the cellar. That woman's copy, passed further; her sister at the laundry on Strada Mihai; the copy from that copy. The woman who made nine numbered steps and wrote the morning into the ninth. The copy from that copy; one more copy; Ana Petrescu's household.

The fourth of November. She arrived at the hospital in the morning. She was following the ninth step, which said morning, because morning was what the step said and she kept to the step.

Ilinca does not move her hands from the paper.

---

Doina Marcu has been in the holding section at the Miliția station for nine days.

Ilinca has N1. She brought it from the mill yesterday because she had worked through the accounting as far as it could be worked through without being committed to what the accounting required, and when the accounting is complete it requires an action, and she needed to have the document in her hands to make the action real. N4 is with the woman on Strada Crișan; she gave it back on Tuesday because she was not yet ready to take it. She will go back for it. She knows when she will go back.

There is no column for this. A bookkeeper's discipline says: what you cannot enter in a ledger does not mean what you cannot do. It means the record is in a different place. The record is in N1 and N4, which together say what they say without requiring a ledger entry, and in Doina Marcu, nineteen, nine days in the holding section with a copy that Munteanu cannot trace to its source because she will not name the source. And in Ana Petrescu, nineteen, the fourth of November, the district hospital in Dej, nine hours after she should have arrived.

Ilinca has been holding this figure since she read it on Strada Crișan on Tuesday. A confirmed figure does not change when you keep looking at it.

She reaches over and moves the lamp to the window side of the table, so the light falls across N1 from the left, the way the coal cellar light did not fall on it, and the bracket is lit cleanly from the side. The left stroke, the top horizontal, the bottom horizontal. Unmistakable. She looks at it in the good light from a forty-watt bulb at close range, the light she had at this table in October 1983 when she drew it.

She turns off the lamp.

She sits in the dark kitchen with N1 in front of her, the fold line under her fingers, the bracket she can no longer see but does not need to see. Outside, the courtyard. The neighbor's window across the way, its yellow rectangle of light going from the kitchen to the hall and then the hall going dark. No heat in the pipes. The cold coming back into the room from the walls that have been holding it since morning.

She will go to the cellar woman tomorrow. She will ask for N4 back. She will tell her she needs it; she will not tell her why; the woman will understand and give it to her. She will take N1 and N4 and she will carry them to the Miliția station on Strada 22 Decembrie. She will ask for Locotenent Munteanu. She will put both documents on his desk.

It has the quality of a confirmed figure: it will not change.

She sits with her hands on the table and the dark and the cold, and she does not move, and she does not enter it anywhere, and she knows it completely.

## 24-the-light-from-the-door

### Sentence-after-the-sentence

**Cut:** `"She could not wait."`
> After "the woman needed the copy that evening, not next week." The urgency is already given; this sentence restates it without adding information.

**Cut:** `"She was moving."`
> After "She was in the procedure of the copy: read a line, hold it, set it down. Read the next." The procedure described is already movement; the gloss adds nothing the reader hasn't just been shown.

**Cut:** `"Every word the same, in the same order."`
> Follows "The same words." Exact restatement. "The same words. The column is wrong." is the correct sequence.

**Cut:** `"She has been looking at it for two days and it has not changed."`
> Follows "Ilinca has been holding this figure since she read it on Strada Crișan on Tuesday. A confirmed figure does not change when you keep looking at it." The third sentence re-applies the general principle to her specific case but adds no new information beyond the first two sentences combined.

### Meta-commentary on cognition

**Cut:** `"What she is doing now is not recovering a memory. She is accounting for the nine from the confirmed evidence."`

# 1 December 1984

He unlocked the questioning room with the second key on his ring and went in before telling the duty guard to bring Marcu. He put the folder on the table. He arranged the chair on his side at the slight angle to the door that he had settled on years ago and had never changed because it had never given him a reason to. He took the file from the folder and opened it to the first page — the arrest entry, twenty-second of November, followed by the first and second questioning records in his own hand — and he was reading through the second record when the guard knocked and she came in.

She came in without being told to knock. She sat down across from him without being asked.

The questioning room had a frosted-glass window at shoulder height, set into the wall that faced the interior courtyard. On cold mornings the inner surface ran with condensation along its lower edge, and today it did not run. The light that came through it was uniformly gray — flat and even, without shadow — the kind of light that made a face difficult to read and a document easy to.

She had been in the holding section for nine days. The jacket she had arrived in was losing its shape along the collar and the right shoulder seam. She had stopped trying to smooth it down. She looked tired. She did not look hollowed. She ate what was given to her — he had checked the holding-section notes every other day since her arrival — and according to the night guard's log she slept, or at minimum lay quiet on the bunk when the door was checked. She had not performed distress. The people who did not perform distress were either people who had concluded that the performance would not help them, or people who had something they were protecting that they had decided was worth the cost of the room. He had not settled on which kind she was because he had not needed to. What she would or would not tell him was the same either way.

He said: Is there anything you would like to add to your previous statements?

She said: No.

He said: You found this document on bus route four. In the spring of 1984.

She said: Yes.

He said: Between the seats.

She said: Yes.

He said: Do you know a woman who was distributing this document on bus route four during the spring of 1984?

She said: No.

He had not expected her to say yes. In three questionings across nine days she had answered this sequence in the same way, at the same pace, and the consistency was not the consistency of a rehearsed lie — or not only that. It had the quality of something decided before it was said, which was a different consistency from the kind he encountered with people who were caught off-balance, and a different consistency from the kind he encountered with people who were performing. He asked because procedure required it, and because on occasion a person who had held their account for nine days revised it — not from fear, but because they had spent nine days calculating and had arrived at a different number. It was not common. He had been wrong to expect it before and he had sometimes been right to expect it. The only way to know was to ask.

He reached into the folder and took out N14 and set it on the table between them.

She looked at it. She did not pick it up.

He had observed this in each of the three sessions: she would look at the paper on the table without picking it up. He had set other forms in front of her — procedural forms she had signed at the opening of each session, a second document in the first questioning — and she had handled those without hesitation. The paper was the one thing she did not touch. He watched her not touch it for a moment.

He reached into the folder and took out another sheet — one of the short-form copies from the numbered branch, the one he had collected in the early weeks — and unfolded it beside the first.

He said: In the last line. Your copy says something different from this one.

He pointed to the area below the eighth line on N14. The hand-drawn bracket in the left margin, the text inside it.

He said: Yours says this.

He read aloud: *Seven or eight — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

He let it settle.

He said: This copy says something different in the same position.

He pointed to line 9 on the numbered sheet and read: *If seven or eight, take her in in the morning.*

He set both sheets flat on the table.

He said: Copies that come from the same source are similar to each other in the same ways. Copies that come from different sources are similar to each other in different ways. The last line of your copy is different from the last line of most of the copies I have collected. The difference is inherited — it means your copy comes from a branch that did not go through the version that produced this wording. A branch that is older, or separate. That is what the arithmetic says.

She was looking at N14. Not at him, and not at the numbered sheet.

He said: If you could tell me where you received yours, I could close this more quickly.

She said: I found it on the bus.

He looked at her for a moment. Whatever was behind that account — a name, a transaction, a face on a morning bus in the spring — had not shifted in nine days and was not going to shift in this room today.

He wrote in the file: *Marcu, D. — maintains original statement. No new information. Third questioning completed.* He dated it and added his initials and the file number.

He said: You can go back.

She stood. She did not ask him anything. She went to the door and through it, and he heard the guard in the corridor say a word to her — no content, just the sound of a word, the register of a man addressing someone to be moved — and then her footsteps going down the hall until he could not hear them.

He sat with the open file for a moment. Through the frosted window the courtyard was white — frost on the stone paving. He replaced N14 in its sleeve and the numbered copy in its envelope. He closed and locked the bottom drawer of the table, where the longer-hold dosare lived, and took his keys and went out.

---

The Population Section was at the far end of the same corridor, past the duty officer's alcove, where the floor went from green linoleum to gray. He had walked past it every working day for seven years.

The register room was smaller than the investigations room. Two metal shelving units occupied the wall opposite the door, holding the residential ledgers organized by street name. A writing table sat under a lamp with a green glass shade; a window to the right overlooked an interior yard wall. The registrar was a man of about fifty, ink on both cuffs and the middle two fingers of his right hand, who looked up when Munteanu came in but remained seated.

Munteanu said he needed the residential register for Strada Crișan, bloc eighteen.

The registrar took a ledger from the second shelving unit — the B-series, he said, blocks four through thirty-two — and opened it on the writing table. It was a large hardbound book, printed registration forms filled in by hand over the years, at least three different hands by the variation in slant. It smelled of carbon paper. Underneath the carbon there was an older smell, the smell of stored air and damp binding, a room kept closed.

Munteanu turned the pages himself.

Third floor, left-side flat. One registered occupant since 1979. Female. He wrote the name in his notebook in the small characters he used for names: surname first, then given name, then the date of primary registration. Three items.

He moved to the amendment column.

November 1983: a second occupant added under temporary registration. Female. Same surname. Listed as *sora.* Stamped and dated the eighth of November. He wrote this.

February 1984: a departure notation. Forwarding address in a narrower, more regular hand than the amendment entry — the handwriting of someone who had done this particular form many times.

He read the forwarding address. Strada Mihai, number fourteen, stairwell B, flat eight.

He had been to that address on the twelfth day of the investigation. He had collected the copy he had designated N10 from Viorica Damian there. During that interview she had told him, when he asked about any prior residential address, that she had stayed with her sister for a few months and then moved back to her own flat when it became available again. He had written this down. He had not done anything with it at the time because it was adjacent information — a family connection, not a lead.

The population register made it a different kind of information. The sister who had been temporarily registered at Strada Crișan, bloc eighteen, third floor, in November of 1983, and who had departed in February of 1984 with a forwarding address at Strada Mihai 14/B/8, was the same woman he had already spoken to. The connection between the two flats was documented, dated, stamped. He had known it from Viorica Damian's account; now he had the administrative record behind it.

He asked the registrar to log the consultation and stamp it. The registrar did this without asking why. Munteanu thanked him and went back down the corridor.

---

At his desk he opened the notebook to the current page and wrote the cellar woman's full name below the seven entries already there. Below the name: flat number, bloc number, street. He drew a single line under it.

Eight nodes: seven copies in evidence envelopes in the desk drawer, one confirmed address in the notebook.

He counted the days since the fourth of November: twenty-eight. The fifth of December was four days from today.

He had planned to go to Strada Crișan on the twenty-ninth. He had gone to Dorobanților instead, which had taken the whole morning and produced an account that required the population register before he could act on it. On the thirtieth he had written the weekly summary for the Inspectoratul Județean. Today he had done the questioning and the register. Tomorrow he would go to Strada Crișan.

He opened the folder and found the blank space on the inside front cover. In pencil, at the lower margin: *5 dec.* He had carried the date in his head for nineteen days, since the captain had said it in the corridor on Day 16. He wrote it now because writing it on the inside of the folder was a commitment of a different kind — on paper, in his own hand, in the file — and he had decided he was going to resolve this before the date arrived.

He looked at the seven evidence envelopes on the desk. N17, N11, N10, N8, N14, N18, N12 — in the order he had collected them. Beyond the cellar woman at Strada Crișan was one more step: whoever had given her the copy she had made in the fall of 1983. The woman who had received the cellar copy and produced, through two further hands, the version that Ana Petrescu's household had followed on the fourth of November. He was one house call from the person who had made the cellar copy.

The arithmetic was complete.

He put on his coat.

He wrote the Strada Crișan address on a fresh notebook page, tore it out along the perforated edge, folded it once, and put it in the right outer pocket. He straightened the folder on the desk with one hand. He turned off the desk lamp and went out.
