# 2 December 1984

She takes the coat from the hook and pulls it on.

At the hallway window, before she buttons it, she stops. The glass is clear — no condensation, which means the temperature last night fell below what the shared pipe requires before the boiler bothers. Through the glass and past the northern roofline she can see the river: brown, flat, moving, the surface catching nothing of the pale early light. She watches it for a moment and then buttons the coat from the bottom up. Five buttons. She has known the bottom three by feel for eleven years; they are slightly smaller than the upper two and require less hand. She takes her gloves from the shelf beside the lamp. She takes the key.

The stairwell is dark. The third-floor light does not come on in the mornings; this is the building superintendent's arrangement and it has been his arrangement for as long as she has lived here. She goes down by the wall, her right hand on the railing, the key in her left.

Outside: frost on the first-floor sill, a white line along the bottom of the glass, already softening at its edges. The air is below zero and dry. The sky is pale and without clouds — the kind of December clarity that follows a hard night and will not last past midmorning, when the valley's moisture finds its way back in. She has not seen a clear sky in Dej since before the fifteenth of November. She walks toward the bridge.

She is going to say, when the door opens: *I need to take the copy back. It is not safe for you to have it anymore.*

She has had this sentence since Thursday morning, worked out on the walk to the mill while the street lamps were still on. She has not revised it because there is nothing in it to revise. Ilinca is going to Strada Crișan, not to a confessional.

The bridge is fifteen minutes from her building. On the approach, the Someș is below and to the left — running full and brown in the clear morning, carrying what the plateau has sent down to it. At the center span, the east railing has been unsettled since at least the spring of 1977. She knows precisely where the intact section resumes. She walks in the center of the lane until she reaches it.

She has not been on this bridge twice in eight days for eleven years.

The last time was November 1973: three crossings in four days with consolidated labor tallies for the district planning office, each one logged on the mill's courier-receipt form. She counts what she can count. She is making her second crossing in eight days.

On the far side she turns west. The river is behind her. She passes the coal depot — iron doors padlocked, a permanent line of fine coal dust at the base of the wall where the wind has carried it. Then the corner bakery, its window fogged, a short queue visible inside: two women with net bags who glance at her as she passes and then look away. She does not know them. She does not know whether they know her, which is a different question and one she cannot answer.

She passes the pharmacy, its window dark at this hour. Past the pharmacy the street widens slightly — the bloc on the left set back from the pavement by a strip of bare ground where a hedge was, no longer — and then narrows again at the entry to the row. She walks on the left, near the wall, which is her habit on streets she does not know well. She knows this one better now than she did eight days ago. She knows bloc eighteen's entry: the latch, the slight resistance of the door, the smell of the stairwell — damp plaster and the cold that an enclosure receives last and holds longest. She goes up. On the second landing there is a folded baby carriage against the wall, the same one or one like it from the visit on the twenty-second. She does not stop. She goes up.

---

The third-floor landing. The water stain above the door frame — old and brown, shaped like nothing — and the patch of darker linoleum, and the draft from the stairwell window that she felt on the last visit and feels again now. She knocks.

The woman who answers is wearing the gray cardigan she wore in October, or one like it. She holds the door at the width she held it before: enough for a face. She looks at Ilinca for a moment without speaking.

Ilinca says: I need to take the copy back. It is not safe for you to have it anymore.

The woman says: a moment. She lets the door fall almost closed.

Inside: footsteps, unhurried. A drawer opening. A pause — the pause of a person who knows where the thing is and is retrieving it, not the pause of a person who is deciding what to do with it. The sound of paper against paper. The drawer closing.

Ilinca stands on the landing and looks at the water stain. It is old and the edges are dry and the center is slightly darker, which means the seep behind the plaster has not resolved itself. She has managed accounts with a discrepancy like this: the surface figure stable for months, the slow wet thing behind it unreported and accumulating. She has managed them by going into the column behind the surface and finding the entry that did not make it out. She is not thinking about accounts. She is waiting.

The door opens. The woman extends one hand through the gap.

N4 is folded twice: once along the long axis, once across. A single sheet. Ilinca takes it and puts it in the right pocket of her coat, flat against the lining. She feels the paper settle against her side — the weight of one sheet, which is less weight than almost anything.

She says: Thank you.

She says: Do not mention this visit to anyone.

The woman says: I know.

The door closes.

When someone comes to this landing — and someone will — the woman will have nothing to produce. She goes down by the wall and out.

---

The wind comes off the river on the return. She walks into it for the first hundred meters, keeping her hands in her coat pockets — left in the left, right in the right, fingers resting on N4 through the lining. One sheet of paper. She does not need to unfold it.

At the center of the bridge she stops.

Below: the Someș, brown and flat and wide, running without urgency in the cold morning. Twenty meters out, where the current presses against something below the surface and then rejoins itself, there is a seam — a long still line in the moving water. She has crossed this bridge more times than she has counted and she has looked at that seam before without stopping. Today she stops. Her breath is visible in the cold air. The railing under her right hand is rough with frost and she can feel the texture of it through her glove.

N4 is in her right pocket.

N1 is in the spine of the 1983 ledger. Second shelf of the mill's administrative wing, between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission. She has opened that ledger three hundred times in the past year, or something near it. She knows the binding by touch — the brown tape she put on in February when the original cracked. Tomorrow morning at seven she will open it again. She will take N1 from the spine. She will fold it: once along the long axis, once across. She will put it in the left pocket.

She has both documents. She has had them both since she walked off this bridge twenty minutes ago.

Doina Marcu has been in the holding section for ten days.

December the fifth is three days from today.

She holds these in the column she keeps for things that cannot go on paper. Confirmed figures. Counting them again does not change them. She has counted them.

*9. 7 or 8 — take her in.*

She knows the rest. She has known it since the twenty-second of November, when she stood in the cellar woman's corridor and read the nine where the bracket should have been. She knows what the nine produced, two hands further down the branch: a careful woman reading nine numbered steps in a column put the ninth in sequence with the eighth, and the eighth spoke of morning, and the ninth inherited it. She knows what will happen when she lays both documents on the desk at Strada 22 Decembrie. The bracket and the nine. Two things she made, provable as hers by the paper and the hand and everything a document is. The distance between them is twenty minutes in a coal cellar on a November night in 1983. The distance between that night and the fourth of November 1984 is twelve months and four women's hands. She has run this arithmetic. She knows what the figure is.

She does not think about what happens after the desk.

She takes her right hand from the railing — frost on her glove where it touched the iron — and walks.

---

Her apartment in the evening is the same temperature it was this morning. Cold enough that she does not take the coat off immediately on arrival; she stands in the hallway for a moment, looking at nothing in particular, and then hangs it on the hook. She does not take N4 from the pocket.

She makes supper: bread, the end of the hard cheese from earlier in the week, water heated for tea. She eats at the kitchen table with the lamp on and the window showing the street lamp at the corner of Strada Avântului and the dark sky beyond it. The sky is still clear. Darker now, fully dark, and when she looks past the northern roofline she can see the river has gone black in the night. She thinks briefly that there will be frost again. She does not write this down.

Tomorrow: the mill at seven. The ledger, the spine, N1 folded and in the left pocket. The walk to Strada 22 Decembrie. She is the kind of person who has already decided and who holds the decision the way she holds everything that cannot go in a column: in the part of the account that is not written down, exact, permanent, requiring nothing further.

She rinses the cup and the plate and sets them beside the sink.

She turns off the kitchen lamp.

In the dark hallway, the coat is on the hook. The right pocket holds a single folded sheet. In the other room the lamp is still on, making a thin line of yellow light under the door.

She goes toward it and then turns off that lamp too.

The coat hangs in the dark. The right pocket holds a single folded sheet. Outside the window the clear sky turns colder and the frost comes down and the river goes on moving in the dark.

# 3 December 1984

The frost had held through the night. He walked from the station on Strada 22 Decembrie north through the market square and then east along the Someș embankment toward Strada Crișan, and the cold was the settled kind — dry and crystalline rather than the wet, fog-heavy cold that had come off the river in the last weeks of November. It had decided to stay. The embankment road was empty except for a woman pushing a pram with a bag of something heavy hung from the handle, and a boy on a bicycle who had to stand up on the pedals to manage the slope. The Someș below the embankment was the color of wet concrete. On the opposite bank, two lines of poplar trees, leafless.

He had not requested the official car. This was one interview on a street he could cover on foot in twenty minutes, and the car's absence would be noted wherever it went. He had not thought further than that; he was a thorough man and he was walking.

Strada Crișan ran north from the embankment for six blocks before it met the park. The eastern side was older construction — five-story buildings close together, the stucco cracked in the horizontal joints, the windows on the lower floors fogged from inside with cooking steam. The western side was panel construction, four stories, each building nearly identical to the ones beside it except in small ways that did not amount to anything: the color of the entrance door frames, the number of functioning windows, whether the concrete on the steps had been swept or left to frost. He walked the length of the street once from south to north, reading the bloc numbers from the entrance panels. Bloc eighteen was on the western side, entrance B. Someone had turned the panel sideways at some point, possibly when hanging a line; it faced the neighboring building rather than the street. He found it on the second pass and went in.

Twenty-eight units. The stairwell smelled of cabbage and damp concrete, which was the smell of every stairwell this deep into November — he corrected himself: December. Third floor left was the last door on the landing before the wall. The light fixture had been taped back to the ceiling at one point with gray insulating tape; one corner of the tape was peeling and the fixture cast its light slightly sideways. He knocked twice.

The woman who answered was somewhere in her mid-thirties. She wore a gray cardigan buttoned to the collar and her hair was in the braid she had slept in. She had opened the door to perhaps forty centimetres and held it there while she read his identification card. Her expression as she looked up at him was not alarm. It was closer to recognition — not of him specifically, but of the question he had come to ask. He could see that in the way her weight settled, very slightly, when she looked up.

He introduced himself: Locotenent Munteanu, Miliția, Investigations Section. "I am here in connection with the Petrescu investigation. May I come in?"

She held the door open.

---

The apartment was one room. A kitchen alcove on the right-hand wall with a two-burner stove and a small refrigerator; a table in the center with two chairs; a narrow wardrobe beside the far wall. The bed was made and pushed against the left wall, a folded blanket at the foot. There was a plant on the windowsill in a tin that had once held marinated peppers — part of the label was still legible. The single window looked onto the rear courtyard. The radiator beneath it was not on; she had a second blanket folded over the back of her chair. There was a cup of tea on the table that had been steaming when she opened the door and was not steaming now.

He sat in the chair that was not hers and opened his notebook.

"I will ask you directly," he said. "Have you at any time had in your possession a handwritten document that has been circulating in the community — a document concerning medical care?"

She looked at her hands. Then at him. "I had something like that. Yes."

"Do you still have it?"

"No."

He wrote this down. "What happened to it?"

"The woman who gave it to me came back and took it."

He wrote: *Document retrieved by original source.* "When was this?"

"Yesterday." She thought about it briefly. "The second. The second of December."

He wrote the date and looked at it. December 2. He had confirmed this address at the Population Section on the afternoon of December 1 — three o'clock, approximately; he had asked the registrar for the Strada Crișan bloc-eighteen ledger, had obtained the registration, had noted the address in his working book while the registrar made the required entry in the consultation log. The following day, in some part of this city, someone had climbed these stairs and removed a document she had not wanted to leave in place.

He did not say anything about this. He wrote: *Retrieval date: 2 December. Document gone the day after Population Section address confirmation.*

"Can you describe the woman who gave you the document?"

"She's older than me." The woman across the table was considering it honestly, not performing the consideration. "Forty, I would say. Perhaps a bit older."

"Where does she work?"

"At the mill. I think in administration — not on the floor. I have seen her from a distance." She paused. "I don't know her family name."

He wrote: *Mill. Administration likely. Age approx. 40. No surname known to witness.* He read these four items back. In his working notes he had three entries under the G1 profile dating from the twenty-third of November, derived from six weeks of interviews and two dead ends: *mill-connected, female, older, document originator.* What the woman across the table had just given him in three sentences was the same profile, confirmed by a witness who had met the G1 source in person. She was either telling him everything she knew, or she was giving him the perimeter of it — precisely the outer edge that would confirm his profile without allowing him to locate anyone.

He asked the next question. "Can you tell me where she gave you the document — the specific location of that first transfer?"

She looked past him at the window for a moment. "I would rather not say."

He wrote: *Refused to specify location of original transfer. Answered all other questions without sign of concealment. Consistent with protection of third party rather than personal exposure.* "I understand," he said. "Is there anything else you can tell me about her — a physical description?"

"I would recognize her face, if that is any use."

He asked two more questions: had she shown the document to anyone, had she copied it. She said no to both, steadily, without the quality that usually accompanied a rehearsed negative — the slight brightening, the half-second before the answer. He believed her. The canvass of this building had turned up nothing. The address on Dorobanților that he had spent the morning of the twenty-ninth working had yielded a woman who had moved out in February; the population register had been what gave him Strada Crișan. The document had come here and had not gone further. He had reached a terminal point.

He stood and thanked her. He told her that if she heard from the woman in question, she should contact the station on Strada 22 Decembrie. She nodded. He went out.

At the top of the stairwell he paused. The door had closed behind him without additional comment. She had given him exactly what she could give him while protecting the woman above her in the chain. He went down.

---

On the street he stood outside the entrance for a moment. The boy on the bicycle was gone. Across the embankment road, the woman with the pram was crossing the bridge in the other direction. A superintendent from one of the eastern-side blocs was scraping ice off the entrance steps with the back end of a shovel. The Someș was still the same color it had been forty minutes ago.

He thought about the consultation log.

The Population Section kept a record of every registry access: date, accessor's name, rank or office, the volume consulted. This was standard administrative procedure for a document with legal relevance. He had known about the log and had not thought about it particularly, because there was ordinarily no reason to think about it. The log was accessible to the court clerk's office, the county inspectorate, and a number of other offices with legitimate interest in civil registration matters.

He was not suggesting that anyone in the Population Section had copied the log entry and passed it to someone outside the building. He was noting that a woman who had been doing careful, deliberate work for more than a year would have developed, over that time, some sense of how information about the investigation was moving. The arrest of Marcu Doina on the twenty-second of November would have been known at the mill by the twenty-third; he was not naive about this. The canvassing of the Strada Mihai building in the second week of November would have been known, perhaps more quickly. A woman working in administration at the same mill where Marcu Doina worked nights would have her own ways of following the direction of the investigation, and those ways would not require her to consult a Population Section access log.

She had taken the document back on December 2. He had confirmed this address on December 1. He preferred not to rely on coincidences.

He turned up his collar and walked south toward the embankment.

---

He was back at his desk by half past twelve.

The Petrescu dosar was in the center of the desk. He opened it to the working notes section, found the most recent entry — the Population Section consultation, December 1, *Moga R., Strada Crișan 18/B/3-left, registered 1979* — and drew a line below it and wrote today's date.

Then he wrote: *Interview, G2 node address, Strada Crișan. Witness: female, mid-thirties, registered resident. Document confirmed received from G1 source and returned to G1 source, 2 December. G1 description: mill-connected, administration likely, age approx. 40. G1 aware of investigation by 1 December at latest. G1 has recovered G2 copy. G1 location: unknown. G1 name: unknown.*

He read the entry back.

The G1 figure had both copies now. The one she had made first, in October of last year, and the one she had made quickly in conditions that did not permit careful work — made quickly enough that something had gone wrong that did not look like anything wrong until two hands later, when a woman reading nine numbered lines had done her careful best to put them in order. The G1 figure had come back for the second copy when she understood that the investigation had its address. She had not had it destroyed in place. She had come herself. A woman going to ground did not need to come back for a second-generation copy that had already dispersed further into the network; she would leave it and move, and the copy would sit in an evidence envelope and point upward at a blank space. Coming back for it meant she intended to do something with both of them. He did not know what.

He picked up the telephone receiver. He held it for several seconds — the ambient click of the station exchange, a distant voice on one of the other lines — and then set it down.

There was nothing he could put in front of his captain that was more than arithmetic: *I have a profile. Mill administration. Approximately forty years old. She is aware of the investigation and has recovered a second-generation copy. She has had two days. I do not have her name.* His captain would say: then go to the mill and find her. And he would have to explain that going to the mill administration section without a name meant walking past a woman who would see a Miliția coat coming and would have the time to decide what to do about it — and that a woman who had taken a document back the day before he reached it would know exactly how to use that time.

He had two days.

He turned to the blank pages at the back of the notebook and wrote at the top: *5 December.* Below it: *If no voluntary approach by 1800 on 4 December — formal charge, Marcu D.* He wrote the article numbers. He looked at this for a moment, then looked away, at the radiator on the far wall, which was making the settling sound it made at this hour. Outside the window the light was already thinning — less than four hours of usable sky this deep into December, and the afternoon had not really started.

Marcu Doina had been in the holding section for eleven days. She had answered his questions in the same words each time, with the same quality of stillness. She ate and slept and did not perform distress. He did not believe she was going to change her account. He believed his arithmetic was sound and that it pointed at someone who was not Marcu Doina; he believed that someone was moving toward some kind of action, because the alternative was going to ground and she had not done that. He believed that if she was going to come to him she would come in the next two days, because two days was when the deadline became something he had to act on.

He was not certain of any of this. He was proceeding as though he were.

He turned back to the working notes section and wrote at the bottom of the entry, below the interview summary, below the G1 profile: *Two days.*

He closed the notebook.

He did not pick up the telephone again.

# 4 December 1984

The administrative wing is dark when she arrives. Seven in the morning, the overhead strip not yet on, the corridor windows still the gray before proper daylight. She can hear the overnight caretaker somewhere at the far end, the sound of the cart's metal wheel against the linoleum. She does not call out to him. She goes directly to Mița's desk and lines the payroll envelopes along the front edge — one per name, alphabetical, sealed and initialed the night before. She counts them as she sets them down. Fourteen. The same as every month.

She does not sign the distribution sheet.

She goes to her own desk. She does not hang her coat. She sets her bag on the floor beside the chair and does not open it. She sits for a moment with her hands flat on the desk and then she opens the bottom shelf of the bookcase and lifts out the 1983 ledger — black cover, her own label starting to lift at the lower right corner, the binding soft from two years on the shelf.

She has produced this ledger on demand three times: the spring audit, the year-end reconciliation, the mill director's signature on the October figures. Each time she has set it on the desk and opened it to the requested page and said nothing while whoever was reading it finished. Each time she has put it back on the shelf afterward and the paper in the spine was still there.

She holds the ledger spine-down over her desk and waits. The paper slides free — a moment of resistance, a small sound, and then it is in her palm. A single sheet, folded in thirds, the creases gone soft from fourteen months in one position.

She sets the ledger back on the shelf, spine straight with the others.

She does not unfold the paper. She folds it once more, the same fold, the same direction, along the same crease, and puts it into her left breast pocket.

She stands. She buttons her coat.

Right coat pocket: N4, where it has been since the second of December.
Left breast pocket: N1, where it has been since October 1983.

She puts on her gloves. She picks up the pen from her desk and sets it parallel to the edge — the way it sits when she has not been in. She turns off the lamp.

She goes out through the side door onto the service road.

---

The cold outside is complete and still — not the cold with wind, but the cold that does not need it. A thin layer of snow from the night before, already dirty along the road edges, pressed hard underfoot and squeaking at every step. The sky is pale yellow to the east, the sun at the rooflines but not above them yet.

She goes around the outer fence to the main avenue and turns toward the market. Strada 22 Decembrie is fifteen minutes at her pace. She does not change her pace.

At the corner of the market, the bread queue is six deep. A woman in a brown coat stands at the front with a canvas bag against her leg. Two schoolchildren go past on the opposite pavement, their breath showing white. Ilinca walks by the end of the queue and does not look at anyone in it.

She passes the post office — the notice board outside with the water-stain across the lower right corner that has been there since September. She passes the pharmacy, grille still down, the window dark. She passes the bloc where Georgeta lives. Third floor, second window from the right — the curtains closed, the light behind them not on. She passes the bloc where Livia Moldovan lives. She does not look up at either of them.

She turns onto Strada 22 Decembrie.

The station is visible from the corner. Stone facade, two stories, the national emblem above the public entrance, an official vehicle parked in the yard to the side. She pushes the door open.

---

Inside: warm air and the smell of floor wax and something underneath it, the particular smell of rooms where forms accumulate over years. A long counter with a frosted glass partition, two stations, only one occupied. The duty officer is young — round-faced, the collar of his uniform one size large for his neck. He looks up from what he is writing.

She says: I need to speak with Lieutenant Munteanu. Regarding the Petrescu matter.

He says: Your name.

She says: Roșca, Ilinca. Mill administration.

He writes this down. He says: Wait there.

There is a bench to her left. Two men are sitting on it, not speaking to each other, both in their fifties, both with the look of people who have been waiting longer than they expected. She stays at the counter. She sets her gloved hands on the counter edge and then takes them off and holds them at her sides.

From behind the partition she can hear a typewriter — three quick strokes, a pause, three more — and then a door somewhere opening. And then a door closing. And then nothing, except the two men on the bench and her own breathing and the sound of a vehicle in the yard outside starting its engine and then going quiet again.

The duty officer comes back through the door at the partition's end. He says: Come through.

---

The corridor beyond is narrower than she expected. Linoleum floor in a color between green and gray, scuffed to nothing along the center. Doors on both sides, most closed. At the far end a window looks out on the courtyard — she can see the official vehicle and the frost still white on the upper course of brickwork on the wall opposite. They go up one short flight of stairs, uncarpeted, and along another corridor. The duty officer stops at the second door on the right. It is open.

---

Munteanu is at his desk. The Petrescu dosar is open in front of him, its cover folded back, and she can see the working pages — forms, notebook sheets, printed headings filled in by hand. Along the left edge of the desk: seven evidence envelopes in a row. She counts them. Seven. She knows the dates they arrived. She knows what each one holds. To the right of the envelopes: his notebook, open to a page of handwriting dense enough that the white of the page is almost gone. At the far corner of the desk, a coffee cup with the coffee dried to a ring at the bottom.

He looks up from the dosar. He looks at her. There is a moment before he says anything. He does not look surprised. He looks at her the way a man looks at a figure that finally matches the column it belongs in.

He says: Tovarășă Roșca?

She says: Yes.

He says: Please, sit down.

The chair across from the desk is wooden and straight-backed, a worn patch on the seat. She sits.

She takes N1 from her left breast pocket, unfolding it as she lifts it free. She takes N4 from her right coat pocket. She sets both documents on the desk in front of him — flat, side by side, N1 to the left, N4 to the right — and removes her hands from both pages.

He looks at them. He does not pick either one up immediately. He reads a few words of each from where he is sitting. Then he picks up N1.

---

1. Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.
2. Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.
3. Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.
4. If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.
5. No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.
6. Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
   [ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why.
     Do not wait for the morning. ]

He reads it line by line. She watches his eyes track down the page. When he reaches line eight he slows. His eyes go to the bracket below it — the indented lines, the closing bracket — and he reads to the end and holds the page.

He sets N1 down. He picks up N4.

---

1. Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.
2. Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.
3. Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.
4. If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.
5. No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.
6. Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.

He reads it and then reads it again from line seven. He sets N4 beside N1 and looks at both pages at the same time. His eyes move from one to the other. He looks at the lower half of the left-hand page — the bracket, the indented lines. He looks at the lower half of the right-hand page — the numbered ninth line, flush with the margin.

She does not speak.

He says: Did you make these?

She says: Yes.

He says: Which one first?

She says: The one with the bracket.

He looks at the two documents once more. Then he reaches for the telephone.

He dials the internal line. It rings twice.

He says: This is Munteanu. I need you to release Marcu Doina from the holding section. She can sign for her things and go.

A pause. She can hear the voice at the other end, small and metallic.

He says: Immediately.

He puts the telephone down.

He picks it up again. He dials a different number. A longer wait this time.

He says: Captain. This is Munteanu. The Petrescu matter — I've resolved it. I have the originating party here in my office. He says her name. Her employer. A pause, the captain's voice rising once. He says: A voluntary approach. This morning. Yes. I can have the full documentation to you by end of business. He listens. He says: Understood.

He puts the telephone down.

---

Somewhere along the corridor a door opens and then closes.

He pulls the right-hand drawer open and takes out a blank form — white, the Miliția heading printed across the top — and sets it on the desk beside the evidence envelopes. He picks up his pen.

He writes her name first, last name before first. Then the date. Then her address.

He writes on.

The two documents are still between them on the desk. N1 to the left, N4 to the right. She can read both from where she is sitting. She has read both so many times that the lines run in sequence whether she means them to or not — eight lines and a bracket on the left; nine lines on the right; the same words in both, and the ninth word in a different place, and everything that came from that. She has not moved. Her coat is still buttoned. Her hands are in her lap.

He writes on.

The writing on both documents is hers.

She sits.

**Result:** "She counts them. Seven."
**Reason:** The label "without deciding to" annotates the cognitive act as automatic/involuntary. The prose already shows the count; labelling its involuntary quality softens the cold-procedure register. The counting beat is preserved; only the meta-gloss is removed.

---

---

---

**Cut:** "He writes with the particular care of a man who knows that what he puts on a form will not come off it — not quickly, and not without consequence."

# The Deadline

5 December 1984

He had been inside the building since six. The overnight duty officer had given him a nod from behind the entry logbook and returned to his numbers. The corridor lights were at half-strength, which they were until eight, when the day shift arrived and someone switched the panel over. In the duty-room kitchen: the powder tin on the upper shelf, water from the tap that ran brown for a moment before clearing. He carried the nechezol back to his desk in the tin cup — the one with the handle that held. The ceramic mugs had handles that separated from the body without warning; he had learned this in his first month at the Dej station, twelve years ago, and had not touched the ceramic mugs since.

The investigations room was empty. His desk held, left to right: his working notebook open to 4 December, the Petrescu dosar open to the blank determination form, and the two documents face-up in the center — he had left them there when he went home the previous evening, which he did not usually do with evidence — and the eleven evidence envelopes stacked on the left edge of the desk, labeled but not yet sealed. He had the labels written from yesterday afternoon. He had wanted to see everything one more time in the morning light before closing it.

He had come in two hours before the office filled because a determination written in an empty room was complete when he signed it, and a determination written while people moved past the desk sometimes needed to be written again. He had written two over twelve years that needed to be written again. He preferred to write things once.

He wrote the section headings in the left margin, uncapped his pen, and began.

---

*Nature of the death.* Petrescu, Ana, born 1965, age nineteen. Admitted to the Dej district hospital at 14:33 on 4 November 1984, died at 18:47 the same date. Cause of death certified by the duty physician: hemorrhagic shock following complications of an illegal procedure. Initial notification to the Procuratură received 5 November 1984. No additional certification required; case opened on that date under the relevant articles.

*The document.* A handwritten document circulating without authorisation among workers and residents of the Dej municipal area. The document contains aftercare instructions pertaining to the management of complications of illegal procedures; it does not describe or specify any procedure. Through examination of twenty-two physical copies and through the voluntary testimony of its originator, it has been established that the document exists in multiple handwritten variant versions, all derived from a single source copy designated Exhibit A. The variants differ from the source by minor transcription incidentals: punctuation, line-break, numbering style. In one branch of transmission, a formatting difference in the source's ninth element propagated a material change in the rendered instruction, resulting in the version present in the Petrescu household. That branch is the subject of this determination.

*Origin.* The source copy — Exhibit A, the master — was produced by Roșca, Ilinca, born 1943, contabil-șef at the Artificial Fiber Enterprise, Dej. Authorship was attested to in a voluntary interview of 4 December 1984. The document was written in October 1983. From the master, the originator produced three copies between October and November 1983: two distributed through named individuals on separate branches of transmission, and one — Exhibit B — made on 3 November 1983.

The originator confirmed that the ninth element of the master was set down in bracket format: a marginal notation attached to the eighth line, not a numbered list item. In Exhibit B, the copy made on 3 November 1983, the same element appears as a numbered line, item 9 of nine. The originator described the conditions of that copying as insufficient light and available time. She stated that she does not know why the transcription took the form it did. She acknowledges that it did, and that Exhibit B was the product of her hand.

*Chain of transmission.* He wrote the names in order from the second generation forward, working from the notebook. He had eleven names: eight women who had spoken to him, plus the responsible party, plus the two household members at the chain's end. Against those eleven he had two entries where a holder had declined to provide a name — recorded as *Name not provided to the investigating officer.* One entry near the bottom read: *Unidentified female, bus route 4, Dej, approximately spring 1984. Contact not established.* He underlined it and moved to the next line.

The chain as established ran ten confirmed nodes from the master to the copy in the Petrescu household. Branches not connected to the fatal variant had been traced and confirmed as dead ends; they were summarised in an appendix. The central chain — from the master through Exhibit B, through two further transmissions, through the regularised copy, and through three further transmissions to the Petrescu household — had been documented through physical copy collection, voluntary interview, and the documentary evidence produced by the responsible party on 4 December 1984.

He reached the mutation section. He looked at the two documents in the center of his desk. He had read them both a dozen times since yesterday afternoon. He wrote.

*Formatting difference and its propagation.* The ninth element of Exhibit A (the master) reads, in relevant part:

[ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning. ]

The same element in Exhibit B (the copy made 3 November 1983) reads:

9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.

The wording was identical in both versions. The formatting differed: a marginal bracket notation in the master became a numbered list item in the copy. Two further transmissions downstream from Exhibit B, a copyist reading nine numbered lines regularised the ninth into sequence with the eighth, producing the following:

9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.

This wording was preserved through three further transmissions and was present in Exhibit C (node seventeen), the copy in Ana Petrescu's household at the time of the events of 4 November 1984. The introduction of the phrase *in the morning* and the omission of the phrase *Do not wait for the morning* both occurred in the course of regularisation from the numbered format of Exhibit B.

He drew a check in the margin and moved to the last heading.

*Responsible party.* Roșca, Ilinca, born 1943, contabil-șef, AFE Dej. Employment address. The relevant articles, which he had from memory. The voluntary interview; the documents produced by the responsible party in person on 4 December 1984. A note that the responsible party had appeared at the station before the end-of-day threshold at which formal preliminary charge would have been placed against the secondary holder. The secondary holder of a document on a clean branch of transmission — Marcu, Doina, born 1965 — had been released from preliminary detention on 4 December 1984, per order of the investigating officer. He wrote that sentence twice, because the first time the handwriting was not clear.

---

The determination was six pages. He read it from the heading. The facts were in the right order. The chain was documented. The mutation was described in the language he had chosen, which said what it said and nothing else. The responsible party was named and the secondary holder was cleared.

He capped the pen.

He picked up the two documents from the center of the desk. He read each one's ninth element once more before the envelopes.

The bracket, in the master: *[ 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning. ]*

The numbered line, in the cellar copy: *9. 7 or 8 — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

Every word the same. He slid Exhibit A into the first envelope and Exhibit B into the second. The labels were already written. He sealed both and set them with the other nine.

Eleven envelopes in a row on the left edge of the desk. He straightened them until the edges aligned and wrote the case number across the strip of paper along the top of the row. He wrote *Petrescu, A., 4.XI.1984 — evidence* and set the completed dosar on top, closed.

---

The file did not contain the reason the document had existed. It did not contain the prior question: why a woman in this town had written eight instructions and a bracketed ninth, what the bracket was there to prevent, what kind of decision it was designed to help someone make.

The file did not contain the reason the cellar had been dark and the time had been insufficient. It contained "insufficient light and time pressure" as the originator's own description of the conditions in which Exhibit B was made.

He had spent thirty-one days on the Petrescu matter. He had not sent up an innocent name. He had sent the correct name, through the correct procedure, on the deadline day.

He closed it there.

---

He telephoned his captain at half past nine. Two rings before the answer.

He said: the determination in the Petrescu matter is on its way to you by messenger.
His captain said: good.
He said: the evidence can be transferred today or tomorrow, whichever is preferred.
His captain said: today. Then: was it as complicated as it seemed?
Munteanu said: it was exactly as complicated as it seemed.
A pause. His captain said: good. Understood. And the call ended.

He set the phone down.

---

The dosar went with the courier at noon. At half past four he carried the evidence envelopes downstairs himself. The evidence room officer — a younger man, two or three years in the post — asked for the case name. Munteanu told him. The officer wrote it in the register. Munteanu watched the entry being written and did not speak again after that.

He went back upstairs and sat at the cleared desk for a few minutes. The notebook was in the inside pocket of his coat. The pen was in the drawer. The tin cup was on the corner, where it had been since six-fifteen that morning.

At six he put on the coat. He picked up the tin cup and drank what was left of the nechezol, which had been cold for several hours. Nobody liked the nechezol warm. Cold was not an additional problem so much as the same problem continued at a lower temperature. He set the cup on the desk and went out.

On Strada 22 Decembrie the air was several degrees below zero and the valley fog had settled back in, low along the Someș — the kind that sat from early evening until late morning, opaque at road level, thickening where the ground fell toward the water. He could make out the shape of the far hillside through the haze. He could not see the river. He turned his collar up.

The case was closed. December fifth, the day it was required to close, and it was closed on that day. Doina Marcu had been released the afternoon before. Ilinca Roșca was in the second-floor holding section, which he had not gone past when he came by it this afternoon.

He walked. His hands were in his coat pockets. The determination was in a folder on its way to Cluj-Napoca. The evidence was in a room in the basement, correctly labeled, signed for, sealed. The fog absorbed the sound of the road and the sound of the Someș below the embankment and the sound of his own boots, so that by the time he reached the corner where the road dropped toward the bridge the only thing he could hear clearly was the one thing he could not see.

He went home.

## 29-the-deadline

### Meta-commentary on cognition

**Cut:** `He thought about what the file contained.`
— Labels the cognitive act; the thoughts that follow render it unnecessary.

**Cut:** `He checked this the way he checked anything: by asking what was missing, and finding nothing.`
— Names the method of verification rather than letting the verification stand.

**Cut:** `Then he thought about what the file did not contain.`
— Announces the pivot rather than making it.

**Cut:** `He understood all of this correctly.`
— Tells the reader Munteanu understands what the preceding paragraphs already showed him understanding.

**Cut:** `He was not comfortable with the things the file did not contain, and he understood that this was not a circumstance that was going to change by his sitting with it at his desk in the morning.`
— Names discomfort ("not comfortable") and labels acceptance ("understood that this was not a circumstance that was going to change"). Both are shown by what precedes; both are dissolved by "He closed it there."

### Redundant transition / re-summary

**Cut:** `It was complete. The origin, the chain, the mutation in exact language, the responsible party named, the secondary holder cleared in the final paragraph. Everything required by procedure was in it.`
— Recaps the determination the reader just read in full. The reader has the file; they do not need the inventory again.

**Cut:** `It described the document, its origin, its chain of transmission, and the consequences of one variant of it.`
— Re-summarises the file's contents inside a paragraph about what the file *didn't* contain. Redundant in both directions.

**Cut:** `He had followed the chain from the death back to the source and had reached the source and had written the source's name in the determination. He had not followed it further than that. The file did not go further than that.`
— Three sentences recapping the investigation's scope, all of which are already carried by the determination text and by the paragraph that correctly names "insufficient light and time pressure" as the end of the traceable chain.

### Post-scene subtext naming

**Cut:** `Whether "exactly as complicated as it seemed" had given his captain what he wanted or not was not something he could determine from this end of the line. He had answered what he was asked.`
— The dialogue does this work. "Exactly as complicated as it seemed" / "Good. Understood." / end of call is the whole scene; the two sentences after it name what the reader already assembled from the exchange.

### Thesis restatement

**Cut:** `That phrase described a condition. It did not describe the condition that produced the condition.`
— Points directly at the regime as the condition behind the condition. Per style.md: "Thesis restatement — an abstract sentence re-stating the book's argument about state culpability, conditions, or what the paper means." The argument is carried by the document tree; the narrator obeys the same rule as the characters.

### Sentence-after-the-sentence

**Cut:** `These were not in the file because the file was not that kind of file. No file he had written in twelve years was that kind.`
— Both sentences gloss "It did not contain the prior question: why a woman in this town had written eight instructions and a bracketed ninth…" The prior sentence does the work; the two following sentences explain it.

---

**Net effect:** The fourth section (between the third and fourth `---`) is reduced from seven paragraphs to four. The phone-call section loses its post-call gloss. The determination text, all sensory/physical detail, all dialogue, and every procedural inventory is preserved intact. Estimated interior/expository reduction in the affected section: ~45%.

# 5 December 1984

The officer who gave me back my coat was not one I'd seen in twelve days of faces, which was the first good thing about the morning. He set the items on the counter in a row: the coat, my buletin, and the bread roll that had been in my coat pocket when they brought me in, which was hard now and slightly flattened from eleven days in an evidence drawer. He put it on the counter with the same procedural neutrality as the buletin and pushed a form across for me to sign. I signed it. It said I was released following the determination of the case, which I knew was what the form would say because it was the only thing that would produce a morning where an officer I didn't know returned my coat instead of an officer I did know collecting me for a fourth session in the second-floor room.

A bread roll in an evidence drawer.

I asked once where my geography book was. Not hopefully — I had worked out, on approximately the fourth day, that the geography book was not coming back, and I had made a kind of peace with that, or at least the functional version of peace that you make with a thing you cannot change while you still have other things to think about. The officer checked a printed list. He said it was retained in evidence. I nodded and picked up the coat.

I put the buletin in my coat pocket and the bread in the other and I walked out through the public entrance. The duty officer at the front desk did not look up. The door was heavier than I remembered, or possibly I was lighter; twelve days of holding-section food takes something from you that you notice most when you have to push a door.

Outside it was cold and barely light. Dej at six in the morning in early December is the idea of a town rather than the actual one — the shapes of blocs in the gray, the outlines of streets, everything the same color as the sky with only texture to tell them apart. I stood on the step and worked out what day it was. I had gone in on a Thursday — I knew it was a Thursday because it was a shift day and I was supposed to be at the mill at six in the evening, and Munteanu had knocked on my hostel door at half past four in the afternoon, which had given me an hour and a half to not go anywhere. Twelve nights from Thursday was Tuesday. I was willing to accept some uncertainty in that count, because some of the nights in the holding section had been long enough to have contained two separate nights inside them — not literally, but in the way that a night without sleep and with nothing to do but recite something to yourself in the dark stretches until it does not resemble a single unit of time anymore.

Tuesday, I decided. Approximately.

I ate the bread standing on the step. It was better than nothing — that is the most accurate thing I can say about the bread, and I have spent some time since trying to arrive at a more nuanced assessment and I cannot manage one. It was cold and hard and stale in a way that suggested it had never been particularly warm, and it was breakfast. When it was finished I was still on the step because I had not decided where to go.

The Someș was two streets over. I could hear the particular quality of quiet that a wide river makes when there is December fog sitting on it — flatter than ordinary quiet, slightly muffled, as if the river has drawn something heavy across itself and is no longer available. I had been inside for twelve days. The fog in the Someș valley had been happening for twelve days without my participation and it had managed fine.

The geography book was in an evidence room somewhere in the building behind me, entered in a register, sealed in an envelope, labelled. The piece of paper that had been inside it for eleven months was in the same room, in a different envelope or possibly the same one — I did not know the procedure for that level of specificity. Either way, both of them were now state property, which meant they were in a place where they would be kept safe and used for nothing. I thought about the state holding that piece of paper and I thought: good luck. You have it. You will file it. You will never know what it is.

Something had determined the case. The form told me that much. I had a theory about what that something was — who it had been, what they had done, what it had cost them — and the theory was detailed enough by the end of twelve days in the second-floor holding section that I am going to leave it here as a theory. Some things I was still not writing down and this was one of them. What I knew was that I was out, and that someone had made that possible, and that I would know more eventually or I would not.

I tested myself.

Line one. I said it quietly, to the empty street in front of me, to the fog that was beginning to move in from the direction of the river.

*Keep her warm, and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.*

Line two.

*Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.*

Line three.

*Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.*

Line four. I started to say *every*. This had been the fault in my memorization from the first time I had tried to recall it — a groove cut into the wrong word, a word-shaped rut that my memory ran into before my attention could prevent it. I had corrected it every time I had gone through the document in the hostel room in November, and on the hostel bathroom floor with the test copy burning in the sink, and on the nights in the holding section when there was nothing else to do with the dark. I corrected it now.

*If she sleeps, wake her each hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.*

Line five.

*No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.*

Line six.

*Burn nothing until she is well. Keep and wash.*

Line seven.

*Two cloths in one hour is too many.*

Line eight.

*A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.*

I stopped there. A pigeon on the cornice of the building across the street watched me with the comprehensive indifference of pigeons. There is no way to draw a bracket in memory. What you have instead is the space where the bracket was: the pause before the thing that overrides the sequence, the one that says the eight steps end here and here is what supersedes them. I had read it right. I had said it right in the hostel room in November when I had first gone through the whole document without the paper, and on the bathroom floor when I burned the test copy and checked it against the original and found the bracket still there, and on the nights in the second-floor room when the document was the thing I held against the dark and the dark didn't win.

I said it quietly, on the step, to the street.

*Seven or eight — take her in. Say she began bleeding on her own and you do not know why. Do not wait for the morning.*

The pigeon left. I went down the steps.

---

The fog was on the Someș when I got to the bank — white and thick, sitting on the surface of the brown water so that the river looked like it went on in both directions indefinitely without going anywhere. The water was running fast from the autumn rains and I could hear it more clearly than I could see it. There was no proper path along the bank, just ground that had been walked flat over enough years to stay flat. I walked along it with my hands in my coat pockets and the fog around me on every side.

I was not going to try to find the woman on the bus.

I want to be clear about this because it has come up since, in various forms, from various people who have heard different versions of the story. I did not know her name. I did not know her stop or where she was going or what she normally did on the number four bus in the morning direction. She had put the paper in my hand the way you pass someone the salt — before I could think of a reason to say no, which I suspect was not accidental, which I suspect was the technique of someone who had done this kind of transaction before and knew that the window for consent is narrower than the window for refusal. I had not said her name in eleven months of having the paper. I had not said it in twelve days of Munteanu asking me questions across the table in the second-floor room, in three sessions across twelve days, the third of which lasted long enough that I lost track of whether it was still the same day. I was not going to say it now, on the Someș bank in the fog, because I was cold and out and the bread was finished and the geography book was in an evidence room. The not-knowing was the correct version of not-knowing. She was safe or she wasn't, and I would go on not-knowing, and that was not going to change because the case was determined and I was standing on the flat ground by the river.

I thought about Ana Petrescu. Not for very long. I find I can hold that thought for a certain stretch before it tips into something I can't do anything useful with, and I try to keep it to the useful part. I didn't know her when she was alive. What I knew about her was what I'd known since November — her name, her house on Strada Someșului, her sister-in-law's account, the time she arrived at the district hospital, the time she did not come out. She was nineteen years old. I kept coming back to that, the way you come back to a number that doesn't add up — nineteen, the same as me, which is not a meaningful coincidence and I know that, it is just the number I could not set aside. She was nineteen and the paper said *in the morning* and she died in the morning, and the paper said *in the morning* because somewhere along the chain of hands through which it had traveled, someone had read a bracket as a ninth step in the sequence and written it down that way. Nobody in that chain had been careless. A girl had died who should not have.

The fog was around me and the water was somewhere to my right, present as sound and smell rather than sight — the brown-water smell of the Someș in December, the cold that comes off a river moving fast in early winter. The far bank was somewhere I had to take on faith. The bloc-tops behind me on my side of the river went in and out of the white as I walked.

I turned around when the concrete apron ended and the bank became proper mud. I walked back the way I had come, into the fog from the other direction.

Eventually I would go back to the hostel. Eventually the hostel would let me in and I would sleep, and then there would be next things, because there are always next things at nineteen — the next shift to figure out, the next month, whatever the determination of the case meant for the rest of it, which I did not know yet and was not going to know on an approximately Tuesday morning on the Someș bank before the town had fully opened for the day. I had my coat. I had my buletin. I had the nine elements in my head, all nine, in order, the bracket included.

The fog did not come up. I got cold first.

### Operative kill list

Doina's longer, digressive, wry sentences are protected by the lean-into clause and were not shortened.

---

### Sentence-after-the-sentence (2 cuts)

**Cut 1.**
> *Cut:* "I have thought about this since and I cannot improve on it as a description of the situation."

Followed the image "A bread roll in an evidence drawer." — which is complete and sharp. The following sentence annotated the image's aptness ("I cannot improve on it"), signalling the reader to notice what the image had already done. The image now sits alone as a one-sentence paragraph.

Positioned between the pigeon image and "There is no way to draw a bracket in memory." Explained why she stopped — but the bracket meditation that follows explains the pause more powerfully and without redundancy. The move from pigeon indifference directly to the bracket passage is stronger.

---

### Thesis restatement (1 cut)

**Cut 3.**
> *Cut:* "The conditions had been the conditions."

Sat between "Nobody in that chain had been careless." and "A girl had died who should not have." — filling the gap between those two facts with an abstract statement naming the systemic cause. The brief is explicit that this argument must be carried by the document tree, not stated. The two flanking sentences now carry the weight without the thesis sentence bridging them; the gap between no-carelessness and death is more productive unmediated.

---

### Flags

None. No continuity gaps opened by any of the three cuts.

## Macro arc assessment

**Overall shape.** The Ninth Line has a well-engineered mechanical clock — two monotonic node-count ladders running in opposite directions against a fixed 31-day deadline — that keeps the race legible throughout. Act I (Ch 1–9) is tight: three POVs established quickly, both collations launched, and the load-bearing dramatic irony delivered correctly at Ch 9 (reader holds `ninth-line-is-a-warning-not-a-step`; Ilinca does not). The climax (Ch 28) is placed correctly, structurally earned, and — crucially — does not depend on external force: Ilinca walks in voluntarily. The final chapter (Doina reciting from memory on the step) is the book's best structural idea and delivers without moralising. The three-act shape holds.

**Midbook sag: the one-node-per-chapter plateau.** The most significant structural risk sits in Act II, chapters 10–17. These eight chapters follow an almost identical beat: one investigator traces one more node on the network. Ilinca chapters 11, 13, 15, and 17 each map one more node on the N4 branch; Munteanu chapters 12, 16, and 20 each collect one more physical copy. Doina chapters 10 and 14 add no nodes at all. The brief's compounding mechanism — each node gain produces a specific new foreclosure — was designed to differentiate these chapters, and the chapter map's foreclosure column is careful. But the structural shape is the same for seven consecutive chapters. If the drafters rendered the foreclosures with enough specificity (a name now burned, a branch now closed), the sag may not materialise on the page. If they fell back on the mechanism as summary rather than scene, chapters 10–17 will read as the book's slowest passage. **This is the single highest-risk zone in the manuscript and deserves close attention in the per-chapter pass.**

**Chapter 19: the zero-advance reaction chapter.** Ch 19 (Ilinca learns of Doina's arrest) is the only chapter in Act II that advances zero node counts and adds no new foreclosure — it is a pure reaction chapter. This is structurally defensible: Doina's arrest in Ch 18 is the midbook event and Ilinca needs a beat to process it. But in a book where every other chapter moves at least one ladder, a rest chapter this late in Act II could land as a stall. The question for the per-chapter pass is whether Ch 19 earns its weight through interiority and through pressure that is qualitatively new (not just restated urgency) — or whether the arrest's implications would land harder by being folded into Ch 21 and leaving Ch 19 to a different kind of advance.

**Double-Ilinca at the Act II/III hinge (Ch 21–22): earned turn or padded decision?** The outline explicitly defends two consecutive Ilinca chapters at the hinge as marking "the turn from the race to the choice." Ch 21 ends with her resolving to go to the cellar woman tomorrow. Ch 22 is the going. A decision chapter followed immediately by its execution chapter is a classic padding pattern: two beats where one would serve. The brief's defence is structural (the hinge needs weight), but the execution should be scrutinised — if Ch 21 reads as "she decides" and Ch 22 reads as "she goes," without Ch 21 independently doing something that Ch 22 cannot also carry, this is a chapter that could be tightened or absorbed.

**Climax/coda balance.** The climax (Ch 28) occupies one chapter and resolves all four threads simultaneously (Ilinca's surrender, Doina's release, Munteanu's correct-but-insufficient understanding, both documents becoming state property). That is a lot of thread to close in a single chapter without feeling rushed; the per-chapter pass should confirm it has enough room. The two-chapter coda (29 Munteanu closes the file; 30 Doina walks out) is structurally sound in concept — two perspectives on aftermath — but Ch 29 risks being the thinnest chapter in the book: Munteanu writes a report, seals eleven envelopes, goes home in the fog. The administrative close is tonally correct for his register, but at a 1,900-word floor, a chapter whose only dramatic movement is bureaucratic closure may feel like an epilogue that overstays. The per-chapter pass should assess whether Ch 29 earns its chapter status or whether its content could be compressed into a scene within Ch 28 or Ch 30.

**Ending-mode distribution.** The planned distribution (literary-fade 8–10, cliffhanger 5–7, mid-action-cut 4–6, turn 4–5, resolved beat 2–3) is deliberately varied and well-designed. The chapter-craft log is the check on whether the drafters honoured it; any run of three or more identical ending modes in Act II would compound the midbook sag risk.

**Padding diagnosis.** This book does not present as padded-to-length in the aggregate. The brief's concern was under-delivery, not over-inflation, and the three-POV braid with 22 tracked document nodes and a live epistemic chain genuinely requires the frame it has. The padding risk is localised: it lives in the repetitive structural beat of the midbook accumulation chapters (10–17), not in the book's total length. A 25% trim would cut into load-bearing material; targeted pressure on the one-node-per-chapter run is the right tool.

# 5 November 1984

The woman from the third floor told us the way you tell a thing you don't want to be the one to tell. She was already in her coat. She said it toward the wall at the end of the hallway — *she died at the hospital in Dej, the younger Petrescu* — and then she went downstairs and left us standing there. Nobody moved first. We all stood in the hallway waiting for someone else to be the person who stopped standing there.

I didn't know Ana Petrescu. I knew the name the way you know names in a mill town — she worked the day shift, I worked nights, we had never been in the same building at the same time as far as I could reckon. What I knew about her was that she was nineteen, which is what I also am, and now she wasn't. The woman from the third floor was already gone. I went back to my room and got my jacket and my gloves and my bag. The shift started at six and if I didn't leave now the section head would have a reason to remember my face, and I didn't want that, and so I put my gloves on and went downstairs, and that was November fifth, 1984, which is where this begins.

---

It was dark at five-thirty. In November in the Someș valley darkness is not an event, it is the default condition that the daytime interrupts briefly and incompletely. The streetlamps along the road to the mill make yellow haloes in the fog rather than light on the pavement, and this is the light I have walked to work by for two years: more fog than lamp, more direction than illumination. I know the road by the soles of my shoes. I know the stretch where the cobbles are loose near the transformer station and the bend where the puddle collects against the cracked kerb and the place where the smell of the mill arrives before you can see the mill's lights — the hot-wet chemical sweetness of the fiber process mixed with the river cold, the smell that lives in my coat whether I notice it or not.

The women ahead of me I knew by their coats. Mariana's was the navy one with the collar lining coming loose on the left side — she had pinned it twice and the pin kept giving way. Costina's was the brown one with the wooden toggles, short on her because she is taller than it was made for. The two women from Shift B whose names I had not learned in fourteen months, for reasons that say something about me or about fourteen months and I am not sure which. I fell in behind their backs and followed them through the dark and the fog and the mill smell and didn't say anything, because it was five-thirty in the morning and the woman from the third floor had said what she said and I didn't have anything to add to it.

By the time the smell of the mill was strong I could see the lights over the production floor. They are always on. It is the most reliable thing about my life in Dej, and I am not going to pretend I don't find it comforting. I showed my cartelă at the gate. I went to put my things in the locker.

The geography book was on the shelf above the coat hooks, where I had put it on my first day two years ago and never moved it since. It was published in 1978, purchased for me by my mother when I was twelve, and neither of us has ever read it. I brought it to Dej because I thought I ought to look like a person who read things, and then when I got to the hostel and understood the situation I decided the factory locker was more private than the hostel room, and I left the book on the shelf and walked away from it. For eleven months it had been just a thing I owned, the way the coat is a thing I own. I did not look at it. I went to work.

---

On the production floor the looms are twelve metres high and if you want to say something to someone standing two metres away, you put your mouth near their ear and shout. If what you want to say is not the kind of thing you shout, you wait. Everyone waits. We have all been waiting for years at whatever volume is required by the job, and we are all very good at it.

What this meant on the morning of the fifth was that I had six hours in which nothing was required of me except to watch the thread and count the revolutions and do what I was there to do. The woman from the third floor had said what she said and Ana Petrescu was in the past tense and the name was in my head and I was on the production floor where the looms make other things impossible. I watched Costina's hands on her machine — she has been here eight years and knows things about it that the maintenance record doesn't, and I have learned more from watching her hands than from anything the section head has ever said directly to me — and I counted what I was supposed to count, and I was very grateful for the noise, which is not something I say lightly because the looms are genuinely very loud.

Six hours. The break is twenty minutes. I had been not-thinking for six hours and I was very tired from it.

---

I went to my locker and took the geography book off the shelf.

Nobody has ever opened my geography book, including me. I want that on the record because of everything that came after: I received the paper that was inside it on the bus from Gherla, eleven months before the fifth of November. The woman who gave it to me had a face like a closed shop and she put it in my hand the way you pass someone the salt — without asking if they wanted salt, without looking at them while they took it. I had eleven minutes between the stop at Bonțida and the stop before Dej and I read what was on the paper in those eleven minutes and I understood that it was the kind of thing you kept somewhere safe and I needed to decide, in eleven minutes, where safe was.

The hostel was not safe. The hostel room has a door with a latch that can be lifted from the outside with a fingernail. I know this because the woman across the hall demonstrated it in the second week, not as a threat but as a fact worth knowing, and I have been grateful for it since. The factory locker locks. I am the only one with the key. I have not lost the key in two years and I do not intend to.

So I put the paper inside the geography book, between pages 34 and 35, which is a double-page diagram of the watershed drainage of the Northern Carpathians, illustrated in blue and grey. I put the geography book on the shelf in the locker. For eleven months it sat there. I want to be clear about this: I never used it. I never showed it to anyone. I could not have told you what was written on any line of it if you had held me upside down. It was just a thing I owned, the same category as the coat — the green wool one with the loose button on the left cuff that I keep meaning to resew.

I took the geography book to the bathroom. There are four stalls and two of them have latches that work. I took one of the ones with a latch.

---

I sat on the edge of the lid with the book on my knees and opened it to pages 34 and 35 and took out the paper. It was folded three times — twice across and once along — and the fold lines had softened over eleven months into the kind of creases that will hold their shape for years without being asked to.

I read it straight through.

Lines one through eight are instructions, numbered, imperative. I am not going to set all of them out here. What I want to say is that I read each one and it was legible and I continued to the next. At the bottom of the page, below the eighth numbered line, there is a bracket. It is drawn in pencil — a hand-drawn rectangle around the last part of the document, with lines that are mostly straight. Inside the bracket it says:

*7 or 8 — take her in.*

And more. The bracket holds more than that — it says what to say when you get there, and one other thing, one line that I didn't retain on the bus and didn't retain in the first week at the hostel and didn't retain now. What I retained, this time, was the bracket itself. The drawn line around it. It was not a ninth step in the same sequence. It was something else — a different kind of instruction, the kind you draw a box around to show it overrides the sequence rather than continuing it.

I had never been able to tell you what was inside that bracket before the fifth. Not if you had asked me on the fourth or the third or at any point in the previous eleven months. I read the paper three times in my life before the fifth of November and each time I read it the way you read something you have been handed and don't know what to do with yet — looking to find out what it is, not to understand it. I retained almost nothing, which I am telling you now because of what came after. I am not asking you to believe it changed anything. I am asking you to believe it is true.

On the fifth of November what I saw was the bracket. It was drawn there. I could see that the thing at the bottom was bracketed, which made it different from the lines above, and today that difference mattered in a way it hadn't mattered before. I didn't know why. I know why now.

---

I folded the paper back along the three creases and put it between pages 34 and 35. I closed the geography book.

The women's bathroom at the AFE production floor has a window above the sinks that is painted shut. In the fluorescent light the walls are a colour that started as pale yellow and has become something else over a number of years I will not guess at. I stood at the sink and ran cold water on my wrists, which does something to my heart rate that is worth doing in certain situations, and then I went back to the locker and put the geography book on the shelf above the coat hooks.

What I told myself: this is still a thing I own, like the coat. Not evidence of anything I did. I had received it on a bus, from a woman I had never seen before and have not seen since, and I had not used it and I had not shown it to anyone and I could not recite a single line of it from memory, including the line inside the bracket. Eleven months of owning it and I had done nothing with it except leave it on a shelf. Same as the coat. Same category entirely.

What I also told myself: the locker locks. The factory has a gate and a guard. I am a woman who tends the looms and has not been in any trouble that mattered, and there is no reason for anyone to open my locker, because there is no reason for anyone to look at me.

I went back to the production floor and worked until two.

---

After the shift I walked back through fog that had not lifted. In November in this valley it often does not. The hostel is ten minutes from the mill gate on a clear day and fifteen when you have to navigate by memory, and on the fifth it was closer to fifteen. I signed in at the desk and went upstairs to my room.

The ceiling of my room has a water stain in the upper left corner. It has been there since before I moved in and it has not grown in two years, which I find reassuring. It does not look like anything. Some water stains resolve into shapes — a face, an animal, a map of somewhere — but this one is just a stain. I find this restful.

I lay on the bed with my coat on.

The geography book was in the locker. The locker was in a building with a gate. I had not used the paper. I had not shown it to anyone. I had not recited it to anyone, could not recite it to anyone. What had gone wrong for Ana Petrescu had gone wrong before the fifth, before I read the bracket or the numbered lines above it, before I ran cold water on my wrists and put the book back on the shelf. I had not been any part of it. I was as innocent as I had been when I got on the bus from Gherla, and the geography book in the locker was the geography book in the locker, and that was the afternoon of the fifth.

Whether that was the right place for it, I did not know. I did not know what the right place was, or whether there was one, or whether the bracket being there rather than not being there made any difference to anything that had already happened or was going to happen next. I lay there with my coat on and I did not know any of it, and so I did nothing, which is itself a kind of decision, as I found out later.

The ceiling stain was in its corner. The light through the curtain was the grey of mid-afternoon fog. I stayed on the bed until it was dark enough that the grey went away.
