# 4 November 1984

She is at the copying room door when the name comes through from personnel.

*Petrescu.* Then the second woman's voice, lower: *at the hospital in Dej.* A pause, something she cannot catch. *The younger one.*

Ilinca is holding October payroll tallies for Shift A. She stands in the corridor long enough to hear nothing more. Then she goes back to her desk.

The adding machine is mechanical, a grey metal instrument with a paper roll she has not changed since September. She feeds it the Shift A wage register — three hundred and twelve names, each with their production coefficient and their October total, which she has already computed twice. The keys require force. The administrative building shares a heating pipe with the weaving hall, but the weaving hall takes precedence and in November there is no heat in the administrative wing before six o'clock. She has kept her coat on since three. She works the keys. The machine returns its additions. The paper roll advances.

One by one the office empties. At five, the accounts assistant from payroll goes without a word — she has a child to collect and a bread queue to stand in before dark. At ten past, the junior planner from the second floor, who has been on the telephone all afternoon. The line is shared with three other offices and every call is audible to the corridor, but Ilinca gave up not-hearing years ago and has learned to hear without retaining. At twenty past, the woman from payroll accounts. At twenty-five past, the two women from the typing pool at the far end of the hall, who are not yet finished but go anyway.

At half past five, Domnu Boteanu from the second floor switches off his light and goes down the stairs. He does not look in. He never looks in.

At five-forty the corridor is quiet.

She puts the monthly register in the right-hand drawer, but she does not close it, because closing it would be finishing and she is not finished — the November overtime sheets are still on the left corner of the desk, untouched. She will do them in the morning.

She looks at the second shelf.

---

The 1983 ledger is where it always is: between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission, the two thickest items on the shelf, which is why she placed it there. A standard four-hundred-page Ministry of Finance form-book. The cover is stamped with the year; the spine is reinforced with brown tape she applied herself in February when the original binding cracked. It is one of six year-ledgers on that shelf. A state auditor arriving without notice — and auditors arrive without notice, always; this is the first thing a bookkeeper learns — could ask her to produce any of them. She would produce them. This one she would produce without hesitation, because her entries in it are correct and complete and every transaction has a supporting document in the adjacent drawer.

She takes it down.

She carries it to her desk and opens it to the spine. The paper is there, folded twice. She works it free with two fingers, careful of the edge of the binding tape, and lays it flat on the desk under the lamp.

She reads it. Not from memory — she knows the document well enough that memory is not the issue — but in order, word by word, the way she was taught to verify a column. You do not trust yourself to have already seen the error. You begin again at the beginning.

Line one. Line two. Line three: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.* When she wrote "by the bed" she had been thinking about what would already be in the room — a chair, a footstool, a folded coat on the floor, a surface for a glass and a pencil. There would always be something. She has reread this line many times since October of last year. She still thinks it is right. Line four. Line five. Line six.

Line seven: *Two cloths in one hour is too many.*

Line eight: *A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.*

Below the eighth line is the bracket. She drew it herself, in the bottom margin, with the ruler from the left-hand drawer. The bracket was necessary because she added the last instruction after the column above it was already full. She needed something to set it apart from the eight numbered lines — not a ninth step in sequence with the others, but a condition, an override, the kind of instruction that applies outside the sequence and over it. She drew the bracket with the ruler. She printed the text inside it.

She reads it. The words are all there.

She folds the sheet back along the original creases and works it into the spine. She closes the ledger and returns it to the second shelf. She straightens the adjacent ledgers so nothing is out of line.

The copying room at the end of the hall is dark. She did not hear anyone switch that light off.

---

She has made three copies of this document, in the thirteen months since October of last year.

The first: the third week of November. A woman she has known since they were both on the third shift eleven years ago, a woman who came to her directly and asked in plain terms, with no pretense of asking about something else. Ilinca trusted her then and trusts her now without qualification. She went to the woman's apartment on a Tuesday evening and copied it at her kitchen table. She left the bracket space before writing anything in the column above it, because a bracket that looks added-on will read as added-on and a bracket that was clearly intended from the start will read as intentional. She checked it twice, let the ink dry, and was home before the building superintendent locked the front entrance.

The second: December, the week before the holidays. A woman from the bloc adjacent to hers, whom she had spoken to twice — once in the bread queue in January darkness, once at the water tap when the third-floor pipes froze. She had asked a question that used none of the words for the question she was asking, and Ilinca understood the question and took a week before she said yes. She made the copy at her own kitchen table, a Sunday night, the district heating off and the kitchen cold enough that her hand was stiff by the end. She checked it twice. She left the bracket space.

The third was different.

November 3 of last year. A coal cellar off the back of a building on Strada Crișan. A woman had asked and could not come to her and could not wait. Ilinca had twenty minutes. The light came through a gap in the door — six centimetres, perhaps eight. She had brought two sheets of paper and a pencil from the administrative building that morning, carried inside the lining of her bag along with the original. She held the original at an angle to the gap and worked down the page. She did not pause between lines. She moved as quickly as she could while keeping each word close to the word it was copied from, because close is not the same as exact but it is the nearest you can get in twenty minutes by the light of a door.

She checked it once: down the lines in order. Yes to each of them. She handed it over and the woman was gone.

She has not seen that third copy since.

She does not write any of this down. She never writes it down. The names live in the column she keeps for everything that cannot be placed in a form — the machine on the second floor of the weaving hall that has run a false coefficient since February and whose correction would open questions she cannot answer, the rounding differences a generous auditor might excuse. She keeps a clean set of books. She also keeps this other one, always current, never on paper.

---

She takes the side passage out of the mill. The main gate is for the shift change — she can hear it through the wall as she passes, the sound of three hundred women going in while three hundred more come out — and she does not want to be counted in that movement this evening.

It is fully dark. The streetlamps along the river road make yellow spheres in the fog without illuminating the pavement beneath them. She knows the route well enough not to need them. The road here is cobbled and the kerb has been broken at the corner since July. She knows where the broken section is. She steps around it.

The Someș is at the bottom of Strada Someșului and she can feel it before she reaches it: the air grows wetter as she descends and the cold changes character, becomes the cold that comes up off moving water rather than the dry cold of the street. The mill's outflow enters the river three hundred metres upstream. In fog, in November, the smell of the process is in the air — hot-wet cellulose, the faint chemical sharpness she stopped noticing years ago and notices again now, because she is not thinking about the smell. The three copies.

The women she gave them to: she knows each one. She is not uncertain about any of them. She chose each for a reason. The reasons hold.

What she has not counted before is the next hand. The women she gave copies to may have passed their copies on to others, who may have passed theirs on. That was the point. That was always the point of the thing — a paper that stays in one hand reaches one person and a paper that moves reaches more. She understood this when she wrote it and she still understands it and the understanding has never before required her to trace the movement.

She needs to trace it now. Without a record. Without asking.

She crosses the bridge. Her hand rests on the railing for two seconds and the cold that comes up through the metal is the cold of the river. Below the railing there is nothing visible but white.

---

The stairwell of the bloc on Strada Avântului is dark on the third floor. The building superintendent switches the light off at five-thirty and does not switch it back on until six-thirty, because the energy reduction programme applies to common areas too, and he applies it without variation and without apology. She goes up by feel, hand on the painted rail, counting the steps from the second-floor landing. Third floor. Her key is on the left ring.

She does not turn on the overhead. She turns on the lamp by the kitchen table. The circle it makes on the oilcloth is the same circle it always makes.

She does not take her coat off.

She sits at the table.

The question still open is not about the three women she gave copies to. She knows the three women. The copies in their first hands she has accounted for.

The question is what happened to the copies after the first hands. Whether any of those hands passed a copy on, and whether any of the copies that followed from that passing eventually reached a house on Strada Gării. Whether there is a connection between the paper in the ledger spine and a nineteen-year-old who arrived at the district hospital on the morning of the fourth of November and did not leave.

She does not say the name. She does not write it.

The lamp makes its forty-watt circle on the oilcloth and nowhere else. Outside the window, across the courtyard, the bloc opposite has one window lit — the yellow of someone else's lamp behind their curtain, the same forty watts, the same circle on someone else's table. Above it and below it, the building is dark. The fog has come up level with the third floor and softened the one lit window until it is just a shape in the white.

She sits in her coat. She counts.

# 6 November 1984

She pulls the November stat de plată from the in-tray and sets it flat on the desk to the left of the adding machine. Forty-seven lines. There are forty-seven workers on the administrative and technical rolls, each of them a column: name, labour category, days worked, deductions, net. She starts at line one.

The adding machine is a Felix 5010, original equipment from 1972, which she has run every working day for twelve years. It adds and subtracts; it keeps a running total on a paper strip and rings a note — more of a click than a ring, though she calls it a ring — when a column clears. She runs column one. It is clean. She tears the strip at the perforation, clips it to the form, and moves to column two.

The window behind her left shoulder gives onto the administrative courtyard. The heat pipe will not come on until after six in the evening, which is the November arrangement on the shared pipe, and the office in the morning is the temperature of the stairwell, which is approximately the temperature of outside. She has dressed for this since October: wool underneath, the heavy coat she keeps on until ten. She runs column three.

She turns to look at the courtyard window twice in the hour: once when a truck from the transportation depot drives in, and once when it drives out. Both times there is nothing that needs seeing. The sky over the courtyard is the grey that will hold all day.

By nine she has worked through line twenty-eight. The materials consumption report for October is in the out-tray, waiting for the floor section chief's signature before she can send it to the district financial office. She does this every first week of the month; having a reason to be on the production corridor is something she is in the habit of accounting for. She finishes through line thirty-one, takes the materials form from the out-tray, and puts her coat on.

---

The passage between the administrative building and the production hall is covered but open at the base, and in November the cold collects along the corridor floor. She reported the gap at the bottom of the connecting door to maintenance in October 1979 and nothing was done. She walks through it and into the production corridor.

The loom floor is to her left, behind the baffle wall. The sound it makes is not quite a sound — it is a vibration below the range of what she identifies as noise, which she stopped distinguishing from silence after the first year. The smell is the synthetic-fiber smell: wet chemistry and steam heat, the exhaust of the wet-spinning process mixed with cold air through every unsealed gap. It has been in the walls of this corridor since 1974 and she stopped registering it years ago. What she registers now is the cold through the soles of her shoes.

The floor section chief's office is the third door on the right. She knocks once and goes in. He is on the telephone — receiver in one hand, a pen in the other, his eyes on the wall. She puts the materials form on the desk in front of him. He signs it without looking at it; she has had it typed cleanly. He does not stop talking. She goes back into the corridor.

Three women from the day shift are near the locker-bay door at the far end. She knows two of them by their coats. She does not turn toward them.

Georgeta Marin, the production supervisor for Hall B, is moving toward the women's bathroom at the far end of the corridor. She walks at the particular pace she uses when she has somewhere to be before the shift bell — not hurried, not slow. She has a ring of keys on a lanyard around her left wrist, tucked into her palm so they do not sound against each other. Three minutes to the shift change, perhaps less.

Ilinca walks to the bathroom.

---

One working bulb in the overhead fixture. Four sinks along the left wall; four stalls, two with latches — one of which has been difficult to close since August. The window above the sinks is painted shut, looking onto the outer wall of the fiber drying unit close enough to touch. The drain smell is more present in November.

Georgeta is at the far sink. Ilinca takes the one next to her and turns the tap.

"I've been thinking about the influenza," Ilinca says. "Whether it's going around. One of the women on the floor was ill last week."

Georgeta does not look up. Her hands are under the tap; she is washing them left over right, carefully.

"I had mine last year," she says. "I gave it to my neighbor on the street. Livia. No one else."

Ilinca runs cold water over her left wrist, then her right.

"And Livia?" she says.

"She's kept it to herself. She's a private woman — she doesn't pass things on. That's just her character."

The water is cold. Ilinca turns the tap off. In the mirror: the painted-shut window behind them, the single bulb above, Georgeta's keys in her palm.

"The influenza passes," Ilinca says.

"It does," Georgeta says, and goes.

---

Ilinca dries her hands and goes back up the corridor, through the connecting door, to her office. She hangs her coat. She sits.

Two pieces of information. She runs them in the order she can act on.

The first: Georgeta holds what Ilinca gave her, and it has not moved. Ilinca has known Georgeta Marin for eleven years — from before the supervisor promotion, from a period when the section rosters put them in proximity and she learned what Georgeta's silences mean and what her assurances mean.

The second: Georgeta gave one copy to her neighbor Livia, on her street, who has not passed it further. Ilinca has seen her perhaps three times in eleven years — grey coming into her hair before it should, a manner of walking with her chin slightly forward. Livia's family name Ilinca does not know by heart. She could find it in the bloc registry at the street committee. She will not need to. She will not look.

Two nodes on this branch: Georgeta, Livia. She runs every name she can place in the Petrescu household, and every name she can place on Georgeta's street, and the two sets do not intersect. The branch does not reach Ana Petrescu.

She thinks of the fourth line, the way she wrote it for Georgeta: *If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.* The copy she made for Georgeta — the third week of November last year, at this desk, by this lamp, in the blue-black ink she uses for fair copies — she can see the page as clearly as if it were in front of her. Line four. Numbered. In its place. The upstroke of the y in *properly*, where the nib caught slightly at the end of the word.

The branch is clean.

She enters both nodes into the account she carries in her head, which has no ledger and no supporting document and which she has maintained for thirteen months by discipline alone. The count is two.

She returns to line thirty-two.

---

Elena Florescu holds the other copy. Third shift now; when Ilinca first knew her they were both on the morning schedule, eleven years ago, when the roster rotation put them in the same section for two seasons. Since 1979 their paths cross in two ways: at the bakery on Strada Lungă, which Elena passes on her way to the morning handover and which Ilinca passes on her way home on certain days; and twice a year at the bloc committee office when the identity documents come up for renewal. Ilinca has counted fourteen exchanges at the bakery in three years. This is not friendship; it is adjacency, which is a more reliable thing.

Elena Florescu is not someone Ilinca knows — what she knows of her is procedural: the schedule she keeps, the coat she wears in November, the way she holds her bag on the same shoulder always.

She cannot go to Elena today. Elena is on the floor, on the machine, and a visit from the contabil-șef without an administrative basis is a visit that anyone nearby can note. The bakery is the correct approach. Elena passes it on Friday mornings at half past five on her way to the handover. Ilinca passes it at that hour only when she has reason to, which she now has. She will be there on Friday.

She does not write any of this down.

---

The stat de plată is finished at quarter past three. She tears the final strip, clips it to the summary line, puts the folder in the out-tray with a rubber band. The next item in the in-tray is a letter from the district financial office about the Q4 consumption norms. She reads it, makes a note in the margin, and puts it in the pending tray.

At four-fifteen the door opens.

A boy she does not know — not older than twenty; she has not seen him in the building before, which means he started recently. He is carrying a folder from the cadres office: she reads the stamp before he speaks. He sets a form on the edge of her desk.

"From the cadres office," he says. "Supplementary materials-usage calculation, Q3. Needs to be back by the fifteenth."

She takes it. "Sign the receipt book."

He finds it in his folder. She signs the line. He closes the folder and goes. She listens: footsteps in the corridor, the connecting door, then nothing.

She holds the form.

It is a Ministry of Finance series form. Q3 is July through September, which closed in October. She submitted the standard materials-usage calculation on the twenty-second of October; the district financial office stamped it received on the twenty-fifth. She ran the numbers four times before submitting because the supplementary ministerial instruction from August had adjusted the Q3 norms mid-quarter, and she wanted the adjustment applied consistently through every line item. It was. If there is a discrepancy in the Q3 accounts, it is not here.

She turns the form over. The back is blank. The watermark is in the lower left corner, the serial number in the upper right, where it belongs. She received a supplementary form for a closed quarter once before, in 1981, during the audit year — but that year all enterprises in the district received supplementary requests for everything, and those circumstances were general and known. This is not that.

She is holding the form and she has not decided what to do with it yet.

In fifteen years she has learned that most things which appear to be something are nothing. She has also learned that a thing which is something looks, from the outside, exactly like the things which are nothing. A form that arrives because a number was transposed two months ago in the district office looks like a form that arrives because someone wants to observe what a person does when a form arrives. She knows what a test looks like. She has not been given one she could verify before, which means she has no way to compare now.

The shift bell sounds in the production hall — muffled through the baffle wall, but she knows the pitch of it, the duration; she has known it for fifteen years and this is it. Footsteps in the corridor. Voices, the brief noise of the shift change, and then the corridor going quiet again under the machines.

She has not moved. The form is in her hand.

# 7 November 1984

He read the folder in his car with the engine off. The station was behind him; the Someș was somewhere ahead in the fog, down past the junction at Strada Gării, invisible from here. The folder held three items: the hospital's notification form, the death certificate stamped by the district procuror's office, and a handwritten sheet giving the name of the next of kin who had been notified. He read them in that order.

Ana Petrescu, nineteen years old. Admitted to the Spitalul Orășenesc at nineteen hundred hours on the fourth of November. Death recorded at twenty-three hundred and twelve on the same date. Cause of death: complications arising from hemorrhage. The hospital's notification form, submitted to the procuror's office on the morning of the fifth, classified the case as requiring investigation under the applicable decree. The hospital had done what it was required to do. His captain had made that clear, yesterday afternoon, when he had put the folder on Munteanu's desk and remained standing in the doorway: it was not the hospital under examination. What remained to establish was whether a criminal act had occurred, and on whose part.

The assignment had come to him on the afternoon of the sixth as an administrative case — the kind his captain classified as requiring a determination, not an investigation. Look at it, write down what happened, decide whether there is a basis for charges, close the file or pass it up. Munteanu had read the file the previous evening and concluded that these instructions would not cover what the file contained. He had not said this to his captain, because the determination had not been written yet and it was possible he was wrong.

He put the three sheets back into the folder in the order he had found them. He started the car and drove to Strada Gării.

---

The valley fog had not lifted by half past eight. It lay in the basin of the Someș below the road, dense in the low places, thinning only at the height of the bloc roofs. He drove with the window cracked. The market square was empty, the bread queue already dispersed — whatever had been available this morning had been available early. Past the square the road narrowed; the houses on Strada Gării ran close together, each with a small winter garden behind wire or concrete fencing: maize stalks cut low, a few cabbages still in the ground, a cold frame with nothing in it. Number forty-one had a metal gate that was not locked.

He parked and looked at the house for a moment before getting out. A single-storey building, extended at the back, with a kitchen light on behind a curtain not quite closed. He noted the gate, the cracked concrete of the garden path, the fact that the curtain had moved slightly while he was looking at it.

---

She came to the door before he had finished latching the gate. She had been watching from the kitchen window. A woman who knew the Miliția would eventually arrive, watching for when it arrived, was a woman who had been thinking about what to say. That was not deception. That was the preparation a person made when they understood that a conversation had consequences.

Her name was Rodica Petrescu. She was the wife of Ana's eldest brother and had been living in the house since the spring. She was not yet thirty and she had not slept.

He introduced himself: Locotenent Munteanu, Secția de Investigații. He said he was sorry for her loss. He was, in the way that he was always sorry at the beginning of this kind of interview.

She asked him in. The kitchen was small. A pot on the stove, the burner turned low, the smell of onions cooked an hour earlier and still in the air. She sat at the table with her hands in her lap; he sat across from her and took the notebook from the inside pocket of his coat.

He asked her to tell him what had happened from the evening of the third of November onward.

She had been telling it to herself for three days. He could hear it in the quality of the account — not rehearsed, exactly, but worn into a groove by repetition, the way a path is worn by the same feet going back and forth across it. Ana came home ill on the evening of the third; this was not the first time she had been unwell, so Rodica did not immediately understand what kind of ill this was. She stayed with her through the night. She counted the cloths, because the paper told her to, and she sat beside her and brought water in small amounts, because that was also on the paper. By noon on the fourth she understood that what she was counting had crossed a threshold. By the evening she understood that staying home was no longer the decision she was making.

She stopped speaking. He waited.

She said: she did not take her to the hospital until the evening of the fourth because going to the hospital was — she stopped again. She said: because she did not know what to say when she arrived.

He wrote: *did not know what to say at the hospital.*

He asked: was there a piece of paper in the house.

She was very still. Then she said yes, and rose from the table and went into the next room. He waited. The pot hissed against the burner and went quiet. Outside, somewhere on the street, a cart moved across frozen gravel.

She came back with a folded piece of paper and put it on the table between them. It had been kept somewhere specific — she had returned without hesitation, without searching. The paper was folded twice, both folds going in the same direction. He could see handwriting through the sheet where the paper had gone thin at the creases.

He looked at it without touching it. Then he took an evidence envelope from his coat, held it open, and she put the paper into it. He sealed the envelope and held it in his lap.

He asked where the paper had come from.

From her neighbor, she said. A woman in the next bloc on the street. She gave the name. He wrote it.

He asked nothing else about the paper. He wrote the time in the margin of his notebook, wrote his station number on a card, and left the card on the table. She did not speak again. He put his coat on and went out the way he had come.

---

The neighbor's bloc was a hundred meters up the street. He walked slowly enough to look at the other houses: a light on behind frosted glass, a light on in an upstairs room, a dog behind a wire fence that watched him and did not bark. The fog was thinning; he could see to the end of the block now, the bare lindens black against the white-grey sky.

He found the address and rang the bell.

The woman who came to the door wore her kitchen apron and her coat at the same time. She read his identification card for a long moment — she read it properly, not just the top line of it — and stepped back.

The kitchen was slightly warmer than the previous one. A clothesline ran along the back wall with two towels folded over it. She stood near the stove with a dish towel in her hands, which were not still: she moved the towel from one hand to the other, set it on the counter, picked it up again.

He asked for her copy of the paper.

She said: what paper.

He said: the one you gave to Rodica Petrescu, on the street.

She was quiet. She looked at the dish towel and then at him. She put the dish towel on the counter and went to a drawer — second from the left, beneath the counter — and took out a folded piece of paper and brought it to him. Her hands were steady when she placed it in the second evidence envelope. It was the pause before the drawer that had not been steady.

He sealed the envelope. He asked her a few further questions: when she had last spoken with Rodica Petrescu, whether she had discussed Ana Petrescu's illness with anyone in the past three days, whether she had anyone else living in the household. She answered each question separately. He wrote the answers. He did not ask her who had given her the paper, and she did not say.

He thanked her. He left his card on the counter and went back out to the street.

---

He drove to the station and sat at his desk with both envelopes in front of him.

The investigations room held four other desks, only one of them occupied — Sandu, on the far side of the room, writing something in a ledger with his back to the window. The overhead fixture cast yellow light that reached only as far as the middle of the room. Munteanu turned on his lamp. He put his coat on the back of the chair. He set the two evidence envelopes side by side and looked at them for a moment.

He opened the first envelope and laid the paper flat on the right side of the desk. He opened the second envelope and laid the paper flat on the left. He moved the stapler to weight the right-hand sheet and a bottle of correction fluid to weight the left. Then he read them.

Line nine on both copies was the same. He read it on the right-hand sheet, then read it on the left: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He read from the top of each copy. Line one: the same on both. Line two: the same. Line three: he stopped.

On the right-hand sheet — the one Rodica Petrescu had given him, the one that had been in the house during the night of the third — line three read: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.*

On the left-hand sheet it read: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper beside the bed.*

He read both sentences again.

The handwriting was different. Not only different hands, but different enough in their letterforms that one person could not account for both. The right-hand script was small and even, the letters placed with some care; the left-hand script was slightly larger, the o's in *cloths* and in *hour* formed differently, opened where the right-hand script closed them. These had not been produced by the same person.

He read lines four through eight on both copies. In line six, the right-hand sheet had a full stop after *well* and the left-hand sheet had a comma — but the word was the same on both. Lines seven and eight were identical between the copies. Line nine was identical: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

He held both sheets up toward the lamp. Not to see through them — the lamp was not strong enough for that — but to hold them in proximity, as two things that were related to each other. Then he set them back on the desk.

He had seen forged documents before. He had seen copied documents: a will transcribed in a different hand, a typed letter produced on two machines. In those cases, the second document had tried to be the same as the first, and what was interesting was where it had not succeeded. This was different. Both of these documents had tried to be the same as some third thing — something they had each been copied from — and both had succeeded, and each had arrived at something slightly different from the other. *By.* *Beside.* Neither of them wrong. Neither of them the other.

The variation between *by* and *beside* was what happened when a person read a word and wrote the word that was in their head, and the word in their head was slightly different from the word on the page. That was not an error of copying. That was copying. That was what copying produced, line by line and hand by hand, generation by generation. A word at a time.

And if both of these copies had drifted one step from the same source, then the source existed. And the source had come from somewhere.

He did not say any of this aloud. He did not write it down.

Line nine was the same on both copies: *take her in in the morning.* Nine numbered lines on both sheets, the ninth sitting square in the column with the rest.

He picked up his pen. He pulled the folder toward him and turned to a fresh page at the back, behind the death certificate and the notification form and his notes from the morning. He wrote the neighbor's name at the top of the page. He drew a line under it.

The neighbor was where the chain between his desk and the Petrescu household stopped, at the moment. Behind her name was whoever had given the paper to her. Behind that name was another, and behind that name another still. He did not know yet how many. He did not know yet where the nine-line version of this document had come from, or when, or in whose hand.

He wrote the date in the margin and began.

# 10 November 1984

The November payroll forms are in the wooden tray beside the secretary's elbow, folded in half the way they come from the print room. She takes them without sitting down.

Pântelimon says: there has been some unpleasantness with the Petrescu matter. A Miliția officer has been speaking with people.

He says it as a statement in an open room. The outer door of the office is propped; two women from the personnel section are at their desks with their coats still on. He is watching Ilinca's hands.

She folds the forms once more and tucks them under her arm. A tragic business, she says. She is glad the family has someone looking into it.

She goes back to her office.

---

She closes the door and puts the payroll forms on the left side of the desk, beside the October figures. She does not open them yet.

An officer has been speaking with people. The secretary told her this in the tone of a man who has information and would like to exchange it. She gave him nothing except the obvious, which is the kind of exchange that costs her nothing and may give him something to think about later, if he is the type who thinks about things later. She does not know what type he is.

He has not come to the administrative building. If she were a name in the file, someone would have been at her door by now. The administrative building is not a production section and it is not a residential bloc. It sits on the other side of the main gate, which is a distance that means something, practically speaking, about whose names come first.

A man working outward from Ana Petrescu's house works from the sister-in-law, then from whoever the sister-in-law named, then outward from there. That is how it goes. There is a sequence to these things and she is not at the front of the sequence.

She opens the middle drawer and takes out the October summary sheet and places it to the right of the payroll forms. She does not look at either of them.

She has time. Not an abundance of it. Enough to do the next thing.

---

At nine she takes the materials-usage report from the filing cabinet behind the door. The October comparison columns for Hall B show a discrepancy on the last week of the month: the production log records sixty-eight kilograms of raw fiber allocation, but the stores ledger shows seventy-two kilograms issued over the same period. Four kilograms. Small enough to be a transcription error; large enough that it cannot stay in the month-end summary without an explanation and a countersignature.

She needs Georgeta for this.

This is the difficulty and also the solution to the difficulty. It is the second time in a week she will have occasion to speak with Georgeta. Once in a week is reasonable. Twice is one more than she prefers, for a woman who has always been careful about how often she appears in the same place as the same person. But the discrepancy is real. The stores ledger is here in her hand. She needs a production supervisor's countersignature before the month-end summary can go to the director's office, and Georgeta is the supervisor for Hall B. She has used worse reasons than this.

She writes the discrepancy figures on a separate sheet: *issued, 72 kg; production log, 68 kg; variance, 4 kg.* She clips the sheet to the October comparison figures and puts both in her document folder.

She waits until ten. She does not look at the clock between nine and ten.

---

At ten she goes to the supplies corridor.

Georgeta is already there. She is doing the quarterly inventory, which she does on the tenth of every month — Ilinca has countersigned the inventory sheets since 1978 and knows the schedule. Georgeta's clipboard is in her right hand; she is making ticks with a pencil, working along the shelves from the door end.

Ilinca sets her folder on the table near the window end and opens it to the October comparison sheet.

A materials discrepancy, she says. Hall B, last week of October. Seventy-two kilograms issued against sixty-eight in the production log. I need to know before the month-end summary which figure is correct, or whether there is a stores entry that explains the difference.

Georgeta does not stop her ticks. She finishes the shelf she is on. She sets the clipboard against the wall and comes to the table.

She looks at the comparison sheet. The last week of October, she says. We had two days of reduced intake on the spooling machines in the second bay. Some of the raw fiber arrived late. I logged it in the first week of November to keep the production records clean. If stores logged it in October because the delivery arrived in October, that is where your four kilograms are.

Ilinca writes this down. She says: I will need the delivery receipt to confirm the date. Can you get me the November intake log for the first four days?

By afternoon, Georgeta says. The materials office will have the receipt; I will send someone.

Ilinca closes the folder and clips the note inside it. She says: that should close it for the month-end summary. Then, without a pause that could be read as a pause: and how is Livia keeping?

Georgeta's pencil is in her hand. She does not tap it against anything.

Her daughter stopped by on Tuesday, she says. She says Livia is fine. Quiet. She's been at home, not seeing people.

Ilinca says: hasn't given anything to anyone?

Georgeta shakes her head, once, as if she is agreeing that the delivery receipt will settle the discrepancy.

No, she says. She kept it to herself.

Good. Ilinca picks up her folder. I'll have the countersignature form ready when the intake log comes. If you send it by two, we can close this before Friday.

She goes back to her office.

---

She closes the door. She sits in the chair.

N2 branch: Georgeta. From Georgeta to Livia — Georgeta's neighbor on her street. Livia gave the copy to nobody. She has been at home, not seeing people. No Miliția contact; Georgeta's daughter went by on Tuesday and she was fine. The branch runs from the master, then to Georgeta, then to Livia, and there it stops. A dead end is what the branch was designed to be; not every copy was meant to go further. Livia had kept it to herself for more than a year and had not used it and had not passed it and was now sitting quietly in her apartment while a man with a notepad asked questions on streets that were not her street. The branch contains no one who is in a file.

*No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.*

She has followed this herself. The cousin, the borrowed pot, the materials discrepancy. She has not made a telephone call she did not need. She has not opened her door to anyone who was not expected. What she has done in the past week to close her accounting of the branches — the routes she took, the words she used, the questions she turned sideways — are all consistent with the instruction on line five. She knows line five the way she knows all of them. She wrote it, which is not the same as reading it: writing a thing is choosing every word separately, and she chose those words and has not needed to reconsider them.

The N3 branch is confirmed through Elena Florescu. The N2 branch closes now, with Livia. What remains is the cellar copy — the third copy she made from the master, on November third of last year, in the coal cellar behind Strada Dorobanților, by the light of the door, in ten minutes, for a woman who could not wait for a better time. She has gone over it. She knows what she wrote. She drew the bracket — two strokes and a corner — and she wrote the words inside it, and the words were the words from the master. She is certain of this the way she is certain of her own handwriting.

Four nodes in her private account. The master. The N2 branch, now closed and clean. The N3 branch, closed and clean. The cellar copy, which she holds as correct. Four entries. She cannot write any of this anywhere. She cannot write the count or the confirmation or the four-kilogram discrepancy in the same column. The private account has no ledger. It exists in the hour between nine and ten when she does not look at the clock.

The man asking questions in the production sections will work outward from what he has and will eventually reach what exists to be reached. What exists to be reached, on the N2 branch, is Livia, who is fine and has kept herself quiet and has given nothing to anyone. That branch is closed. If he reaches it, it dead-ends.

She opens the payroll forms.

---

The November columns are blank. She fills them from the October summary, adjusted for the two new employees in Hall C and the reduced hours from the repair week. She uncaps her pen and writes the first entry at the top of the column. She checks the form header. Alphabetical, surname-first, which has been the format since October per the new directive from the financial office. The entry is in the right place.

The numbers go in one column at a time. Gross hours, deductions, net. She runs the figures by hand first, then checks the tape. The tape agrees with her column for the first twelve entries and disagrees by three lei on the thirteenth. She finds the error: a transposition in the gross hours, twenty-two where the source sheet says twenty-two point five. She corrects it with a single line through the wrong figure and the right figure beside it.

She fills the column to the end of the first page. She turns to the second.

She leans back in the chair. The chair has a creak at the back joint that she has meant to report to the maintenance office since spring. She has not reported it. A creak is not a problem; it is the kind of sound that stops being heard after the first week, the kind that only a person paying close attention to her office and her habits would notice in the middle of a morning.

She sits forward and puts both hands flat on the desk.

The delivery receipt will arrive by two.

She uncaps the pen and pulls the October comparison sheet back into the light and reads the figures again from the beginning. The thing you miss is always in the line you read first, when your eye has not yet learned what it is looking for. She has learned this about herself over fifteen years and she does not argue with it.

The lamp is off. She has not needed it since the fog cleared.

# 12 November 1984

He had left the two copies on his desk the previous evening, spread flat and held at their corners by the evidence folder, and when he came in Monday morning they were as he had left them.

He took off his coat and hung it on the back of the door. Sandu's desk at the far end of the investigations room was empty; Sandu was in the field on the Cuzdrioara registration matter and would not be in until afternoon. The coal stove in the corner had been lit by whoever was on overnight duty and was burning with the damp smell of lignite that never quite cleared in November, which meant it had been going long enough to take the edge off the cold without quite producing warmth. He moved the folder to the left side of the desk and sat down.

He had read both copies on Thursday — the day he had collected them — and again on Friday before the weekend. He knew what they said. What he was doing now was not reading for content. He was reading the way he had learned, over twelve years, to read a statement taken from two different people about the same event: not for what the words said but for where the words diverged, and whether the divergence was something that would have happened accidentally or only by design.

He was not a graphologist. He was a man who had spent twelve years reading statements.

Line one of the first copy: *Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.* Small careful hand. The o in 'lying' and the o in 'whole' pressed closed by a pen held at a narrow angle.

Line one of the second copy: the same line, the same words. Different hand. Larger letters, a slight rightward lean, the downstrokes of the l and the y in 'lying' longer than was strictly necessary, as though the writer had thought they were about to run out of room and then discovered they had more than enough.

He went line by line.

Lines one through eight: close to identical. He noted where they were not. Line three on the first copy: *Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.* Line three on the second copy: the same sentence, until the last four words — *on the paper beside the bed.* He looked at the two phrases. The instruction was the same. The prepositions were not. Someone had written *beside* where the other document, or its source, said *by.* That was either a copying error — the copyist's own preposition substituting itself for the original's — or it was a variation already present in whatever the second copy had been made from.

He had no way to know yet which of these was true.

He turned to the back page of his cardboard folder, which served as his case notes, and wrote below Saturday's entry: *L3 variant: 'by the bed' / 'beside the bed'. Two hands, two sheets, different paper stocks. L9: identical — see below.*

Line nine was the same on both copies. He read it on the first document — *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning* — and then on the second, the words arriving in the same order, set down in a different hand on different paper, but unchanged: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* He held the two sheets up briefly, each in one hand, and read the ninth line again on each.

A woman who had stayed until morning had been following a document that told her to wait for morning. What he was looking at now was something additional: the instruction had not entered the chain at the point where the first copy had passed to the Petrescu household. It was present in the neighbor's copy as well, which was a separate document obtained separately from a separate address. If the instruction was already in both copies, and both copies had been made by different people from whatever they had each received, then the instruction had been present in what they had each received. The instruction was earlier.

He closed the folder.

---

The address he needed was a three-story bloc on Alecsandri street, east of the mill workers' market. Three hundred metres. He walked.

November had gone cold and wet in the last week, the kind of damp that came off the Someș in the morning and did not lift before noon. The market was open but thin — mid-month, the queues had already moved through whatever there was to move through. A woman at the corner stand near the market entrance had something under an oil cloth. She watched him come up the street and watched him go past without moving. He did not stop. He counted the doorways until he had the right building.

Interior stair. The third floor smelled of cabbage soup and wet wool. He knocked at the indicated door.

The woman who answered had the expression of someone who had been expecting a particular knock for some number of days and had made a decision about how she would receive it. She was in her late forties, heavy-shouldered, her hair pinned close to her head, wearing a house coat. She was holding a dish cloth. When she looked at him she folded the cloth in half, and then in half again, until she had a square she had nowhere particular to put.

He introduced himself. He said he was investigating the death of Ana Petrescu and that he had questions about a document she might be able to help with.

She said: come in.

The flat was a kitchen and one other room. The kitchen had a table in the centre and two cups on it, which she moved to the counter without comment. She put the folded dish cloth on the counter beside them and sat down across from him at the table.

Her name was Lucia Gal. She worked the day shift in the second weaving hall at the AFE mill. She had worked there since 1972.

He told her: he was aware that a document of a certain kind had been circulating in the area. That he was trying to understand how it had moved. That if she had such a document and was willing to give it to him now, that cooperation would be noted in the file. Voluntary surrender was better than the alternative. He said this simply, without emphasis on the word 'alternative,' because emphasis was the thing that made people stop cooperating. He had learned this.

She got up and went to the counter. Second drawer from the left. She took out a folded sheet, carried it to the table, and set it in front of him.

He put on his gloves before he picked it up.

The paper was different from the other two copies. It was lighter, greyer, the stock of a mill production form — the front side carried official printing, department designation and output-tracking columns and a foreman's signature box, in the regulation black ink. On the reverse: the document, written in blue pencil. He had not seen blue pencil before on any version of this document. The handwriting was careful — more careful than either of the copies he had collected on Thursday, the numerals at the start of each line formed with a deliberateness that was close to elegance, the lines spaced evenly from top to bottom of the sheet.

He put it in an evidence envelope and wrote her name and address on the flap.

He asked: had she given a copy of this document to anyone else?

She said: no. She held his eyes when she said it. He wrote *denies further transmission* in his case notes.

He asked: where had she received this document?

She said: from a woman she worked with, on the production floor, in the second hall. She gave him the name without prompting. He wrote it. He wrote the hall number and the shift.

He asked: and did the woman she named live in this building, or elsewhere?

She gave him the address. He wrote it.

He thanked her. She held the door.

---

He had three copies.

He laid them side by side on his desk and weighted the corners with whatever was nearest, which turned out to be a stapler and three unopened tins of shoe polish. He read each copy through separately first, going from line one to line nine. Read separately, they said nearly the same thing. He read them again together, line by line across all three sheets.

He put the grey mill-form paper on the left, the two Thursday copies on the right, and went from the top.

Lines one through eight: close to identical across all three, with the same minor scribal variations he had already noted. Line three was the exception. The grey-paper copy said *by the bed*. The first of the Thursday copies said *by the bed*. The second Thursday copy said *beside the bed.*

He stopped.

Two of his three copies agreed in line three. The third differed from both of them by one word. He marked the positions in his notes. It was a small difference — a preposition, nothing more, the instruction unchanged — but it told him something about the arrangement. Two copies that agreed with each other in a particular line were either copied from each other or copied from the same source. A third copy that differed from both of them had either introduced the variation itself or had inherited it from a different source. He was looking at two copies that agreed, and one that did not. The two that agreed were probably closer to each other in the chain.

Line nine he read last, going left to right across all three sheets. It was the same on all three: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* He had taken his pen up when he started and he set it back down without writing anything.

The instruction had been present in the grey-paper copy, which was a step earlier in the chain than the two Thursday copies. The grey-paper copy was the one the woman in the flat on Alecsandri street had given him — the woman who had named a woman on the production floor as the person she had got it from. If the instruction was already present in the grey-paper copy, it had not been introduced by Lucia Gal. It had been there when she received it. It had been present before the grey-paper copy was made.

He looked at the three sheets again. The grey-paper copy and the first Thursday copy agreed in line three — *by the bed*. The second Thursday copy said *beside the bed.* That meant the second Thursday copy had probably been copied from the grey-paper copy or from something that had already introduced *beside* — but either way, the grey-paper copy was probably the oldest document in front of him, or closest to the oldest. And the oldest document in front of him already had the morning instruction in line nine.

He turned to the fresh page at the back of the cardboard folder and wrote: *Three copies in evidence. L3 variant: 'by the bed' (x2) / 'beside the bed' (x1). L9 consistent across all three: 'take her in in the morning.' Instruction not introduced at points of collection. Present at minimum in copy acquired today (earlier in chain). Source is upstream. Next: [the name from the Gal interview].*

It was the kind of finding that would not survive being described to his captain in its present form. Captain Niculescu had looked at the file on Wednesday and asked when Munteanu expected to have something writable. He had said: by the end of the week. That had been a realistic estimate at the time. He had thought, on Wednesday, that the chain would be short — three, maybe four people, the kind of small informal thing that didn't go far and died at the edges for want of someone to carry it. The instruction in line nine had been present before the three copies he held. Before the woman on Alecsandri street, before the woman on Strada Gării, before the Petrescu household. The chain behind it was longer than three people.

He was going to have more names in this file before he was done.

He stood and took his coat from the back of the door.

The name from the Gal interview was the production-floor woman who had given Lucia Gal her copy. One step further back. One step closer to wherever the instruction had entered. She worked the same hall, the day shift. She had not been expecting him this morning, because he had not known her name this morning. Now he did.

He put on his coat and picked up his case notes.

# 12 November 1984

She is on the last two lines of the October column when the knock comes.

Stela Ionescu, from the personnel section: a maintenance request across the desk, the boiler-room work order for the second heating pipe joint, which has been leaking since October and bleeds heat from the second-floor corridor before it reaches the administrative wing. The description of the repair is specific — sealing the joint with a wool-and-resin compound, three hours of work after the Sunday shift. The date is correct. The series number matches the maintenance register. Ilinca picks up her pen.

She has known Stela by the corridor and the elevator and the bathroom sink at the end of the hall: eleven years of proximity without occasion for more. Stela has a quiet manner and flat shoes and keeps her coat buttoned in the building until the heating comes on, which in November means until six, which in the administrative wing means until somewhat after that.

While Ilinca signs, Stela says — as a separate sentence, outside the transaction — that her friend from the bloc committee was called in this morning. About the Petrescu matter. Someone had been asking about a piece of paper that was going around the district. Something about what to do when a person was ill.

Ilinca hands the form back.

Stela says: the person asking had a copy with him, and he had read the ninth line aloud from it. The exact wording, as her friend had told her: *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.*

She says she thought Ilinca would want to know, given that everyone in the building is talking about it.

Ilinca says thank you. Stela goes, pulling the door not quite shut behind her. A two-centimeter gap of corridor light. Ilinca watches it for a moment. Then she gets up and closes the door properly.

She goes back to her desk. She sets her pen on the blotter. She does not pick it up.

---

The 1983 ledger is on the second shelf between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission. The brown tape at the top of the spine has held since February. It is a Ministry of Finance form-book, four hundred pages, a state document she is required to produce on demand.

She takes it down from the shelf and carries it to her desk. She sets it flat with the spine uppermost and holds it by the boards, opening the spine at the top, fitting two fingers along the gap between the pages and the board where the paper sits. The paper is folded twice in one direction and once across, a small square. She takes it out by the corner.

She opens it flat on the desk between the ledger and the lamp. She does not touch it again.

The paper has been folded and refolded many times in the fourteen months since she wrote it in October of last year. The creases have gone slightly furry — the fiber pressing up at each fold line into a faint nap — and the outer edge has taken on a soft, handled quality. The ink is still sharp. She used the blue-black she keeps for fair copies. The page shows everything she has asked of it.

She reads from the beginning.

---

1. Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.
2. Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.
3. Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.
4. If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.
5. No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.
6. Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
   [ 7 or 8 — take her in. Do not wait for the morning. ]

---

She reads the bracket three times.

She drew it in October of last year because she understood, before she finished writing, that the ninth instruction was not the same kind of thing as the other eight. A numbered list is a sequence. Lines one through eight are a sequence: what to do first, what comes next, what follows. The bracket is not a step in a sequence. It is a different order of information entirely — not what comes after eight, but what overrides everything above it when the conditions are met. In fourteen years of bookkeeping she has used brackets for the same reason every time: to mark what operates on the column, not what continues it. An item inside a bracket is not the next entry. It is the instruction that changes what the other entries mean.

*Do not wait for the morning.*

She reads the phrase once more. Then she looks away from the document without looking at anything in the room.

She has been given the exact wording of the ninth line as it exists in another copy. *If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.* She holds the two texts beside each other and reads the difference.

The bracket: *take her in. Do not wait for the morning.*

The numbered line: *take her in in the morning.*

Both contain the word *morning*. In the bracket, *morning* is the limit — the threshold you do not wait for. In the numbered line, *morning* is the time — it is when you go. The bracket says: the sequence has ended; when condition 7 or 8 is true, go now. The numbered line says: when condition 7 or 8 is true, go in the morning.

A bracket given a number has become a step in a list. The word *now* is gone from it. What is left is a sequential instruction with a time attached: *morning.* The woman who made that copy was being tidy. She saw nine pieces of information and she numbered them one through nine, because that is what a careful copyist does with nine pieces of information and a numbered list on the page in front of her. The hand that has just written *8.* has the *9.* ready.

Ilinca counts down the page. Eight numbered lines. Then the bracket.

She counts again. Eight. Then the bracket.

---

She puts the two accounts together and runs the entry that reconciles them.

The master is here, in front of her — eight numbered lines and a bracket, exactly as she wrote it. The three copies she made from the master in the thirteen months since October 1983 are the second generation. She has traced two of those three branches.

The N2 branch goes from Georgeta to Livia: dead end, closed, no Miliția contact, no further transmission. Clean.

The N3 branch goes through her cousin to Elena Florescu: confirmed clean on Day 5, no outside approach, no contact.

The N4 branch — the cellar copy, Strada Crișan, the third of November of last year, twenty minutes, by the light of the door gap — she has not confirmed directly, because confirming it directly means identifying herself in the chain. She has no route to N4 that does not require a name.

But she made N4. She holds the memory of making it the same way she holds a column: in order, line by line. The cellar: the smell of coal dust, the cold at the door, the paper on her knee. The pencil moving down the page. Eight numbered lines, written in sequence — one through eight, each checked as she went. And then the bracket: two strokes and a corner, the corner at the bottom of the last stroke. The text inside the bracket, written inside it, not below it, inside. She checked the copy once after finishing. She is almost certain the bracket was there when she handed it over.

If the N2 branch is clean and the N3 branch is clean, and if N4 is clean — and she is almost certain — then the mutation entered in a generation after her second generation. Someone downstream received a copy with a bracket at the bottom and copied it as a numbered step, because that is what the hand does when it has been moving down a numbered list and arrives at the bottom of the page with the number nine ready. The mutation entered there. Not in anything she made.

This is the direction the entries point.

She knows the wording of the mutation now exactly. She has added one node to her accounting: the fact of the mutant line, confirmed, the exact words of it, the distance between those words and the words in front of her on the desk. Her count is five.

---

She refolds N1 along the furry creases. Once in one direction, once across. The paper makes a soft sound that is the sound of paper that has made this fold many times before. She tucks it into the ledger spine, fitting it along the gap between the pages and the board until it seats at the outer edge. She carries the ledger to the second shelf and sets it between the quarterly labour plan compliance records and the annual balance submission, spine flush with the edge of the shelf.

She goes back to her desk. She picks up the pen.

But before she takes the October column from where she left it, she does what she always does when two accounts that cannot both be correct must be held together: she sets them in the same column and reads what is there.

She knows lines one through eight. She wrote them. She holds each of them complete and exact.

She has been given line nine verbatim — read aloud by a man she has never met, repeated by a woman she has known for eleven years by proximity, delivered to her desk at a quarter past four in the afternoon. She sets both texts in the same column and she reads:

---

1. Keep her warm and lying down. Someone stays with her the whole night.
2. Small sips of water, often. Nothing else by mouth for six hours.
3. Count the cloths. Write the number and the hour on the paper by the bed.
4. If she sleeps, wake her every hour and speak to her until she answers you properly.
5. No visitors. No telephone. If anyone asks, she has the influenza.
6. Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.
7. Two cloths in one hour is too many.
8. A fever that will not come down by morning is too long.
9. If 7 or 8, take her in in the morning.

---

Lines one through eight: hers. Correct.

Line nine: not hers. The error is in the being careful.

She puts her pen to the October column and begins.

The heat comes on at twelve minutes past six: the knock of the joint at the baseboard corner, and then the dull expansion of the pipe along the wall. She does not look up. The figures run to the end of the page. She checks the column twice. Both times it totals correctly.

She caps her pen and sets it in the groove at the right side of the desk. She takes her coat from the hook behind the door and turns off the lamp. The office goes dark except for the yellow line of corridor light under the door. She steps through, closes the door, tries the handle once.

N1 is in the ledger spine. The ledger is on the second shelf. The mutation entered somewhere downstream — in a copy she did not make, in a hand she cannot name, in a generation she has not yet reached.

She walks.

# 14 November 1984

She does the variance three times. The third time it comes back twelve lei.

The October third-shift payroll: seventeen line discrepancies, all resolved since Tuesday, and one aggregate variance of twelve lei that has had no explanation since she found it. She has been doing the rest of the column around it, leaving the line empty, returning after other work to see if the answer has appeared. It has not appeared each time she has returned. She marks the line with a pencil stroke and turns the page.

She will find it. It is twelve lei and it has been here since Tuesday and it will be there when she finds it.

What she is thinking about this morning is the N4 branch.

She made the copy on the third of November of the year before, in the coal cellar of a building she had been brought to by someone she trusted — a connection specific to that night, not a connection before and not a connection after. The woman from that night was waiting in the coal smell. Ilinca had the pencil. The light came in through the door from the courtyard; not enough light but enough to write by if you were fast. She had written the lines while saying each one aloud, and had watched the pencil to see if it was keeping up.

She can account for eight lines from that recitation.

*Burn nothing until she is well. Wash and keep.* Line six. She had said it clearly. The woman had written it without stopping. Line six is the one that appears to go against the line before it and does not; she had been deliberate with it in the dark because of this. She can account for line six the way she can account for each of the eight: said it, watched the pencil move, line complete.

What she cannot account for is the bracket. The ninth element. She had said it. She is almost certain the pencil was still moving when she said it. She cannot say with certainty that the bracket was in the right position on the page, or in any position at all, because it is a margin note and not a numbered line and the difference between those two things in the dark, with a pencil moving fast, is a difference she could not audit in real time.

She has been proceeding on the assumption that it was correct. She has treated the cellar copy as: one transaction, her end closed. Made the copy, gave it over, left. What came after was the woman from that night's management, not a column Ilinca had any reading of.

This morning she does not believe the column ends there.

The woman from that night is not a full stop. She received the paper. People who receive this paper, and who know people who might need it, do with it what it is for: they pass it on, when the time comes, to someone they know. Ilinca has been counting on this. It is how the paper gets where it needs to go. It is also how a branch extends past a single transaction, and she has been treating the cellar branch as one transaction and nothing after, and she does not now believe that is accurate.

What she does not know: whether the woman from that night gave a copy to anyone, and if so to whom. She cannot ask directly. The cellar woman is not part of her usual network; a visit to that part of the city would be its own kind of visibility, the kind she cannot afford. She needs a route.

---

She has one.

The pharmacy is on Eminescu, near the second bloc, fifteen minutes from the mill gate. The woman at the counter knows her from the market queue and the monthly aspirin requisition and the bus stop on Thursdays. They have spoken about the bread allocation. They have spoken about the flour, about the new forms, about the bus that does not run on Saturdays when it should. They have not spoken about anything that matters.

She has needed aspirin since Monday. This is the first mid-morning she has had free.

She tells Lenuta from accounts she will be back before eleven and goes out through the rear exit, past the clinic door, which is still locked at this hour.

---

The cold on the street outside is particular to this valley in November: not at the floor yet, but past the point where the body argues about it. The boulevard trees have been finished with their leaves for several days. The pavement is wet with something that happened earlier without reaching the level of rain. She keeps her pace at the pace of a woman going somewhere she goes regularly, which she is. The market stand at the corner is closed until Thursday; she passes it.

Dorobanților runs behind Eminescu and connects to it at the north end. She does not go down Dorobanților. She goes straight to Eminescu and turns toward the pharmacy.

The pharmacy occupies a narrow single-story building between the corner post office and a shoe repair. Inside: the counter, the shelves with the permitted stock behind it, a warmth that is not present on the street. The woman at the counter has glasses repaired with thread at the right hinge and a way of standing that suggests she has been standing in the same position for a long time and has found it sufficient.

She copies Ilinca's buletin number into the register while the identity document lies open between them. She produces the aspirin. Ilinca presses the requisition form flat with one finger and signs it.

She says, while tucking the identity document away: there is a woman I've been meaning to find. She gives a description — roughly her own age, a round face, a dark coat with a grey collar, the kind you see everywhere; adds: her husband worked at the chemical plant on the south road. I thought she lived somewhere near here, on Eminescu or behind it. Do you know the family?

The woman at the counter restocks a shelf while she thinks.

She says: there is a woman on Dorobanților — just behind the second bloc on Eminescu — who recently moved her sister in from the village. The sister works at the communal laundry on Strada Mihai. That's the closest I know to what you're describing.

She says: the husband at the chemical plant, that was the main thing I remembered about them.

The pharmacy woman says: I don't know about a husband. That family, that's all I know of them.

Ilinca thanks her. She says: perhaps it's not the right person. Don't trouble yourself.

She goes out.

Three items to carry: *sister, laundry, Strada Mihai.*

She takes the longer route back to the mill — eight minutes more, away from the bloc side of town — and arrives at her desk at twelve minutes past eleven.

---

She opens the November preliminary and starts the December headers. At six minutes past noon she finds the twelve lei: a digit misread in the October second-week line transfer, a three entered as an eight in the fourth column, a small error dated to the twenty-second. She corrects the entry and rules the line. The column closes.

Then she works. The afternoon documents come through: two sets of revised production tallies from the third shift, a ministry form that requires countersignature, an internal memo about the December heating schedule for the administrative building that requires no action but has to be filed. She processes them.

At half past two, through her window, she sees the delivery boy from the pharmacy cross the forecourt below with a cardboard box held level. He goes past the personnel door, past the door she is sitting behind, and turns toward the clinic two doors down.

He does not come to her. She did not expect him to.

At twenty minutes to three, Lenuta knocks and opens the door: the clinic nurse has stepped out to the toilet, can Ilinca sign for the pharmacy delivery.

Ilinca goes into the corridor.

The box sits on the shelf by the clinic door with the delivery notice folded flat on top. She lifts the notice and reads it and signs the incoming column in the delivery ledger; while she is doing this she takes from beneath the notice a slip of paper that she folds once and puts into the pocket of her coat; she carries the box the three steps to the clinic ledge and sets it inside and comes back and returns the delivery ledger to its hook.

Lenuta is already back at accounts. The door between the two rooms is closed.

Ilinca sits at her desk. She takes the slip from her coat pocket.

The pharmacy woman's handwriting: small, regular, not hurried. Three sentences about the December aspirin allocation and the new Ministry dispensing form taking effect in January, which all mill clinics will receive notice of separately. Below that, set a little apart, one sentence that is not the same kind of sentence as the others: *Regarding the family you were asking after — the sister is at the communal laundry on Strada Mihai, I am told, Tuesdays through Saturdays.*

She reads the last sentence three times.

Then she folds the slip and places it in the ledger between the October summary and the first November sheet, where it is a piece of paper among other pieces of paper, and she sits.

---

The cellar woman has a sister. The sister is in Dej. She works the laundry on Strada Mihai, Tuesdays through Saturdays.

This is not the same as knowing there is a copy at the laundry. A sister recently arrived from the village is not automatically a woman who has received a copy of a specific document from a specific source. But: the cellar woman received a paper she would not have requested for herself, because the emergency had been resolved by the time Ilinca brought the copy to her that night — resolved or past. She took the paper anyway. People take the paper for the reason people take anything useful that they cannot buy and cannot request through official channels: because someone they know may need it and they may need to give it.

She adds the new entry. Five, and now this: six.

The problem is the laundry. She has no route to Strada Mihai. The laundry is not on her circuit; she has no contact there; a visit without a reason is the same problem as Eminescu. She needs a second route, the way she needed the pharmacy for the first. She does not have one yet. This is a problem with a solution she has not found.

She reopens the December forecast and begins the first column.

---

The shift bell rings at half past three. The building clears in its usual sequence. Accounts first: she hears Lenuta and the two junior staff go down the corridor, the familiar pattern of their conversation about the Victoriei bread shop, which is closed on Tuesdays apparently. Then the personnel office, two women who have worked there since before Ilinca arrived and who leave without speaking to anyone on the way out, which is their habit and not unfriendliness. Then, at a quarter to four, the two senior clerks at the far end of the corridor, whose footsteps she has learned to distinguish without intending to: the one with the uneven heel first, then the other.

She stays at her desk.

Her office lamp is the only one burning in this part of the building. The lamp at the end of the corridor went off when Lenuta left. The clinic door lamp has been off since three. Through the window: the forecourt is dark except for the gate lamp, and beyond it the street, and beyond that the production building with its row of small high windows lit orange from inside. From three buildings over she can hear the frequency of the night shift at full run — not individual machines but the aggregate of them, the forty-eight looms at their register.

She still needs the route to Strada Mihai. She has six nodes and a gap she cannot close from her desk.

The December first column is not going to finish itself.

She bends over the ledger and keeps working.
